About this text

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, known in Sanskrit as the Avadānaśataka and in Tibetan as Gang po la sogs pa'i rtogs pa brjod pa brgya pa, is a great collection of one hundred avadānas, or stories of noble deeds, illustrating how actions bear fruit across lifetimes. Grouped in decades, each introduced by a short summary verse, its tales tell of brahmins, merchants, kings, gods, and spirits who, through acts of faith, generosity, and devotion toward the Buddha and his community, come to receive predictions of future awakening, to attain arhatship, or to reap the results of their past deeds, while the Buddha reveals the karmic histories behind their fortunes. The collection closes with accounts of the Buddha's passing and of King Aśoka, a century later, learning from the elder Upagupta the deeds that shaped a remarkable monk's life. It is Toh 343 in the Kangyur, belonging to the General Sūtra section, and was translated into Tibetan by the Indian preceptor Jinamitra together with the Tibetan editor-translator Devacandra.

Translation

In the language of India: Pūrṇapramukha Avadānaśatika. In the language of Tibet: The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa. The first section.

Homage to the Omniscient One.

The summary:

The good Pūrṇa and Yaśomatī,
The lazy one and the caravan leaders,
Great Candra and Padma,
Pañcāla and the incense,
And the king, named at the end:
This is the summary of the chapter.

In a certain region there lived a brahmin called Pūrṇa. At that time the Blessed Buddha was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, the people of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Blessed Buddha, worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, was endowed with great merit and received robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites. The Buddha had newly appeared, and the time had come to drink the essence of the scriptures. He taught perfectly to all, from the gods down to human beings. Together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, he was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka feeding ground.

Not long after the Blessed One had become a perfectly and completely awakened buddha, the world was filled with his fame. Now, in the region called Dakṣiṇāgiri, there lived a great and eminent brahmin called Pūrṇa. He was rich, with much wealth and great means, with extensive and vast possessions; he had wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He was also endowed with faith, virtuous and of good intention, dedicated to his own benefit and to the benefit of others, greatly compassionate and of great nobility, eager for the Dharma, keen to give away, delighting in generosity, rejoicing in giving abundantly, and dwelling in great liberality. For a time he held a sacrificial feast for all who had gone forth, and many thousands of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and others ate food there.

At the time when the Blessed One had tamed King Bimbisāra and his retinue, and through his taming many hundreds of thousands of living beings had been tamed, relatives of Pūrṇa came from Rājagṛha and spoke in praise of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha in front of Pūrṇa. When the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa heard of the Blessed One's qualities, he was filled with great joy. Then he went up onto the roof of his house, sat facing in the direction of Rājagṛha, set both kneecaps on the ground, scattered flowers, offered incense and water, and made this request to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please come to my sacrificial feast! Please look upon the enclosure of my sacrifice!"

Then, through the buddha power of the buddhas and the divine power of the gods, those flowers became a house of flowers above the Blessed One. The incense became like a canopy of cloud. The water became like a column of beryl.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and asked the Blessed One, "Venerable One, where has this invitation come from?"

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, in the region called Dakṣiṇāgiri there lives a great and eminent brahmin called Pūrṇa, and we must go there. Monks, get ready!"

Then the Blessed One, attended by a thousand monks, set out wandering through the region of Dakṣiṇāgiri. When he had come to a place near the enclosure of the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa's sacrifice, he reflected, "I shall bring the brahmin Pūrṇa to faith by a miraculous display of magical power." Then the Blessed One made those thousand monks invisible, and, all alone, carrying his alms bowl and water pot in his hand, went to a place near Pūrṇa.

Then the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa saw the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessed of a light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, excellent in every way. On seeing him, he went very quickly up to the Blessed One and said to him: "Welcome, Blessed One! Blessed One, please be seated. For my benefit, will you consent to partake of food?"

The Blessed One declared, "If you are giving it away completely, give it into this alms bowl."

Then the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa, attended by five hundred brahmin youths, began to fill the Blessed One's alms bowl with various kinds of food: cakes, cooked dishes, soft foods, foods to be licked, foods to be sucked, and so on. And the Blessed One transferred that food from his own alms bowl into the alms bowls of the thousand monks. When the Blessed One knew that the alms bowls of the thousand monks were full, at that moment he showed his own alms bowl to be full. Then he made the thousand monks appear, seated in the shape of a crescent moon, with their alms bowls full. And the gods abiding in the sky also proclaimed aloud, "The alms bowls of the Blessed One and of the thousand monks have been filled!"

Then, through that display of miracles, the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa was delighted. Joyful, pleased, overjoyed, rejoicing, delighted and happy in mind, he fell at the feet of the Blessed One like a tree cut off at the root, bowed down, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, by this arousing of the mind, and by this complete giving away of what is to be given, in this world that is blind, without a guide and wholly without a leader, may I become a buddha who ferries across the beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not freed, gives relief to those who have not found relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing how the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa's causes followed one upon another and how his actions followed one upon another, smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever the blessed buddhas smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth from their mouths at that time. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells: Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana and Avīci; and the Blistering hell, the hell of Bursting Blisters, the hell of Chattering Teeth, the hell of Crying "Alas!", the hell of Crying "Achoo!", the hell Split like a Blue Lotus, the hell Split like a Lotus, and the hell Split like a Great Lotus. Into those that are hot hells they descend as coolness; into those that are cold hells they descend as warmth. Then the particular torments of those beings are soothed. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to arouse faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, who has appeared, that our particular torments have been soothed." Then their minds become joyful toward the emanation, and the karma that was to be experienced in hell is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, wherever they may become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the gods of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light and Clear Light, the gods of Limited Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue and Expansive Virtue, the Cloudless gods, the Merit-Born gods, the gods of Great Fruit, the gods Not Greater, the gods Without Torment, the gods of Fine Appearance, the gods of Perfect Vision, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sound of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Undertake renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will completely abandon the cycle of birth
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm, the world-system of a thousand million worlds, and follow along behind the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past deeds, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future deeds, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell a birth in hell, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell a birth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king of force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the space between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Variegated, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Many rays have come forth from the doorway of your mouth.
They have lit up every direction,
Just as the rising sun does."

And again he spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free of agitation, who have abandoned pride and displeasure,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Show a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast One, since with your own understanding you know the time has come,
O Lord of Victors among śramaṇas, for the listeners who are in doubt,
With the supreme, steadfast and excellent words of the bull among sages,
Please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not show a smile without reason.
The reason for which the heroes show a smile,
A great many people long to hear from you."

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, so it is; it is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this great and eminent brahmin pay me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this arousing of the mind, and this complete giving away of what is to be given, this great and eminent brahmin will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be fully accomplished over three incalculable eons. He will perfect the six perfections, wholly suffused with great compassion, and will become a perfectly and completely awakened buddha called the good Pūrṇa, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this one, through which his mind became joyful toward me."

At the time when the Blessed One foretold the great and eminent brahmin Pūrṇa's unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, Pūrṇa fed the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas for three months in the enclosure of his sacrifice, and beyond that he also generated roots of virtue of many different kinds.

"Monks, therefore you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall esteem him. We shall revere him. We shall worship him. Having honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped the Teacher, we shall live in dependence on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and highly praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Yaśomatī.

The Blessed Buddha was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, the people of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Blessed Buddha, worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, was endowed with great merit and received robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites. Together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, he was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Kūṭāgāra Hall on the bank of the Markaṭa Pond.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went into Vaiśālī for alms. Having gone on his alms round through Vaiśālī in due order, he went to the house of General Siṃha, and when he arrived he sat down on the seat that had been prepared.

Now General Siṃha had a daughter-in-law called Yaśomatī, who was beautiful, good to look upon and lovely. When she saw the Blessed One, blazing with the major and minor marks of every kind, she was filled with great joy. She asked her father-in-law, "Is there perhaps some means by which I too might come to possess such qualities?"

Then General Siṃha thought, "Ah, this girl is inclined toward what is vast. If she meets with the right condition, she will make an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening." Knowing this, he said, "Girl, if you take up the cause correctly and keep to it, you too will become just like the Blessed One." Then, to increase Yaśomatī's faith, General Siṃha gave her much money, gold and many jewels.

Then Yaśomatī invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to her house for the midday meal on the following day, and the Blessed One consented, in order to benefit her. Then the girl Yaśomatī had flowers made of gold, silver and jewels, and she gathered much incense, many garlands of flowers and many ointments. Having also laid out food of a hundred flavors, she sent a messenger to the Blessed One to announce the meal: "Venerable One, the time for the midday meal has come and the food is ready. Now, if the Blessed One sees that the time has come, please come."

Then the Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went to the house of General Siṃha, and when he arrived he sat down on the seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks. Then the girl Yaśomatī, seeing that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, satisfied them with her own hands with food of a hundred flavors, and scattered flowers over the Blessed One. Then, through the buddha power of the buddhas and the divine power of the gods, those flowers became, above the Blessed One, a house of jewels and a pavilion with jewel banners, such as not even a smith or a smith's apprentice, however well trained, could make.

Then, when the girl Yaśomatī saw that utterly wondrous miracle, which brings gods and humans to faith, she fell at the feet of the Blessed One with her whole body, like a tree cut off at the root, bowed down, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, by this arousing of the mind, and by this complete giving away of what is to be given, in this world that is blind, without a guide and wholly without a leader, may I become a buddha who ferries across the beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not freed, gives relief to those who have not found relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing how the girl Yaśomatī's causes followed one upon another and how her actions followed one upon another, smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever the blessed buddhas smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth from their mouths at that time. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend having become cool, and into those that are cold hells they descend having become warm. In this way the various torments of those beings are soothed. Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

Set out upon renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever in this very Dharma and Vinaya
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will utterly abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

So they recite. Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, return and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past deeds, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to foretell future deeds, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a king who turns the wheel by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the space between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

Variegated, interspersed with a thousand hues,
Many rays have issued from the door of your mouth;
They have made all the directions shine
Just as the rising sun does.

And again he addressed him in verse:

Free of agitation, rid of pride and dejection,
The buddhas, who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not, without cause or condition,
Show a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O lord of ascetics, for the listeners who are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme, firm
And excellent words, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not show a smile without reason.
That for whose sake, O hero, you show a smile,
The great multitude longs to hear from you.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this girl Yaśomatī pay me such honor?"

"Reverend One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the mind of awakening, and this complete giving away of things to be given, Yaśomatī will accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having perfected the six perfections, permeated by great compassion, she will become a perfectly and completely awakened buddha named Ratnavat, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and will appear in the world. Her gift is this: that her mind rejoiced in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Lazy One.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and great mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and great mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a merchant who was rich, of great wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love and enjoyed himself with her. Yet though he played, made love and enjoyed himself, he had neither son nor daughter. Resting his cheek on his hand, he sat brooding, thinking, "Although my house is endowed with much wealth, I have neither son nor daughter. Since I have no son, after I pass away everything I own will fall to the king."

Then ascetics, brahmins, soothsayers, friends, relatives and other kinsfolk urged him, "Pray to the gods!" There is a saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, then each person would have a thousand sons, like a wheel-turning king. In fact, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together aroused by desire; the mother is in her season and fertile; and a gandharva is present. Sons and daughters are born from the coming together of these three conditions. Nevertheless, prompted by the ascetics, brahmins, soothsayers, friends, relatives and kinsfolk, he, being without a son and wanting a son, prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra (Indra), Brahmā and others, and to other particular gods as well: that is, he prayed to the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads, the gods of three-way junctions, the gods who receive offerings, and the gods who are born together with one, who share one's nature, and who constantly follow one. And while he was devoting himself to prayer, a certain being died and passed away from a certain class of beings and entered his wife's womb.

Some women of wise nature have five special qualities. What are the five? They know when a man is passionate and when he is not passionate; they know the right time and know their fertile period; they know when they have conceived and know from whom they have conceived; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl: if it is a boy, it rests on the right side of the womb; if it is a girl, it rests on the left side of the womb.

Then she, overjoyed, told her husband, "My lord, I have conceived a child. Since it rests on the right side of my womb, it is certain to be a boy. Please rejoice!" He too was overjoyed, and lifting the upper part of his body and stretching out his right hand, he uttered these joyful words: "I shall see the face of the son I have long wished for! May my son be well formed, and not ill formed! May he do my tasks! May he support us in return for having been supported! May he enjoy his inheritance! May my lineage long endure! And after we have passed away and died, may he give gifts and make merit on our behalf, whether much or little, and dedicate the offering, saying, 'Wherever these two have been born and gone, may this go to them!'"

Knowing that she had conceived, he placed her at ease in the upper part of the mansion so as to care for the child. In the cold season she had things for the cold, and in the hot season things for the heat. She ate the foods prescribed by the physician, foods not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent, and not too astringent: foods free of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency and astringency. Her body adorned with necklaces and garlands, like a daughter of the gods roaming in the Nandana Grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat and did not come down to the ground below, and he saw to it that she heard no unpleasant sound whatsoever.

When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and bore a boy who was handsome, good to look upon and beautiful. When he was born, everyone in the household rejoiced. They held a birth feast for his birth, and then they named him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" The relatives said, "Since at his birth everyone in the household rejoiced, let this boy be named Delighter." And so he was named Delighter.

Then the boy Delighter was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away dirt, and two nurses to play with him. The eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other fine provision, so that he grew up quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, when he had grown and was five or six years old, he became a lazy one, exceedingly lazy, not wanting even to rise from his bed and seat. Being sharp and clear-minded, he studied the treatises while remaining at home.

Then the merchant thought, "After I propitiated the gods, a son was born to me, as rarely as once in a hundred times, and yet he has become a lazy one, exceedingly lazy, who does not even rise from his bed and seat. Though his body is normal, he just sits there like a cripple. What use is a son like this?"

Now the merchant was devoted to Pūraṇa. He invited the six non-Buddhist (tīrthika) teachers to his house, thinking, "If the boy sees them, perhaps he will be inspired to follow them and will at least get up from his bed." But when the lazy boy saw those teachers, he did not even look at them, let alone rise, speak respectfully, or offer them a seat. When the merchant saw this state of affairs he was even more deeply distressed, and resting his cheek on his hand, he sat brooding.

Now for the buddhas, the blessed ones, there is nothing that they do not know, do not see, do not realize or do not understand. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion, engaged in benefiting the world, the sole protectors, the sole heroes without equal, who never speak with a double tongue, who abide in calm abiding and insight, who illuminate the three knowledges, who are well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand most firm, who have long practiced the four means of attraction, who are fearless with the four fearlessnesses, who roar the great, true lion's roar of the bull, who have entirely abandoned the five factors, who have wholly transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six factors, who have perfected the six perfections, who dwell in the six constant abidings, who are rich in the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame pervades the ten directions, and who are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. By the nature of things, three times by day and three times by night, they look upon the world with the eye of a buddha, and the vision of their wisdom engages, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted? Who is in want, in danger and afflicted? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I lift out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation and in the fruit? Whom shall I pull out by the hand from sinking in the mire of sensual desire? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom, where the roots of virtue have not been produced, shall I produce them? In whom, where the roots of virtue have already been produced, shall I bring them to maturity? Whom, already matured, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, the abode of sea monsters,
May perhaps let its tide pass by its time;
But for the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time pass by.

Then the Blessed One saw: "If the lazy boy sees me, he will begin to exert diligence, and his mind will be turned toward unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening." Then, in order to cut through the arrogance and pride of the tīrthikas and to produce roots of virtue in the boy, the Blessed One sent forth golden rays of light surpassing the light of a thousand suns, and they illuminated that whole house. He also sent forth rays of loving-kindness, cultivated over a thousand eons, and as soon as they touched the boy's body it was filled with ease. He thought, "By whose power has my body been filled with ease?" and he looked all around.

Then the Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks, entered that house, and the lazy boy saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. Seeing him, he was overjoyed, and at once he got up by himself, arranged a seat for the Blessed One, and said, "Come, Blessed One! Welcome, Blessed One! Blessed One, please be seated on the seat that has been arranged." When his parents and the household saw this eager respect, never seen before, they were utterly amazed.

Then the lazy boy, with eyes bright with joy, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One spoke to him in many ways about the faults of laziness and the benefits of exerting diligence, and he also gave him a sandalwood staff and said, "Boy, strike this staff!" When he struck the staff, a sweet sound was heard, and he also saw various treasures of jewels. Then he thought, "Ah! Exerting diligence has such great advantages. I must certainly exert diligence again and again." He had it proclaimed in Śrāvastī with the sound of a bell, announcing that he himself would act as caravan leader, and he crossed the great ocean six times. Having accomplished the purpose of his voyages, he gathered great jewels, and he invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to a meal in his house and made an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

Then the Blessed One, knowing how the lazy boy's causes followed one upon another and how his actions followed one upon another, smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth at that time from the door of their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend having become cool, and into those that are cold hells they descend having become warm. In this way the various torments of those beings are soothed. Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in that emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

Set out upon renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever in this very Dharma and Vinaya
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will utterly abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

So they recite. Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, return and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past deeds, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to foretell future deeds, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a king who turns the wheel by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

Variegated, interspersed with a thousand hues,
Many rays have issued from the door of your mouth;
They have made all the directions shine
Just as the rising sun does.

And again he addressed him in verse:

Free of agitation, rid of pride and dejection,
The buddhas, who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not, without cause or condition,
Show a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O lord of ascetics, for the listeners who are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme, firm
And excellent words, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not show a smile without reason.
That for whose sake, O hero, you show a smile,
The great multitude longs to hear from you.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this lazy boy pay me such honor?"

"Reverend One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the mind of awakening, and this complete giving away of things to be given, this lazy boy will accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having perfected the six perfections, permeated by great compassion, he will become a perfectly and completely awakened buddha named Fully Endowed with Strength, Diligence and Prowess, possessed of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and will appear in the world. His gift is this: that he rejoiced in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, Second Section.

The Caravan Leader.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and great mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and great mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in Śrāvastī there was a great caravan leader whose ship capsized on the great ocean, and he came back. Two and three times he prayed to all the gods, but whenever he set out on the great ocean, his ship still capsized and he came back. Then great dejection arose in him, and he thought, "By what means can I gather wealth? What means is there?" Then he thought further, "This Buddha, the Blessed One, is far more exalted than all the gods. He is engaged in benefiting himself and benefiting others; he is compassionate, magnanimous, devoted to the Dharma, and kind to living beings. Now, relying on him, I shall set out again on the great ocean, and when I have successfully accomplished the purpose of my voyage and come back, I shall make offerings to him with half my wealth."

Having resolved in this way, he set out once more on the great ocean, and by the Buddha's power he reached the island of jewels. He gathered great jewels and returned to his home safely and without mishap. When he had rested and unpacked his containers, he saw the many kinds of jewels, and great attachment arose in him. He began to think, "How could I give half of jewels such as these to the ascetic Gautama? Instead, I shall sell them to my wife for a quarter of a coin, and I shall certainly offer incense to the Blessed One."

With the quarter coin he bought aloeswood incense and went to the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta. Then, very much ashamed, he stayed by the doorway and burned the aloeswood. Then the Blessed One performed a miracle such that the incense he had burned rose up into the sky above, pervaded all of Śrāvastī, and remained there like the crest of a great cloud. When the caravan leader saw that most marvelous wonder, which inspires faith in gods and humans, great joy arose in him. Restraining his own mind, he said, "It is not for me to cheat the Blessed One of the jewels."

Then the caravan leader invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to a meal in his house. He satisfied them with fine food and then strewed great jewels over them. Then, through the buddha power of the buddhas and the divine power of the gods, those jewels rose into the sky above the Blessed One's head and turned into a jeweled house and a jeweled pavilion with jeweled banners, such as even a well-trained smith or smith's apprentice could not make. When the caravan leader saw that wonder, intense joy arose in him, and falling like a tree cut at the root, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and made this aspiration: "Through this root of virtue, this generation of the mind of awakening, and this complete giving away of things to be given, in a world that is blind, without a guide and wholly without a leader, may I become a buddha who ferries across the beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not freed, gives relief to those who have not found relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing how the caravan leader's causes followed one upon another and how his actions followed one upon another, smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth at that time from the door of their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend having become cool, and into those that are cold hells they descend having become warm. In this way the various torments of those beings are soothed. Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go among the gods: the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and so on up to the gods of Akaniṣṭha. There they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, and they also utter two verses:

Set about renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
Like an elephant crushing a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will completely abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

So they proclaim. Then, having encircled the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, those rays follow back after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they disappear into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they disappear into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they disappear into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they disappear into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human being, they disappear into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a king who is a cakravartin by force, they disappear into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a cakravartin king, they disappear into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they disappear into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they disappear into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Blessed One:

A many-colored cluster, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Has come forth from between your lips,
And by it all directions everywhere have been illumined,
Just as they are by the rising sun.

And again he addressed him in verse:

Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of dejection and pride,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
Victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile white as a lotus root or a conch.

Steadfast one, since you know by your own understanding that the time has come,
For the listeners, O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, who are in doubt,
O bull among sages, with your steadfast, supreme,
And excellent speech, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for no reason.
The purpose for which the hero displays a smile,
That is what the great multitude of people wish to hear from you.

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfect and complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, did you see this caravan leader pay me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the resolve, and this giving away of a gift, this caravan leader will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished through three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, permeated by great compassion, he will become a perfect and complete buddha called Gandhottama, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Candra. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, remedies for the sick, and medicines, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now in Śrāvastī there lived a weaver called Candra, who was poor, utterly poor. However much work he did, he earned no more than that day's food, and he could not set aside even a little. Then he thought, "I came here from the other world without having made merit, and here too I do no virtue. So I may well have to go from here to the other world without having made merit, without having done virtue, and without having made a protector and refuge against fear and terror. It would be good if I made an offering to the Blessed One with a few things."

Then he wove cloth for another householder, took from it some strips of fringe, and went out into the street. In the morning the Blessed One put on his lower garment and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. Then the weaver saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, beautiful in every way. And having seen him, his mind took delight in the Blessed One.

In order to benefit him, the Blessed One for his part showed his own Dharma robe as torn. Then the weaver offered those strips of fringe to the Blessed One, and at once the Blessed One showed the Dharma robe as mended. Then, filled with great joy, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and made this aspiration:

The gift is small, but the field is vast.
Since you, Great Powerful One, have accepted it,
By this, which has become a great gift,
May I become a buddha of vast renown.

Though this gift is small,
My mind is vast and immeasurable;
Accepted by the Victor, supreme among humans and gods,
Even a small gift becomes a great fruit.

The Blessed One declared:

In the future you, peaceful and of great power,
Of vast renown, worshipped by humans and gods,
Self-arisen, a benefactor of the world, endowed with compassion,
Will become a Victor called Supreme Fringe.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the succession of causes, one after another, and the succession of deeds, one after another, of the weaver Candra, smiled. It is the nature of things that when buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. Thereby the various torments of those beings are soothed. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go among the gods: the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and so on up to the gods of Akaniṣṭha. There they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, and they also utter two verses:

Set about renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
Like an elephant crushing a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will completely abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

So they proclaim. Then, having encircled the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, those rays follow back after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they disappear into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they disappear into his front. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they disappear into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Blessed One:

A many-colored cluster, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Has come forth from between your lips,
And by it all directions everywhere have been illumined,
Just as they are by the rising sun.

And again he addressed him in verse:

Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of dejection and pride,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
Victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile white as a lotus root or a conch.

Steadfast one, since you know by your own understanding that the time has come,
For the listeners, O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, who are in doubt,
O bull among sages, with your steadfast, supreme,
And excellent speech, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for no reason.
The purpose for which the hero displays a smile,
That is what the great multitude of people wish to hear from you.

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfect and complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, did you see this weaver Candra pay me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the resolve, and this giving away of a gift, the weaver Candra will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished through three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, permeated by great compassion, he will become a perfect and complete buddha called Supreme Fringe, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Great. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, remedies for the sick, and medicines, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī the son of a guild master, called Great. He was one in whom outbursts of anger were very strong, and he made offerings to the six teachers, Pūraṇa and the rest. Later he was struck by a severe illness, and, having no physician, no medicine, and no one to nurse him, he came close to death. He thought, "Now who else is there, other than the Buddha, to be a refuge for me in my suffering or to grant me the life I hold dear?" Having thought this, he prayed to the Blessed One.

Now, there is nothing that buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion, engaged in benefiting the world, possessed of a single guardianship, solely heroic, without peer, never speaking in two ways, abiding in calm abiding and insight. They illuminate the three knowledges, are well trained in the three trainings, and are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods; the soles of their feet, the four bases of miraculous power, are firmly planted; they have long been accustomed to the four means of attraction; they are fearless with the four fearlessnesses; they roar the great, true lion's roar of the bull. They have entirely abandoned the five factors and have passed completely beyond the five destinies. They are endowed with the six factors, have perfected the six perfections, and abide in the six constant abidings. They are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, teach the eightfold path, are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, and possess the strength of the ten powers. Their renown pervades the ten directions, and they are far superior even to those who hold sway over a thousand. By the nature of things, three times by day and three times by night, they look upon the world with the eye of a buddha, and the vision of their wisdom arises, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who is in danger? Who is afflicted? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruit? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I bring to mastery over the wealth of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I generate roots of virtue not yet generated? In whom shall I ripen roots of virtue already generated? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, the abode of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide pass by,
But for the children to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time pass by.

Then the Blessed One, seeing the condition of the guild master's son Great, sent forth golden rays surpassing the light of a thousand suns, and they illuminated that entire house. He also sent forth rays of loving-kindness, cultivated thoroughly for a thousand eons, and as soon as they touched his body he was deeply refreshed. Then the Blessed One went to his door, and the doorkeeper announced to him, "The Blessed One is standing at the door."

Then the guild master's son Great was overjoyed, and, his breathless distress giving way to relief, he said, "Welcome, Blessed One! Please, Blessed One, come inside. I long to see the Blessed One's face." Then the Blessed One went inside and sat on the seat that had been prepared. Once seated, the Blessed One said to Great, "Great, what ails you?"

Great replied, "I suffer from an affliction of the body and an affliction of the mind."

Then, with a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, the Blessed One gave him instruction, declaring, "This is the antidote to the suffering of your mind." Then he formed a worldly intention, thinking, "Oh, it would be good if Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, were to bring the śirika herb from Mount Gandhamādana." The moment the Blessed One formed this intention, Śakra, lord of the gods, took the śirika herb from Mount Gandhamādana and offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One took it in his own hand and gave it to Great, declaring, "This will soothe the suffering and fever of your body."

Then he attained the bliss of complete pliancy of body and mind, and his mind delighted in the Blessed One. His mind delighted, he informed King Prasenajit, served a meal to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, offered a robe worth a hundred thousand, and also made offerings with every kind of flower, incense, and garland. Then, having steadied his mind, he made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, this generation of the resolve, and this giving away of a gift, just as the Blessed One, the unsurpassed king of physicians, has healed me, so may I too, at a future time when the world is blind, without a guide and without a leader, become a buddha who ferries across beings who have not crossed, liberates those not liberated, brings relief to those without relief, and leads to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the succession of causes, one after another, and the succession of deeds, one after another, of Great, smiled. It is the nature of things that when buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. Thereby the various torments of those beings are soothed. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation, and when they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go among the gods: the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and so on up to the gods of Akaniṣṭha. There they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, and they also utter two verses:

Set about renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
Like an elephant crushing a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will completely abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

So they proclaim. Then, having encircled the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, those rays follow back after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they disappear into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they disappear into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they disappear into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they disappear into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human being, they disappear into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a king who is a cakravartin by force, they disappear into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a cakravartin king, they disappear into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they disappear into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they disappear into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Blessed One:

A many-colored cluster, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Has come forth from between your lips,
And by it all directions everywhere have been illumined,
Just as they are by the rising sun.

And again he addressed him in verse:

Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of dejection and pride,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
Victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile white as a lotus root or a conch.

Steadfast one, since you know by your own understanding that the time has come,
For the listeners, O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, who are in doubt,
O bull among sages, with your steadfast, supreme,
And excellent speech, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for no reason.
The purpose for which the hero displays a smile,
That is what the great multitude of people wish to hear from you.

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfect and complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, did you see this guild master's son Great pay me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the resolve, and this giving away of a gift, the guild master's son Great will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished through three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, permeated by great compassion, he will become a perfect and complete buddha called Śākyamuni, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Padma. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, remedies for the sick, and medicines, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Before the Blessed One had appeared in the world, King Prasenajit used to honor other gods three times a day with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments. When the Blessed One had appeared in the world and had tamed King Prasenajit by means of the examples in the Daharasūtra, the king found faith in the teaching of the Blessed One. From then on, filled with joy and gladness, he went to the Blessed One three times a day and made offerings with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.

Then, at one point, a gardener picked a freshly bloomed lotus flower and was taking it into Śrāvastī to King Prasenajit, when a lay follower of the non-Buddhist sects saw him and asked, "Hey, you there, is that lotus for sale?"

"It is for sale," he replied.

As that man wanted to buy it, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada arrived on the scene and raised the price to double, and the two bid against each other until it had risen to a hundred thousand. Then the gardener thought, "This householder Anāthapiṇḍada is not a frivolous man; he is a steady person, so there must be some purpose in this." Doubt arose in him, and he asked the man who favored the non-Buddhists, "For whose sake are you bidding like this?"

He said, "I am bidding for the sake of the blessed Nārāyaṇa."

Anāthapiṇḍada said, "I am bidding for the sake of the Blessed One, the Buddha."

The gardener asked, "Who is this one called the Buddha?" Then Anāthapiṇḍada described to him at length the qualities of the Buddha. Then the gardener said to Anāthapiṇḍada, "Householder, I myself will make an offering to that Blessed One."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took the gardener with him and went to where the Blessed One was. There the gardener saw the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, beautiful in every way. As soon as he saw him, the gardener tossed the lotus to the Blessed One, and as soon as he tossed it, the lotus became the size of a cartwheel and remained above the Blessed One.

Then, when the gardener saw that miracle, he fell at the feet of the Blessed One like a tree cut off at the root. Joining his palms, he made his mind steadfast and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, may I, in a world that is blind, without a guide and without a leader, become a buddha who ferries across those beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not free, gives relief to those who have found no relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the gardener's succession of causes, one after another, and his succession of actions, one after another, smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth from their mouths. Some go downward, and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into all the hot hells they descend having become cool, and into all the cold hells they descend having become warm. As a result, the various torments of those beings are relieved. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been relieved." Then, their minds delighted in the emanation, the karma that would have made them experience the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Undertake renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Lives with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of birth
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a thousand million worlds, and follow right behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wishes to foretell past actions, they vanish into his back. If he wishes to foretell future actions, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a balacakravartin king, a wheel-turning king by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-hued, interlaced with a thousand colors,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth.
They have lit up all the directions
Just as the rising sun does."

And again he said in verse:

"Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of pride and dejection,
Have become the supreme cause for beings.
Victors, conquerors of the foe, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile white as lotus root or conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own wisdom you know the time has come,
Lord of Victors among ascetics, for the listeners who long to know,
Bull among sages, with your excellent, steadfast and virtuous words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

Not without reason do the protectors, the perfect buddhas,
Steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains, display a smile.
The great multitude of people longs to hear from you
That for whose sake, O hero, you displayed your smile."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition.

"Ānanda, do you see the honor this gardener has paid me?"

"I see it, venerable one."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, this gardener will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, imbued with great compassion, he will become a perfectly complete buddha called Padmottara, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Pañcāla.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, people of the court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the king of Northern Pañcāla fell into discord with the king of Southern Pañcāla. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you are the unsurpassed king of the Dharma, the protector of beings in distress, who reconciles those who bear enmity toward one another. This king of Northern Pañcāla is in discord with the king of Southern Pañcāla, and the two of them are bringing many people to ruin against each other. Out of your loving kindness, may the Blessed One please pacify the enmity that has long existed between the two of them."

The Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kosala by remaining silent. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by remaining silent, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, rose from his seat and departed.

Then, early in the morning of the following day, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and set out wandering toward the towns of the Kāśis in the direction of Vārāṇasī. Wandering by stages, he reached Vārāṇasī, and in Vārāṇasī he stayed at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

Then, after a while, those two learned that the Blessed One had come to their country. Then, through the Blessed One's miraculous power, a fourfold army was emanated, and the king of Northern Pañcāla, terrified and afraid, mounted a chariot and went into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him a Dharma that would bring an end to enmity. Having heard that Dharma, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, and by striving, effort and exertion he abandoned all afflictions and realized arhatship.

The king of Southern Pañcāla, for his part, invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas for three months, served them food with a hundred flavors, and also offered robes worth a hundred thousand. Then he made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, may I, in a world that is blind, without a guide and without a leader, become a buddha who ferries across those beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not free, gives relief to those who have found no relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the succession of causes, one after another, and the succession of actions, one after another, of that king of Southern Pañcāla, smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth from their mouths. Some go downward, and some go upward.
