Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend having become cool, and into the cold hells they descend having become warm. As a result, the various torments of those beings are relieved. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing that emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been relieved." Then, their minds delighted in the emanation, the karma that would have made them experience the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Undertake renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Lives with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of birth
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a thousand million worlds, and follow right behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wishes to foretell past actions, they vanish into his back. If he wishes to foretell future actions, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a balacakravartin king, a wheel-turning king by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-hued, interlaced with a thousand colors,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth.
They have lit up all the directions
Just as the rising sun does."

And again he said in verse:

"Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of pride and dejection,
Have become the supreme cause for beings.
Victors, conquerors of the foe, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile white as lotus root or conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own wisdom you know the time has come,
Lord of Victors among ascetics, for the listeners who long to know,
Bull among sages, with your excellent, steadfast and virtuous words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

Not without reason do the protectors, the perfect buddhas,
Steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains, display a smile.
The great multitude of people longs to hear from you
That for whose sake, O hero, you displayed your smile."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor this king of Pañcāla has paid me?"

"I see it, venerable one."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, this king of Pañcāla will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, imbued with great compassion, he will become a perfectly complete buddha called Gandhottama, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the third section.

The story called Incense.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, people of the court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, in Śrāvastī, two merchants fell into discord with each other. Of the two, one had faith in Pūraṇa, and the other had faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One. The two of them then settled on a debate with each other. Pūraṇa's lay follower said, "Pūraṇa is far more distinguished than the Buddha."

The Buddha's lay follower said, "The Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha, is far more distinguished."

Then the two of them laid down a wager in which all their possessions were staked. After a while, King Prasenajit heard of it and ordered his ministers, "Put those two to the test." Then those ministers had the bell rung throughout the land, proclaiming, "Seven days from now, the two lay followers, the Buddha's and the non-Buddhist's (tīrthika's), will be put to the test. Whoever wishes to see something marvelous, come!"

When seven days had passed, in a spacious place where many hundreds of thousands of people had gathered, with many hundreds of thousands of gods gathered in the sky, a maṇḍala was made with cow dung, and incense, flowers and garlands of every kind were gathered there. First of all, the non-Buddhist lay follower made an invocation of truth: "By the truth and the words of truth that the six teachers, Pūraṇa and the rest, are supreme, by that truth and those words of truth, may these flowers, this incense and this water go to them!"

The moment he said this, the flowers fell to the ground, the fire died out, and the water sank into the ground, was used up and dried away completely. Then that great crowd of people raised an uproar and laughter and shouted loudly. When the non-Buddhist lay follower saw this, he sat without a word. Dejected, his shoulders slumped, his eyes cast down, his confidence gone, his mind withdrawn into itself, he sat brooding with his cheek resting on his hand.

Then the disciple of the Blessed One, overjoyed, his eyes bright and shining with delight, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, and made an invocation of truth: "By the truth and the words of truth that the Blessed One is supreme among all beings, by that truth and those words of truth, may these flowers, this incense and this water go to the Blessed One!"

The moment he said this, the flowers rose into the sky like a line of geese and went off facing toward the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta. The incense became like a canopy of cloud, and the water became like a pillar of beryl. Then that great crowd of people, seeing that miracle, raised an uproar and laughter, shouted loudly, and went along following behind them. Then the flowers remained above the Blessed One, and the incense and the water remained before him.

Then that great crowd of people, delighted, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and sat before him in order to hear the Dharma, and the Blessed One taught them this sūtra:

"Brahmins and householders, these three are declared supreme. What are the three? The Buddha is declared supreme, the Dharma is declared supreme, and the Saṅgha is declared supreme.

"What is the declaration that the Buddha is supreme? Brahmins and householders, whatever beings there may be, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed or many-footed, whether having form or formless, whether having perception, without perception, or neither with perception nor without perception, among them the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha is taught to be supreme. Whoever delights in the Buddha delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be solely the highest among those who become gods among the gods, or among those who become humans among humans. Brahmins and householders, this is called the declaration that the Buddha is supreme.

"What is the declaration that the Dharma is supreme? Whatever dharmas there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, among them the Dharma of freedom from desire is taught to be supreme. Whoever delights in the Dharma delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be solely the highest among those who become gods among the gods, or among those who become humans among humans. Brahmins and householders, this is called the declaration that the Dharma is supreme.

"What is the declaration that the Saṅgha is supreme? Whatever gatherings, groups, multitudes or assemblies there may be, among them the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas is taught to be known as supreme. Whoever delights in the Saṅgha delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be solely the highest among those who become gods among the gods, or among those who become humans among humans. Brahmins and householders, this is called the declaration that the Saṅgha is supreme."

When this discourse on the Dharma had been taught, some of those brahmins and householders gained faith in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha. Some took refuge and took up the bases of training. Some went forth and, understanding that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and having determined that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, abandoned all afflictions and realized arhatship.

The non-Buddhist lay follower, too, gained faith in the Blessed One. Then, falling at his feet like a tree cut off at the root, he made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, may I, in a world that is blind, without a guide and without a leader, become a buddha who ferries across those beings who have not crossed, frees those who are not free, gives relief to those who have found no relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the succession of causes, one after another, and the succession of actions, one after another, of that non-Buddhist lay follower, smiled.

It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red and white, come forth from their mouths. Some go downward, and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend having become cool, and into the cold hells they descend having become warm. As a result, the various torments of those beings are relieved. Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been relieved." Then, their minds filled with faith in the emanation, the karma that would have made them experience the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Undertake renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and discipline,
Lives with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of birth
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a thousand million worlds, and follow right behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wishes to foretell past actions, they vanish into his back. If he wishes to foretell future actions, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a balacakravartin king, a wheel-turning king by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the curl of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-hued, interlaced with a thousand colors,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth.
They have lit up all the directions
Just as the rising sun does."

And again he said in verse:

"Buddhas, free of agitation, rid of pride and dejection,
Have become the supreme cause for beings.
Victors, conquerors of the foe, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile white as lotus root or conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own wisdom you know the time has come,
Lord of Victors among ascetics, for the listeners who long to know,
Bull among sages, with your excellent, steadfast and virtuous words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

Not without reason do the protectors, the perfect buddhas,
Steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains, display a smile.
The great multitude of people longs to hear from you
That for whose sake, O hero, you displayed your smile."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor this non-Buddhist lay follower has paid me?"

"I see it, venerable one."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, this non-Buddhist lay follower will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, imbued with great compassion, he will become a perfectly complete buddha called Acala, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Now, the one called "The King." The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townsfolk, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kiṃnaras, and by great mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and great mahoragas, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick, and medical supplies, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time King Prasenajit of Kosala and King Ajātaśatru fell into hostility with each other. King Ajātaśatru then equipped his fourfold army, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry, and led it out to do battle with King Prasenajit of Kosala. King Prasenajit of Kosala heard: "King Ajātaśatru has equipped his fourfold army, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry, and has led it out to do battle with me." Having heard this, he too equipped his fourfold army, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry, and led it out to do battle with King Ajātaśatru.

Then King Ajātaśatru captured the whole of King Prasenajit of Kosala's elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry. King Prasenajit of Kosala, defeated, terrified, and routed, utterly defeated and turning his back in flight, went off to Śrāvastī with a single chariot. Three times this same thing happened. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala went into the chamber of sorrow and sat with his cheek propped on his hand, brooding.

Now in Śrāvastī there lived a merchant who was rich, of great wealth and great means, whose holdings were broad and vast, who possessed wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, wealth that rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He heard how King Prasenajit of Kosala, defeated, terrified, and routed, utterly defeated and turning his back in flight, had gone off to Śrāvastī with a single chariot. Having heard this, he went to where King Prasenajit of Kosala was. On arriving, he hailed King Prasenajit, saying, "Victory to you! May you live long!" and then said, "Your Majesty, why are you so downcast? Your Majesty, I wish to offer Your Majesty as much gold as it will take for Your Majesty to be glad and content once more."

He then heaped up for him a great heap of gold and presented it, a heap so great that a person sitting on one side could not see a person standing on the other, nor could a person standing see one who was sitting.

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala sent spies out all through his own country, saying, "Listen to what people are saying." Once, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, two old men were talking with each other. They said, "There is a battle stratagem called the Lotus Filament. In it, the men who are cowardly are sent out first, as the fodder of battle. Those who are middling are placed in the middle. The men who are supremely brave are placed at the rear."

They reported this to the king. King Prasenajit of Kosala, having heard it, equipped his fourfold army accordingly and led it out to do battle with King Ajātaśatru. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala captured the whole elephant corps of King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī. He captured his cavalry, his chariot corps, and his infantry as well. King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, in turn defeated, terrified, and routed, utterly defeated and turning his back, was taken alive. Prasenajit put him in a single chariot and went to where the Blessed One was. On arriving, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, for a long time this King Ajātaśatru has borne enmity toward me though I am no rival of his, and has acted as an enemy though I am no foe of his. Yet because he is the son of my friend, I do not wish to kill him; I wish to let him go."

The Blessed One said, "Great king, let him go," and then on that occasion spoke these verses:

"When one is victorious, enmities are many;
When one is defeated, one dwells in suffering.
But when victory and defeat are both abandoned,
One is fully at peace and dwells in happiness."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala thought, "That I have regained my kingdom is owing to the kindness of this merchant. I shall give him the chance of whatever reward he wishes." So King Prasenajit of Kosala offered the merchant whatever reward he wished, and the merchant replied, "I ask for a reward that I would enjoy: grant me the kingship for seven days, to do with as I please."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala had it proclaimed by bell throughout all his country: "My kingdom has been given to the merchant for seven days." In due course the merchant invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, together with King Prasenajit and his retinue, to the midday meal for seven days.

He also sent messengers to all the multitudes of people living in the lands of the Kāśis and of Kosala, saying, "For seven days, free of taxes and levies, live as you please, contented, and enjoy yourselves in happiness. Come here too, and go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Seek out my feast as well, and attend upon the Tathāgata." Then for seven days he honored the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with great honors, and many hundreds of thousands of people were also brought to happiness.

When the seven days had passed, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet, made his mind resolute, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, in a world that is blind, without a guide and without a leader, may I become a buddha who ferries across those beings who have not crossed over, frees those who are not freed, gives relief to those who have not found relief, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the merchant's chain of causes, one after another, and his chain of actions, one after another, smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, rays of light, blue, yellow, red, and white, issue from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend having become cool, and into those that are cold hells they descend having become warm. In this way the various torments of those beings are allayed. Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our various torments have been allayed." Then, their minds delighting in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, wherever they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sound of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also utter two verses:

"Set about renunciation;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching.
Like an elephant in a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness,
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they proclaim. Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, return and follow behind the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past actions, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future actions, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will be a wheel-turning king ruling by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will be a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown protuberance on the Blessed One's head.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many rays, of every kind, interspersed with a thousand hues,
Have come forth from the door of your mouth,
And they have lit up all the directions,
Just as the rising sun does."

And again he spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free of agitation, rid of pride and of displeasure,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The Victors, the conquerors of foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fibers and of conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O lord of ascetics, for the listeners who are in doubt,
O bull among sages, with your supreme and steady speech,
Excellent one, please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steady as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without a reason.
The reason for which you, O hero, display this smile,
That the great multitude wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. It is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor this merchant has shown the Tathāgata together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and how he has established a great multitude of people in virtue?"

"I see it, venerable one."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, this merchant will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having brought to completion the six perfections, imbued with great compassion, he will become a perfectly complete buddha called Abhayada, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this: that his mind delighted in me."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the first summary verse is complete.

The summary:
The Ferrymen, the Pillar, the Bath,
The Epidemic, the Miracle,
The Five-Year Festival, Praise, the Boon-Giver,
The Kāśi Cloth, and Divine Food.

Now, the one called "The Ferrymen." The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townsfolk, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kiṃnaras, and by great mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and great mahoragas, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick, and medical supplies, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas near Śrāvastī, at the ferrymen's village at the landing on the river Ajiravatī.

Then those ferrymen went to where the Blessed One was. On arriving, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed those ferrymen with a talk on the Dharma, led them to take it up, inspired them, and gladdened them. Having instructed them, led them to take it up, inspired them, and gladdened them with talk on the Dharma in many ways, he remained silent.

Then those ferrymen rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, set their right knees on the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, would you, together with the Saṅgha of monks, consent to take the midday meal with us tomorrow there on the bank of the river Ajiravatī? We would also like to ferry you across by the boat bridge." The Blessed One consented to the ferrymen by remaining silent.

Then those ferrymen cleared the bank of the river Ajiravatī of stones, gravel, and potsherds. They raised victory banners and flags, scattered flowers of many kinds, burned incense in censers, set out fine food, and prepared a great many flowers. They also adorned the top of the boat bridge with pavilions of flowers. Then they sent a messenger to announce the midday meal to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, it is time for the midday meal, and the food is ready. Please, Blessed One, consider that the time has now come, and come."

Then the Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went to the ferrymen's village. On arriving, he sat down on the seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks. Then, seeing that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, the ferrymen with their own hands served them pure and excellent foods, hard and soft, satisfying them and giving them all they wished. Having with their own hands satisfied them with pure and excellent foods, hard and soft, of many kinds, and having given them all they wished, they saw that the Blessed One had finished his meal, set aside his alms bowl, and washed his hands. Then they took low seats and sat before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the dispositions, the latent tendencies, the temperaments, and the natures of those ferrymen, taught them the Dharma in such a way that they would realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, many of the ferrymen attained the fruit of stream entry. Some attained the fruit of once-returning. Some attained the fruit of non-returning. Some abandoned all afflictions and realized arhatship. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a śrāvaka. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.

Some generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. And the whole assembly was established in devotion to the Buddha, inclination toward the Dharma, and attraction to the Saṅgha.

Then those ferrymen, with great honor, ferried the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks across by the boat bridge. The monks, too, were glad at heart on seeing this veneration of the Buddha, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, "Where did the Blessed One create these roots of virtue?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated actions whose requisites had been gathered and whose conditions had matured, actions that have now come upon him like a flood and that must inevitably bear fruit. That is why this veneration has been offered to the Tathāgata. Monks, do you wish to hear about it?"

"Blessed One, we wish to hear."

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, a guide who tames persons, unsurpassed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one called Bhagīratha. Attended by sixty-two thousand arhats, he was traveling through the countryside and came to the bank of the Ganges. At that time a caravan leader, together with a retinue of many hundreds, was ferrying travelers across the river Ganges. In that region there was also great danger from robbers.

"Then the caravan leader saw the perfectly complete buddha Bhagīratha, attended by sixty-two thousand arhats. Seeing him, he was glad at heart, and glad at heart he said to the Blessed One, 'I wish to ferry the Blessed One across first of all.' The perfectly complete buddha Bhagīratha consented to the caravan leader by remaining silent. Then that caravan leader, with great magnificence, ferried the perfectly complete buddha Bhagīratha, attended by sixty-two thousand arhats, across by the boat bridge, satisfied them with fine food as well, and made an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the caravan leader at that time, on that occasion, was I. Through the ripening of that action, in which I ferried across by the boat bridge the perfectly complete buddha Bhagīratha, attended by sixty-two thousand arhats, satisfied them with fine food, and made an aspiration, I experienced great and boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and now too, when I have fully awakened into unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, such veneration has been offered to me. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall revere him. We shall esteem him. We shall worship him. Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall live in reliance on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Now, the one called "The Pillar." The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townsfolk, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kiṃnaras, and by great mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and great mahoragas, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick, and medical supplies, was traveling with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas through the Kuru country and came to the city of the Kurus. The multitudes of Kuru people there were to be tamed by the Buddha; they were of broad mind, and every one of them delighted in giving.

Then the Blessed One thought, "I shall summon Śakra, lord of the gods, surrounded by his retinue of gods, for on seeing him the virtue of these people will increase." Then the Blessed One brought forth a worldly thought: "Oh, how good it would be if Śakra, lord of the gods, attended by the hosts of gods, were to come bringing pillars of gośīrṣa sandalwood!" The very moment he brought forth that thought, Śakra, lord of the gods, attended by the hosts of gods, together with Viśvakarman and the Four Great Kings, and attended by many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kumbhāṇḍas, arrived, bringing pillars of gośīrṣa sandalwood. Crying "Ha ha!", making a clamor of laughter and raising a great shout, they built a fine palace of gośīrṣa sandalwood for the Blessed One.

Then in that palace Śakra, lord of the gods, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with divine food, divine bedding and seats, divine perfumes, and garlands of flowers. When the multitudes of Kuru people saw that divine splendor, they were filled with the greatest wonder and thought, "Since the gods together with their lord worship the Blessed One in this way, surely he is supreme in the world!" With their minds drawn to him, they went to the Blessed One, bowed at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the multitudes of Kuru people felt great delight in that palace.

Then the Blessed One made the palace vanish and taught them the Dharma, bound up with impermanence, in such a way that they would realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, some of the Kuru people attained the fruit of stream entry. Some attained the fruit of once-returning. Some attained the fruit of non-returning. Some abandoned all afflictions and realized arhatship. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a śrāvaka. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. Some generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. And the whole assembly was established in devotion to the Buddha, inclination toward the Dharma, and attraction to the Saṅgha.

The monks, too, were glad at heart on seeing this veneration of the Buddha, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, "Where did the Blessed One create these roots of virtue?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated actions whose requisites had been gathered and whose conditions had matured, actions that have now come upon him like a flood and that must inevitably bear fruit. That is why this veneration has been offered to the Tathāgata. Monks, do you wish to hear about it?"

"Blessed One, we wish to hear."

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, a guide who tames persons, unsurpassed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one called Brahmā. The perfectly complete buddha Brahmā, attended by sixty-two thousand arhats, was traveling through the countryside and came to a certain royal city. The king, a head-anointed kṣatriya, heard: 'The perfectly complete buddha Brahmā, attended by sixty-two thousand arhats, traveling through the countryside, has come into my land.' Having heard this, he went with great royal splendor and great royal power to where the Blessed One, the perfectly complete buddha Brahmā, was. On arriving, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete buddha Brahmā and sat down to one side. When he was seated to one side, the Blessed One fully established the head-anointed kṣatriya king in the qualities that bring about the attainment of awakening.

"Then the king, delighted, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: 'I wish to serve the Blessed One with robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick, and medical supplies. Would the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, consent to stay here in this royal city for three months?' The perfectly complete buddha Brahmā consented to the king by remaining silent.

"Then the head-anointed kṣatriya king had a palace of gośīrṣa sandalwood built for the Blessed One. He adorned it with cloths and ornaments of many kinds, scattered flowers of many kinds, and perfumed it with incense burners. He offered it to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, satisfied them with fine food for three months, presented them with fine robes of many kinds, and also made an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the head-anointed kṣatriya king at that time, on that occasion, was I. Through the ripening of the action of offering such veneration to the perfectly complete buddha Brahmā, I experienced great and boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and now too, when I have fully awakened into unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, such veneration has been offered to me. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall revere him. We shall esteem him. We shall worship him. Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall live in reliance on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, fascicle four.

Now, the one called "The Bath." The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townsfolk, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kiṃnaras, and by great mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and great mahoragas, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick, and medical supplies, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time some five hundred merchants of Śrāvastī set out on a road through the wilderness. They lost their way and came into a sandy desert. Exhausted by the hardship of the road, their provisions used up, and scorched by the heat of the sun at midday, they writhed on the ground like fish thrown onto dry land, experiencing feelings that were fierce, unbearable, burning, and disagreeable. They prayed one by one to Śiva, to Varuṇa, to Kubera, to Śakra, and to some thousand other gods, yet none was able to save them from it.

Among them was a layman who was familiar with the teaching of the Buddha, and he said to the merchants, "Go for refuge to the Buddha!" Then all of them, with one voice, went for refuge.

Now, for the buddhas, the blessed ones, there is nothing whatever that they do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion and engaged in benefiting the world. They are the sole protectors, the sole heroes, without equal, who never speak with a double tongue. They abide in calm abiding and insight, illuminate the three knowledges, are well trained in the three trainings, and are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods; the soles of their feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand firm; and they have long been practiced in the four means of attracting disciples. Fearless through the four fearlessnesses, they roar the great, true lion's roar of the bull among men. They have thoroughly abandoned the five factors, have completely transcended the five destinies, and are endowed with the six qualities. They have perfected the six perfections and abide in the six constant abidings. They are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, they teach the eightfold path, and they are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions. They possess the strength of the ten powers, their fame pervades the ten directions, and they are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. By the nature of things, three times each day and three times each night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, and their gaze of wisdom goes forth with the thought: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted by harm? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not generated roots of virtue shall I generate them? In whom who has already generated roots of virtue shall I bring them to full ripeness? Whom, already fully ripened, shall I bring to complete liberation?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, dwelling place of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide go by,
But toward the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then, at a certain moment, the Blessed One saw the many merchants who were in want and had fallen into danger. Then, in the time it takes to blink an eye, attended by the assembly of monks, he vanished from the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta and went to that place. The merchants saw the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks, and when they saw him they raised a great cry.

Then the Blessed One formed a worldly intention, thinking, "It would be good if Śakra, lord of the gods, were to send down a great rain and also send forth a cool breeze." The very moment the Blessed One formed this intention, Śakra sent down a great rain and also sent forth a cool breeze. Because of this the merchants were no longer thirsty, and their torment from the heat subsided as well. Then the merchants were refreshed, and the Blessed One also showed them the way, so that they reached Śrāvastī.

Then, when they had recovered from their weariness, they went before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One taught them the Dharma in such a way that they came to realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, some attained the fruit of stream-entry, some attained the fruit of once-returning, and some attained the fruit of non-returning. Some abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a śrāvaka, some generated the mind set on the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and some generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. The whole assembly was established in inclining toward the Buddha, sloping toward the Dharma, and bending toward the Saṅgha.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wonderful how the Blessed One rescued these merchants from the wilderness in this way, and how, the very moment he formed the intention, a great rain fell and a cool breeze arose."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the Tathāgata himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations had matured and whose conditions had come together, which came on like a flood and were bound inevitably to arrive. Since I myself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor do they ripen in the elements of water, fire, or wind. Virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfect and complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames persons, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Candana. Then, as the perfect and complete buddha Candana was wandering through the country, he came to a certain royal capital. The king there, a kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, went to where the perfect and complete buddha Candana was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfect and complete buddha Candana and sat down to one side. When the kṣatriya king anointed on the crown of his head was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed him well in the teachings that lead to the attainment of awakening."

"Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the perfect and complete buddha Candana, and said this to the perfect and complete buddha Candana: 'Would the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, consent to stay in this royal capital for three months?' Then the perfect and complete buddha Candana consented to the king by remaining silent.

"At that time a great drought occurred, and because of it the rivers and wells ran low, and the trees too were left without flowers or fruit. Then the king made a request to the perfect and complete buddha Candana: 'Blessed One, if you would allow a pool filled with scented water to be made within this city, I pray that the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, bathe there. If the Blessed One bathes in this way, I hope that rain will fall from the sky in my land.' Then the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Candana, consented to the king by remaining silent.

"Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, commanded his ministers, 'Prepare scented water and jeweled vases, and with them I shall bathe the Buddha, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas.' Then the king, together with his retinue of ministers, cleared the city of stones, gravel, and potsherds. Banners and flags were raised, all kinds of flowers were strewn, it was sprinkled with scented water, it was perfumed with all kinds of incense, and in the center a pool was made. Then the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Candana, for the sake of benefiting beings, put on a bathing cloth and entered the pool. Then the king, together with his retinue of ministers, bathed the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Candana, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, with water infused with all kinds of fragrances. The very moment the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Candana, bathed, Śakra, lord of the gods, sent down a great rain of such a kind that all the crops flourished. On that account a great many people also gained faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One, and they built many stupas anointed with fragrances and consecrated them.

"All those there who went for refuge to the perfect and complete buddha Candana have passed into complete nirvāṇa; of them I alone remain. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher, revere him, esteem him, and make offerings to him. Having served, revered, esteemed, and made offerings to the Teacher, we shall live in reliance upon him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Epidemic.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and offered to by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, the people of the royal capitals, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time a pestilence broke out among the many people of the Reed Grove country. A great many of the people there were stricken by the disease, and though they prayed one by one to Śiva, to Varuṇa, to Kubera, to Śakra, and to some thousand other gods, the epidemic did not abate. Then a layman who lived in the Reed Grove country said this to the brahmins and householders of the Reed Grove: "Come here! Go for refuge to the Buddha, and invite the Blessed One to come here; and also make this request: 'May the Blessed One please bring the epidemic to an end with little trouble.'" Then the brahmins and householders of the Reed Grove made a request to the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, please come here and free us from this want and misery."

Now, for the buddhas, the blessed ones, there is nothing whatever that they do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion and engaged in benefiting the world. They are the sole protectors, the sole heroes, without equal, who never speak with a double tongue. They abide in calm abiding and insight, illuminate the three knowledges, are well trained in the three trainings, and are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods; the soles of their feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand firm; and they have long been practiced in the four means of attracting disciples. Fearless through the four fearlessnesses, they roar the great, true lion's roar of the bull among men. They have thoroughly abandoned the five factors, have completely transcended the five destinies, and are endowed with the six qualities. They have perfected the six perfections and abide in the six constant abidings. They are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, they teach the eightfold path, and they are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions. They possess the strength of the ten powers, their fame pervades the ten directions, and they are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. By the nature of things, three times each day and three times each night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, and their gaze of wisdom goes forth with the thought: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted by harm? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not generated roots of virtue shall I generate them? In whom who has already generated roots of virtue shall I bring them to full ripeness? Whom, already fully ripened, shall I bring to complete liberation?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, dwelling place of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide go by,
But toward the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then in the morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe and Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went to the Reed Grove. Then the Blessed One pervaded all the people of that town with loving-kindness, and because of this the nonhuman beings departed and the epidemic subsided. Then those brahmins and householders, on seeing the Blessed One, were filled with great joy. Filled with joy, they offered the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas the opportunity to receive whatever they wished of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick.

Then the Blessed One taught them the Dharma in such a way that they came to realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, many brahmins and householders attained the fruit of stream-entry, some attained the fruit of once-returning, and some attained the fruit of non-returning. Some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhatship. Some generated the mind set on the awakening of a śrāvaka, some generated the mind set on the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and some generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. All the people of that town were established in inclining toward the Buddha, sloping toward the Dharma, and bending toward the Saṅgha.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wonderful how these beings, through the joy that arose in them toward the Blessed One, have been freed from their want."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the Tathāgata himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations had matured and whose conditions had come together, which came on like a flood and were bound inevitably to arrive. Since I myself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor do they ripen in the elements of water, fire, or wind. Virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfect and complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames persons, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Candra. Then, as the perfect and complete buddha Candra was wandering through the country, he came to a certain royal capital. The king there, a kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, heard, 'The perfect and complete buddha Candra has come to my land.' Having heard this, he went, with great royal splendor and great royal might, to where the perfect and complete buddha Candra was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfect and complete buddha Candra and sat down to one side. When the kṣatriya king anointed on the crown of his head was seated to one side, the perfect and complete buddha Candra instructed him well in the teachings that lead to the attainment of awakening. Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, rejoicing, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the perfect and complete buddha Candra, and said this to the perfect and complete buddha Candra:

"'Since I wish to serve the Blessed One with robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick, would the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, consent to stay here for three months?' Then the perfect and complete buddha Candra consented to the king by remaining silent.

"At that time a pestilence broke out among the many people in that royal city, and it caused great harm to a great many of them. Then, in order to bring the disease to an end, the king made a request to the perfect and complete buddha Candra: 'Blessed One, would you consent to provide a means by which this epidemic may be brought to an end?' Then the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Candra, said to the king, 'Great king, go and fasten this patched Dharma robe of mine to the top of a banner, and with great honor have it carried around your land. Hold a great festival for it as well, and have all the multitude of people properly keep the recollection of the Buddha. By this you will come to well-being.' Then the king did everything exactly as he had been instructed, and by that cause and that condition the epidemic was completely ended. Then those multitudes of people rejoiced, and the king, the ministers, and the people of the royal capital went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I. Through the ripening of the karma of having made great offerings to the perfect and complete buddha Candra, I experienced in saṃsāra the great happiness of attaining births among gods and humans, and now too I am endowed with the prosperity that has arisen from that cause. Therefore, whatever I have thought of and whatever I have wished for has all been accomplished accordingly. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher, revere him, esteem him, and make offerings to him. Having honored, revered, esteemed, and made offerings to the Teacher, we shall live in reliance upon him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Miracle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and offered to by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, the people of the royal capitals, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At the time when, at Devadatta's instigation, King Ajātaśatru had killed his father, the righteous king who lived by the Dharma, and had himself assumed the kingship, those who were without faith became powerful, and those who had faith became weak. Then, at a certain time, an old minister who was without faith and hostile to the teaching of the Blessed One held a sacrificial offering for the brahmins. Many hundreds of thousands of brahmins assembled there, and among themselves they made a rule that no one should go to see the ascetic Gautama. Then the brahmins, having made this rule, gathered in harmony and, overjoyed, in the middle of the street, following the rite that comes from the Vedas, made supplication to Śakra, saying, "Come, O husband of the Boneless Lady! Come!"

Now, for the buddhas, the blessed ones, there is nothing whatever that they do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion and engaged in benefiting the world. They are the sole protectors, the sole heroes, without equal, who never speak with a double tongue. They abide in calm abiding and insight, illuminate the three knowledges, are well trained in the three trainings, and are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods; the soles of their feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand firm; and they have long been practiced in the four means of attracting disciples. Fearless through the four fearlessnesses, they roar the great, true lion's roar of the bull among men. They have thoroughly abandoned the five factors, have completely transcended the five destinies, and are endowed with the six qualities. They have perfected the six perfections and abide in the six constant abidings. They are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, they teach the eightfold path, and they are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions. They possess the strength of the ten powers, their fame pervades the ten directions, and they are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. By the nature of things, three times each day and three times each night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, and their gaze of wisdom goes forth with the thought: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted by harm? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not generated roots of virtue shall I generate them? In whom who has already generated roots of virtue shall I bring them to full ripeness? Whom, already fully ripened, shall I bring to complete liberation?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, dwelling place of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide go by,
But toward the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then the Blessed One saw those brahmins: through having generated roots of virtue again and again in the past, they had become fit for liberation; they had found what was to be sought; they were facing inward toward nirvāṇa and facing away from saṃsāra. Seeing them, he thought, "Now, because they rely on unwholesome spiritual friends, they have become hostile to my teaching. I shall make an effort to train them."

Then the Blessed One emanated himself in the guise of Śakra, lit up the sacrificial assembly hall with divine light, and went there. Then those brahmins were glad, delighted, overjoyed, and elated, joyful and happy in mind, and with one voice they said, "Come, Lord! Come! Welcome, Lord!" Then the Blessed One, remaining in the guise of Śakra, sat on the seat that had been prepared. Then throughout the city of Rājagṛha the report also spread, "Śakra, lord of the gods, has come to the sacrifice!" Hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that the brahmins had come to have faith, made the guise of Śakra disappear, took on the guise of a buddha, and taught the Dharma in such a way that they came to realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, sixty-two thousand brahmins destroyed with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable aggregates, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings also gained faith in the Blessed One.

Then doubts arose in those monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wonderful how these brahmins, having met the Blessed One in this way, came to see the truths, and how many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained great joy."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the Tathāgata himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations had matured and whose conditions had come together, which came on like a flood and were bound inevitably to arrive. Since I performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor do they ripen in the elements of water, fire, or wind. Virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfect and complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames persons, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Indradamana. As he was wandering through the country, he came to a certain royal capital, and that royal capital had fallen under the sway of the tīrthikas. Then the king there, a kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, heard, 'The perfect and complete buddha Indradamana has come to my land.' Having heard this, he went, with great royal splendor and great royal might, to where the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana, and sat down to one side. When the kṣatriya king anointed on the crown of his head was seated to one side, the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana instructed him in the teachings that lead to the attainment of awakening.

"Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of his head, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana, and said this to the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana: 'Since I wish to serve the Blessed One with robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick, would the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, consent to stay here for three months?'

"The Blessed One said, 'Great king, is there in your land any monastery suitable as a lodging for monks who arrive and depart?'

"The king replied, 'Blessed One, there is none at present, but may the Blessed One accept my invitation, and I ask that you permit me to build a monastery suitable as a lodging for monks who arrive and depart.'

"Then the king had a monastery built for the Tathāgata, with walls, a portico, windows, and doorways, adorned with latticework, crescent-moon ornaments, and railings, furnished with coverings, filled all around with pools, and surrounded by many trees bearing flowers and fruit. When it was built, he offered it to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas.

"Then he asked the Blessed One to perform a great miracle. Since the king had asked, the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana, displayed the great miracle of the play of a multitude of buddhas. As a result the king, the ministers, the townspeople, the country folk, and all the people of the royal capital rejoiced, and they came to cherish the protection of the teaching.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I myself. Through the karmic maturation of that deed, the offering I made in that way to the perfect and complete buddha Indradamana, I experienced boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and now that I have become a tathāgata, this teaching of mine has also become beautiful. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall revere him. We shall esteem him. We shall make offerings to him. Having honored the Teacher, revered him, esteemed him, and made offerings to him, we shall dwell in reliance on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Five-Year Festival.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, courtiers, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit and receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time the foolish Devadatta, though he had done the Blessed One's teaching a thousand harms, had not been able to stir even a single hair of the Blessed One's body. So he said to King Ajātaśatru, "Great king, issue a decree that no one from Rājagṛha is to go to the ascetic Gautama or give him food. If that is done, he will gain neither profit nor honor, and he will surely move away to another country." The king did just that.

Then the lay followers living there who had seen the truth wept, lamenting, "Alas! Though we have met with the appearance of a buddha, a blessed one, as rare as the udumbara flower, we are not even able to attend on him. The people of the city of Rājagṛha have become without a protector!" The monks heard those very words here and there, and the venerable Ānanda reported them to the Blessed One just as he had heard them.

The Blessed One declared, "Ānanda, in this the Tathāgata himself knows the right time, so do not be disheartened. Moreover, for as long as my teaching endures, the śrāvakas will never be without their requisites, so what need is there to speak of now?"

On that occasion Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, turned his knowing gaze to the world below, and he saw what had befallen the teaching of the Blessed One. The very moment he saw it, in order to stir the enthusiasm of patrons and donors, to show truly the greatness of a buddha's appearance, to cut down the arrogance and pride of Ajātaśatru and Devadatta, and to show his own faith, he lit up the whole of Rājagṛha with a great light and called out in a loud voice, "From this day forward I shall serve the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with divine robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick!" Having said this, he went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One, "For as long as I live, here in this very city of Rājagṛha, I wish to serve the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with divine robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick. May the Blessed One please grant me permission."

The Blessed One declared, "Kauśika, there are many in the world who desire merit. That you have brought your mind to faith in me in this way is enough."

Śakra said, "In that case, I wish to hold a Five-Year Festival for the Tathāgata for five years. May the Blessed One please grant me permission."

The Blessed One declared, "Kauśika, there are many in the world who desire merit. That you have brought your mind to faith in me in this way is enough."

Śakra said, "Then may the Blessed One please grant me permission for five years."

Then, in order to make manifest the power of his own merit, to benefit Śakra, lord of the gods, and so that in future times the festival of the fifth day would continue without interruption, the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by remaining silent, made the Bamboo Grove appear like the palace Vaijayanta, and he also made divine seats, divine pools, and divine food of ambrosia appear. Then the Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, understanding that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, together with an attendant retinue of many hundreds of thousands of gods, with his own hands satisfied them and served them whatever they wished. When he had satisfied them in many ways with his own hands and served them whatever they wished, and understood that the Blessed One had finished his meal, put away his bowl, and washed his hands, he took a very low seat and sat before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, with a talk on the Dharma, instructed Śakra, lord of the gods, together with his retinue, inspired them, fired them with enthusiasm, and delighted them.

King Ajātaśatru, who was on the upper terrace of his palace, also saw such offerings being made to the Blessed One in the Bamboo Grove. Having seen it, he was struck with remorse and gained great faith.

The courtiers living in Rājagṛha, moved by the force of the Dharma, also went before the king and said, "Alas, great king! Since even the gods, who live intoxicated and heedless, have left the realm of the gods to make offerings to the Blessed One, the courtiers living in Rājagṛha will be put to shame. It would be well if Your Majesty's decree were revoked."

Then King Ajātaśatru revoked the decree and had a bell rung through the royal city with the proclamation, "Honor the Blessed One as you please!" Then the courtiers living in Rājagṛha, together with their households, glad, pleased, delighted, rejoicing, and filled with joy and happiness, took flowers, incense, and garlands and went to see the Blessed One. Then gods and humans paid great honor to the Blessed One. On that basis the Blessed One taught gods and humans a Dharma such that they would realize the Four Noble Truths, and on hearing it many gods and humans came to see the truth.

Then the monks, having seen the offerings made to the Blessed One, were filled with doubt, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wondrous that such a festival has been held in the teaching of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One declared, "Monks, in other former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations were complete and whose conditions had ripened, deeds that are bound to come forth like a flood and will inevitably arrive. Since I myself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor do they ripen in the element of water, the element of fire, or the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they are complete and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in a time gone by, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfect and complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one called Jewel Mountain. As he traveled through the land, he came to a certain royal capital, and in that royal capital an epidemic broke out. Then, in order to quell the epidemic, the king invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas for the midday meal for three months. When the three months had passed, the epidemic subsided. Then the king and the townspeople, whose minds had become filled with faith, held a Five-Year Festival for the Tathāgata together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas."

Here it is said:

Ānanda, when I had become a king,
To Jewel Mountain of great light
I made my request, wishing for peace,
And held the Five-Year Festival.
