"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I myself. Through the karmic maturation of that deed, the Five-Year Festival I held for the perfect and complete buddha Jewel Mountain, I experienced great happiness in saṃsāra, and now that I have become a tathāgata, such honor has also been paid to me. Even after my parinirvāṇa, many hundreds of Five-Year Festivals will be held in my teaching. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall revere him. We shall esteem him. We shall make offerings to him. Having honored the Teacher, revered him, esteemed him, and made offerings to him, we shall dwell in reliance on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa. Section five.

Praise.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, courtiers, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit and receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time about five hundred musicians, all members of a single troupe, were living in Śrāvastī. At that time a king of musicians called Supriya newly arrived, and his skill was such that he knew how to bring forth seven notes and twenty-one modulations from a single string. He had proclaimed six great cities to be no great places, and then he came to Śrāvastī. The musicians living in Śrāvastī reported this to the king. The king said, "I know the right time for this, so do not be disheartened."

Then Supriya, the king of musicians, thought, "It is said that King Prasenajit is highly skilled in music, so I shall compete with him." Then Supriya, the king of musicians, went to where Prasenajit, king of Kosala, was, and when he arrived, he said to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, "O king, I have heard that you are highly skilled in music. If it would not trouble you, I would like to put you to the test."

Then King Prasenajit, putting him off, said to him, "Good sir, I have a teacher, the unsurpassed king of musicians, who is staying in the Jeta Grove. Come, let us go there." Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, attended by about five hundred musicians, went to the Jeta Grove with Supriya, the king of musicians, and many hundreds of thousands of people.

On that occasion, for the buddhas, the blessed ones, there is nothing that is not known, not seen, not understood, or not comprehended. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion, devoted to benefiting the world, possessed of a singular guardianship, singular heroes, without a second, never speaking in two ways, abiding in calm abiding and insight, illuminators of the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, crossed over the four floods, with the soles of their feet firmly planted on the four bases of miraculous power, long familiar with the four means of attraction, fearless through the four fearlessnesses, proclaimers of the great true lion's roar of a supreme bull, rid of the five factors, gone wholly beyond the five destinies, possessed of the six factors, perfect in the six perfections, abiding in the six constant abidings, rich in the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, teachers of the eightfold path, skilled in the nine successive absorptions, strong with the strength of the ten powers, adorned all about with renown in the ten directions, and far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. By their very nature, three times by day and three times by night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, and they turn their gaze of wisdom upon it, thinking, "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who is in danger? Who is afflicted? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and set in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Who is sunk in the mire of sensual desire, that I may pull him out by the hand? Who lacks the seven noble riches, that I may make him master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I produce the roots of virtue that have not yet been produced? In whom shall I ripen the roots of virtue that have already been produced? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, abode of sea monsters,
Might perhaps let the time of its tide go by,
But for the children he is to tame
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then, in order to benefit the people to be tamed, the Blessed One formed a worldly thought: "Oh, it would be good if Pañcaśikha, son of the gandharvas, surrounded by seven thousand gandharvas, were to come to me bringing a lute whose body is made of beryl." The very moment he formed that thought, Pañcaśikha, son of the gandharvas, surrounded by seven thousand gandharvas, came, made offerings to the Blessed One in the proper manner, and presented the Blessed One with a lute whose body was made of beryl.

Then Supriya, the king of musicians, took up his lute in the presence of the Blessed One and showed how seven notes and twenty-one modulations could be brought forth from even a single string. On hearing it, King Prasenajit and the many other people present were utterly amazed.

Then the Blessed One too strung the lute whose body was made of beryl, and he showed how many different kinds of notes and many kinds of modulations could be brought forth from even a single string. And they resounded as emptiness and as selflessness. He showed that this body is like the lute, that the notes are like the sense faculties, and that the modulations are like the elements of mind.

On hearing this, Supriya, the king of musicians, gave rise to faith. He offered his lute to the Perfumed Chamber and went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Through diligence, application, and effort, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is shifting and unstable, and he ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction. Having abandoned all afflictions, he realized arhatship. Having become an arhat, free of desire for the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, and his mind was like space and like the palm of the hand. He became cool like sandalwood paste. With knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg. He attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, and he turned his back on worldly gain, attachment, and honor. He became worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas gained faith and set about protecting, guarding, and preserving the teaching of the Blessed One.

The five hundred musicians were also glad and happy, and they thought, "We carry on a lowly trade and make our living with difficulty. Why should we not ask the king and invite the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to come to the city?" In time those musicians obtained permission and invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to come to the city, and the Blessed One consented to those musicians by remaining silent.

Then those musicians, the king, the ministers, the courtiers, and the country folk joined together and cleared the whole city of Śrāvastī of stones, gravel, and potsherds. They sprinkled it with scented water, strewed it with various flowers, perfumed it with various incenses, and adorned it with canopies of flowers. The musicians, each bringing his own lute, paid homage with clay drums, flutes, round drums, and many special kinds of music. And with fine food they satisfied the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. Then the Blessed One smiled.

Now it is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward. Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. In the hot hells they descend as coolness, and in the cold hells they descend as warmth. As a result, the particular torments of those beings are soothed. Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, who has appeared, that our particular torments have been soothed." Then their minds delight in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, wherever they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

Set about renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

Thus they recite.

Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, return to the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to reveal a past deed, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to reveal a future deed, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to predict a rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to predict a rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to predict a rebirth as a preta, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to predict a rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to predict that someone will become a king who turns the wheel by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to predict that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to predict a rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to predict the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to predict the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the hair curl between his eyebrows. If he wishes to predict unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the hair curl between the Blessed One's eyebrows. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

Many-hued, interwoven with a thousand colors,
A multitude came forth from the door of your mouth,
And it lit up all the directions
Just as the rising sun does.

And again he spoke in verse:

Free of agitation, rid of pride and of displeasure,
The buddhas, the supreme cause for beings,
The victors, conquerors of the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast One, since with your own mind you know the time has come,
Lord of victors, for the monks, your listeners, who are in doubt,
With the supreme, steady, and excellent words of the bull among sages,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for no purpose.
The purpose for which you, O hero, display this smile,
The great multitude wishes to hear from you.

The Blessed One declared, "Ānanda, it is so. It is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfect and complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor these musicians have paid me?"

"Venerable One, I see it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this giving away of things to be given, these musicians will in due course achieve the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and in a future time they will all become pratyekabuddhas called Sweet Voice. Compassionate toward the wretched and destitute, living in remote dwellings, they will become the sole worthy recipients of offerings for the world. Their gift of things to be given is this: that their minds took delight in me."

Then the monks were filled with doubt, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, where did you perform the roots of virtue through which such power came about?"

The Blessed One declared, "Monks, in other former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations were complete and whose conditions had ripened, deeds that are bound to come forth like a flood and will inevitably arrive. Since I myself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor do they ripen in the element of water, the element of fire, or the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they are complete and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in a time gone by, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfect and complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one called Realizer. As he traveled through the land, he came to a certain royal capital. There was a royal pleasure garden there, rich with excellent fruit in every season. The Blessed One went to that pleasure garden and, in order to benefit the king, settled at the foot of a tree. Then he sat down on the seat that had been spread out and entered the absorption of the fire element.

"Then that king, a consecrated kṣatriya, went to the pleasure garden with women sounding cymbals and music. As the king was strolling about the pleasure garden, he saw the Blessed One, the perfect and complete buddha Realizer, handsome and pleasing to behold, his senses at peace, his mind at peace, possessed of supreme discipline and tranquility of mind, blazing with splendor like a golden pillar. When he saw him, the king was delighted, and together with his retinue of queens he sounded cymbals of many kinds and requested the Blessed One to arise from that samādhi. He also served him fine food, and then he made an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I myself. Because of the very offering I made to the perfect and complete buddha Realizer, the musicians have now paid me such homage. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall revere him. We shall esteem him. We shall make offerings to him. Having honored the Teacher, revered him, esteemed him, and made offerings to him, we shall dwell in reliance on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Boon-Giver.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, courtiers, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit and receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now in Śrāvastī there was a man who lived in the stain of committing adultery with other men's wives. The king's men seized him and brought him before the king, and the king handed him over to the executioners to be punished. Then the king's men, wearing blue garments, bearing weapons, and wearing garlands of karavīra flowers around their necks, proclaimed his crime aloud on the highways, the streets, the crossroads, and the junctions, and led him to the southern gate of the city.

At that time, there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. The buddhas, the blessed ones, are endowed with great compassion. They are engaged in benefiting the world. They are possessed of a single protection, singular heroes, without equal, never speaking in two ways. They abide in calm abiding and insight. They illuminate the three knowledges. They have trained well in the three trainings. They are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods. The soles of their feet are firmly planted upon the four bases of miraculous power. For a long time they have made themselves familiar with the four means of attraction. Through the four fearlessnesses they are without fear. They roar the great and true lion's roar of the supreme bull. They have fully abandoned the five factors. They have entirely passed beyond the five destinies. They are endowed with the six qualities. They have perfected the six perfections. They abide in the six constant abidings. They are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening. They teach the eightfold path. They are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments. They possess the power of the ten powers. Their renown pervades the ten directions. They are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world. As is their nature, three times by day and three times by night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, and the vision of their wisdom engages, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is beset with harm? Who is beset with want, danger, and harm? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruit? Whom shall I pull out by the hand from where he is sunk in the mire of desire? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I bring to mastery over the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I generate the roots of virtue not yet generated? In whom shall I bring to maturity the roots of virtue already generated? Whom, already matured, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, the abode of sea monsters,
May let the time of its tide go by;
But for the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then in the morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. Then that man saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. Having seen him, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, since I am worthy of the sublime gift, please grant me the life I hold so dear."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, go and say this to King Prasenajit: 'Great king, give this man to me, and I shall have him go forth.'"

Then the venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Blessed One had said, went to where King Prasenajit of Kosala was. When he arrived, he gave King Prasenajit of Kosala the Blessed One's message in these words: "Great king, please permit this man to go forth under the Blessed One." King Prasenajit of Kosala, recognizing this as entirely fitting, gave his permission. The Blessed One had him go forth and gave him full ordination.

Through diligence, practice, and effort he came to understand that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable. Having ascertained that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction, he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, he became free of attachment to the three realms. Gold and a clod of earth were the same to him. His mind was like empty space and the palm of the hand. He became cool, like refined sandalwood. Through knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg. He attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. He turned his back on the gains of craving, on attachment, and on honors. He became one worthy of being worshiped, revered, and spoken to with respect by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable, it is wondrous that everything is accomplished by the Blessed One's mere intention."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated those actions which, having gained their accumulations and possessing fulfilled conditions, arise like a flood and will come about without fail. Since I myself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide of beings to be tamed, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Indradhvaja. As he was wandering through the countryside, he came to a certain royal capital. In that royal capital there lived, in the king's city, a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their ancillary sciences. Then the perfectly complete Buddha Indradhvaja, in the morning, put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into that royal capital for alms.

Then that brahmin saw the perfectly complete Buddha Indradhvaja, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. Having seen him, he fell like a tree cut down at the root, bowed at the Blessed One's feet, and said, "Blessed One, I am worthy of receiving the sublime. Sugata, since I am worthy of receiving the sublime, Blessed One, please be seated wherever you will."

Then, in order to benefit him, the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Indradhvaja, sat down there. When the perfectly complete Buddha Indradhvaja had sat down, the brahmin praised him with a hundred words. He also served him fine food, and then made an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. On that basis faith arose in the king, the ministers, and the people of the capital.

"Monks, what do you think? I myself was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the brahmin. Because of the worship I offered to the perfectly complete Buddha Indradhvaja, I experienced boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and now too, whatever I think of and whatever I wish, all of it is accomplished. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the Teacher, hold him supreme, revere him, and worship him. Having shown honor to the Teacher, held him supreme, revered him, and worshiped him, we shall dwell relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Kāśi Cloth.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the capital, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

When King Bimbisāra, together with many hundreds of thousands of his followers, had come to see the truths, he invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to the royal capital for the midday meal, in order to show his repayment of kindness for the benefit he had received, to establish the worship of the Buddha as a custom, to show the openness of his house, and to show how precious is the appearance of a buddha.

Then he commanded the people of the Magadhan capital, "When the Blessed One comes into the city, make offerings of flowers, garlands, incense, and ointments. Clear the whole city of Rājagṛha of stones, gravel, and potsherds. Strew it with all kinds of flowers and raise victory banners and pennants. Cover the whole road from the Bamboo Grove to Rājagṛha with cloth." The ministers carried all of this out.

Then King Bimbisāra with his own hand held a parasol of a hundred ribs over the Blessed One's head, and other people of the capital held parasols for the thousand monks.

Then the Blessed One, tamed and with a tamed retinue, peaceful and with a peaceful retinue, liberated and with a liberated retinue, consoled and with a consoled retinue, purified and with a purified retinue, an arhat and with a retinue of arhats, free of desire and with a retinue free of desire, beautiful and with a beautiful retinue, was like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle, like an elephant surrounded by a herd of young elephants, like a lion surrounded by a pack of beasts of prey, like a king of geese surrounded by a flock of geese, like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of birds, like a skilled physician surrounded by a crowd of patients, like a hero surrounded by a body of soldiers, like a guide surrounded by a band of travelers, like a caravan leader surrounded by a company of merchants, like a guild master surrounded by the people of the city, like a vassal king surrounded by his ministers, like a wheel-turning king surrounded by his thousand sons, like the moon surrounded by the hosts of stars, like the sun surrounded by its thousand rays, like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by the hosts of gandharvas, like Virūḍhaka surrounded by the hosts of kumbhāṇḍas, like Virūpākṣa surrounded by the hosts of nāgas, like Dhanada (Kubera) surrounded by the hosts of yakṣas, like Vemacitrin surrounded by the hosts of asuras, like Śakra (Indra) surrounded by the hosts of the gods of the Thirty-Three, and like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika gods. Brimming and still like the ocean, like a cloud laden with rain, like a king of elephants free of rut, with his senses utterly serene, his deportment never faltering, adorned with the many unshared qualities of a buddha, the Blessed One entered that city.

When the Blessed One set his foot upon the threshold of the gate, this great earth shook in six ways, and when the Blessed One entered the city, such marvels as these occurred. Moreover, narrow gateways became wide, and low ones became high. The elephants trumpeted, the horses neighed, and the bulls bellowed.

All the various musical instruments kept in house after house sounded of their own accord. The blind came to see with their eyes. The deaf came to hear with their ears. The mute became able to speak. Those whose other faculties were impaired obtained complete faculties. Those drunk with liquor became sober. Those who had drunk poison became free of poison. Those who bore enmity toward one another attained minds of loving-kindness. Pregnant women gave birth with ease. Those in bonds were freed. Those without wealth found wealth. The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas dwelling in the sky rained down a shower of divine flowers.

Then, with such splendor, the Blessed One went to the royal palace. King Bimbisāra himself, with his own hands, took up water scented with the finest sandalwood for cooling the feet at the outer gatehouse, and bathed the feet of the Blessed One and of the Saṅgha of monks. Then, seeing that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, he served them food of a hundred flavors. When they had eaten, he also presented them with robes of Kāśi cloth. Because of this, the people of the Magadhan capital became filled with faith.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable, where did the Blessed One create the roots of virtue by which the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks have received such worship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated those actions which, having gained their accumulations and possessing fulfilled conditions, arise like a flood and will come about without fail. Since I myself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide of beings to be tamed, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Śaṅkara. As he was wandering through the countryside, he came to a certain royal capital. The king, a kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, heard that the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara, wandering through the countryside, had come to that royal capital. Having heard this, he went, with great royal splendor and great royal might, to where the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara, was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara and sat down to one side. When the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, had sat down to one side, the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara caused him to take up properly the teachings that bring about the attainment of awakening. Then the king, overjoyed, invited the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara to the royal palace and served him food of a hundred flavors. He also presented him with robes worth a hundred thousand. And he built a stūpa of his parinirvāṇa one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.

"Monks, what do you think? I myself was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king. Because I made such offerings to the perfectly complete Buddha Śaṅkara, I experienced boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and through that very cause, now that I have become a tathāgata, King Bimbisāra too has made such offerings. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the Teacher, hold him supreme, revere him, and worship him. Having shown honor to the Teacher, held him supreme, revered him, and worshiped him, we shall dwell relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Divine Food.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the capital, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

There lived a guild master, rich, of great wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in wealth, who was devoted to the tīrthikas. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana brought him to faith and introduced him to the teaching, and he became deeply devoted to the Blessed One. That householder was one inclined toward generosity on a vast scale, and he said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "I wish to make an offering to the Blessed One, so please be my helper." The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the householder by remaining silent.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took that householder with him and went to where the Blessed One was. When they arrived, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. When they had sat down to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable, this householder wishes to offer the midday meal to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. Out of kindness to him, may the Blessed One please consent."

Then the Blessed One consented to the householder by remaining silent. Then the householder, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by remaining silent, laid out food of a hundred flavors, flowers, incense, garlands, and ointments.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana urged Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, saying, "Be this householder's helper." Then Śakra, lord of the gods, transformed the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground into the likeness of the Nandana Grove. He also brought many thousands of elephants like Airāvaṇa and Supratiṣṭhita, and they held parasols of a hundred ribs over the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. He also brought many thousands of goddesses, led by Gatherer of Bliss, and they fanned the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with yak-tail whisks with jeweled handles. He also brought many thousands of gandharvas, led by Supriya, Pañcaśikha, and Tumburu, and they struck up all kinds of excellent music. He also prepared divine food of nectar.

Then the householder, having served the Blessed One with the requisites of gods and humans, bowed at the Blessed One's feet with his whole body and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, by this generation of the mind, and by this complete giving of a gift, in this blind world that has no guide and no leader at all, may I become a buddha who carries across those who have not crossed, frees those who are not free, consoles those who are not consoled, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not attained complete nirvāṇa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the succession of that householder's causes, one after another, and the succession of his actions, one after another, smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend having become cool, and into the cold hells they descend having become warm. As a result, the particular torments of those beings are soothed. Then they think, "Oh, have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to arouse their faith, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh, we have neither died and passed away from here nor been born somewhere else. Rather, through the power of this being, never seen before, who has appeared to us, our particular torments have been soothed." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, they exhaust the karma that was to be experienced in the hells, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

Set about renunciation;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching;
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Destroy the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of birth
And make an end of suffering.

Thus they recite.

Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, return and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to reveal past actions, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to reveal future actions, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to predict rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to predict rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to predict rebirth as a preta, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to predict rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to predict that someone will become a wheel-turning king of force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to predict that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to predict rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to predict the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth.

If he wishes to predict the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the ūrṇā hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to predict unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, they vanish into the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the Blessed One's head. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and asked the Blessed One:

Variegated, interlaced with a thousand hues,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth;
They have lit up all the directions everywhere,
Just as the rising sun would do.

And again he asked in verse:

Free of agitation, having abandoned pride and displeasure,
The buddhas, who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered their foes, do not, without cause or condition,
Display a smile the color of lotus root and conch.
Steadfast one, since with your own mind you know the time has come,
Lord of victors, for the śramaṇas who listen and are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your steadfast and supreme speech
And with excellent words, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.
The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without a reason;
The purpose for which the hero displays a smile,
That the great multitude longs to hear from you.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. It is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor this householder has shown me?"

"Venerable, I see it."

"Ānanda, by this root of virtue, this generation of the mind, and this complete giving of a gift, this householder will fully accomplish the awakening that is to be fully accomplished over three incalculable eons. Having perfected the six perfections, wholly suffused with great compassion, he will become a perfectly complete buddha called Giver of Divine Food, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared applications of mindfulness, and great compassion, and he will appear in the world. His gift is this one, through which his mind rejoiced in me."

On this occasion, King Bimbisāra of Magadha and his retinue heard this and were supremely amazed.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, see how this householder has worshiped the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with the riches of gods and humans!"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated those actions which, having gained their accumulations and possessing fulfilled conditions, arise like a flood and will come about without fail. Since I myself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, knower of the world, guide of beings to be tamed, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Pūrṇa. Then the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa, wandering through the countryside, came to a certain royal capital. The king, a kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, heard that the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa, wandering through the countryside, had come to that royal capital. Having heard this, he went, with great royal splendor and great royal might, to where the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa and sat down to one side. When the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, had sat down to one side, the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa caused him to take up properly the teachings that bring about the attainment of awakening.

"Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, invited the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to receive robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick for three months. The perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa consented by remaining silent. Then the king, the kṣatriya anointed on the crown of the head, understanding that the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa had consented by remaining silent, served him for three months with robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick. He also had an image of the Blessed One made of precious substances and held a festival for the Buddha, at which many hundreds of thousands of living beings gained great faith; by that cause and that condition, they attained complete nirvāṇa.

"Monks, what do you think? I myself was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king. Because I made such offerings to the perfectly complete Buddha Pūrṇa, I experienced boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and through that very cause, now that I have become a tathāgata, the guild master and Śakra have made such offerings to me. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the Teacher, hold him supreme, revere him, and worship him. Having shown honor to the Teacher, held him supreme, revered him, and worshiped him, we shall dwell relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the second summary verse is complete.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the sixth section.

The summary:

Candana and Padma,
Likewise the Wheel, the Ten-Headed,
Soft Complexion and Cool Light,
The Boatman and Rising Fragrance,
And those called Vimala and Sweet Voice:
These are taught in this group.

The story called Candana.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and recognized by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was wandering through the land of Magadha together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and he arrived at the bank of the river Ganges.

At that time, not far from the bank of the river Ganges, there stood a stūpa that had fallen into ruin, worn away by wind and the heat of the sun. When the monks saw it, they asked the Blessed One, "Blessed One, whose stūpa is this?"

The Blessed One said, "There once was a pratyekabuddha called Candana. It is his."

The monks asked, "Blessed One, from where did the pratyekabuddha Candana come? From what was his name given?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, do you wish to hear where the pratyekabuddha Candana came from and from what his name was given?"

They replied, "Venerable One, we wish to hear it."

He said, "Then, monks, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, a king called Brahmadatta ruled in the city of Vārāṇasī. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and blessed with good harvests, and full of many people and folk. Quarrels and fighting were stilled, and there was no unrest, no internal strife, no robbery and theft, no famine, and no disease. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffaloes. That king, too, was righteous, a Dharma king endowed with the Dharma, and he ruled in accordance with the Dharma.

"He had no son, and wishing for a son, he prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and others, and to other particular gods as well, namely: he prayed also to the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads where four roads meet, the gods of places where three roads meet, the gods who receive the torma offerings, and the gods who are born together with one, who share one's nature, and who constantly follow one about.

"There is indeed the saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, then each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch. Rather, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together, aroused by desire; the mother is in season and fertile; and a gandharva has arrived. It is from the coming together of these three conditions that sons and daughters are born.

"While he remained intent on prayer, in a great pond in his pleasure garden there grew an exceedingly large lotus. Day by day it grew larger, yet it did not open. The keeper of the park reported this to the king, and the king commanded, 'Guard that lotus well!'

"Some time later, at sunrise, the lotus opened, and in the heart of the lotus sat a boy, handsome, pleasing to behold, and beautiful, of fine complexion, golden in color, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a high nose, a well-formed nose, and thick eyebrows. His body was well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks. He was sitting with his legs crossed. From his mouth came the fragrance of a lotus, and from his body came the fragrance of sandalwood.

"The keeper of the park reported this as well to the king. Then the king, together with his ministers and queens, went to the pleasure garden. As soon as the boy saw him, he said to the king, 'Come here, father! I am the son of you who have no son.'

"The king was delighted, gladdened, and overjoyed, and said, 'Son, it is just as you say.' Then the king entered the pond, took the boy from the heart of the lotus, and placed him in his hands. Wherever the boy then set his foot, lotuses sprang up there. So they gave him the name Candana.

"When the boy Candana had gradually grown up, the people of the city said to the king, 'Your Majesty, if a festival takes place in this city of ours, it would be fitting to send the prince Candana. Then he will enjoy the festival together with us, and every place will be adorned with lotuses.'

"The king said, 'Let it be done so.'

"Then Candana, adorned with every ornament, accompanied by the sons of the ministers with their servants and retinue, and with the sounds of many kinds of music being played, went out from the royal palace in order to enjoy the city festival. As he went along, at every step lovely and captivating lotuses sprang up, but as soon as the rays of the sun struck them, they withered and dried up.

"Then he, a being who was pure, of virtuous intention, and who had generated roots of virtue toward buddhas in the past, saw this, and proper attention arose in him. He thought, 'Just as these lotuses are beautiful the moment they spring up, yet, scorched by the rays of the sun, wither and dry up, so too this body is just like them.'

"As he thought in this way, weighing it and examining it closely, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening became manifest to him, and right there, while still sitting amid the crowd of people, he directly realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.

"Then, after a while, the gods of the Pure Abodes offered him garments of colored cloth. He put them on, rose up into the sky, and performed miracles of many kinds. Seeing this, the king, together with his ministers and the people of the town, was filled with great joy, and they also generated roots of virtue of many kinds."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, that is where the pratyekabuddha Candana came from, and that too is how his name was given."

The monks asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, "Venerable One, what deeds did the pratyekabuddha Candana do and accumulate, such that his body was fragrant and his five faculties were keen?"

The Blessed One said, "He went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa. There he offered a sprinkling of perfumed water to a stūpa containing that Buddha's hair and nail clippings, and he also hung flowers on it. And there he cultivated the path to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the Teacher, hold him supreme, revere him, and worship him. Having shown honor to the Teacher, held him supreme, revered him, and worshiped him, we shall dwell relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Padma.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and recognized by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, following the custom of those who live in the Middle Country, the park keepers would gather lotuses and go into the streets to sell them.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms.

A woman, too, was going along the street carrying a little boy on her hip. The boy saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a mountain of jewels in motion. On seeing him, joy arose in the boy, and on a sudden impulse he stretched out his hand, took a lotus from a park keeper, and threw it onto the head of the Tathāgata.

Then that lotus grew to the size of a chariot wheel and stayed in the sky above him: when the Blessed One walked, it moved, and when he stood still, it stayed. Then the Blessed One emitted rays of light the color of rubies, and with them he illuminated the whole of Śrāvastī. Through this, the king, the ministers, and the people of the palace retinue were brought to faith.

Then the Blessed One smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light come forth from their mouths, and some go downward while some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend as coolness, and into those that are cold hells they descend as warmth. Thus the particular torments of those beings are soothed.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our particular torments have been soothed." Then, their minds delighting in the emanation, they exhaust the karma that was to be experienced in hell, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, wherever they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness.

They also proclaim two verses:

"Set out, and go forth;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching;
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they proclaim.

Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, follow along right behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wishes to explain a past deed, they disappear into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain a future deed, they disappear into his front. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a preta, they disappear into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a human, they disappear into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that one will become a universal monarch ruling by force, they disappear into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that one will become a universal monarch, they disappear into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a god, they disappear into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they disappear into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many rays, of every kind, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Have come forth from the door of your mouth;
They have lit up all directions everywhere,
Just as the rising sun would do."

And he spoke further in verse:

"Free of agitation, having abandoned pride and displeasure,
The buddhas, who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and of conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
For the śramaṇas, Lord of Victors, the listeners who are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme and steadfast words,
Excellent one, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for nothing.
The reason, hero, for which you display this smile,
That is what the great crowd of people wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, it is so. It is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this boy, filled with faith, throw a lotus onto the Tathāgata?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, through the resolve he has generated, and through this giving away of a gift, this boy will not fall into the lower realms for fifteen eons. Having experienced the happiness of gods and humans, he will become a pratyekabuddha called Padmottara. His gift is this one, through which his mind became joyful toward me.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called the Wheel.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and recognized by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time a caravan leader from Rājagṛha had set out on the great ocean. His wife, in the prime of youth, longing for her husband and utterly disheartened, uttered laments, yet her husband did not come. So she bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and made a vow: "If my husband comes back quickly, I shall offer you a golden wheel."

Then her husband quickly returned from the great ocean and came back safely, without mishap. Then she had a golden wheel made, and, surrounded by a group of her maidservants, she set out for the temple carrying the wheel, along with perfumes, incense, and flowers.

Now on that occasion, there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not comprehend. Yet the buddhas, the blessed ones, possessed of great compassion, engaged in benefiting the world, the sole guardians, the solely heroic, without equal, who do not speak in two ways, who dwell in calm abiding and insight, who illuminate the three knowledges, who are well trained in the three trainings, who are skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand firm, who have long been familiar with the four means of attraction, who are fearless through the four fearlessnesses, who roar the great and genuine lion's roar of the bull, who have entirely abandoned the five factors, who have wholly passed beyond the five destinies, who are endowed with the six factors, who have brought the six perfections to completion, who dwell in the six constant abidings, who are rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive absorptions, who are powerful with the power of the ten strengths, whose fame spreads everywhere in the ten directions, and who are far more exalted even than the lord of the thousandfold world, by the nature of things look upon the world with the eye of a buddha three times each day and three times each night. Their wisdom and vision turn to it, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted with harm? Who is in want, in danger, and afflicted with harm? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding into the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Whom shall I take by the hand and pull out from sinking in the mire of desire? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I bring to command the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not generated roots of virtue shall I generate them? In whom who has already generated roots of virtue shall I bring them to full ripening? Whom, already fully ripened, shall I bring to liberation?"

On this it is said:

"The ocean, the abode of sea monsters,
May perhaps let its tide pass by its time;
But for the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time pass by."

Then the Blessed One saw: "If that young woman sees me, she will generate roots of virtue for a pratyekabuddha's awakening."

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went into Rājagṛha for alms.

Then that young woman saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a mountain of jewels in motion. The moment she saw him she was filled with joy, and she was about to throw the golden wheel to the Blessed One. Then her maidservant stopped her, saying, "This is not Nārāyaṇa!" Yet even as she was being stopped, her heart was drawn by intense faith, and she threw the golden wheel over the Buddha, the Blessed One. She also offered perfumes, incense, and flowers.

Then the Blessed One smiled. Now it is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light come forth from their mouths, and some go downward while some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into those that are hot hells they descend as coolness, and into those that are cold hells they descend as warmth. Then the particular torments of those beings are soothed.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, it is through the power of this being, never seen before, that our particular torments have been soothed." Then, their minds delighting in the emanation, they exhaust the karma that was to be experienced in hell, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, wherever they will become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also proclaim two verses:

"Set out, and go forth;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching;
As an elephant crushes a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they proclaim.

Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, follow along right behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wishes to explain a past deed, they disappear into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain a future deed, they disappear into his front.

If he wishes to foretell a rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a preta, they disappear into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a human, they disappear into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that one will become a universal monarch ruling by force, they disappear into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that one will become a universal monarch, they disappear into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell a rebirth as a god, they disappear into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they disappear into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many rays, of every kind, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Have come forth from the door of your mouth;
They have lit up all directions everywhere,
Just as the rising sun would do."

And he spoke further in verse:

"Free of agitation, having abandoned pride and displeasure,
The buddhas, who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and of conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
For the monks, Lord of Victors, the listeners who are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme and steadfast words,
Excellent one, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile for nothing.
The reason, hero, for which you display this smile,
That is what the great crowd of people wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, it is so. It is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this young woman throw a golden wheel over the Tathāgata?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, through the resolve she has generated, and through this giving away of a gift, this young woman will not fall into the lower realms for fifteen eons. Having experienced the happiness of gods and humans, she will become a pratyekabuddha called Cakrottara. Her gift is this one, through which her mind became joyful toward me.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to the buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called the Ten-Headed.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, held supreme, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and recognized by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was wandering through the land of Magadha together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and he arrived at the bank of the river Ganges.

Then the monks saw, from a long way off, an old stūpa worn away by wind and the heat of the sun. Having seen it, they asked the Blessed One, "Venerable One, whose stūpa is this?"

The Blessed One said, "It belongs to the pratyekabuddha the Ten-Headed."

The monks asked, "Blessed One, from where did the pratyekabuddha the Ten-Headed come? From what was his name given?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, do you wish to hear where the pratyekabuddha the Ten-Headed came from and from what his name was given?"

They replied, "Venerable One, we wish to hear it."

He said, "Then, monks, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, a king called Brahmadatta ruled in the city of Vārāṇasī. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and blessed with good harvests, and full of many people and folk. Quarrels and fighting were stilled, and there was no unrest, no internal strife, no robbery and theft, no famine, and no disease. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffaloes. That king, too, was righteous, a Dharma king endowed with the Dharma, and he ruled in accordance with the Dharma.

"Then that king, having no son and wishing for a son, prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and others, and to other particular gods as well, namely: he prayed also to the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads where four roads meet, the gods of places where three roads meet, the gods who receive the torma offerings, and the gods who are born together with one, who share one's nature, and who constantly follow one about.

"There is indeed the saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, then each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch.

Rather, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother, aroused by desire, come together; the mother is in season and has her menses; and a gandharva has arrived. From the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.

He nevertheless kept devoting himself to prayer. Now in his park there was a great pond filled with utpala, padma, kumuda, and white lotuses, its banks made beautiful by geese, ducks, cranes, and many other kinds of birds. In it there unexpectedly grew a lotus of immeasurable size. Day by day it grew larger, yet its petals did not open. The keeper of the park reported this to the king, and the king ordered, "Guard that lotus well!"

Some time later, at sunrise, the lotus opened, and in its heart sat a boy, cross-legged: handsome, pleasing to behold, lovely, of fine complexion, golden in color, his head shaped like a parasol, with long arms, a broad forehead, a high nose, a well-formed nose, and thick eyebrows, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks. The keeper of the park reported this to the king as well.

When the king heard it, he went to the park together with his ministers and queens and saw the boy sitting so beautifully in the heart of the lotus. Seeing him, he was delighted, overjoyed, and thrilled; he rejoiced, and joy and happiness arose in him. He went into the pond, took up the boy, and with great honor carried him to his own palace. He told the matter to the ascetics, the brahmins, and the readers of signs, held a lavish birth celebration for three weeks, twenty-one days, and gave him the name the Ten-Headed.

Then the boy, the Ten-Headed, was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other excellent provision, so that he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

The boy was full of faith, of good and virtuous disposition, devoted to benefiting himself and benefiting others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, and loving toward all creatures. While his father occupied the throne, the boy saw him performing deeds both blameworthy and blameless. Seeing this, the boy was displeased and said to his father, "Father, please permit me to go forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya."

His father gave him permission, and he shaved his hair and beard, put on dyed robes, and with true faith went forth from home into homelessness. Then, without having received instruction from anyone, he made manifest the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and actualized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. Rising into the sky, he displayed various kinds of miracles to his father. His father then invited him to receive meals for three months. Then, wearied of having a body, he displayed various kinds of miracles and passed into nirvāṇa like a fire whose fuel is spent. This is his stupa."

Then the monks, feeling doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did the pratyekabuddha the Ten-Headed perform that he was not born from a mother's womb but was born from a lotus?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the Ten-Headed himself, in other, earlier lives, performed and accumulated deeds which, once the accumulations were gathered and the conditions complete, come forth like a flood and will inevitably arrive. Since the Ten-Headed himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

Monks, long ago, in times past, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one. The perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin was staying in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī.

Then one morning the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went into the royal capital Bandhumatī for alms. A certain caravan leader, carrying a lotus, had entered the street. He saw the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, altogether excellent, like a moving Jewel Mountain. As soon as he saw him, he threw the lotus over the Blessed One. As soon as he had thrown it, the lotus became as large as a chariot wheel above the Blessed One; when the Blessed One walked, it moved, and when he stopped, it stayed.

Then, after a while, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin prophesied that the caravan leader would attain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. Delighted, overjoyed, and thrilled, the caravan leader went to his own home. At that moment his wife was giving birth and was crying out in distress. He asked a servant woman, "What is this?" and she told him just what was happening.

Then the caravan leader, dismayed, made this aspiration: "May I never, while in saṃsāra, be born in a mother's womb!"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the caravan leader is none other than the pratyekabuddha the Ten-Headed. Through that root of virtue, for ninety-one eons he was never born in a mother's womb, and in his final existence, too, he came to have such splendor. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to buddhas, to pratyekabuddhas, and to śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.
