Soft Complexion.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, members of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a merchant who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with abundant riches and possessions, with many dependents, and with many friends, ministers, relatives, and elders. That householder was full of faith, virtuous and of good disposition, devoted to benefiting himself and benefiting others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.

Then he thought, "These riches are by nature like the moon reflected in water, like a mirage: impermanent, unstable, not lasting, untrustworthy, subject to change, and held in common with the five great harms. So I would do well to give the Buddha, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, a properly arranged bath and satisfy them with fine food."

He then invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to bathe and to take the midday meal. Then, in order to benefit him, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, attended by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to the properly arranged bath. The merchant brought scented sesame oil, went into the bathhouse, and himself attended upon the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas.

Then, when the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas had finished bathing, the householder with his own hands satisfied the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, with fine, pure food both hard and soft, serving them as much as they wished. Having with his own hands satisfied them with many kinds of fine, pure food both hard and soft, and having served them as much as they wished, he saw that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had put away his bowl, and had washed his hands. He then took a very low seat and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One instructed him with a talk on the Dharma, inspired him, roused his enthusiasm, and delighted him. Having instructed him with many kinds of talk on the Dharma, inspired him, roused his enthusiasm, and delighted him, he remained silent.

Then the merchant, having gained faith, fell like a tree cut at its root and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and he set his mind firmly on an aspiration.

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward. Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. In those that are hot hells they fall as coolness, and in those that are cold hells they fall as warmth. As a result, the particular torments of those beings are eased.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to arouse their faith, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been born somewhere else; rather, through the power of this being who has never appeared before, our particular torments have been eased." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, they exhaust the karma that was to be experienced in the hells, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out upon renunciation;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching.
As an elephant tramples a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, follow behind the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain a past deed, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain a future deed, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell a birth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell a birth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a preta, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell a destiny as a balacakravartin, a wheel-turning king of force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell a destiny as a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows. Then the venerable Ānanda, joining his palms and bowing, asked the Blessed One:

"Many-colored, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth,
And they have illumined every direction
Just as the rising sun would do."

And again he said in verse:

"Buddhas free of agitation, who have abandoned pride and displeasure,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
Victors who have conquered their foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
Lord of victors among ascetics, for those listeners who are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme and steadfast words,
Your excellent words, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

Protectors, perfectly complete buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without reason.
The reason for which you, hero, have displayed a smile,
That the great multitude longs to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is; it is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this merchant show me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, through this generation of the resolve, and through this relinquishing of a gift to be given, this merchant will become a pratyekabuddha called Soft Complexion. His gift to be given is this: that his mind rejoiced in me. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to buddhas, to pratyekabuddhas, and to śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the seventh section.

Cool Light.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, members of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a householder who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He was full of faith, virtuous and of good disposition, devoted to benefiting himself and benefiting others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, and loving toward all creatures.

Then he thought, "These riches are by nature like the moon reflected in water, unsteady like an elephant's ear: impermanent, unstable, not lasting, untrustworthy, subject to change, and held in common with the five great harms. So I would do well to extract the essence from these essenceless riches."

When the hot season arrived, he invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to the midday meal. He cleared his house of stones, gravel, and potsherds, sprinkled it with sandalwood water, set out vessels of various fragrances, perfumed it with sweet-smelling incense, strewed it with various flowers, and laid out seats of flowers. Then, having prepared cool drinks, pastries, and food, he sent a messenger to summon the Blessed One to the midday meal, saying, "Venerable One, the time for the midday meal has come and the food is ready. May the Blessed One, considering that the time has now come, please come."

Then in the morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to the house of that householder. Having arrived, he sat on the seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the householder, seeing that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, with his own hands satisfied them with fine, pure food both hard and soft, serving them as much as they wished. Having with his own hands satisfied them with many kinds of fine, pure food both hard and soft, and having served them as much as they wished, he saw that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had put away his bowl, and had washed his hands. He then took a very low seat and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One instructed the householder with a talk on the Dharma, inspired him, roused his enthusiasm, and delighted him. Having instructed him with many kinds of talk on the Dharma, inspired him, roused his enthusiasm, and delighted him, he remained silent. Then the householder, having gained faith, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and set his mind firmly on an aspiration.

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward. Those that go downward go to the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. In those that are hot hells they fall as coolness, and in those that are cold hells they fall as warmth. As a result, the particular torments of those beings are eased.

Then they think, "Oh! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to arouse their faith, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been born somewhere else; rather, through the power of this being who has never appeared before, our particular torments have been eased." Then, their minds rejoicing in the emanation, they exhaust the karma that was to be experienced in the hells, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they become fit vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward go to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and as far as the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out upon renunciation;
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching.
As an elephant tramples a house of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, follow behind the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain a past deed, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain a future deed, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell a birth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell a birth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a preta, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell a destiny as a balacakravartin, a wheel-turning king of force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell a destiny as a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell a birth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda, joining his palms, asked the Blessed One:

"Many-colored, interwoven with a thousand hues,
Many rays have come forth from the door of your mouth,
And they have illumined every direction
Just as the rising sun would do."

And again he said in verse:

"Buddhas free of agitation, who have abandoned pride and displeasure,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
Victors who have conquered their foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus root and conch.

Steadfast one, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
Lord of victors, for the monks who listen and are in doubt,
Bull among sages, with your supreme and steadfast words,
Your excellent words, please dispel the doubts that have arisen.

Protectors, perfectly complete buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without reason.
The reason for which you, hero, have displayed a smile,
That the great multitude longs to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is; it is just so. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, did you see this householder show me such honor?"

"Venerable One, I saw it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue of this householder, through this generation of the resolve, and through this relinquishing of a gift to be given, he will become a pratyekabuddha called Cool Light. His gift to be given is this: that he set his mind in faith on me. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall show honor to buddhas, to pratyekabuddhas, and to śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Boatman.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, members of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, while wandering through the land of Magadha together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, arrived at the bank of the river Ganges.

Then the Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to where the boatmen were. Having arrived, he said to the boatmen, "Friends, ferry me across this river."

The boatmen said, "Give us the fare."

Then the Blessed One said to those boatmen, "I too was once a boatman. I ferried Nanda across when he had fallen into the river of desire. I ferried Aṅgulimāla across when he had fallen into the ocean of hatred. I ferried the brahmin's son who was swollen with pride across when he had fallen into the ocean of pride. I ferried Uruvilvā Kāśyapa across when he had fallen into the ocean of delusion. Yet I did not take a fare."

Even though he spoke thus, they did not agree to ferry him across.

Then one boatman, hearing the Blessed One's voice endowed with the eight qualities and seeing his perfect form, gained faith and said, "I wish to ferry the Blessed One across, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas."

Then, as the monks boarded the boat, the Blessed One by his miraculous power arrived on the far bank even before that boatman. When the boatman saw that miraculous display, his mind was delighted, and he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet. The Blessed One then taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would come to realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, the boatman, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and he actualized the fruit of stream entry.

Having seen the truth, he three times uttered words of joy: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up the ocean of my blood and tears, carried me across the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and the host of my relatives, nor by the departed ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils,
Utterly unbearable, by your power has been cut off.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, has been opened,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.

Today, relying on you, I have gained
The utterly pure eye from which faults are removed.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And gained the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.

Supreme among humans, lord, worshiped by humans and gods,
You who have abandoned the sickness of birth, aging, and death,
Hard to behold even in a thousand existences,
O Sage, today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then one of the boatmen there was seized by great remorse. He bowed at the Blessed One's feet, confessed his fault, and served a meal to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas.

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. In this way the various torments of those beings are relieved.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, through the power of this being, never seen before, our various torments have been relieved." Then their minds rejoice in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become worthy vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out on renunciation,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching,
And as an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Discipline,
Practices with heedfulness,
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a powerful wheel-turning king (balacakravartin), they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell awakening as a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell awakening as a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-colored, interwoven with a thousand hues,
A multitude of rays has come forth from your mouth.
They have illuminated every direction,
Just as the rising sun does."

And he further spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free from levity, who have abandoned pride and discontent,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered their foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and conch.

O Steadfast One, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, for those who wish to hear and are in doubt,
O Bull among Sages, with your supreme, steadfast, and excellent words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without reason.
O Hero, the reason for which you display this smile,
The great multitude wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see how this boatman has brought forth joy toward me?"

"Venerable One, I see it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, through this arising of the mind, and through this giving away of something to be given, this boatman will in the future become a pratyekabuddha called Crosser of Saṃsāra. His gift is this: that he made his mind faithful toward me.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We will show reverence to buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Wafting Fragrance.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the one who knows, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time the people who lived in the Middle Country, by custom, mostly anointed their bodies with various unguents. Now, at that time there was a householder's son who had a servant girl who was faithful, virtuous, and of good intentions, and she was grinding red sandalwood.

Then in the morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went into Rājagṛha for alms. Then that girl saw the Blessed One, the Buddha, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, entirely beautiful. Seeing him, great faith arose in the girl. Having found faith, she thought, "Although I have found such a field of merit, if through the fault of poverty I am unable to show reverence to the Blessed One, what use is such a life as mine?"

Then, without regard even for her own life, she smeared both her hands with red sandalwood and anointed the Blessed One's two feet. And the Blessed One, by his miraculous power, filled the whole city of Rājagṛha with the scent of sandalwood. Then, when the girl saw that miracle, her mind was filled with joy. She bowed at the Blessed One's feet and made this resolve: "Through this root of virtue, this arising of the mind, and this giving away of something to be given, may I realize the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. In this way the various torments of those beings are relieved.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, through the power of this being, never seen before, our various torments have been relieved." Then their minds rejoice in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become worthy vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out on renunciation,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching,
And as an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Discipline,
Practices with heedfulness,
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a powerful wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel.

If he wishes to foretell awakening as a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell awakening as a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-colored, interwoven with a thousand hues,
A multitude of rays has come forth from your mouth.
They have illuminated every direction,
Just as the rising sun does."

And he further spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free from levity, who have abandoned pride and discontent,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered their foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and conch.

O Steadfast One, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, for those who wish to hear and are in doubt,
O Bull among Sages, with your supreme, steadfast, and excellent words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without reason.
O Hero, the reason for which you display this smile,
The great multitude wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see how this girl has shown me such reverence?"

"Venerable One, I see it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this arising of the mind, and this giving away of something to be given, this girl will in the future become a pratyekabuddha called Wafting Fragrance. Her gift is this: that she made her mind faithful toward me.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We will show reverence to buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Vimala.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the one who knows, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in Śrāvastī there was a park keeper. He took a tooth stick and went into Śrāvastī. A soothsayer was sitting at the city gate, and he said, "Whoever chews this tooth stick will come to eat food of a hundred flavors."

When the park keeper heard these words, he thought, "To whom should I give this tooth stick, so that because of it I might be greatly honored?" Then he further thought, "This Blessed One, the Buddha, is a field of merit in the world of the moving and the unmoving, a destination that bears fruit. I shall offer it to the Blessed One, the Buddha."

Then the park keeper took that tooth stick and went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the park keeper said this to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Blessed One, out of compassion for me, please accept this tooth stick."

Then the Blessed One, in order to benefit the park keeper, stretched out his golden-colored arm, which was like an elephant's trunk, and accepted it. Having accepted it, he chewed it in front of the park keeper. Having chewed it, he planted the tooth stick in the ground. The very instant it was planted, it became a great nyagrodha tree, as tall as it was broad, perfect in branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. The Blessed One sat in its shade and taught the Dharma to many gods and humans. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada served him food of a hundred flavors.

Then the park keeper, his mind made faithful by the Blessed One's miracle, fell at his feet like a tree cut at the root, and made this aspiration: "Through this root of virtue, may I realize the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. In this way the various torments of those beings are relieved.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, through the power of this being, never seen before, our various torments have been relieved." Then their minds rejoice in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become worthy vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out on renunciation,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching,
And as an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Discipline,
Practices with heedfulness,
Will abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a powerful wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell awakening as a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell awakening as a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Many-colored, interwoven with a thousand hues,
A multitude of rays has come forth from your mouth.
They have illuminated every direction,
Just as the rising sun does."

And he further spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free from levity, who have abandoned pride and discontent,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered their foes, do not without cause and condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and conch.

O Steadfast One, since by your own understanding you know the time has come,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Victors, for those who wish to hear and are in doubt,
O Bull among Sages, with your supreme, steadfast, and excellent words,
Please dispel the doubt that has arisen.

The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast as the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without reason.
O Hero, the reason for which you display this smile,
The great multitude wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, so it is. So it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see how this park keeper has shown me such reverence?"

"Venerable One, I see it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, this arising of the mind, and this giving away of something to be given, this park keeper will not fall into the lower realms for thirteen eons. Then, having attained his last existence, his last abode, his last body, and his last embodiment, he will become a pratyekabuddha called Vimala. His gift is this: that he made his mind faithful toward me.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We will show reverence to buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Sweet Voice.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the one who knows, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and provisions for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then in the morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. Meanwhile a large band of companions, drunk and intoxicated with liquor, were making all kinds of music with lutes, flutes, clay drums, and round drums, dancing and singing. They had hung many garlands of flowers around their necks, of utpalas, padmas, kumudas, white lotuses, vārṣikī jasmine, and others, and wearing the finest clothes, they came out of Śrāvastī.

Then that band of companions saw the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, entirely beautiful. The moment they saw him, they sobered from their drunkenness. Sobered from their drunkenness, their minds became joyful and faithful, and they paid homage to the Blessed One with dancing, song, and the sound of music. They also scattered blue utpalas over the Blessed One, and these remained above the Blessed One, becoming like a blue pavilion, a blue chamber, and a blue parasol. When the Blessed One walked, they moved; when he stopped, they stayed. The Blessed One, too, sent forth blue light, and that light made Śrāvastī look the color of sapphire.

Then faith in the Blessed One arose in that band of companions, and they made this resolve: "Through this root of virtue, this arising of the mind, and this gift, may we realize the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."

Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light come forth from their mouths. Some go downward and some go upward.

Those that go downward reach the hells Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Into the hot hells they descend as coolness, and into the cold hells they descend as warmth. In this way the various torments of those beings are relieved.

Then those beings think, "Oh! Have we died and passed away from here, or have we been born somewhere else?" Then, in order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they see the emanation, they think, "Oh! We have not died and passed away from here, nor have we been born somewhere else. Rather, through the power of this being, never seen before, our various torments have been relieved." Then their minds rejoice in the emanation, the karma that was to be experienced in the hells is exhausted, and they take rebirth among gods and humans, where they will become worthy vessels for the truths.

Those that go upward reach as far as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha, and there they proclaim the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also recite two verses:

"Set out on renunciation,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching,
And as an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, in this very Dharma and Discipline,
Practices with heedfulness,
Will abandon the cycle of births
And dispel suffering."

So they recite. Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm and follow after the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they vanish into the Blessed One's back. If he wishes to explain future karma, they vanish into his front. If he wishes to foretell rebirth in the hells, they vanish into the soles of his feet. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as an animal, they vanish into his heels. If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a hungry ghost, they vanish into his big toes.

If he wishes to foretell rebirth as a human being, they vanish into his two knees. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a king who turns the wheel by force, they vanish into the palm of his left hand. If he wishes to foretell that someone will become a wheel-turning king, they vanish into the palm of his right hand. If he wishes to foretell rebirth among the gods, they vanish into his navel. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a śrāvaka, they vanish into his mouth. If he wishes to foretell the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they vanish into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. If he wishes to foretell unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, they vanish into the crown protuberance on his head.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into the tuft of hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows. Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Blessed One:

"Varied, interlaced with a thousand colors,
Many rays have come forth from your mouth;
They have made all the directions bright,
Just as the rising sun would do."

And again he spoke in verse:

"The buddhas, free of excitement, who have abandoned pride and displeasure,
Who have become the supreme cause for beings,
The victors who have conquered the foe, do not without cause or condition
Display a smile the color of lotus fiber and of conch.
Steadfast one, since you know by your own mind that the time has come,
For the śramaṇas, the kings, and the listeners who are seeking amid doubt,
With the supreme and steadfast speech of the Bull among Sages,
Excellent one, please dispel the doubt that has arisen.
The protectors, the perfect buddhas, steadfast like the ocean and the king of mountains,
Do not display a smile without purpose.
The reason for which the Hero displays a smile:
This the great multitude wishes to hear from you."

The Blessed One said, "So it is, Ānanda. So it is. Ānanda, the tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, do you see the honor these members of the association have paid me?"

"Venerable One, I see it."

"Ānanda, through this root of virtue, through this arising of their resolve, and through this relinquishing of a gift, these members of the association will not fall into the lower realms for twenty eons. When they attain their final existence, their final abode, their final body and their final individual being, every one of them will become a pratyekabuddha called Sweet Voice. Their gift is this one that they gave to me with a faithful mind. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall pay honor to the buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas and the śrāvakas.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the third set summarized by a verse is complete.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the eighth fascicle.

The summary verse:

Padma, and Morsel,
Dharmapāla, and likewise Peaceful,
Surūpa, Maitrakanyaka,
The Hare, and Dharmagaveṣin,
Anāthapiṇḍada, and Subhadra:
These are taught in this set.

Padma. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, townspeople, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, known to and worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessing great merit, receiving robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling with the community of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then, in the autumn season, the monks were struck by jaundice and became emaciated and weak in body. The Blessed One was free of illness, unharmed, untouched by sickness, and strong. When the monks saw this, they said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, some monks have been struck by jaundice, a disease caused by grahas, and have become emaciated and weak in body. The Blessed One is free of illness and unharmed; he is strong, naturally free of illness, his digestive heat is even, and he digests well."

The Blessed One looked at them and said, "Monks, in other, former lives the Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together, whose conditions have ripened, which approach like a flood, and which will inevitably come. Since I myself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen on the external earth element; they do not ripen on the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely on the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense bases.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time has come,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king called Padma ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing and happy, with good harvests, and full of many people and folk. Fighting and quarrels had been quelled, and there was no unrest, internal strife, banditry, theft, famine or disease. It was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free of harm and with its thorns cleared away, he protected the kingdom as one would care for an only child.

That king, moreover, was full of faith, virtuous and of excellent intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, kind to his subjects, one who gave everything, who gave everything away, who gave away without attachment, and who abided in great generosity.

At that time, because the seasons and their junctures fell out of balance, a great epidemic broke out in Vārāṇasī, and most beings were struck by jaundice. When the king saw them, compassion arose in him, and he thought, "I must protect these people and heal them." So he gathered the physicians who lived throughout the land and instructed them, and once they had determined the basis of these beings' disease, its seat and its earlier origin, he himself had all the remedies and medicines collected. Then the sick were treated, and although they were provided with wealth, medicine and attendants, for a long time those beings could not be cured.

The king then summoned all the physicians, treated them with respect, and said, "Sirs, why have these beings become so hard to cure?"

The physicians examined the matter, weighed its merits and faults, and having reached agreement, they said, "Your Majesty, since this has come from an imbalance of the seasons and an imbalance of the elements, we have not fully understood it. Yet, Your Majesty, there is one medicine: there is a fish called the rohita, and if it can be found, it will be able to cure them."

So the king set about searching everywhere for the rohita fish. He sent out many people to search, but though they searched, they did not find it, and they reported this to the king.

Some time later, when the king went out for a walk, the sick gathered together, sat down, and said to the king, "Great king, please protect us from this disease and grant us our lives!"

When the king heard the words of the sick, crying "Have pity, have pity!" and crying "It hurts, it hurts!" and speaking in despair, his heart was stirred with compassion. Shedding tears and weeping, he thought, "If I cannot even bring relief to others who are tormented by suffering, what use to me is such a life as this, and such sovereignty over a kingdom?"

Having thought this, the king gave away most of his wealth. He installed his eldest son as king, confessed his faults to his relatives and the people, praised the townspeople and the ministers, and comforted the suffering sick. Then he took up the eightfold observance, went up onto the top of the palace, scattered incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands and ointments, faced east, and made this aspiration: "By the truth and the words of truth that, seeing beings fallen into dire need and tormented by disease, I have given up my own precious life, by this truth and these words of truth, may I be born as a rohita fish in this river, the Turner-Back!" When he had said this, he threw himself down from the top of the palace. The moment he landed there, he died, and he was born in the river Turner-Back as a great fish called a rohita.

Then the gods proclaimed throughout the whole land, "The great fish called the rohita that has been born in the river Turner-Back is like nectar for those who have long been tormented by grave disease!"

As soon as they heard this, a great many people took weapons in their hands, carried baskets, and went there, and they began to cut the flesh from the living fish with sharp weapons of every kind. While his body was being cut in this way, that bodhisattva pervaded those beings with loving-kindness, and warm tears streamed down his face. He thought, "That these beings become well through my flesh and blood is a gain that I have truly gained!" In this way, for twelve years, he satisfied those beings with his own flesh and blood, and he never turned his mind away from unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

When the disease of those beings had subsided, the great rohita fish proclaimed, "O beings, listen! I am that king called Padma. For your sake I gave up my own life and took on such a body as this. So have a joyful mind toward me, and when I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, I will again free you from disease forever, and I will establish you in nirvāṇa, the ultimate end, accomplished and blissful."

When they heard this, those crowds of people, the king, the ministers and the townspeople gained faith. They made offerings of flowers, garlands and ointments and made this aspiration: "You who do what is supremely difficult, when you fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, may we become your śrāvakas!"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king called Padma was none other than I. Because I made such a sacrifice, while I wandered in saṃsāra I experienced boundless happiness, and now too, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, my digestive heat is even and I digest well. Therefore what I eat, drink, chew and taste is digested well and comfortably, and I am free of illness, unharmed, and by nature free of disease. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall cultivate compassion for all sentient beings.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Morsel. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, townspeople, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, known to and worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessing great merit, receiving robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling with the community of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

There the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, if beings knew the fruit of giving and knew the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts, just as I know the fruit of giving and know the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts, then even with the very last morsel, the final morsel that remains, if they found a worthy recipient, they would not eat it until they had given it or shared it, and their minds would not remain entangled by the stinginess that arises. But because beings do not know the fruit of giving and do not know the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts, as I know the fruit of giving and know the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts, they eat with a grasping mind, without giving or sharing, and their minds remain entangled by the stinginess that arises."

When the Blessed One had said this, when the Sugata had spoken thus, the Teacher further said this:

"If beings knew, as the Great Sage has said,
How the ripening of sharing out
Comes to be of such great benefit,
They would not eat until they had given,
They would not become stingy,
And a grasping mind
Would never arise in them.
But because the childish, obscured
By delusion, do not know it,
With grasping minds
They always eat without giving.
And, stinginess having arisen in them,
Their minds remain entangled."

When the Blessed One had spoken this sūtra, doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wonderful that the Blessed One has spoken in praise of giving and has also spoken of the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what is so very wonderful in the Tathāgata's speaking in praise of giving and speaking of the ripened fruit of sharing out gifts in this way? Listen well and carefully, and keep it in mind, and I shall tell you how in a past time, for the sake of one who begged, I gave away even the morsel that had already reached my mouth as I was eating.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king called Brahmadatta ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing and happy, with good harvests, and full of many people and folk. Quarrels and fighting had been quelled, and there was no unrest, internal strife, banditry, theft, famine or disease. It was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free of harm and with its thorns cleared away, he protected the kingdom as one would care for an only child. That king, moreover, was full of faith, virtuous and of excellent intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, kind to his subjects, one who gave everything, who gave everything away, who gave away without attachment, and who abided in great generosity.

"Some time later a great famine broke out, like the intermediate eon of famine. Then crowds of people, afraid of dying before their time in the famine, starving, their throats and cheeks sunken, their bodies like those of hungry ghosts, gathered and assembled, thronged together, and went to the king. They praised him, saying, 'May you be victorious! May you live long!' and said, 'Your Majesty, please protect us from this terror of famine and grant us our lives!'

"Then the king called his treasurer and said, 'Hey, treasurer! Is there enough food and drink in the treasury for us and for these crowds of people?'

"When he heard this, the keeper of the treasury said, 'I would like to make a count and then report to Your Majesty.'

"Then those skilled in reckoning made the count and reported, 'For such and such a period, everyone living in the land may have one morsel each per day, and the king may eat two morsels.'

"Then the king called the crowds of people and told them, 'In that case, come to the royal palace every day, eat one morsel each, and go.'

"So every day they came, each person ate one morsel, and they went wherever they pleased.

"Then a certain other brahmin who had not been included in the count heard the news from others and said to the king, 'Your Majesty, I have heard among the people of the land about the count you made, so please grant me too that single morsel.'

"Then, of the two morsels he himself ate, the king gave one morsel to the brahmin, and ate one morsel, the same as the people of the land.

"Śakra, lord of the gods, turned his gaze of knowledge to the world below, and he thought, 'Oh! The one who rules as king in the land of Vārāṇasī is doing something extremely difficult. I shall test him.'

"Then Śakra, lord of the gods, magically transformed himself into the guise of a brahmin, and at mealtime he went before the king. Praising him with the words, 'Victory to you! May you live long!' he said, 'Your Majesty, I am hungry. Please help me with that single morsel of Your Majesty's own.'

"Then the king, resolved to give up his own life, out of compassion gave that single morsel of his to the brahmin and remained fasting. In this way he went without food for six days. Yet seeing all those many people eating, he felt supreme joy.

"Then Śakra, lord of the gods, seeing that the king was doing something extremely difficult, made his brahmin guise disappear, and, remaining in his own form, he praised the king: 'Excellent, great king! Well done! I am delighted by this hardship you have undertaken. Since there is such a protector of beings, this multitude of people has a guardian. Now have it proclaimed throughout the land: "Obtain every kind of seed!" In seven days I shall send down such a great downpour of rain that the grains will flourish.'

"The king had it done just so, and Śakra sent down just such a great downpour. Thereby the famine was averted, and there was a good harvest."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king called Brahmadatta was none other than I. When such a famine occurred, I gave up my own life and gave such gifts. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall give gifts; we shall make merit.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Dharmapāla.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, renowned and possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time the foolish man Devadatta, in order to kill the Blessed One, had sent out the elephant Dhanapāla, had scattered poisoned powder, and had dispatched assassins. For a long time he had been murderous, hostile, and unfriendly toward the Blessed One, while the Blessed One remained toward him with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benevolence, and a mind of compassion. Then the monks said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, see how this Devadatta strives to kill the Blessed One, while the Blessed One remains toward him with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benevolence, and a mind of compassion."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what is so wonderful in this, now that the Tathāgata is free of attachment, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and agitation, omniscient, knowing all aspects, and has attained mastery over all wisdom and all that is to be known? In the past, when I still had attachment, aversion, and delusion, even when he came to kill me while I was young in years, I did not harbor hatred toward him. Listen well and carefully, and bear it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī a king called Brahmadatta ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Strife and disputes were stilled, and there was no unrest, no internal conflict, no banditry, no famine, and no disease. It abounded in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Without causing harm, having cleared away the thorns of the realm, he ruled his kingdom as one cares for an only son.

"That king was faithful, virtuous, and of good intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and loving toward his subjects. He gave everything, relinquished everything, and relinquished without attachment; he abided in great generosity.

"That king had a queen called Evil-Minded, who was fierce, wrathful, and cruel, and his only son, called Dharmapāla, was born of that same Evil-Minded. The young prince Dharmapāla was also faithful, virtuous, and of good intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and loving toward beings. The brahmins and householders living in Vārāṇasī, whenever they saw him, held him dear, cherished, beloved, and pleasing. Then he went to a teacher and learned to read and write together with the other children.

"Some time later, in springtime, when the trees were in full blossom and the forest resounded with the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds, the king, attended by his retinue of queens together with the chief queen, went to the pleasure garden. In that pleasure garden, while the king was sporting with his retinue of queens, Queen Evil-Minded, overcome by jealousy and anger, became enraged.

"The king sent her half of the drink he had been drinking, but she, enraged, sent a message to the king: 'If I should drink half of what you have drunk, then let me drink my son's blood!'

"For one given over to desire there is no evil deed that he will not do. Then King Brahmadatta, although he was righteous and had been free of entanglement in sensual passion, though the retinue of queens tried to calm him, blazed with the fire of anger. Growing ever more furious, he commanded, 'This very day cut the throat of the boy Dharmapāla and give her his blood to drink!'

"Then the boy Dharmapāla, who was in the children's schoolroom, heard this, and weeping he said, 'In saṃsāra, beings at enmity with one another are the lowest of all: thus, under the sway of anger, one will kill even the son born of one's own body.'

"Then the boy Dharmapāla adorned himself with all his ornaments, bowed at his father's feet, and said, 'Father, I bow to you. I am your beloved son, and I have done no wrong. Please grant that I not be killed.'

"The king said, 'Beloved son, if your mother forgives you, then I too shall forgive.'

"Then Dharmapāla, weeping, went before his mother, bowed at her feet, joined his palms, and said, 'Mother, have forbearance, and do not have me killed!'

"Though she heard him speaking thus, crying out 'Have pity, have pity!' and 'Alas, alas!' and speaking in anguish, she did not relent. Then the executioners cut the throat of the boy Dharmapāla with a sharp blade and gave the blood to Queen Evil-Minded to drink, and even so Evil-Minded felt no remorse. The boy Dharmapāla died with a gladdened mind toward his father and mother and toward the executioners."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the boy called Dharmapāla was none other than I. Queen Evil-Minded was this very Devadatta. At that time, even when I had fallen into the hands of the executioners, I gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward him; and now too, while he strives to kill me, I regard him with loving-kindness, I regard him with benevolence, I regard him with compassion. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Peaceful.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, renowned and possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in Śrāvastī the monks had formed two great assemblies. One had undertaken to keep the rains retreat in the middle month of summer; the other had undertaken to keep the rains retreat until the full moon of the last month of autumn. There the monks were coloring their alms bowls, washing, boiling, and dyeing their robes, and sewing their seams.

Then at one point a certain monk, wanting to sew his robe, could not get the thread into the eye of the needle. Crying out "Have pity, have pity!" and "Alas, alas!" and speaking in anguish, he said, "Who in the world desires merit? Who in the world desires merit?"

The Blessed One was walking up and down on a walkway not far from him. Then the Blessed One stretched out his arm, like an elephant's trunk, and with a voice deep, sweet, and articulate, pleasing like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, and resonant like the sound of a great drum, he said, "Monk, I am one in the world who desires merit."

Then that monk, hearing the Blessed One's voice endowed with the five qualities, with reverent and eager attention took hold of the Blessed One's hand, placed it on his own head, and said, "Blessed One, with this hand of yours you have accumulated generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for three countless eons; and yet does the Blessed One still say, 'Monk, I am one in the world who desires merit'?"

The Blessed One said, "Monk, I am never sated with merit. Monk, because I have tasted the flavor of merit, I am never sated with merit."

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Blessed One, it is wondrous that the Blessed One is never sated with meritorious formations."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what is so wonderful in this, now that the Tathāgata is free of attachment, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and agitation, omniscient, knowing all aspects, and has attained mastery over all wisdom and all that is to be known? In the past, when I still had attachment, aversion, and delusion, and was not yet completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and agitation, I was never sated with meritorious formations. Listen well and carefully, and bear it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the royal palace called Great Sound of Peace, a king called Peaceful ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and strife were stilled, and there was no unrest, no internal conflict, no banditry, no famine, and no disease. It abounded in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Without causing harm, having cleared away the thorns of the realm, he ruled his kingdom as one cares for an only son.

"That king was faithful, virtuous, and of good intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and loving toward his subjects. He gave everything, relinquished everything, and relinquished without attachment; he abided in great generosity.

"He would rise early in the morning and go to the hall of offerings, and there he gave food to those who wanted food, drink to those who wanted drink, and clothing to those who wanted clothing, and he gave away wealth, grain, cowries, gold, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, and coral. Yet even so he was not sated with meritorious formations. He went to the queens' quarters and gave food and drink to the retinue of queens. He gave food and drink to his sons, to the ministers, to the warriors, to the commanders, to the townspeople, and to the people of the countryside.

"Then King Peaceful thought, 'I have satisfied the people, but with what shall I satisfy the tiny creatures that remain?'

"Having given away all his possessions, he was left wearing no more than a single garment, with nothing but his body remaining, and he thought, 'I shall give my own body to the tiny creatures.' He bared his body and lay down where there were gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, and he satisfied them with his blood, as one would care for a beloved only son.

"Śakra, lord of the gods, turned his gaze of knowledge to the world below, and he thought, 'Is this King Peaceful doing this for the sake of beings, or is he doing it out of compassion? I shall test him.'

"Then he magically transformed himself into a vulture of fearsome, overbearing aspect, black as ink, and went to King Peaceful. Yet even when the bird made as if to pluck out his eyes with its beak, the king was not frightened; looking at the vulture with great eyes of loving-kindness, he said, 'Son, take from my body whatever you wish, as much as you please.'

"Then Śakra, lord of the gods, was delighted. Transforming himself into the guise of a brahmin, he stood before King Peaceful and said, 'King, please give me your two eyes.'

"The king said, 'O brahmin, no one will hinder you from this body of mine. Take whatever you wish.'

"Then Śakra, lord of the gods, was even more delighted. He made his brahmin guise disappear, and, remaining in his own form, he encouraged the king and said, 'O king, excellent, excellent! Your mind is utterly resolute, and your aspiration cannot be shaken. The stream of your great compassion has flowed out toward beings. Since you are thus fearless in the face of things that inspire fear, through this effort you will before long fully awaken into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was King Peaceful was none other than I. If even then I was not sated with performing meritorious deeds, what need is there to speak of now? Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall give gifts; we shall make merit.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Surūpa.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, renowned and possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At one time the Blessed One, having risen from inward meditative seclusion, taught the fourfold assembly a teaching wholly imbued with the flavor of the Dharma, like honey from bees that has not been boiled. Many hundreds of people in the assembly listened to the Blessed One's teaching, wholly imbued with the flavor of the Dharma, with their senses unmoving. At that time doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, see how these beings have become vessels for the precious Dharma and are intent on listening with respect."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, listen well and carefully to how the Tathāgata, with respect, listened to the Dharma and held it in mind, and bear it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī a king called Surūpa ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Strife and disputes were stilled, and there was no unrest, no internal conflict, no banditry, no famine, and no disease. It abounded in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Without causing harm, having cleared away the thorns of the realm, he ruled his kingdom as one cares for an only son.

"That king was faithful, virtuous, and of good intention, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and loving toward his subjects. He gave everything, relinquished everything, and relinquished without attachment; he abided in great generosity.

"That king had a queen called Sundarī, fair of form, lovely to behold, and beautiful, perfect in all her limbs and features. He also had an only son called Sundara, dear, cherished, beloved, and pleasing, patient and free of contrariness.

"Some time later King Surūpa came to long for the Dharma. He assembled all his ministers and commanded them, 'Leaders of the land, I long for the Dharma. Seek out the Dharma for me!'

"Then those ministers joined their palms and said, 'Great king, the Dharma is rare. It is said that only when a buddha appears in the world does the Dharma appear.'

"Then the king fastened a vessel containing a hundred thousand pieces of gold to the top of a banner and had a proclamation made by bell throughout the land: 'Whoever in my land can speak the Dharma, to him I shall give this vessel containing a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and I shall also honor and praise him with great honors.'

"Yet even after a long time had passed, no one who could speak the Dharma appeared. Then the king grieved and despaired for want of the Dharma.

"Śakra, lord of the gods, turned his gaze of knowledge to the world below, and seeing the king pining for the Dharma, he thought, 'I shall test King Surūpa.'

"Then he magically transformed himself into a yakṣa with hideous hands, feet, and eyes, and said to the king, who was seated amid his large retinue, 'If you long for the Dharma, I shall teach you the Dharma.'
