"When the king heard the word 'Dharma,' joy and supreme delight arose in him, and he said to the yakṣa, 'O Guhyaka, speak the Dharma, and I shall listen.'

"The yakṣa said, 'Ah, great king, it is the one who sits at ease who speaks the Dharma, but I am hungry. Give me food first!'

"When the king heard this, he commanded his servants, 'Bring him all kinds of food and delicacies.'

"The yakṣa said, 'I eat the flesh and drink the blood of those freshly slain. Give me your only son, Sundara!'

"When the king heard this he became deeply unhappy, and he thought, 'Once in a hundred times, as today, one may meet with the sound of the Dharma, and that too is beyond price; it must be bought.'

"Then young Sundara heard this, bowed at his father's feet, and said, 'Your Majesty, be patient, fulfill Your Majesty's wish, and please give me as food to the Guhyaka.'

"Then the king, for the sake of the Dharma, gave to the yakṣa his only son, dear, cherished, beloved, and pleasing, patient and free of contrariness. Then the yakṣa, by the power of his magic, made it appear to the king and his retinue that he was cutting off the boy's limbs and parts one by one and eating them, and drinking his blood as well. When the king saw this, because he longed for the Dharma, he did not become displeased.

"Then the yakṣa said to the king, 'King, I am not satisfied. Give me more!'

"The king gave him his beloved wife as well. Then he made it appear that he ate her too in the very same way. Then again he said to the king, 'O king, I am still not satisfied.'

"Then the king said to the yakṣa, 'Son, I have given you my only son and my beloved wife; what more do you want?'

"The yakṣa said, 'Give me your own body, and then I will be satisfied.'

"The king said, 'If I give you my own body, how shall I hear the Dharma? First teach me the Dharma, and after I have heard the Dharma I shall give up my own body.'

"Then the yakṣa, having bound the king by his promise, taught the Dharma before many hundreds of people in the assembly:

'From what is dear arises sorrow;
From what is dear arises fear.
For those wholly freed from fears,
Having no sorrow, how could there be fear?'

"As soon as the king heard this verse, his mind was thoroughly refreshed; his senses rejoiced, gladness arose in him, and he said to the yakṣa, 'Yakṣa, do with this body of mine as you please.'

"Then Śakra, lord of the gods, knowing that the king was as unmoving as Mount Meru from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, made the yakṣa form disappear, and, remaining in his own form, with eyes shining with joy, holding the son with one hand and the wife with the other, he encouraged the king and said, 'Excellent, excellent, holy being! Through this effort of your steadfast armor, you will before long fully awaken into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And here is your reunion with those dear to you.'

"Then the king said to Śakra, lord of the gods, 'Kauśika, excellent, excellent that you have fulfilled my wish for the Dharma!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king called Surūpa was none other than I. Young Sundara was Ānanda. Sundarī was Yaśodharā. Monks, if even at that time I gave up my dear kin and gave up my own life for the sake of the Dharma, what need is there to speak of now? Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Dharma, esteem it, revere it, and worship it.

Having honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped the Dharma, we shall abide relying upon it.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the ninth section.

Maitrakanyaka.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, renowned and possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, those households in which the mother and father are well revered, well worshiped, and well served are households that have Brahmā within them. Why is that? Because, monks, the mother and father of a son of good family are, rightly considered, like Brahmā.

"Monks, those households in which the mother and father are well revered, well worshiped, and well served are households that have teachers within them. Why is that? Because the mother and father of a son of good family are, rightly considered, like teachers.

"Monks, those households in which the mother and father are well revered, well worshiped, and well served are households that have those worthy of offerings within them. Why is that? Because, monks, the mother and father of a son of good family are, rightly considered, worthy of offerings.

"Monks, those households in which the mother and father are well revered, well worshiped, and well served are households that have the sacred fire within them. Why is that? Because, monks, the mother and father of a son of good family are, rightly considered, like the sacred fire.

"Monks, those households in which the mother and father are well revered, well worshiped, and well served are households that have the gods within them. Why is that? Because, monks, the mother and father of a son of good family are, rightly considered, like gods."

The Blessed One spoke thus, and when the Sugata had said this, the Teacher further declared:

"Mother and father are Brahmā,
And likewise they are the first teachers.
They are worthy of their son's offerings;
They are human, and they are gods as well.
Therefore those two are worthy of homage.
With massage and with bathing,
And with washing of their feet,
Or else with food and drink,
With clothing, bedding, and seats,
The wise should show them honor.
Because they have honored mother and father,
Those wise ones, therefore,
Are not reproached here in this life,
And when they die, they rejoice in the higher realms."

When the Blessed One had spoken this sūtra, doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable Blessed One, it is wondrous that the Blessed One has spoken praise of showing great respect to mother and father."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, now that the Tathāgata is free of attachment, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and agitation, omniscient, knowing all aspects, and has attained mastery over all wisdom and all that is to be known, what is so wonderful in his speaking such praise of showing great respect to mother and father? In the past, when I still had attachment, aversion, and delusion, and was not yet completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and agitation, I experienced great suffering from doing my mother even a small harm, and I experienced great happiness from showing her even a little honor. Listen well and carefully, and bear it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a caravan leader called Maitra, rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal rank, and he played, made love, and took his pleasure with her. As he played, made love, and took his pleasure, sons were born to them, but they died.

"He rested his cheek on his hand and sat brooding, thinking, 'Although my house is full of wealth, I have neither son nor daughter, so after my death, because I have no son, the king will take possession of everything I own.'

"Then someone gave him this advice: 'If a son is born to you, give him a girl's name. If you do that, he will live long.'

"Having no son and longing for one, he prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā and the rest, and to other particular gods as well: the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads where four ways meet, the gods of junctions where three ways meet, the gods who receive bali offerings, the gods born together with him, the gods who share his nature, and the gods who constantly follow close behind him. To all these he prayed. In the world there is indeed a saying that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, then each person would surely have a thousand sons, like a wheel-turning king. Rather, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together, aroused by desire; the mother is in season and in her fertile time; and a gandharva, a being between death and rebirth, is present. From the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.

"So he went on, devoted to prayer, and a certain being died, passed from some class of beings, and entered his wife's womb. Some women of wise nature have five special qualities. What are the five? They know when a man is attached to them and know when he is not; they know the right time and know their fertile season; they know when they have conceived; they know from whom they have conceived; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl: if it is a boy, it rests on the right side of the belly, and if it is a girl, it rests on the left side of the belly. Overjoyed, she told her husband, 'My lord, I have conceived a child. Since it rests on the right side of my womb, it will certainly be a boy. Rejoice!'

"He too was overjoyed. Raising the upper part of his body and stretching out his right hand, he spoke these words of joy: 'I shall see the face of the son I have long wished and prayed for! May my son be sound and not unsound. Once raised, may he do what I need done. May he repay the care of his raising. May he enjoy his inheritance. May my family line long endure. And after we have passed away and died, may he give gifts on our behalf, whether many or few, perform meritorious deeds, and dedicate the reward, saying, "Wherever those two are born and go, may this follow them there."'

"Then, knowing that she had conceived, he placed her at ease in the upper story of the mansion so that the child would be cared for. In cold weather she had what was needed against the cold, and in hot weather what was needed against the heat. She was sustained with the foods the physician prescribed: foods not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent, and not too astringent, foods free of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency and astringency. Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces. Like a daughter of the gods roaming in the Nandana Grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat and never stepped down to the ground below, and she was made to hear no unpleasant sound at all.

"After eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son: a boy handsome and pleasing to behold, beautiful and of fine complexion, golden in color, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a high nose, a well-formed nose, thick eyebrows, and complete in all his limbs and lesser limbs. When he was born, they held a birth feast and then set about naming him, asking, 'What name shall be given to this boy?' The relatives said, 'This boy is the son of Maitra, and he is also a daughter. Therefore let this boy's name be Maitrakanyaka.'

"Then the boy Maitrakanyaka was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to hold him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. The eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other kind of excellent provision, and he grew swiftly, like a lotus in a lake.

"His father went to the great ocean and died there. Then, when Maitrakanyaka had grown up, he said to his mother, 'Mother, by what work did my father make his living in the past? I wish to follow him and do the same.'

"His mother thought, 'If I tell him that his father traded on the great ocean, he too will likely go to the great ocean and die there.' So she said, 'Son, your father used to be a local trader. If you wish, you too should be a local trader.'

"So he took up the work of a local trader, and on the first day he earned four kārṣāpaṇas. He gave them to his mother, saying, 'Mother, give these as gifts to ascetics and brahmins, to the wretched and destitute, and to beggars.'

"Some time later someone else said, 'Your father used to trade in perfumes.' So he gave up local trading and dealt in perfumes, and he earned eight kārṣāpaṇas. These too he gave to his mother.

"Some time later yet another said, 'Your father used to trade in gold and silver.' So he gave up selling perfumes and dealt in gold and silver. On the first day he earned sixteen kārṣāpaṇas, and these too he gave to his mother. On the next day he earned thirty-two kārṣāpaṇas, and these too he gave to his mother.

"Then, some time later, the gold and silver merchants, being of jealous nature and realizing that the boy understood the ways of buying and selling in every place, said to him, 'Maitrakanyaka, your father traded on the great ocean. What need have you of this unrighteous livelihood? Who put you to the petty trading work of lowly people?'

"Then, spurred on by the words of the gold and silver merchants, he went to his mother and said, 'Mother, they say that my father used to trade on the great ocean. I too wish to go out onto the great ocean, so please give me your permission.'

"His mother said, 'My only son, that is true. But you are a child, and you are my only son. Do not leave me and go out onto the great ocean.'

"But, led on by bad friends of jealous nature, he could not be turned back. He did not listen to his mother's words. He had a bell rung throughout the city of Vārāṇasī, proclaiming, 'Hear me, merchants who live in Vārāṇasī! The caravan leader Maitrakanyaka is setting out on the great ocean. Those among you who wish to go out onto the great ocean together with the caravan leader Maitrakanyaka, without paying customs dues, without paying tolls at the passes, and without paying boat fares, make ready your goods for the voyage on the great ocean!' Then he performed the rites for good fortune, auspiciousness and well-being, and set out with a company of five hundred merchants. They loaded the goods for the voyage on the great ocean onto carts, into loads carried on the back, into sacks and into baskets, and onto camels, oxen and donkeys.

"His mother, out of the love in her heart, did not know what to do. With tears streaming and weeping, she went out, clasped his feet, and said, 'My only son, do not leave me and go out onto the great ocean!' Though she cried out, 'Have pity, have pity!' and 'Alas, alas!' and raised wailing and lamenting cries, he hardened himself, struck his mother on the head with his foot, and set out with the travelers. Then his mother said, 'Son, may you not experience the ripening of this deed!'

"After some time, having seen towns, provinces, royal capitals and great countries, he reached the shore of the great ocean. There he bought a ship for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and hired the five kinds of men who work for wages: a captain, a bailer, a boatman, a keeper of the shore-finding birds, and a helmsman. Three times he had the bell rung, and then they set out onto the great ocean.

"After some time, a makara, a sea monster of the fish kind, wrecked the ship and capsized it. Maitrakanyaka caught hold of a plank and reached dry land. Then, as he went on and on across the land, he saw from far off a city called Ramaṇaka. When he approached it, after a while four daughters of the gods came out of it, handsome, pleasing to behold and beautiful. They said, 'Maitrakanyaka, come here! Welcome! These are our storehouses for food, our storehouses for drink, our storehouses for clothing, and our bedchambers. They are filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, and gold and silver of every kind. Come here, and let us enjoy ourselves!' And with them he enjoyed delight for many years, because he was one who had made merit, one who had done virtue, and one of great miraculous power and great might.

"Then they would not let him go along the road to the south. Because they would not let him go along that southern road, he wanted all the more to go that way. After some time he went south again and saw a city called Sadāmatta. When he came to its gate, after a while eight daughters of the gods came out of it as well, even more handsome, even more pleasing to behold, and even more beautiful. They said, 'Maitrakanyaka, come here! Welcome! These are our storehouses for food, our storehouses for drink, our storehouses for clothing, and our bedchambers. They are filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, and gold and silver of every kind. Come here, and let us enjoy ourselves!' And with them he enjoyed delight for many years, because he was one who had made merit, one who had done virtue, and one of great miraculous power and great might.

"Then again they would not let him go along the road to the south. Because they would not let him go along that southern road, he wanted all the more to go that way. After some time he went south again and saw a city called Nandana. When he came to its gate, after a while sixteen daughters of the gods came out of it as well, even more handsome, pleasing to behold, and even more beautiful. They said, 'Maitrakanyaka, come here! Welcome! These are our storehouses for food, our storehouses for drink, our storehouses for clothing, and our bedchambers. They are filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, and gold and silver of every kind. Come here, and let us enjoy ourselves!' And with them he enjoyed delight for many years, because he was one who had made merit, one who had done virtue, and one of great miraculous power and great might.

"Then again they would not let him go along the road to the south. Because they would not let him go along that southern road, he wanted all the more to go that way. After some time he went south again and saw a palace called Brahmottara. When he came to its gate, after a while thirty-two daughters of the gods came out of it as well, even more handsome, even more pleasing to behold, and even more beautiful. They said, 'Maitrakanyaka, come here! Welcome! These are our storehouses for food, our storehouses for drink, our storehouses for clothing, and our bedchambers. They are completely filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, and gold and silver of every kind. Come here, and let us enjoy ourselves!' And with them he enjoyed delight for many years, because he was one who had made merit, one who had done virtue, and one of great miraculous power and great might.

"Then again they would not let him go to the south. Because they would not let him go along that southern road, he wanted all the more to go that way, and the farther south he went, the more his desire grew. After some time he went south again and saw a fortress of iron. He went inside it, and as soon as he had gone in, its gate was shut. Then he went still farther in, and that gate too was shut. He went still farther in, and after a while he saw a huge man. On that man's head an iron wheel was turning, blazing, ablaze, utterly ablaze, one single mass of flame, and the pus and blood that dripped from his head was what he ate as his food.

"Maitrakanyaka asked that man, 'Hey, man, who are you?'

"He replied, 'I am one who harmed his mother.'

"As soon as the man had said this, Maitrakanyaka remembered that deed and thought, 'I too am one who harmed his mother. I too must have been led here by that very deed.'

"Then at that moment a voice came from the sky, saying, 'Let whoever is bound be freed, and let whoever is free be bound.' As soon as it had said this, the wheel vanished from that man's head and appeared on Maitrakanyaka's head.

"Then the man, seeing Maitrakanyaka tormented by suffering, spoke these verses:

'You went past the palaces
Of Ramaṇaka and Sadāmatta,
Of Nandana and Brahmottara.
Why then have you come here?'

"Maitrakanyaka said:

'I went past the palaces
Of Ramaṇaka and Sadāmatta,
Of Nandana and Brahmottara,
And came here through great desire.
Karma leads one far away;
From far away, too, karma leads one back.
Wherever karma ripens,
There karma leads one.
By what ripening of karma
Has this wheel that takes my life,
Blazing and ablaze,
Come to turn upon my head?'

"The man said:

'With a heart full of hatred
You struck with your foot the head
Of your mother, who did so much that was hard for you.
This is the fruit of that deed.'

"Maitrakanyaka said:

'For how many thousands of years
Will this wheel that takes my life,
Blazing and ablaze,
Turn upon my head?'

"The man said:

'For sixty thousand years
And sixty hundred more,
The blazing iron wheel
Will turn upon your head.'

"Maitrakanyaka said, 'Hey, will anyone else come here?'

"The man said, 'Whoever does such deeds as this will come.'

"Then Maitrakanyaka, oppressed by the feeling of suffering, gave rise to compassion for beings and said to the man, 'Hey, I wish to bear this wheel upon my head for the sake of all beings. May no one else who does such deeds as this ever come here!'

"As soon as he had said this, the wheel of the bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka rose up from his head and stayed in the sky at the height of seven palm trees. He died and was reborn among the Tuṣita gods.

"The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? I myself was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was Maitrakanyaka. Through the ripening of that deed, my trading and giving kārṣāpaṇas to my mother, I experienced great happiness in the four great cities. Through the ripening of that deed, the small harm I did my mother, I experienced such suffering. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: you should honor your father and mother, and you should not harm them. Further, monks, you should train in this way: 'May faults such as those that befell Maitrakanyaka while he was an ordinary being not arise, and may we attain such qualities as he had there when he became a god.'

"Why is that? Because, monks, a son's father and mother do much that is hard for him: they give him drink, nurture him, raise him, suckle him, and show him the many-colored world of Jambudvīpa. Even if a son were to carry his father and mother, one on his right shoulder and one on his left, for a hundred years, or were to make them sovereign rulers over this great earth filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, gold, silver, emerald, sapphire, ruby, right-coiling conches and the like, that alone would not repay his father and mother's kindness or benefit them. But when he leads his father and mother from lack of faith to perfect faith, trains them, settles them and establishes them in it; when he leads them from broken moral discipline to perfect moral discipline, from miserliness to perfect generosity, and from faulty wisdom to perfect wisdom, and trains them, settles them and establishes them in these, by that much a son repays his father and mother's kindness and benefits them."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hare.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the royal court, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, renowned, the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with great merit, received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick. Together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, he was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a guild master who was rich, with great wealth and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal rank, and he played, made love, and took his pleasure with her. As he played, made love, and took his pleasure, after some time his wife conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth. A boy was born, and he was nurtured and raised until he grew up.

Then his father's wealth ran out, and his possessions ran out as well. But he had a great circle of friends, relatives and kin, and from time to time he would send his son to stay with the relatives. The boy grew so close to those relatives that they became ever more fond of one another.

Some time later he went to the Jeta Grove, and there he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessed of light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, beautiful in every way. On seeing him he became joyful, and bowing his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma. The Blessed One then taught him a Dharma that brings disenchantment with saṃsāra. Hearing it, he came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa, and with the permission of his father and mother he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Having gone forth in this way, he kept company and stayed with those relatives. The Blessed One turned him away from mixing with householders and set him to dwelling in the wilderness, but he took no pleasure there. Three times the Blessed One turned him away from mixing with householders, saying, "Son, this mixing with householders has many faults. There are forms known by the eye that are pleasing, dear, delightful and attractive, that arouse desire and lead to attachment, and that are like thorns; and there are sounds known by the ear, smells known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body that are pleasing, dear, delightful and attractive, that arouse desire and lead to attachment, and that are like thorns." And in many ways he praised the virtues of the wilderness, where, if one settles there, wholesome qualities increase.

Then after some time that son of good family, relying on the Blessed One as his spiritual friend, and through constant diligence, practice and effort in dwelling in the wilderness, understood that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unstable and unsteady. He thoroughly ascertained that all kinds of formations are subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship directly. As an arhat, free of desire for the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, and his mind was like space and like the palm of the hand. He became cool, like sandalwood paste. With knowledge he had broken the eggshell of ignorance. He had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges. He turned away from the gains of existence, from attachment and from honors, and he became one worshiped, revered and respectfully addressed by the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Then he recalled his former lives, and seeing the extremely difficult deeds the Blessed One had done, he went to the Blessed One and with reverence praised and honored him.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, see how the Blessed One turned this son of good family back from the village three times, set him to dwelling in the wilderness, and brought him all the way to arhatship."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, now that the Tathāgata is free of desire, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress, omniscient, possessing omniscience, and has gained mastery over wisdom and over all that is to be known, what wonder is there in this, that I turned this son of good family back from the village three times, set him to dwelling in the wilderness, and brought him all the way to arhatship? In the past, when I was still with desire, with aversion and with delusion, when I was not yet completely liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress, I gave up my own life to turn this son of good family back from the village and set him to dwelling in the wilderness. Listen well and carefully, and keep it in mind, and I shall tell you.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in a mountain valley where water flowed and which was rich in flowers, fruits and rocks, there lived a sage who practiced fierce austerities. He lived on fruits, roots and water for food, wore deerskins and bark, and performed the fire offering. That sage had a friend, a hare who understood human speech. Every day the hare went to the sage three times. Going there, he would speak to him respectfully and delight him with all kinds of talk, and the two became ever closer friends, like father and son.

"Some time later a great drought came. Because of it the rivers and wells ran low on water, and the trees bore neither flowers nor fruit. Then that sage, having nothing to eat in that place, grew unhappy there, and he rolled up his deerskins and his bark garments. The hare, seeing him like this, asked, 'Great sage, where are you going?'

"The sage said, 'Now I am going to the village. There I will live on alms of cooked food.'

"Hearing the sage's words, the hare was stricken with grief, feeling as if he were being parted from his father. He bowed at the sage's feet and said, 'Please do not abandon me. After all, the household life is full of many faults, while the life of the wilderness is endowed with perfect virtues.' Though he said this many times, the sage could not be turned back.

"Then the hare said, 'If you really must go, then at least stay just for today, and tomorrow go as you please.'

"The sage thought, 'Those born as animals are fond of hoarding and of what they have stored up. Perhaps this one wants to offer me some kinds of food today.' And so he agreed.

"Then, when the day's tasks were done and evening had come, the hare came, circled the sage respectfully, and asked his forgiveness: 'Great sage, since I was born as an animal and do not know what should and should not be done, please forgive me for whatever small wrong I may have done you.' Having said this, without hesitation he leapt into the fire.

"The sage was dismayed. Weeping, he snatched him up as one would a beloved only son and said, 'Son, what are you doing?'

"The hare said, 'Great sage, because you delight in the life of the wilderness, eat my flesh and sustain yourself for one day. As for me:

For a hare born in the forest thickets,
What lentils, sesame or rice are there to give?
Roast this body of mine in the fire,
Eat it, and stay just today in the grove of austerities.'

"Hearing the hare's words, the sage was dismayed and said, 'If that is so, then for your sake, dear to my heart, and for the sake of the wilderness, dear to my heart, I would sooner give up my life right here. I will not go to the village.'

"Hearing these words, the hare's mind was filled with joy. Looking up into the sky, he made this prayer:

'If, since I came to the wilderness,
My mind has delighted in solitude,
By the power of this truthful word,
May the rain of Mahendra fall!'

"As soon as he had said this, by the power of the bodhisattva the abode of Mahendra shook in every direction. The gods turned the sight of their knowledge downward, wondering what had caused it, and they saw that it was the power of the bodhisattva. Then, after a while, Śakra, lord of the gods, sent down the rain of Mahendra on that dwelling place, and once again grass, shrubs, herbs, flowers and fruits flourished in abundance.

"Then that sage, relying on the hare as his spiritual friend and staying on in that place, directly realized the five superknowledges. The sage said to the hare, 'Hey, hare, what do you intend to accomplish by this difficult practice, this diligence and this compassionate nature?'

"The hare said, 'May I become a buddha who, for a blind world without a guide and without a leader, brings across beings who have not crossed over, frees those who are not freed, consoles those who are not consoled, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not passed into complete nirvāṇa.'

"Hearing these words, the sage said to the hare, 'When you become a buddha, remember me too.'

"The hare said, 'I shall do so.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? I myself was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the hare. The sage was none other than this son of good family. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: you should keep to a virtuous spiritual friend, a virtuous companion and a virtuous support, and you should not keep to an evil friend, an evil companion or an evil support. Monks, you should train in this way."

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, here, when I was alone in solitude and absorbed in inward meditation, this thought came to my mind: 'A virtuous spiritual friend, a virtuous companion and a virtuous support are half of the holy life, but an evil friend, an evil companion and an evil support are not so.'"

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, do not say, 'A virtuous spiritual friend, a virtuous companion and a virtuous support are half of the holy life, but an evil friend, an evil companion and an evil support are not so.' Why is that? Ānanda, a virtuous spiritual friend, a virtuous companion and a virtuous support are the entire holy life: unmixed, complete, pure and cleansed. An evil friend, an evil companion and an evil support are not so. Why is that? Ānanda, it is because, by relying on a virtuous spiritual friend, beings subject to birth become completely free of being subject to birth, and beings subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress become completely free of being subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress. Therefore, Ānanda, by this very line of reasoning you should understand it thus: a virtuous spiritual friend, a virtuous companion and a virtuous support are the entire holy life, unmixed, complete, pure and cleansed, and an evil friend, an evil companion and an evil support are not so. Ānanda, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Dharmagaveṣin.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, people of the royal court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying at Śrāvastī, together with the saṅgha of śrāvakas, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the householder Anāthapiṇḍada would, as was his custom, rise early in the morning and go to see the Blessed One, and he would sweep the Jeta Grove with his own hands. Then, on a later occasion, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had some business to attend to. So, in order to show sentient beings who desire merit a field of merit, the Blessed One himself took up a broom and began to sweep the Jeta Grove. When the great śrāvakas Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Revata and others saw the Blessed One, they too joined in the sweeping.

When the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas had swept the Jeta Grove, they went to the assembly hall and sat down on the seats prepared in the midst of the saṅgha of monks. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, these five are the benefits of sweeping. What are the five? One's own mind becomes joyful; the minds of others become joyful; the gods are pleased; one gathers roots of virtue that lead to beauty; and after the breakup of the body one is reborn among the gods in the happy realms, in the heavenly world."

Then Anāthapiṇḍada too came to that place. When he heard that the Blessed One, together with the great śrāvakas, had taken up brooms and swept the Jeta Grove, he thought, "How could I walk over the ground where the Blessed One, together with the great śrāvakas, has swept with brooms?" And so Anāthapiṇḍada, his mind full of great scruple and shame, stayed right where he was.

Buddhas, the blessed ones, ask even though they know, and so the Blessed One said to the monks, "Who is this?"

The monks replied, "Venerable One, it is Anāthapiṇḍada. With a mind full of great scruple and shame before the Blessed One, he does not dare to tread with his feet upon the ground that the Blessed One, together with the great śrāvakas, has swept with brooms in the Jeta Grove, and so to come into the Blessed One's presence."

Then the Blessed One said to him, "Householder, the buddhas, the blessed ones, revere the Dharma, and the Dharma is the teacher of the arhats. So recite the words of the Buddha and come in!"

Then Anāthapiṇḍada, reciting verses, went into the Blessed One's presence. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat before him in order to listen to the Dharma. The Blessed One then instructed him with a talk on the Dharma, inspired him, filled him with enthusiasm and delighted him. When the Blessed One had instructed him with talks on the Dharma in many ways, inspired him, filled him with enthusiasm and delighted him, Anāthapiṇḍada left the Blessed One's presence.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable Blessed One, it is wonderful that the Blessed One, having developed esteem and reverence for the Dharma, speaks nothing but praise of the Dharma."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what is there so wonderful in this: that now the Tathāgata, free of attachment, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress, all-knowing, knowing all aspects, having gained mastery over all wisdom and all that is to be known, has developed esteem and reverence for the Dharma and speaks nothing but praise of the Dharma? In times past, even when I still had attachment, aversion and delusion, and was not yet completely liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress, I gave up my own life for the sake of the Dharma. Listen well and carefully, keep it in mind, and I shall explain it.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, a king called Brahmadatta ruled in the city of Vārāṇasī. In his reign the land was rich, prosperous, peaceful, with good harvests, and full of people and many inhabitants. Quarrels and fighting were stilled; it was free of strife, internal unrest, robbers, famine and disease; and it was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Without causing harm, with its thorns cleared away, he cared for his kingdom as one cares for an only son. That king was full of faith, virtuous and good-hearted, devoted to his own benefit and the benefit of others, of great compassion, magnanimous, loving the Dharma, kind to his subjects, one who gave everything, relinquished everything, relinquished without attachment, and abided in great generosity.

"Then, on a later occasion, he played, delighted and made love with his queen. After he had played, delighted and made love with her, at a later time the queen became pregnant, and a longing arose in her mind: 'I wish to hear well-spoken words.' She told this to the king. The king summoned the soothsayers and spoke to them, and they replied, 'Your Majesty, this is the power of that being.'"

Then, in order to find someone who could speak well-spoken words, the king had ten million pieces of gold carried around the villages, towns, provinces and royal capitals, but even so those well-spoken words were not found. In time, when nine months had passed, a child was born: a boy who was handsome, pleasing to behold and lovely, of fine complexion and golden hue, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a high nose, a well-formed nose, and thick eyebrows, complete in all his limbs and lesser limbs. When he was born, a birth feast was held, and they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give the boy?" The ministers said, "Since this boy was seeking well-spoken words even before he was born, let this boy be named Subhāṣitagaveṣin, Seeker of Well-Spoken Words." So he was named Subhāṣitagaveṣin.

Then the boy Subhāṣitagaveṣin was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. The eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, the finest cream of ghee, and every other excellent provision, and he grew swiftly, like a lotus in a lake. When he had grown up, he too searched for well-spoken words, but did not find them.

After his father died, he was placed on the throne, and he commanded his ministers, "Leaders of the land, I need well-spoken words. Seek out well-spoken words for me!" Then, in order to search for well-spoken words, the ministers displayed ten million pieces of gold throughout all of Jambudvīpa, but even so they did not find any well-spoken words. Then they reported this to the king, and the king, longing to hear well-spoken words, was tormented and despondent.

Now Śakra, lord of the gods, directs his vision of knowledge toward those below. Seeing that the king was deprived for want of hearing well-spoken words, he thought, "I shall test the king." So Śakra transformed himself into the guise of a yakṣa with hideous hands, feet and eyes, and before the king he spoke this verse:

Practice the Dharma of good conduct;
Do not engage in bad conduct.
In this world and in the next,
The one who practices the Dharma rests in happiness.

At this the king was filled with wonder, his face brightened, and he said to the yakṣa, "Guhyaka, speak that verse so that I may hear it. Speak it!"

The yakṣa said to the king, "If you do just as I tell you, then I too will do whatever you command."

The king said, "What is it you command of me?"

The yakṣa said, "For seven days and nights, kindle a fire of khadira wood in a fire pit. If you then leap into it yourself, I will recite the verse for you."

When the king heard this, he was glad at heart and said to the yakṣa, "I shall do so."

Then the king, having bound the yakṣa by a pledge, had it proclaimed with bells throughout the whole country: "Seven days from today, in order to hear well-spoken words, the king is resolved to throw himself into a fire pit. Whoever among you wishes to see this marvel, come here!"

Then, wishing to understand the bodhisattva's pure superior intention and to behold the marvel, many hundreds of thousands of people gathered, and many hundreds of thousands of gods assembled and took their places in the sky. In their midst the yakṣa rose into the sky and said to the bodhisattva, "Great king, do just as you promised!"

Then the king consecrated his eldest son as king, asked forgiveness of the ministers, the townspeople and the people of the country for his faults, and, having comforted the multitude, went to the edge of the fire pit and spoke this verse:

For the sake of the Dharma I am resolved to leap into this pit of embers,
Blazing like a blood-red sun, utterly terrifying; I have no fear for my life.
By the power of my merit, may this fire pit truly become a most excellent pool,
Filled with cool water fragrant with sandalwood paste, and filled with lotuses.

Having spoken these words, the bodhisattva leapt into the fire pit, and the moment he leapt, that fire pit became a pool.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, seeing this marvelous miracle that inspires faith in gods and humans, made the form of the yakṣa vanish, appeared in his own form, and spoke the verse:

Practice the Dharma of good conduct;
Do not engage in bad conduct.
In this world and in the next,
The one who practices the Dharma rests in happiness.

Then the bodhisattva committed the verse to memory, had it written on golden tablets, and had it carried around all the villages, towns, provinces and royal capitals throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa.

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? I was the one who was the king at that time, on that occasion. If even then I gave up my own life in order to hear well-spoken words, what need is there to speak of now? Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We will honor the Dharma, revere it, respect it and venerate it; and having honored, revered, respected and venerated the Dharma, we will abide in reliance upon it.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, respected and venerated by kings, chief ministers, the wealthy, citizens, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit and a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with his community of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. After some time, proceeding gradually, he came onto the highway, and a brahmin also came onto that highway. The brahmin saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. When he had seen him, he looked him over for a very long time, then drew a line on the ground and said to the Blessed One, "O Gautama, until you give me five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, you shall not cross this line."

Then the Blessed One, in order to show that karma is never wasted and to turn beings away from taking what is not given, remained standing there like a door-post set firmly in the ground.

Then word spread throughout the whole of Śrāvastī: "On the highway a brahmin will not let the Blessed One go, for the sake of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas."

The moment Prasenajit, king of Kosala, heard of it, he went, attended by his host of ministers, to where the Blessed One was, and when he arrived he said to the Blessed One, "I will pay it. Please go on, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said, "Great king, these are not for you to give; they must be given by someone else."

In the same way Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, Ṛṣidatta, the chief of the queen's retinue, and Purāṇa, as well as the gods, Śakra, Brahmā and the rest, and Vaiśravaṇa and others, brought gold and silver and went before the Blessed One; and to them too the Blessed One said, "These are not for you to give either."

Then, after a while, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard of it. He placed five hundred kārṣāpaṇas on top of a golden basin filled with gold and silver, went before the Blessed One, and said, "Blessed One, please accept this."

The Blessed One said, "Householder, these are for you to give. Give them to the brahmin."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave the brahmin the full golden basin.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, consider how this brahmin would not even let the Blessed One go, and Anāthapiṇḍada had to pay the kārṣāpaṇas. Blessed One, since when has this debt been owed to him?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, do you wish to hear?"

"Venerable One, we wish to hear."

"Monks, then listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall tell you.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta ruled the kingdom. In his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful and abundant in harvests, and filled with many people and folk. Quarrels and fighting had been quelled, and there was no tumult, no internal strife, no robbers, no famine and no disease. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Without harm, with its thorns cleared away, he protected the kingdom as one would care for an only son.

"Later, at a time when his son was acting as viceroy, in springtime, in a forest where the trees were in full bloom and geese, ruddy geese, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos and pheasants were singing, the prince, attended by the sons of ministers, played, delighted and made merry. He had a friend, the son of a minister, who played at dice with another man, a gambler, and that man beat the minister's son by five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. The king's son had stood surety for him, but being powerful, and thinking, 'I am the king's son,' he did not pay.

"Monks, what do you think? I was the one who was the king's son at that time, on that occasion. The minister's son was the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The gambler was none other than this brahmin. Because I stood surety and then, thinking, 'I am the king's son,' did not give the kārṣāpaṇas to that gambler, I experienced endless poverty of wealth in saṃsāra, and even now, when I have fully and perfectly awakened to enlightenment, this man has pressed me for the debt.

"So, monks, deeds that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; deeds that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed deeds have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed ones, and devote yourselves solely to deeds that are wholly white. Strive also to abandon taking what is not given. Monks, you should train in such a way that you never fall into a fault such as this."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, tenth section.

Subhadra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, respected and venerated by kings, chief ministers, the wealthy, citizens, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit and a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with his community of śrāvakas near the city of Kuśinagara, at Upavartana of the Mallas, in the grove of the twin sāla trees.

Then, at the very time when the Blessed One was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, tonight at midnight the Tathāgata will pass into parinirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. Prepare the Tathāgata's couch between the twin sāla trees, with its head toward the north."

"Venerable One, I will do so," said Ānanda. Having heard what the Blessed One had told him, he prepared the couch between the twin sāla trees with its head toward the north, and then went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, the Tathāgata's couch has been prepared between the twin sāla trees, with its head toward the north."

Then the Blessed One went to where the couch was, and when he arrived he lay down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, with the perception of light, mindful and vigilant, and fixed his mind solely on the perception of nirvāṇa.

At that time there was in the city of Kuśinagara a wandering ascetic named Subhadra. He was old, aged and advanced in years, a hundred and twenty years since his birth, and the Mallas living in the city of Kuśinagara honored, revered, respected and venerated him, and held him to be an arhat.

Then the wandering ascetic Subhadra heard, "Tonight at midnight the ascetic Gautama will pass into parinirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates," and he thought, "I have uncertainties and doubts about certain matters, and I have hope that this Gautama can dispel my uncertainty." As soon as he heard it, he went to Kuśinagara, to where the twin sāla trees were.

At that time the wandering ascetic Subhadra saw the venerable Ānanda walking up and down on the walking path in the open ground outside the dwelling. Seeing the venerable Ānanda from afar, he went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and when he arrived, he exchanged with the venerable Ānanda, face to face, many kinds of pleasant and cordial talk, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wandering ascetic Subhadra said to the venerable Ānanda:

"O Ānanda, I have heard that tonight at midnight the ascetic Gautama will pass into parinirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. I have uncertainties and doubts about certain matters, and I have hope that this Gautama can dispel my uncertainty. So, Ānanda, if it is no trouble to you, and if he would grant me the opportunity to answer my questions, I would come in and ask about a few points."

Ānanda said, "Subhadra, the Blessed One is weary; the Sugata is exhausted. Subhadra, let it be. Do not trouble the Blessed One."

A second and a third time the wandering ascetic Subhadra said to the venerable Ānanda, "O Ānanda, I have heard that tonight at midnight the ascetic Gautama will pass into parinirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. I have uncertainties and doubts about certain matters, and I have hope that this Gautama can dispel my uncertainty. So, Ānanda, if it is no trouble to you, and if he would grant me the opportunity to answer my questions, I would come in and ask about a few points."

A second and a third time the venerable Ānanda said to the wandering ascetic Subhadra, "Subhadra, the Blessed One is weary; the Sugata is exhausted. Subhadra, let it be. Do not trouble the Blessed One."

Even so, the wandering ascetic Subhadra spoke once more to the venerable Ānanda: "O Ānanda, I have heard from the great teachers of old, the aged and venerable wandering ascetics of the various schools, that tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas appear in the world only very rarely, now and then, like the udumbara flower; so it is said. And now this Gautama will pass into parinirvāṇa tonight at midnight in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. I have uncertainties and doubts about certain matters, and I have hope that this Gautama can dispel my uncertainty. So, Ānanda, if it is no trouble to you, and if he would grant me the opportunity to answer my questions, I would come in and ask about a few points."

Then once again the venerable Ānanda said to the wandering ascetic Subhadra, "Subhadra, the Blessed One is weary; the Sugata is exhausted. Subhadra, let it be. Do not trouble the Blessed One."

The Blessed One, with his divine hearing, purified and surpassing that of humans, heard the conversation that the venerable Ānanda was having with the wandering ascetic Subhadra. Having heard it, he said to the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, do not speak so. Do not hold back the wandering ascetic Subhadra; let him come in and allow him to ask whatever he wishes. This will be my last conversation with wandering ascetics of other, non-Buddhist (tīrthika) schools. This wandering ascetic Subhadra will also be the last of the śrāvakas in my own presence to whom it is said, 'Come, monk, practice the holy life.'"

Then the wandering ascetic Subhadra, given leave by the Blessed One, was glad, pleased, delighted and overjoyed, and with joy and happiness arising in him he went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he exchanged with the Blessed One, face to face, many kinds of pleasant and cordial talk, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wandering ascetic Subhadra said to the Blessed One, "O Gautama, there are in the world various non-Buddhist schools, namely those of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the wandering ascetic Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambala, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Have these each realized what they profess?"

Then the Blessed One spoke these verses:

I was twenty-nine years of age
When I went forth to seek what is wholesome.
Subhadra, since I went forth,
Fifty-one years have passed.
Moral discipline, concentration, knowledge and conduct
I have cultivated with a one-pointed mind.
Outside of this, among other ascetics,
There is not even one who speaks a part of the Dharma of reason.

"Subhadra, in whatever Dharma and Vinaya the noble eightfold path is not found, there is no first ascetic, nor is there a second, third or fourth ascetic. Subhadra, in whatever Dharma and Vinaya the noble eightfold path is found, there is a first ascetic, and there are a second, third and fourth ascetic as well. Subhadra, since the noble eightfold path is found in this Dharma and Vinaya, the first ascetic is found here, the second is found here, the third is found here, and the fourth is found here. Outside of this there are no ascetics or brahmins; the opposing schools are empty of ascetics and brahmins. Thus do I rightly roar the lion's roar here in this assembly."

When this discourse on the Dharma had been spoken, the stainless, immaculate eye of Dharma regarding phenomena arose in the wandering ascetic Subhadra. The wandering ascetic Subhadra saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma and fathomed the depths of the Dharma; he crossed beyond uncertainty and crossed beyond doubt, and in the Teacher's teaching he no longer depended on others and was no longer led by others. Having gained fearlessness regarding the Dharma, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, and said to the venerable Ānanda, "Venerable Ānanda, that the Great Teacher has consecrated you with the consecration of the Great Teacher's personal attendant is a great gain well gained by the venerable Ānanda. For my part too, if I could go forth, receive full ordination and attain the state of a monk in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, it would be a great gain well gained."

Then the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, this wandering ascetic Subhadra wishes to go forth, receive full ordination and become a monk in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya."

Then the Blessed One said to the wandering ascetic Subhadra, "Come, monk, practice the holy life." By that very word the venerable one went forth; that was his full ordination, and that was his becoming a monk.

Having gone forth in this way, the venerable one dwelt alone in seclusion, heedful, ardent and resolute. He realized in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, the final goal of the unsurpassed holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beards, put on saffron robes, and with genuine faith go forth from home into homelessness. Having realized it, he accomplished and understood it, and fully knew, "My birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and I know no further existence beyond this." The venerable one became an arhat, his mind fully liberated.

Then the venerable Subhadra, having attained arhatship and experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, thought, "It is not my part to witness the Teacher's parinirvāṇa; surely I must pass into parinirvāṇa before him." So the venerable Subhadra passed into parinirvāṇa first, and after that the Blessed One passed into nirvāṇa.

When the Blessed One, lying on his final bed, experiencing feelings that struck at his vital points, as his vital points were giving way and his joints were parting, established Subhadra in arhatship and brought many of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara to the Dharma, the monks became doubtful, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, it is wonderful that even while the Blessed One's vital points were giving way and his joints were parting, he freed this wandering ascetic Subhadra from the grip of saṃsāra and established him in the accomplishment that is the final and ultimate security, the bliss of nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what is so very wonderful in this: that now, when I am free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion, and completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and agitation, I have freed the wandering ascetic Subhadra from the grip of saṃsāra and established him in the accomplishment that is the final and ultimate security, the bliss of nirvāṇa? In times past, when I still had attachment, aversion and delusion, and was not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and agitation, even when I was born in the womb of an animal that does not know what should and should not be done, I gave up my own life and brought the wandering ascetic Subhadra and the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara from fear to fearlessness. Listen well and closely to this, keep it in mind, and I shall tell you.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there lived in a mountain valley the leader of a herd of deer, with a following of many thousands of deer; he was wise, clear-minded and of upright mind. A hunter spied out the herd of deer and reported it to the king. Then the king set out with his fourfold army and surrounded that whole herd of deer.

"Then the leader of the herd thought, 'If I simply keep these deer together here, today they will be wiped out entirely.' So the leader of the herd looked all around, wondering, 'On which side might this herd of deer escape?' He saw a river flowing through that valley. The river was swift and strong and swept things away violently, and the deer were all weak.

"Then, without hesitating, the leader of the herd entered the river and stood in the middle of it, and called out, 'Come here! Leap from this bank, use my back as a stepping-place for your feet, and cross to the far bank. By this means I see that you will escape; if you do not do this, you will die.'

"The deer did just as he said. As they planted their hooves on his back, his hide was torn open, until all that remained of him was flesh, blood and bone. Yet, moved by compassion for those deer, he did not give up his effort. When all the deer had crossed, he thought, 'Surely none are left here who have not crossed?' Looking back, he saw a single fawn that had not yet crossed. Then the leader of the herd, though his vital points were giving way and his joints were parting, heedless of his precious life, came to the bank, took the fawn onto his back, carried it across the river and set it down on the bank. Seeing that the whole herd of deer had crossed, at the point of death he made this aspiration: 'Just as I have saved the precious lives of these deer and of this fawn, and protected them from loss, so in the future, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect and complete enlightenment, may I also free them from the grip of saṃsāra.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? I was the one who was the leader of the herd of deer at that time, on that occasion. The deer were these Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara. The fawn was none other than this Subhadra."

Then the monks became doubtful, and asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Subhadra do, that he became the last of the śrāvakas in your presence?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Subhadra himself, in other former lives, did and accumulated deeds that have reached their accumulation, whose conditions have matured, that come on like a flood, and that are certain to come. Who else would experience the deeds that Subhadra did and accumulated? Monks, deeds done and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Wholesome and unwholesome deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense bases.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruits.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide of beings to be tamed, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One named Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"Now a nephew of the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, named Aśoka, wishing for liberation, went forth under the Blessed One; but he regarded liberation as something merely within his own power, and made no effort. After a long time had passed, Aśoka undertook to spend the rains retreat in the countryside.

"The Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, having carried out all the activities of a buddha, was lying on his final bed, like a fire whose wood is exhausted. The monk Aśoka, meanwhile, had entered into inner meditative seclusion at the foot of an aśoka tree. The god who dwelt in that aśoka tree heard that the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, and sat weeping, and the tears he shed as he wept fell onto Aśoka's body.

"Then Aśoka looked up and said to the weeping god, 'Divine one, why are you weeping?'

"The god said, 'Tonight at midnight the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, will pass into parinirvāṇa.'

"When Aśoka heard the god's words, he was stunned, as if struck in a vital point, and he too wept in a pitiful voice."

"Then the god asked him, 'Why are you weeping?'

"Aśoka said, 'Because I am being parted from a kinsman and parted from a preceptor. The perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa is my maternal uncle, and so I simply lived at my ease and did not exert myself with diligence. Now he is a long way off, and I am left an ordinary person. Because the way is so long, I am unable to attain any distinction.'

"The god said, 'If I were to bring you into the presence of the Blessed One, would you be able to attain some distinction?'

"Aśoka said, 'I feel in my mind that the very moment I see the Blessed One, I will attain distinction.'

"Then, by the power of his miraculous abilities, the god carried Aśoka into the presence of the Blessed One. When Aśoka saw the Blessed One, joy arose in him. When joy had arisen in him, the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught him the Dharma in such a way that, on hearing it, he would directly realize arhatship, and he did directly realize arhatship. First the venerable Aśoka passed into parinirvāṇa, and after that the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, passed into parinirvāṇa.

"Then the god, seeing that the venerable Aśoka had passed into parinirvāṇa, felt joy and made this resolve: 'Whatever distinction this venerable one has attained, all of it came about through me. In the same way, in time to come, the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, will prophesy to the brahmin youth Uttara, "Brahmin youth, when the lifespan of beings is a hundred years, you will become the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha called Śākyamuni." When that Buddha lies down on his final bed, may I too become his last disciple in his own presence, and pass into parinirvāṇa before the Blessed One, and may the Blessed One Śākyamuni pass into parinirvāṇa after that.'

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the god at that time, on that occasion, is this Subhadra. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall keep to spiritual friends, good companions and good support, and we shall not keep to evil friends, evil companions and evil support.' Monks, that is how you should train."

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, while I was here alone in seclusion, absorbed in inner meditative concentration, this reflection arose in my mind: 'Spiritual friends, good companions and good support are half of the holy life; evil friends, evil companions and evil support are not so.'"

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, do not say, 'Spiritual friends, good companions and good support are half of the holy life; evil friends, evil companions and evil support are not so.' Why is that? Ānanda, spiritual friends, good companions and good support are the whole of the holy life, unmixed, completely perfect, completely pure and completely cleansed; evil friends, evil companions and evil support are not so. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, by relying on a spiritual friend, beings subject to birth are completely freed from being subject to birth, and beings subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress are completely freed from being subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress. Therefore, Ānanda, by this very line of reasoning you should understand it in this way: 'Spiritual friends, good companions and good support are the whole of the holy life, unmixed, completely perfect, completely pure and completely cleansed; evil friends, evil companions and evil support are not so.' Ānanda, that is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From the Hundred Avadānas, the fourth group of ten under a summary verse, the Birth Stories of the Bodhisattva, is complete.

The summary verse:

The sugar mill, the food,
The water, and the pots of excrement,
Maudgalyāyana, the lower stream,
The one born blind, the merchant,
The sons, and the cesspit:
These are taught in this group.

The story called "The Sugar Mill."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, members of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with his saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

When the Blessed One had become fully and perfectly awakened into unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, the two, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, made this vow: "Until we have freed at least one single being from among the hell beings, animals and hungry ghosts, we will not eat food."

Then, from time to time, those two venerable ones would sometimes go wandering among the beings of the hells.

At other times they would go wandering among the animals, and at other times they would go wandering among the hungry ghosts. There they heard the wretched cries of beings tormented by all kinds of harm, and when they returned from their wanderings they would tell the fourfold assembly about it. Those who heard it were stricken with weariness of saṃsāra. Then the two of them, having described this, would teach the Dharma in accordance with it, and so many beings, on hearing it, attained distinction, and it became an occasion for hearing the Dharma and for discussion.

Some time later, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while wandering among the hungry ghosts, saw a hungry ghost whose belly was the size of a mountain and whose mouth was the size of the eye of a needle, covered by its own hair, blazing, flaring and blazing all around, burning as a single mass of flame, uttering cries of distress, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering, and wandering around wherever there was excrement and urine, yet unable to find even that with ease.

Then the elder asked that hungry ghost, "Hey, what deed did you do, that you are now experiencing such intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering?"

The hungry ghost said, "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp. Ask the Blessed One about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had arisen from inner meditative concentration and was teaching the fourfold assembly the Dharma, rich in flavor like unboiled honey, and an assembly of many hundreds, their senses unmoving, was listening to the Blessed One's Dharma, rich in its flavor.

Now, the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak openly and speak sweetly, saying, "Come, welcome!" and smiling first. So the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, come here. Welcome to you. Where have you come from just now?"

Maudgalyāyana replied, "Venerable One, I have come back from going wandering among the hungry ghosts. There I saw a hungry ghost whose belly was the size of a mountain and whose mouth was the size of the eye of a needle, covered by its own hair, who seeks as food excrement that stinks, utterly stinks, that is foul, utterly foul, and yet cannot find even that with ease."

And he said further:

"Its great body is like a lofty mountain;
Its lips and throat are parched, and it is wretched in the extreme.
Its face covered by its own hair, it goes about naked;
The opening of its lips is as narrow as a needle's eye, and it is utterly emaciated.
Thus naked and covered by its hair,
Like a skeleton standing upright,
Carrying a skull, unbearable to behold,
It weeps and runs about everywhere.
Exhausted by hunger and by thirst,
Tormented by sufferings,
It utters cries of distress
And experiences feelings of suffering.
What dreadful evil did it commit
In the world of humans,
That because of it it has come to experience
Suffering as terrible as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, that hungry ghost was a doer of evil deeds. Do you wish to hear the nature of its deeds?"

"Venerable One, I wish to hear it."

"In that case, Maudgalyāyana, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Maudgalyāyana, long ago, in times past, in the city of Rājagṛha there lived a guild leader who was rich, had much wealth and great possessions, with broad and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He had five hundred places for pressing sugarcane, and in them his sugarcane was pressed.

"At times when buddhas do not appear in the world, pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, compassionate toward the wretched and destitute, living in remote dwellings, the sole worthy recipients of offerings in the world. At one time a pratyekabuddha had appeared, compassionate toward the wretched and destitute and living in a remote dwelling. In the morning he put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Rājagṛha for alms.

"That venerable one had been struck by a wasting illness, and a physician had advised him that sugarcane juice would help it, so he went to that great guild leader. The guild leader saw the pratyekabuddha, beautiful in body and beautiful in mind as well, and on seeing him the guild leader said, 'Noble one, what do you wish?'

"The pratyekabuddha said, 'Householder, I would like some sugarcane juice.'

"Then the householder instructed a workman, 'Offer the noble one some sugarcane juice,' and the householder himself set out on some business.

"Then that man grew miserly over another's property, thinking, 'If I give him sugarcane juice now, he will keep coming back here later.' Inclined toward the precipice of the three unpleasant destinies, having cast away the two destinies that all desire, having put the noble paths far from himself, he gave rise to an evil thought and said to the pratyekabuddha, 'Monk, hand me your bowl and I will give you sugarcane juice.'

"Arhats among the śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, do not engage their vision of knowledge unless they turn their attention to something. Out of compassion for the wretched and destitute, he thought, 'I shall benefit this man,' and gave him the bowl. Then that man of wicked conduct, with no compassion in his heart, took it, went to a hidden place, and filled it with urine, covered the top with the froth of sugarcane juice, and offered it to the pratyekabuddha. The pratyekabuddha perceived what it was and thought, 'This wretched man has committed a great evil, and there is no help for it.' He went off to one side, poured it out, and went away."

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, what do you think? The one who was the workman at that time, on that occasion, is this hungry ghost. Through the karmic maturation of that deed he experienced endless suffering in saṃsāra, and now too he has become a hungry ghost and is experiencing unbearable suffering. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, so that faults such as that hungry ghost's may not arise, you should strive to abandon miserliness."

"Thus, Maudgalyāyana, entirely black deeds have an entirely black maturation; entirely white deeds have an entirely white maturation; and mixed deeds have a mixed maturation as well. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed ones, and devote yourself solely to entirely white deeds. Maudgalyāyana, that is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called "Food."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, members of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas.
