The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with his saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was sitting at the foot of a tree for his daytime rest, and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard the voice of a female hungry ghost, crying out in distress and experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering. Begging for food, she was saying, "Friends, I am hungry! Friends, I am thirsty!"

Then the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw that female hungry ghost and asked her, "What deed did you do, that you are now experiencing sufferings such as these?"

The female hungry ghost said, "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp. Ask the Blessed One about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had arisen from inner meditative concentration and was teaching the fourfold assembly the Dharma, rich in flavor like unboiled honey, and an assembly of many hundreds, their senses unmoving, was listening to the Blessed One's Dharma, rich in its flavor.

Now, the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak openly and speak sweetly, saying, "Come, welcome!" and smiling first. So the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, come here. Welcome to you. Where have you come from just now?"

Maudgalyāyana replied, "Venerable One, I have come back from going wandering among the hungry ghosts. There I saw a female hungry ghost whose belly was the size of a mountain and whose mouth was the size of the eye of a needle, covered by her own hair, going naked and crying out in distress, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering."

And he said further:

"Her great body is like a lofty mountain;
Her lips and throat are parched, and she is wretched in the extreme.
Her face covered by her own hair, she goes about naked;
The opening of her lips is as narrow as a needle's eye, and she is utterly emaciated.
Thus naked and covered by her hair,
Like a skeleton standing upright,
Carrying a skull, unbearable to behold,
She weeps and runs about everywhere.
Exhausted by hunger and by thirst,
Tormented by sufferings,
She utters cries of distress
And experiences feelings of suffering.
What dreadful evil did she commit
In the world of humans,
That because of it she has come to experience
Suffering as terrible as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, that female hungry ghost was a doer of evil deeds. Do you wish to hear the nature of her deeds?"

"Venerable One, I wish to hear it."

"In that case, Maudgalyāyana, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Maudgalyāyana, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"Now in that city of Vārāṇasī there was the wife of a certain householder who was miserly and stingy, clinging to all her possessions. She would not give even a bali offering to the crows, so what need is there to speak of other beggars? Whenever she saw ascetics, brahmins, the wretched and destitute, or the hungry, she felt hatred in her mind.

"One day a monk on his alms round came to her house. When she saw him, miserliness arose in her and her mind turned to hatred, and she thought, 'If I show him respect, he will keep coming back here later.' Then that wicked woman, disregarding the unpleasant consequences in her next life, called the monk inside, shut the door, and made him go without food. She reviled him at length as well, saying, 'Monk, this is the disrespect done to you. From now on, do not come to this house!'

"Then, because she had indulged in miserliness, cultivated it and made much of it, she was reborn as a hungry ghost, and experiences sufferings such as these.

"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, so that faults such as that female hungry ghost's may not come about, you should strive to abandon miserliness."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, along with gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called "Water."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, members of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with his saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while wandering among the hungry ghosts, saw a female hungry ghost like a tree stump scorched by fire, covered by her own hair, her belly the size of a mountain and her mouth the size of the eye of a needle, blazing, flaring and blazing all around, burning as a single mass of flame, crying out in distress, tormented by thirst, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering. At her mere glance, rivers and wells would dry up, and whenever rain fell, a rain of embers shooting out sparks fell upon her.

On seeing her, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to her, "Hey, what evil did you do, that you are now experiencing suffering such as this?"

The female hungry ghost said, "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I was a doer of evil. Ask the Buddha, the Blessed One, about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds. When they hear it, other beings too will give up evil deeds."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had arisen from inner meditative concentration and was teaching the fourfold assembly the Dharma, rich in flavor like unboiled honey, and an assembly of many hundreds, their senses unmoving, was listening to the Blessed One's Dharma, rich in its flavor.

Now, the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak openly and speak sweetly, saying, "Come, welcome!" and smiling first. So the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, come here. Welcome to you. Where have you come from just now?"

Maudgalyāyana replied, "Venerable One, I have come back from going wandering among the hungry ghosts. There I saw a female hungry ghost like a tree trunk scorched by fire, covered by her own hair, her belly the size of a mountain and her mouth the size of the eye of a needle, blazing, flaring and blazing all around, burning as a single mass of flame, crying out in distress, tormented by thirst, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering. At her mere glance, rivers and wells dry up, and whenever rain falls, a rain of embers shooting out sparks falls upon her."

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, that female hungry ghost was a doer of evil. Do you wish to hear the nature of her deeds?"

"Venerable One, I wish to hear it."

"In that case, Maudgalyāyana, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Maudgalyāyana, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa.

"While he was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park, a monk there set out on the road and became tormented by thirst. He went to a well, where a young woman was sitting with a pitcher filled with water, and the monk said to her, 'Sister, I am tormented by thirst. Please give me some water.'

"But she clung to her possessions, and miserliness arose in her, and she said to the monk, 'Monk, my pitcher would be diminished. Even if you die, I will not give you water.'

"Then the monk, still tormented by thirst, went away in despair.

"Then, because that young woman had indulged in miserliness, cultivated it and made much of it, she died and was reborn as a hungry ghost, and she is experiencing such intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering.

"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should train in this way: 'We shall strive in order to abandon miserliness.' Maudgalyāyana, that is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the eleventh section.

The story called "The Pot of Excrement."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy householders, members of the royal court, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. The Buddha, the Blessed One, worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with his saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

Then, in the morning, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Rājagṛha for alms. Having gone on his alms round in Rājagṛha and eaten his meal, he gave up taking any further food, put away his bowl and robe, and went to Vulture Peak. When he arrived, he climbed Vulture Peak and sat at the foot of a tree for his daytime rest.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw a female hungry ghost like a tree stump scorched by fire, naked and covered by her own hair, her belly the size of a mountain and her mouth the size of the eye of a needle, blazing, flaring and blazing all around, burning as a single mass of flame, crying out in distress, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering. She ate as her food excrement, stinking and utterly stinking like excrement, and yet could not find even that with ease.

When he saw her, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was saddened, and he asked the female hungry ghost, "What evil did you do in the past, that you are now experiencing such a result?"

The female hungry ghost said, "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I was a doer of evil. Ask the Buddha, the Blessed One, about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds. When they hear it, other beings too will give up evil deeds."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had arisen from inner meditative concentration and was teaching the fourfold assembly the Dharma, rich in flavor like unboiled honey, and an assembly of many hundreds, their senses unmoving, was listening to the Blessed One's Dharma, rich in its flavor.

Now, the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak openly and speak sweetly, saying, "Come, welcome!" and smiling first. So the Blessed One said this to the venerable Maudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, come here. Welcome to you. Where have you come from just now?"

Maudgalyāyana replied, "Venerable One, while I was going wandering among the hungry ghosts, I saw there a female hungry ghost like a tree stump scorched by fire, naked and covered by her own hair, her belly the size of a mountain and her mouth the size of the eye of a needle, blazing, flaring and blazing intensely, burning as a single mass of flame, crying out in distress, experiencing intense, unbearable, burning and disagreeable feelings of suffering. At her mere glance, rivers and wells dry up, and whenever rain falls, a rain of embers shooting out sparks falls upon her. She seeks as her food excrement, stinking and utterly stinking like excrement, and yet cannot find even that with ease."

And he said further:

"She utters cries of distress
And experiences feelings of suffering.
Wherever there is a place of excrement,
There she runs, wretched as she is.
When she longs to eat or drink excrement,
Even that she cannot easily find.
What dreadful evil did she commit
In the world of humans,
That because of it she experiences
Suffering as terrible as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, that female hungry ghost was a doer of evil. Do you wish to hear the nature of her deeds?"

"Venerable One, I wish to hear it."

"In that case, Maudgalyāyana, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Maudgalyāyana, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a pratyekabuddha, compassionate toward the wretched and destitute and living in a remote dwelling. He was unwell, and he went into Vārāṇasī for alms. On one occasion a physician had prescribed suitable food for him, and he went to where a certain guild leader lived. The guild leader saw him and asked, 'Noble one, what do you wish?'

"He said, 'I would like some suitable food.'

"Then the guild leader instructed his daughter-in-law, 'Offer the noble one some suitable food.'

"Then miserliness arose in his daughter-in-law, and she thought, 'If I give him food today, he will come back tomorrow as well.' She went off to one side, filled the bowl with excrement, covered the top with rice, and offered it to the pratyekabuddha.

"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not engage their vision of knowledge unless they turn their attention to something, so he accepted it. Having accepted it, he perceived what it was and thought, 'Since this stinks, she must certainly have filled it with excrement.' Then that great being threw it away somewhere and left."

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, what do you think? The one who was the guild leader's daughter-in-law at that time, on that occasion, is this female hungry ghost. Having committed such an evil deed, from then on she has always been born among the hell beings, animals and hungry ghosts, and has always eaten excrement as her food.

"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, strive to abandon miserliness, so that faults such as that female hungry ghost's may not come about. Maudgalyāyana, that is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, and the others as well, the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and so forth, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Maudgalyāyana.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townspeople, by guild leaders, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kinnaras and by mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time, beyond Rājagṛha and on this side of the Bamboo Grove, in the space between them, there were hungry ghosts like charred tree stumps, naked and covered only by their own hair, with bellies the size of mountains and mouths the size of a needle's eye. They were burning, blazing, blazing all over, ablaze as a single mass of flame, and as they burned they cried out in misery. Experiencing feelings that were fierce, harsh, burning and disagreeable, five hundred of them wheeled about in the sky like a hovering flock of crows, finding nowhere at all to rest.

Then in the morning the venerable Maudgalyāyana put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Rājagṛha for alms, and he saw those hungry ghosts. The hungry ghosts too saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Then, crowding together, they went up to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and crying out, "Pity, pity!" and "Misery, misery!" and wailing, they spoke with one voice:

"Venerable Maudgalyāyana, we were five hundred guild leaders in Rājagṛha. We were miserly and stingy, clinging to our possessions. Not only did we give no gifts ourselves, we also obstructed others who were giving. We often reviled those worthy of gifts with words such as 'hungry ghost,' saying, 'You prowl around other people's houses like those born as hungry ghosts.' Because of that, after we died we were born as hungry ghosts such as these. Therefore, great venerable Maudgalyāyana, please make known to our relatives who live in Rājagṛha the nature of our deeds, and rouse their faith, and have them invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal and have the dedication of the offering recited for our sake. Then perhaps we may be freed from birth as hungry ghosts. Please tell them this."

The venerable Maudgalyāyana consented to the hungry ghosts by remaining silent. Then the venerable Maudgalyāyana went from house to house among their relatives, rousing their faith, and they invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal on the following day. He also informed the hungry ghosts, saying, "The Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks has been invited to a meal, so you too must come there." And to their relatives he said, "You too must come, and at the feast you are holding for your kin you will see those hungry ghosts." Then the venerable Maudgalyāyana himself took charge of overseeing the feast.

When dawn came the food was set out, but when midday arrived those hungry ghosts did not appear. Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana searched for those hungry ghosts with his divine eye, but they were not to be seen anywhere in the whole land of Magadha. He looked further and further, as far as the four continents, but they were not to be seen there either. Then he looked as far as the vision of his wisdom could reach, yet they were not to be seen there either.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana grew dismayed and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, those patrons of mine are nowhere to be found."

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, let it be; do not be dismayed. There are countless world systems that lie beyond the range of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they have been hurled into these by the wind of karma. Nevertheless, Maudgalyāyana, today behold the power of the Tathāgata. I shall make manifest the vision of omniscient wisdom, and I shall also display the miraculous transformation of the Tathāgata. Strike the gong."

When the gong was struck, the whole Saṅgha of monks assembled, and the relatives of the hungry ghosts and other beings who wished to see the hungry ghosts also came to watch the spectacle and gathered there. Then the Blessed One displayed a miracle of such a kind that the hungry ghosts would see the Buddha, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas being served the meal, and would come to recall, "Our relatives are serving a meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for our sake, and they are seated here."

Then, with his voice endowed with five qualities, the Blessed One spoke the dedication of the offering:

"Whatever merit there is from this gift,
May it go after the hungry ghosts;
From the terrifying world of hungry ghosts
May they swiftly be set free!"

So he spoke. Then, on that basis, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in keeping with it, and when they had heard it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings abandoned the stain of miserliness and came to see the truths. Those hungry ghosts too became gladdened in mind toward the Blessed One, and when they died they were born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

It is the nature of things that not long after a god's son or a god's daughter is born, three thoughts arise in their mind: "From where have I died and passed on? Where have I been born? By what karma have I been born?"

They saw that they had died and passed on from among the hungry ghosts, that they had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because their minds had become gladdened toward the Blessed One. Then those sons of the gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts thought, "It is not fitting for us to wait until the night has passed and only then go to see the Blessed One. We shall go to see the Blessed One before the night has passed."

Then those sons of the gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts, wearing earrings and bracelets that jingled and swayed, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing diadems studded with all kinds of jewels, their bodies anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, that very night filled their laps with divine flowers, utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndāravas. They lit up the whole of the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground with a great radiance, strewed the flowers over the Blessed One, and sat down before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the inclinations, latent tendencies, constituents and natures of those sons of the gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts, taught them the Dharma in keeping with these. When they had heard it, those sons of the gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts attained a great distinction. Like merchants who have made a profit, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished on the spot.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Maudgalyāyana, you established many hungry ghosts among the gods, and last night they came to me. I taught them the Dharma, and they gained what was to be gained, gained the vision of the truth, and departed. The oversight you undertook has borne fruit. Excellent, excellent!"

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana made this known to their relatives as well. When they heard it they were utterly amazed, their minds became gladdened toward the Blessed One, and they paid him honor.

"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should strive to abandon miserliness, so that faults such as those of these hungry ghosts may not come about."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the others as well, the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and so forth, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Uttara.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townspeople, by guild leaders, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kinnaras and by mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time there lived in the city of Rājagṛha a guild leader who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in wealth. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played with her, enjoyed himself and made love. From his playing, enjoying himself and making love, his wife conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a boy. When the boy was born they held a birth celebration for him, and when it came to naming him they asked, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "Since this boy was born under the lunar mansion Uttarāṣāḍhā, let his name be Uttara." And so they named him Uttara.

Then the boy Uttara was raised and nourished until he grew up, and when his father died he became the master of his own household. He set up a shop in the market and traded, making his living by buying and selling, and every day he would go to the Blessed One. By seeing the Blessed One and hearing the true Dharma, he gained faith in the Blessed One's teaching, and the wish to go forth arose in him. He made this request to his mother: "Mother, I wish to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Please give me your permission."

His mother replied, "Son, you are my only son. Do not go forth as long as I live. After I die, do whatever you wish."

So Uttara gave everything he earned to his mother, saying, "Mother, give gifts with this to śramaṇas and brahmins, and to the wretched, the needy and the destitute."

But his mother was greedy and stingy, clinging to her possessions. She hid those kārṣāpaṇa coins, and whenever monks or brahmins came to the house wanting food, she abused them, saying, "You go prowling around houses begging, like those born as hungry ghosts." She also deceived her son, saying, "Every day I give food to such and such a number of monks."

Some time later she died and was born as a hungry ghost, and her son Uttara mourned at being parted from his mother.

He gave gifts and made merit, and then went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through striving, effort and exertion he understood that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable. He fully ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction, and having abandoned all afflictions he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; he had a mind like space and like the palm of his hand; he had become cool like sandalwood paste; he had broken the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge and attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he paid no heed to worldly gain, desire or honor; and he became worthy of the worship, veneration and respectful address of the gods together with Indra and Upendra. He made a hut of leaves on the bank of the river Ganges and meditated there.

His mother, who had been born in the world of hungry ghosts, was like a charred tree stump, naked and covered only by her own hair, with a belly the size of a mountain and a mouth the size of a needle's eye. Burning, blazing, blazing all over, ablaze as a single mass of flame, she cried out in misery, and she went to the venerable Uttara. Then Uttara saw the female hungry ghost and asked her, "Who are you, looking like this?"

The female hungry ghost said:

"I am the loving mother
From whom you, my only son, were born.
I have been born among the hungry ghosts,
Deprived of food and drink.
Since the time of my death
Twenty-five years have passed;
I have not seen even a trace of water,
So how could I ever see food?
When I go to the foot of trees bearing fruit,
They become fruitless;
Even when I go to the shores of brimming lakes,
They too dry up.
Reverend one, the shade at the foot of your tree is pleasant,
And the water in your vessel is cool.
Take pity on me, destitute as I am;
I am tormented by thirst: give me water!"

Then Uttara said to his mother, "Mother, when you were human, did I not have you give gifts and make merit?"

The female hungry ghost said, "My only son, overcome by miserliness I gave no gifts and made no merit. With an evil mind I hid all the wealth I received in a pit. Therefore, my only son, rouse the faith of others, and for my sake invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal and request that the dedication of the offering be recited. Then perhaps I may be freed from birth as a hungry ghost."

Uttara said, "I will do so. And you too must sit in front of the elder at the head of the row."

The female hungry ghost said, "My only son, I am naked, and I am ashamed; I could not bear it."

Uttara said, "Mother, at the time you were doing evil you were not ashamed. Why are you ashamed now, when you are experiencing its result?"

The female hungry ghost said, "Then I shall come, just as you say."

Then Uttara went from house to house among his relatives rousing their faith, and they invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal on the following day. When midday came, the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha assembled, and the female hungry ghost sat in front of the elder at the head of the row. The many hundreds of thousands of living beings who had gathered saw the female hungry ghost. When they saw the repulsive body of the female hungry ghost, a deep weariness with saṃsāra arose in them, and their minds became gladdened toward the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Uttara, having satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with fine food, requested that the dedication of the offering be recited for the female hungry ghost. Then the Blessed One himself, with his voice endowed with five qualities, spoke the dedication of the gift:

"Whatever merit there is from this gift,
May it go after the hungry ghost;
From the terrifying world of hungry ghosts
May she swiftly be set free!"

So he spoke. Then, on that basis, the Blessed One taught the female hungry ghost and many people the Dharma in keeping with it, and when they had heard it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings came to see the truths. The female hungry ghost too became gladdened in mind, and when she died she was born as a hungry ghost of great magical power. The venerable Uttara knew that she had been born as a hungry ghost of great magical power.

Then the venerable Uttara said, "Mother, now that you have power, give gifts generously."

The hungry ghost of great magical power said, "My only son, I take no delight in giving; I cannot do it."

Then the venerable Uttara said to the hungry ghost of great magical power:

"Your eyes were thoroughly veiled by the darkness of craving,
And so you brought about the world of hungry ghosts.
Your great bones without flesh,
Your bones, your skin and your hide, remain even now."

Then, after the venerable Uttara had spoken to her many times, reproaching her, he afterward obtained a pair of cloths from her. Uttara offered them to the Saṅgha, and the monk who acquired the pair of cloths from the Saṅgha placed it on his clothes rack. Then the female hungry ghost came at night and stole it. The monk reported this to the venerable Uttara, and Uttara went, reproached the female hungry ghost, took it back, and gave it to him. In the same way, three times she stole it from the monk, and three times the venerable Uttara took it back and gave it to him. Then the monk cut it up and patched it onto a seat for the Saṅgha of monks of the four directions, and after that she stole it no more.

Therefore, seeing how miserliness thus brings beings to grief, one should strive to abandon miserliness, so that faults such as those of that female hungry ghost may not come about.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks, and the others as well, the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and so forth, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Blind Woman.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townspeople, by guild leaders, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kinnaras and by mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then in the morning the venerable Nandana put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. When he had gone on his alms round in Śrāvastī and eaten his meal, he refrained from taking any food afterward, put away his alms bowl and robe, and went wandering through the realm of the hungry ghosts. There the venerable Nandana saw a female hungry ghost like a charred tree stump, blind, covered by her own hair, with a belly the size of a mountain and a mouth the size of a needle's eye. Foul smelling like a charnel ground, she was surrounded by crows, vultures, dogs and jackals, which tore and tore at her flesh from every side and devoured it. Struck in her vital points, in extreme agony, she cried out in misery, and she remained there experiencing suffering that was fierce, harsh, burning and disagreeable.

Then the venerable Nandana, dismayed, asked her, "Sister, what evil deed did you do in the past, that you are experiencing suffering such as this?"

The female hungry ghost said, "When the sun has risen there is no need for a lamp. Ask the Blessed One about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds. When they hear it, other beings too will abandon evil."

Then the venerable Nandana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had risen from his meditative absorption and was teaching the four assemblies a Dharma full of flavor, like pure honey from the bees, and an assembly of many hundreds, their senses unmoving, was listening to the Dharma full of flavor from the Blessed One.

Now the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak clearly, speak pleasantly, say "Come, welcome!", and smile before they speak. So the Blessed One said this to the venerable Nandana: "Nandana, come; welcome to you. Where have you come from just now?"

Nandana said, "Reverend, I have come from where the hungry ghosts wander. There I saw a female hungry ghost like a charred tree stump, blind, covered by her own hair, with a belly the size of a mountain and a mouth the size of a needle's eye. Foul smelling like a charnel ground, she was surrounded by crows, vultures, dogs and jackals, which tore and tore at her flesh from every side and devoured it. Struck in her vital points, in extreme agony, she cried out in misery, and she remained there experiencing suffering that was fierce, harsh, burning and disagreeable."

And he said further:

"Her great body is like a lofty mountain;
Her lips and throat are parched; she is utterly wretched.
Her face covered by her own hair, she goes naked;
Her mouth is narrow like a needle's eye; she is utterly emaciated.
Naked like this, covered by her hair,
Like a contraption of bones set upright,
She carries a skull cup, dreadful to see,
And runs about everywhere, weeping.
Worn out by hunger and thirst
And afflicted by sufferings,
She cries out in misery
And experiences painful feelings.
What terrible evil did she commit
In the world of humans,
That she should now experience
Suffering as frightful as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Nandana, that female hungry ghost was one who did evil deeds. Do you wish to hear the ripening of her karma?"

"Reverend, I wish to hear it."

"Then, Nandana, listen well and carefully and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Nandana, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of those to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"Now in that city of Vārāṇasī there lived a guild leader's daughter who longed for the Dharma. When she heard the Dharma, she came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa, and having asked her parents' leave, she went forth in the teaching of that Blessed One. Then her relatives built a nunnery for her, and she lived there together with nuns who were still in training and nuns beyond training. After some time, under the sway of carelessness, she grew lax in the bases of training, and the nuns expelled her for her immoral conduct.

"Then she caused the patrons, the householders, to cut off even the regular offerings they made out of faith. She spoke dispraise of the nuns who were still in training and those beyond training. And whenever she saw monks of good moral discipline, she would sit with her eyes shut.

"Nandana, what do you think? The one who was the guild leader's daughter is this female hungry ghost. Because she was miserly about the nunnery, she was born as a hungry ghost. Because she cut off the regular offerings, she is surrounded by crows, vultures, dogs and jackals. Because she spoke dispraise of the nuns who were still in training and those beyond training, her body has become foul smelling. Because she shut her eyes whenever she saw monks of good moral discipline, she has become blind.

"So, Nandana, wholly black deeds have a wholly black ripening; wholly white deeds have a wholly white ripening; and mixed deeds have a mixed ripening.

"Therefore, Nandana, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed ones, and devote yourself only to wholly white deeds. Nandana, that is how you should train."

When this Dharma discourse was taught, countless living beings came to see the truths.

Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, understand these and other drawbacks of miserliness and of misconduct in speech, and strive to abandon miserliness and misconduct in speech. Monks, that is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks, and the others as well, the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and so forth, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Guild Leader.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the townspeople, by guild leaders, by caravan leaders, by gods, by nāgas, by yakṣas, by asuras, by garuḍas, by kinnaras and by mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, renowned, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a guild leader who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in wealth. One day he went to the Jeta Grove. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body beautifully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and graced with the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly lovely, like a Jewel Mountain in motion. When he saw him, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma, and the Blessed One taught him a Dharma that brings weariness with saṃsāra. When he had heard it, he came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa. He went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and became renowned to all and possessed of great merit, a receiver of clothing, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites.

He hoarded every requisite he received and held on to, and did not share it with his fellow practitioners of the holy life. Then, because he had indulged in, cultivated and repeatedly practiced miserliness, he died still greatly attached to his own possessions and was born as a hungry ghost in his own dwelling.

Then his fellow practitioners of the holy life struck the gong without pause and carried his remains outside. They performed the rites of veneration for his remains and returned to the monastery. Then they opened the door of his dwelling and began to distribute his robes and alms bowl in turn, and at once they saw a hungry ghost, with ugly hands, feet and eyes and a body most terrifying, sitting there clutching the robes and the alms bowl. When they saw this ugly being, the monks were dismayed, and they told the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, in order to benefit that son of good family, to rouse weariness in the assembly of his disciples, and to show plainly the ugly ripening of miserliness, went to that dwelling escorted by the assembly of monks, with the Saṅgha of monks going before him. Then the ghost saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body beautifully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and graced with the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly lovely, like a Jewel Mountain in motion. The moment he saw him, his mind became gladdened toward the Blessed One, and he was filled with shame.

Then the Blessed One, with a voice deep as the thunder of rain clouds and like the sound of a drum, reproached the hungry ghost: "Good sir, to your own ruin you accumulated these robes and this alms bowl, and so you were born as a hungry ghost. Now gladden your mind toward me, and do not let your mind cling to these possessions either; that will be good. Otherwise, when you die from this state, you will be born among the beings of the hells."

Then the hungry ghost offered the robes and the alms bowl to the Saṅgha, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, and confessed his fault. Then the Blessed One spoke the dedication of the offering for the hungry ghost:

"Whatever merit there is from this gift,
May it go after the hungry ghost;
From the terrifying world of hungry ghosts
May he swiftly be set free!"

Then the hungry ghost became gladdened in mind toward the Blessed One, and when he died he was born as a hungry ghost of great magical power. Then that hungry ghost of great magical power, wearing earrings and bracelets that jingled and swayed, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a diadem studded with all kinds of jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, that very night filled his lap with divine flowers, utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndāravas. He lit up the whole of the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground with a great radiance, strewed the flowers over the Blessed One, and sat down before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One taught him the Dharma suited to him, and when he had heard it, joy arose in him and he departed. At that time the monks, who did not sleep in the first and last watches of the night but remained devoted to diligent practice, saw that a great radiance had appeared near the Blessed One. Seeing it, they were seized with doubt and asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night, did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not the lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. That hungry ghost died and was reborn as a hungry ghost of great magical power. Last night he came to me, I taught him the Dharma, and joy arose in him and he departed. Therefore, monks, so that a fault such as that of the merchant who became a hungry ghost may not befall you, strive to abandon avarice. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others besides, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Sons.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, known far and wide, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

Then early in the morning the venerable Maudgalyāyana put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Rājagṛha for alms. Having gone for alms in Rājagṛha, he ate his meal and, having given up taking food afterwards, he put away his robe and bowl and went wandering in the realm of the hungry ghosts. Near Vulture Peak he saw a hungry ghost woman who looked like the sister of Yama. Her body was smeared with blood, and as though she dwelt in a charnel ground, she was surrounded by skeletons. Each day and each night she gave birth to five sons, and so she underwent such suffering; and although she loved her sons, tormented by hunger she was eating them.

Then the elder Maudgalyāyana asked her, "What deed did you do in the past, that you undergo suffering such as this?"

The hungry ghost woman said, "When the sun has risen, there is no need of a lamp. Ask the Blessed One about this matter, and he will explain to you the nature of my deeds. Having heard it, other beings too will give up evil deeds."

Then the venerable Maudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One had risen from his meditative absorption and was teaching the four assemblies a Dharma full of flavor, like honey from bees unboiled; and many hundreds in the assembly, their senses unmoving, were listening to the Dharma full of flavor from the Blessed One.

Now the buddhas, the blessed ones, speak openly, speak pleasantly, say "Come, welcome!", and smile before they speak. So the Blessed One said to the venerable Maudgalyāyana, "Maudgalyāyana, come! You are welcome. Where have you come from just now?"

Maudgalyāyana replied, "Venerable Blessed One, I have come back from going among the hungry ghosts. There I saw a hungry ghost woman who looked like the sister of Yama, her body smeared with blood, surrounded by skeletons as though she dwelt in a charnel ground." And he said further:

"'Every day I bear five sons,
And every night I bear five more;
Though I devour them once they're born,
I am never satisfied,' she says.
What terrible evil did she do
Within the world of human beings,
That she should come to undergo
Such dreadful suffering as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, that hungry ghost woman is one who committed evil deeds. Do you wish to hear the nature of her deeds?"

"Venerable One, I wish to hear it."

"Then, Maudgalyāyana, listen well and closely, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Maudgalyāyana, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a merchant who was rich, of great wealth and abundant possessions, whose holdings were vast and extensive, who possessed the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played with her, made love, and enjoyed himself. But although he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, no son was born to him, nor any daughter. Resting his cheek on his hand, he sat brooding, thinking, 'Although my household has great wealth, I have neither son nor daughter. When I have passed away, since I have no son, everything I own will fall to the king.'

"Then that woman, wishing for a son, prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā and other eminent gods as well: to the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads where four roads meet and where three roads meet, the gods who receive the torma offerings, and the gods born together with one, the gods who share one's nature, and the gods who constantly follow behind one. There is indeed a saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, then each person would surely have a thousand sons, like a universal monarch.

Rather, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together, aroused by desire; the mother is in her season and has her menses; and a gandharva has arrived. From the coming together of these three conditions sons and daughters are born. So although she propitiated the gods, neither son nor daughter was born.

Then such thoughts as these arose in him: "If I were to take a second wife, perhaps there is some chance that I would have a son." So he took a second wife from a family equal to his own, and he played with her, made love, and enjoyed himself. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, after some time she became pregnant. Delighted, pleased and overjoyed, she told her husband, "My lord, I have conceived a child, and since it rests on the right side of my womb, it will certainly be a boy. Please rejoice!"

He too was overjoyed. Raising the upper part of his body and stretching out his right hand, he uttered these words of joy: "I shall see the face of the son I have long wished and wished for! May my son be sound and not unsound! May he do my duties! May he repay us for raising him! May he enjoy his share of the wealth! May my family line long endure! And after we have passed away and died, may he give gifts, whether many or few, and make merit on our behalf, and dedicate the reward, saying, 'Wherever these two are born and go, may this follow them there!'"

Then, knowing that she was pregnant, in order to care for the child he settled her at ease in the upper storey of the mansion. In the cold season she was attended with things for the cold, in the hot season with things for the heat, and with foods prescribed by the physician: things not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent, not too astringent, foods free of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency and astringency. Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and like a divine maiden roaming in the Nandana Grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat and never set foot on the ground below, and he made sure that she heard no unpleasant sound at all.

Then the first wife, seeing how he honored and cherished her, grew jealous and thought, "If this woman gives birth to a son, he will do me harm. I must find some way to deal with this." For one who is wholly given over to desire there is no restraint whatever against doing evil deeds. Gazing over the precipice of the wretched destinies, she won the other's trust and gave her an abortifacient drug, such that merely from drinking it that afflicted woman's child miscarried.

Then the second wife gathered all the relatives and summoned the first wife to judgment, saying, "You won my trust and gave me an abortifacient drug, and because of it my child has miscarried."

Then the first wife swore an oath among the relatives, saying, "If I gave you an abortifacient drug, may I become a hungry ghost woman and devour every son I bear!"

"Maudgalyāyana, what do you think? She who was the merchant's wife is that hungry ghost woman. Because of the jealousy she showed in the past, she was born as a hungry ghost woman. Through the karmic maturation of the deed of lying and swearing that oath, she gives birth to five sons each day and five each night, and devours them. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should strive to abandon faults of speech, so that faults such as those of that hungry ghost woman do not arise. Maudgalyāyana, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others besides, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, twelfth fascicle.

Jāmbāla.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, known far and wide, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Vaiśālī, in the Kūṭāgāra Hall on the bank of the Monkey Pond.

At that time in Vaiśālī, in one of the city's moats, there lived five hundred hungry ghosts who ate vomit, ate what had been thrown away, lived on phlegm, snot and urine, and ate pus, blood and excrement, unbearable and miserable by their very nature. It is also said:

They eat vomit and eat what is thrown away,
They live on phlegm and snot and urine,
They eat pus and blood and excrement,
Unbearable and wretched by their nature.

In Vaiśālī there also lived a certain brahmin. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played with her, made love, and enjoyed himself. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife became pregnant, and her body came to smell foul. Then the brahmin summoned the soothsayers and asked them, and they said, "This is the power of the boy who is in her womb."

After eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and the child she bore was a boy, ill-colored, unpleasant to look at, ugly, his body smeared with filth and foul-smelling. Though he was extremely unlovely, his parents raised him, bound to him by the force of love. He delighted only in filthy places: he would roll in heaps of refuse and in cesspits and put filth into his mouth, and so he came to be named "Cesspit," Jāmbāla.

One day, as he was wandering here and there, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa saw him and thought, "Since he delights in places like these, he must be a man of unbroken accomplishment. I shall ordain him." So he ordained him, and the boy went about naked, and he also settled into the practice of austerities.

Then, as he went wandering, he saw the five hundred hungry ghosts who dwelt in the moat of Vaiśālī, and because of his connection with the karmic maturation of his former deeds, he went down into that city moat, gathered and met with them, took delight in them, and became their friend.

Some time later the boy Jāmbāla, busy with some errand, went into Vaiśālī. The Blessed One too came to that city moat, and those hungry ghosts saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly splendid, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as they saw him, they bowed at the Blessed One's feet and said, "Blessed One, we are in want."

The Blessed One said, "What do you lack?"

The hungry ghosts said, "Blessed One, we are thirsty."

Then from his five fingers the Blessed One sent down five streams of water possessing the eight qualities, and with them he satisfied those five hundred hungry ghosts. Then their minds became joyful toward the Blessed One, and when they died they were reborn in the fair realm of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

It is the nature of things that when a god or goddess has been born, not long afterward three thoughts arise: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what deed was I born here?" Then they saw that they had died and passed on from the hungry ghosts, that they had been born in the fair realm of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because their minds had become joyful toward the Blessed One.

Then those gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts thought, "It would not be fitting for us to wait until a day has passed before going to see the Blessed One. We will go to see the Blessed One before the day is out." Then those gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts, wearing earrings and bracelets that jingled and swayed, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing diadems studded with all kinds of jewels, their bodies anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, that very night filled their laps with divine flowers, utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndāravas. They lit up the whole of the Kūṭāgāra Hall with a great radiance, strewed the flowers over the Blessed One, and sat down before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions and natures of those gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts, taught them the Dharma in such a way that they would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the five hundred gods shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truth, with the very splendor with which they had come before the Blessed One, a splendor like that of a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times and went back to their own abode.

Then the boy Jāmbāla came to the city moat and did not see those hungry ghosts. He began to search, and searching everywhere for them he grew weary, but he did not find them.

Now there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize, or do not understand. Yet the buddhas, the blessed ones, possessed of great compassion, devoted to benefiting the world, the sole protectors, the sole heroes, without equal, whose speech is never double, who abide in calm abiding and insight, who make the three knowledges shine, who are well trained in the three trainings, who are skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet, the four bases of magical power, stand most firm, who have long been practiced in the four means of attraction, fearless through the four fearlessnesses, who proclaim the true and great lion's roar of a bull among men, who have entirely abandoned the five factors, who have wholly passed beyond the five destinies, who possess the six factors, who have perfected the six perfections, who abide in the six constant abidings, who are rich in the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame pervades the ten directions, who far surpass even the lord who holds sway over a thousand, by the nature of things survey the world with the eye of a buddha three times by day and three times by night. Their wisdom gaze proceeds, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into distress? Who is afflicted with harm? Who is in want, distress and harm? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding into the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation and in its fruits? Whom shall I take by the hand and pull out of the mire of sensual desire in which he is sinking? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the sovereignty of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not yet produced roots of virtue shall I produce them? In whom who has already produced roots of virtue shall I bring them to maturity? Whom who has already matured shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, dwelling place of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide go by;
But for his children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by.

Then, in order to benefit the son of good family Jāmbāla, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe early in the morning, took his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, went into Vaiśālī for alms. After some time, as he made his alms round in due order and came into a street, Jāmbāla too, wandering here and there, came and stood before the Blessed One.

Then he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly splendid, like a moving mountain of jewels. And as soon as he saw him, his mind became joyful toward the Blessed One. Joy having arisen, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet, joined his palms, and said, "Blessed One, if even beings such as I may go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and it would be fitting, then I too wish to go forth."

Then the Blessed One, possessed of great compassion, who knows the dispositions and latent tendencies of beings, understanding that he was supremely fortunate, stretched out his golden-colored arm, like the trunk of an elephant, and spoke these words: "Come, monk, live the pure life!" The moment the Blessed One had spoken these words, his hair and beard were shaven as if seven days before, and with the deportment of one fully ordained he stood as though he had been ordained a hundred years, holding an alms bowl and a water pot in his hands. Here it is said:

When the Tathāgata said to him, "Come!"
His head was shaven, his body clad in the patched robe;
Robed by the Buddha's intention,
At once he stood with his senses wholly calmed.

Then the Blessed One gave him instruction in mental cultivation. By striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is in motion and unstable. He saw thoroughly that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, and abandoning all afflictions he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like empty space and like the palm of his hand; he became cool like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he turned his back on worldly gain, attachment and honor; and he became one worthy to be worshiped, revered and respectfully addressed by the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Even after he had attained arhatship, he still delighted in what was lowly. So the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, this monk of mine, Jāmbāla, is foremost among my monk śrāvakas who are inclined toward what is lowly."

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts off all doubts, "Venerable One, what deed did the elder Jāmbāla do, that he underwent such suffering as this?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Jāmbāla himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds which, once their accumulation was complete and their conditions fulfilled, arise like a flood and come about without fail. Since Jāmbāla himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense bases.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and their time arrives,
They ripen as their fruits.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for forty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, called Krakucchanda, and he was staying at a royal capital called Sundara.

"At that time a householder in that royal capital built a monastery, and he took care of the monks from various regions and lands who came, went and stayed there. In that monastery there lived a monk who was an ordinary person, and he was extremely possessive of his dwelling. When he saw monks newly arriving, he would seethe with resentment, become agitated and bear them ill will; he would sit sullen and stir up quarrels. But when he saw monks departing from the monastery, he would be greatly pleased and overjoyed, and would see them off and speak with them.

"Some time later a monk who was an arhat came from some other land. The owner of the monastery was a non-returner, and he knew from his deportment that he was an arhat. Then, joy having arisen, he invited him together with the Saṅgha of monks for the ceremonial bath and a meal on the following day. The resident monk was not there. When the next day came and the ceremonial bath had been offered and the meal set out, the resident monk too arrived. He went to the place of the ceremonial bath and saw the owner of the monastery, who had come early, attending to the newly arrived monk. Then jealousy arose in him, and with a hostile mind he spoke harsh words: 'Monk, you, whose body is smeared with filth, are not fit to accept the service of such a patron as this!'

"Then that arhat thought, 'It must not be that this poor afflicted man becomes destined for a fate still more terrible than this,' and saying nothing at all, he bore it patiently.

"After some time, when the assembly had gathered and the morning had come, the resident monk heard people saying to him, 'You harbored hostility toward an arhat.' Having heard this, he was filled with remorse. Then he bowed at the feet of that monk who was an arhat and said, 'Noble one, I beg you to forgive the harsh words I spoke to you.'

"Then, in order to inspire faith in him, that arhat rose into the sky and displayed various kinds of miracles. At that his remorse grew still greater, and he confessed and acknowledged that wrongful deed before him and purified it by confession. Nevertheless, he was unable to give rise to the ultimate wisdom.

"Then after some time, when the hour of his death had come, he made this aspiration: 'May I not experience the karmic maturation of the deed of harboring hostility toward an arhat and speaking harsh words. By the karmic maturation of whatever deeds I have done in reading and reciting, in giving gifts and great gifts, and in serving the Saṅgha, may I in a future time please a Buddha, a Blessed One!'

"Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time and on that occasion was the resident monk is none other than this Jāmbāla. Because of the karmic maturation of the deed of speaking harsh words to an arhat, he experienced endless suffering in saṃsāra, and because a remainder of that same deed was left, even now that he has reached his last existence, he was foul-smelling, exceedingly foul-smelling, and delighted in filth and muck. And because he had practiced recitation, and had become skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible, he went forth in my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhatship.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: you should strive to abandon avarice. Why is that? So that faults such as those Jāmbāla had while he was an ordinary person do not arise, and so that you may come to have such a host of qualities as he gained in attaining arhatship. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and others besides, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Here ends the fifth decade, with its summary verse, of the Hundred Avadānas.

The summary verse:

The Black Snake and the Moon,
The Sāla and Śrīmatī,
The Robe, the Parrot, the Messenger,
The Buffalo and the Poṣadha,
And the Goose, told last of all.

The Black Snake.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, known far and wide, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time in the city of Rājagṛha there lived a householder who was rich, of great wealth and abundant possessions, whose holdings were vast and extensive, who possessed the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. But he was avaricious and miserly, clinging to his possessions, one who would not give an offering even to a crow. Whenever he saw ascetics, brahmins, the wretched, the needy or beggars, his mind would turn hostile.

Then he hid a great heap of gold and silver in his own park, and he died still attached to it and clinging to it intensely. When he died, he was reborn right on top of it as a venomous snake, a great black snake with a poisonous gaze. Then whatever crowds of people went into that park, he would kill merely by looking at them. And word spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha: "Everyone who goes into such and such a park will perish."

The crowds of people reported this to King Bimbisāra. Then King Bimbisāra thought, "Apart from the Buddha, the Blessed One, who else is there who could tame it?"

Then King Bimbisāra, with a large retinue of people, went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. When he was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed King Bimbisāra with a talk on the Dharma, inspired him, roused him and delighted him. Having instructed, inspired, roused and delighted him with many kinds of talk on the Dharma, he remained silent.

Then King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Blessed One with palms joined, and said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, here in Rājagṛha, in a certain pleasure garden, there lives a venomous snake, a great black snake with a poisonous gaze, and it is destroying many people. Out of compassion, may the Blessed One please tame it." The Blessed One consented to King Bimbisāra by remaining silent. Then King Bimbisāra, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by remaining silent, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

Then, when that very night had passed, the Blessed One dressed in the morning in his lower garment and robe, took his alms bowl, and went to the pleasure garden. Having arrived, the Blessed One sent forth golden-colored rays of light whose brilliance surpassed that of a thousand suns, and they lit up the whole of that pleasure garden. He also sent forth rays of loving-kindness, which he had thoroughly cultivated for a thousand eons, and as soon as they touched the snake's body, it became deeply soothed and cooled.

Then the venomous snake looked this way and that, wondering, "By whose power has my body become so soothed?" And it saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, beautiful in every way. As soon as it saw him, it gave rise to faith in the Blessed One. When it had come to have a mind of faith, the Blessed One taught it the Dharma in keeping with this: "Good sir, it is because you yourself amassed this wealth that you have been made to fall into the state of a venomous snake. Now arouse faith in me, and do not let your mind cling to this treasure either; that would be well. For when you die and pass on from here, you would otherwise be born among the beings of hell." Then, when the Blessed One caused it to remember its former lives, it wept. At that the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"You have been born as an animal;
Now there is nothing I can do.
Since you are already born in a state without freedom,
What good will pointless weeping do?
Here, toward me, the compassionate Victor,
Arouse a mind of faith.
It is well to leave behind an animal birth;
Then you will go to the higher realms."

Then, for a while, the Blessed One placed the snake inside his alms bowl and carried it to the Bamboo Grove. At that time the king and the people of the land of Magadha heard how the Blessed One had tamed the venomous snake. Then the venomous snake, loathing its own body, gave up eating, and with its mind rejoicing in the Blessed One, it died and was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Not long after a son or daughter of the gods is born, three thoughts arise in them by the very nature of things: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then he saw that he had died and passed on from the state of a venomous snake, that he had been born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because his mind had rejoiced in the Blessed One.

Then the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake thought, "It would not befit me to go and see the Blessed One only after a night has passed. I shall go to see the Blessed One before the night is out." Then the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake, wearing earrings and bracelets that gleamed and swayed, his body adorned with necklaces and garlands, wearing a crown studded with all kinds of jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and other fragrances, filled the fold of his garment that very night with divine flowers: blue lotuses, lotuses, night lilies, white lotuses and māndārava blossoms. He lit up the whole of the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, with a great light, scattered the flowers over the Blessed One, and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he spoke these words of joy: "Venerable Blessed One, you have dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, carried me across the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and kinsfolk, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, beset with many faults,
Most terrible, has been cut off by your power.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, is opened,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have gained
The utterly pure eye from which all faults are gone.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And reached the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.
Supreme among humans, lord, worshipped by humans and gods,
You who are free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Hard to behold in a thousand existences:
Sage, today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then the wearer of the necklace, filled with joy,
Bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And circling the Conqueror of Foes,
Turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake, with the same splendor in which he had come before the Blessed One, went that very night to King Bimbisāra. He lit up the whole royal palace with a great light, roused the king, and said this: "Great King, get up! Why lie sleeping?" Then the king awoke and saw the great light and the god's son. Seeing them, delighted and glad, he asked, "Who are you?"

He replied, "I am the venomous snake that the Blessed One tamed in that pleasure garden. When I died, I was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. I have also paid homage to the Blessed One, and I have seen the truths. Now I shall show you something: go, and from a certain spot in that pleasure garden dig up a great treasure, and for my sake offer a meal to the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and ask that the dedication of the offering be recited for me as well." King Bimbisāra assented to the god's son by remaining silent. Then the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake, understanding that the king had assented by remaining silent, vanished on the spot.

Then that very night King Bimbisāra gave orders to the townspeople and the country people of the land of Magadha, went to that pleasure garden, and dug up the treasure. For three months he offered meals to the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and he asked the Blessed One, "Blessed One, what karma did the god's son who had formerly been the venomous snake commit, that he was born as a venomous snake? And what karma did he perform, that he was born among the gods and came to see the truths?"

The Blessed One said, "Because he gave rise to intense attachment, and gave rise to hostile thoughts toward śramaṇas and brahmins, toward the wretched and destitute, and toward the poor, he was born as a venomous snake. Because he made his mind rejoice in me, he was born among the gods. In the time of Kāśyapa, the perfectly complete Buddha, he was a layman; because he went for refuge and took up the precepts, he came to see the truths. Therefore, Great King, you should train yourself thus: striving to abandon stinginess, so that faults such as becoming a venomous snake do not arise, and so that you come to have a host of good qualities like those of that very god's son."

Then King Bimbisāra praised and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, rose from his seat, and departed. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story of Candra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas.
