Worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a brahmin farmer, who took a wife from a family of equal standing. He played with her, enjoyed himself, and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife conceived a child, and after eight or nine months had passed, a child was born: she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, lovely to behold and beautiful, a delight to the eyes of all people. The brahmin had obtained him only with difficulty, for he had no other sons or daughters. The boy was nursed and raised and grew up, and because he delighted the whole world, the brahmins and householders gave the boy the name Candra, the Moon.

The brahmin boy Candra was passed from hand to hand and carried about all through the city, and the brahmin came to love the boy all the more, always taking great care to protect him well whenever he walked, sat or lay down. The brahmin's house stood near that of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the brahmin boy, keeping company with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, went to the Jeta Grove, heard the Buddha's words, and found faith in the Blessed One's teaching. But he was short-lived; he died and was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Not long after a son or daughter of the gods is born, three thoughts arise in them by the very nature of things: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then he saw that he had died and passed on from the human state, that he had been born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because his mind had rejoiced in the Blessed One.

Then the god's son who had formerly been a brahmin thought, "It would not befit me to go and see the Blessed One only after a night has passed. I shall go to see the Blessed One before the night is out." Then the god's son who had formerly been a brahmin, wearing earrings and bracelets that gleamed and swayed, his body adorned with necklaces and garlands, wearing a crown adorned with all kinds of jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and other fragrances, filled the fold of his garment that very night with divine flowers: blue lotuses, lotuses, night lilies, white lotuses and māndārava blossoms. He lit up the whole of the Jeta Grove with a great light, scattered the flowers over the Blessed One, and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the god's son who had formerly been a brahmin, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the god's son who had formerly been a brahmin shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he spoke these words of joy three times: "Venerable Blessed One, you have dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, carried me across the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and kinsfolk, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, beset with many faults,
Most terrible, has been cut off by your power.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, is opened,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have gained
The utterly pure eye from which all faults are gone.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And reached the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.
Supreme among humans, lord, worshipped by gods and humans,
You who are free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Hard to behold in a thousand existences:
Sage, today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then he with the swaying necklace, filled with joy,
Bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And circling the Conqueror of Foes,
Turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, the god's son who had formerly been a brahmin returned to his own abode with the same splendor in which he had come before the Blessed One.

The monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were intent on diligent practice, and they saw that a great light had appeared near the Blessed One. Seeing it, doubts arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night, did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. A brahmin's only son was short-lived and died. Because his mind had rejoiced in me, he was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Last night he came to me, and when I had taught him the Dharma, he came to see the truths and returned to his own abode.

"At that time the brahmin had carried his only son, beloved and cherished, dear to his heart and pleasing to his mind, patient and never contrary, to the charnel ground. He laid him in his lap and called out, crying, 'Alas, my son! Alas, my eldest son! Alas, my only son!' Though his relatives urged him to, they could not get him to rise, and he sat there surrounded by crows, magpies, vultures and jackals, keeping company with women with disheveled hair, while many people looked on.

"Then his son, reborn as a god, saw his father lamenting, and his heart was moved with compassion. To dispel his father's grief, he magically took on the appearance of a sage, and sat at the edge of the charnel ground practicing the five austerities. Then the brahmin asked the sage, 'O great sage, what are you trying to accomplish with these austerities?'

"The sage said, 'I am seeking kingship. I wish to have a golden chariot adorned with all kinds of jewels, with the sun and the moon as its two wheels, drawn in front by the four world protectors, and to ride in that chariot around this great earth.'

"The brahmin said:

'Even if for a full hundred years
You were to practice austerities without pause,
And even if you practiced the supreme austerity,
You could never hope to reach that state.'

"The sage said, 'And what are you trying to accomplish with this corpse, so utterly foul-smelling and impure, like a log of wood?'

"The brahmin said, 'My beloved only son has died, and I am trying to bring him back.'

"The sage said:

'Even if for a full hundred years
You were to keep on weeping without pause,
You could never hope to gain back that son.
What good does your weeping do?'

"Then the brahmin, thinking, 'The sage's words are true,' gave rise to faith. Having given rise to faith, he asked, 'Who are you?' Then the sage made that appearance vanish, remained in his own form, and said to his father, 'I am your only son. Because my mind rejoiced in the Blessed One, when I died I was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and I have come here to dispel your grief. Father, come here! Go for refuge to the Blessed One, and you too may yet pass beyond saṃsāra.'

"Then the brahmin set down the remains of the dead, went to where the Blessed One was, and when he arrived, bowed at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the brahmin shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry."

Having attained distinction and gained what was to be gained, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, circled him three times, and departed.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, behold how this god's son has dispelled his father's grief in this way and has also established him in seeing the truths."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what great wonder is there in this, that now, having seen the truths, he has completely saved his father? In the past too, while he was still an ordinary person, when his father came to the point of being executed, he saved him three times. Listen well and carefully to this, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there was in the city of Vārāṇasī a man who committed adultery with other men's wives. His son had faith, was virtuous and good-hearted, and was greatly esteemed by people. Then at one point his father committed a theft, and the king commanded the executioners, 'Kill him!' Then the son petitioned the king three times, and so his father was granted his precious life."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The man who at that time, on that occasion, committed adultery with other men's wives was this brahmin. The adulterer's son was this brahmin youth."

The monks asked, "Blessed One, what karma did they perform, that both father and son came to see the truths?"

The Blessed One said, "In the time of Kāśyapa, the perfectly complete Buddha, both of them were laymen. Because they went for refuge and took up the precepts, they have therefore come to see the truths in this way. Therefore, monks, you should strive for nirvāṇa, thinking, 'All conditioned things are impermanent, all phenomena are without self, and nirvāṇa is peace.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks, and also others, gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas and the rest, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story of Sāla.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time a festival called the Plucking of the Sāla took place in Śrāvastī. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered there, picked the flowers of the sāla trees, and played, enjoyed themselves and made merry. At one point a merchant's daughter, having picked sāla flowers, was going into Śrāvastī. The Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, had gone for alms in Śrāvastī and was returning, and the girl saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, beautiful in every way. Seeing him, she was filled with joy, and scattered sāla flowers over the Blessed One. Then she circled the Blessed One and turned back, thinking, "I shall pick some more, since I need them for the house." And at one point, climbing a sāla tree, she fell and died. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Then at one point, her body and her celestial mansion adorned with sāla flowers, she went into the assembly hall of the gods. At that time Śakra, lord of the gods, was in Sudharmā, the assembly hall of the gods, in the midst of the hosts of gods, speaking the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha. Śakra, lord of the gods, saw the goddess, her body and her celestial mansion adorned with sāla flowers, blazing with her roots of virtue. Seeing her, he addressed her in verse:

"Why has your body's hue become like pure gold, like the lotus and the blue lotus?
Here, you whose bodily splendor has no equal, from what have these lights streaming from your body come?
For what reason has the color of your face become like a blossoming lotus, like the hue of gold?
Of which deeds is this the fruit you now enjoy? Goddess, tell me this."

The goddess said:

"Over the Sun of Humanity, rich with the supreme marks,
Together with his śrāvakas,
I scattered well
Fine, spotless sāla flowers.
Because I did such a virtuous deed,
I am radiant beyond others,
My face like the lotus and the moon,
Pure, luminous and lovely to behold."

Śakra said:

"Ah! In that very field of good qualities,
Wholly free of every fault,
In order to be born in the lovely higher realms,
You have sown your seed.
O fair-faced one, with eyes like the broad petals of a lotus,
The Buddha, honored by the finest of women,
With eyes like the broad petals of a blossoming lotus,
Radiant like a heap of the finest gold: who would not worship him?"

Not long after a son or daughter of the gods is born, three thoughts arise in them by the very nature of things: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?"

Then she saw that she had died and passed on from the human state, that she had been born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because her mind had rejoiced in the Blessed One. Then that goddess thought, "It would not befit me to go and see the Blessed One only after a night has passed. I shall go to see the Blessed One before the night is out."

Then the goddess, wearing earrings and bracelets that gleamed and swayed, her body adorned with necklaces and garlands, wearing a crown adorned with all kinds of precious jewels, her body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and other fragrances, attended by many hundreds of thousands of goddesses, went that very night to the Blessed One, together with that same celestial mansion of sāla flowers. Then she scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding that goddess's disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the goddess shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she spoke these words of joy three times: "Venerable Blessed One, you have dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, carried me across the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and kinsfolk, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And she said further:

"The path to the lower realms, beset with many faults,
Most terrible, has been cut off by your power.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, is opened,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have gained
The utterly pure eye from which all faults are gone.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And reached the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.
Supreme among humans, lord, worshipped by gods and humans,
You who are free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Hard to behold in a thousand existences:
Sage, today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then she with the swaying necklace, filled with joy,
Bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And circling the Conqueror of Foes,
Turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, that goddess returned to her own abode with the same splendor in which she had come before the Blessed One.

The monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were intent on diligent practice, and they saw that a great light had appeared near the Blessed One. Seeing it, doubts arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night, did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "It was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Did you see the girl who scattered flowers on the road?"

"Venerable One, we saw her."

"Having made her mind rejoice in me, she died and was born in the fair divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. She came to me, and when I had taught her the Dharma, she came to see the truths and returned to her own abode. Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher, revere him, esteem him and worship him. Having honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped the Teacher, we shall live relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the thirteenth section.

The story of Śrīmatī.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was dwelling with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time King Bimbisāra was reigning in the city of Rājagṛha. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, blessed with good harvests and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and fights had been quelled, and there were no riots, no civil strife, no robbers, no famine and no diseases. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free from harm, with every thorn rooted out, he ruled his kingdom as one would care for an only son.

Then, from the time King Bimbisāra saw the truths through the Blessed One, he went to the Blessed One three times a day, together with his retinue of queens.

Then later, when the season of spring had come, and the trees were in full blossom, and geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos and jīvaṃjīvaka birds were calling in the groves, King Bimbisāra went to the pleasure garden together with his chief queen and his retinue of queens. There the retinue of queens said to the king, "Your Majesty, since we are not able to go to the Blessed One every day, would Your Majesty please build a stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails here within the queens' quarters and consecrate it? We would then constantly honor it with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, parasols, victory banners and flags."

Then King Bimbisāra said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, please grant me hair and nails. I will build a stūpa of the Tathāgata within the women's quarters of the palace and consecrate it."

Then the Blessed One gave him hair and nails, and King Bimbisāra, together with his retinue of queens, with great reverence built a stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails within the queens' quarters and consecrated it. There the retinue of queens made offerings to it with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, parasols, victory banners and flags.

Then King Ajātaśatru, incited by Devadatta, killed his father, the righteous king who ruled according to the Dharma, and took the throne himself. At that time he cut off everything that was to be given to the Blessed One's teaching, and he also laid down a law: "No one is to honor the stūpa of the Tathāgata!"

Then, when the time of the festival on the fifteenth day came, no one swept the stūpa of hair and nails, nor offered it lamps, incense or flowers. The retinue of queens saw the stūpa of hair and nails in that state, and remembering King Bimbisāra, they wept piteously and lamented, "Alas! Parted from the righteous king, we have fallen away from merit!"

Among them, a queen called Śrīmatī, staking her own life, recollected the qualities of the Buddha, swept the stūpa of hair and nails, and lit a garland of lamps.

Then King Ajātaśatru came up onto the top of his many-storied palace, and seeing that great light, he asked, "What is this?" Someone answered, "It is Śrīmatī, who has lit a garland of lamps at the stūpa of hair and nails."

Then he summoned Śrīmatī and said, "Why have you broken the king's command?" She replied, "Although I have broken your command, I have not broken the command of the righteous King Bimbisāra."

At that he flew into a rage, hurled a discus, and killed her. Then, her mind gladdened toward the Blessed One, she died and was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

At that time an assembly of gods had also gathered, and the goddess Śrīmatī, possessed of a halo, a maṇḍala of divine light that shone a full league all around, entered the gods' assembly hall. Then Śakra, lord of the gods, seeing that great radiance and divine light a league across, asked her:

"Why has the color of your body become like pure gold, like the lotus and the utpala?
O you whose bodily splendor here is unequaled, from what have these lights streaming from your body come?
Why has the complexion of your face become like a lotus in bloom, like the hue of gold?
Through what deeds do you now enjoy this fruit? Goddess, tell me this."

The goddess said:

"I saw the Buddha, protector of the three worlds,
The single lamp for beings, rich in the supreme marks.
To the supreme speaker, who dispels the darkness of afflictions,
I offered as a gift lamps that dispel the dark.

Seeing light the color of the moon's rays,
Faith in the Sage arose from my very heart.
Delighted at the sight of those rays,
I bowed down to the Teacher, supreme among speakers.

Because I did such a virtuous deed,
I am radiant beyond measure;
My face is like the lotus and the moon,
Pure, shining, and lovely to behold."

Śakra said:

"Ah! In that very field of qualities,
Who has utterly abandoned every fault,
So as to be born in lovely form in the heavens,
You have planted a seed.

O fair-faced one, whose eyes are like broad lotus petals,
Who would not worship the Buddha, honored by the finest of women,
Whose eyes are like the broad petals of a lotus in bloom,
Radiant and bright like a heap of the finest gold?"

By the nature of things, a god or goddess, not long after being born, gives rise to three thoughts: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then she saw that she had died and passed from among humans, that she had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because her mind had been gladdened toward the Blessed One.

Then the goddess Śrīmatī thought, "It is not fitting for me to go and see the Blessed One only once a day has passed. I will go to see the Blessed One before the day is over."

Then that very night the goddess Śrīmatī, filled with the radiance of divine light, filled the fold of her garment with divine flowers: utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndāravas. Lighting up the whole of the Kalandaka Feeding Ground at Rājagṛha with a great light, she strewed the flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the goddess Śrīmatī's disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she came to realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, the goddess Śrīmatī shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she three times uttered words of joy:

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, has carried me over the mountain of bones, has shut the doors to the lower realms, has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and has established me among gods and humans. What he has done for me was not done by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my kin and the host of my relatives, nor by the departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And she said further:

"The path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils,
Utterly dreadful, has been cut off by your power.
The way to the heavens, richly endowed with merit, has been opened,
And I have also gained the path to nirvāṇa.

Today, relying on you, I have obtained
The eye that is utterly pure, rid of faults.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering,
And shall attain the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.

O lord of supreme humans, worshipped by humans and gods,
You who have abandoned the sickness of birth, aging and death,
O Sage, so hard to behold in a thousand existences,
To have seen you today has borne fruit."

Then, delighted, her necklace swaying,
She bowed down and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
She turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then the goddess Śrīmatī, like a merchant who has made a profit, like a farmer whose crops have flourished, like a hero victorious in battle, like a sick person freed from every illness, went back to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had come to the Blessed One.

The monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were dwelling intent on diligence, and they saw that a great light had appeared near the Blessed One. When they had seen it, doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Rather, a queen of King Bimbisāra called Śrīmatī, staking her own life and recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, lit a garland of lamps at the stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails, and King Ajātaśatru, in his anger, killed her. Having brought forth a mind of joy toward me, she died and was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Last night she came to me, and when I had taught her the Dharma she saw the truths and went back to her own abode.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Teacher. We shall esteem him. We shall revere him. We shall worship him. Having honored the Teacher, esteemed him, revered him and worshipped him, we shall dwell relying on him.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called The Garment.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and had gradually offered a hundred koṭis, that is, a billion, gold coins to the Blessed One's teaching, this thought arose in him: "What is so wonderful about my giving gifts and making merit in this way? To benefit the poor, I shall collect offerings of faith from the people living in Śrāvastī and serve the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. If I do so, I shall also benefit many people and generate much merit as well."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada told the king what he had been thinking, and the king had a bell rung throughout all of Śrāvastī and proclaimed: "Listen, all you townspeople living in Śrāvastī! Seven days from today the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, riding on an elephant, wishes to collect offerings of faith for the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. Whatever each of you intends to give, and however much, give it!"

Then, when seven days had passed, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada mounted an elephant and set out to collect offerings of faith for the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. There, people gave as much as each of them had. Some gave necklaces, some gave bracelets, some gave armlets, some gave gold chains, some gave ornamental rings, some gave pearl necklaces, some gave gold, some gave silver, and some gave even as little as an eighth of a māṣaka. And the householder accepted it all in order to benefit others.

Now at that time a very poor woman, toiling to exhaustion, had after three months obtained a single length of cotton cloth. She was wearing that cloth and had gone out into the street, when she saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍada coming from afar, with conches blowing and round drums beating. She asked a layman, "How is it that this householder, who is rich, with great wealth and vast possessions, who can even see treasures hidden beneath the ground, goes around begging from other people's houses?"

The layman replied, "It is to benefit others. For the sake of those who are unable to offer a meal to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, he does them this kindness: he gathers together many small gifts and has them offered to the Blessed One."

Then this thought occurred to the young woman: "Well then, I am someone who has made no merit, and I have no means to offer a meal by myself to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. Surely I should offer him something, however little." Then she looked to see what she possessed, and saw nothing at all apart from that single length of cloth. She thought, "If I offer this cloth while I stand here, I will be left naked. I will go up onto the roof and throw the cloth down."

So she went up onto the roof, took the cloth off her body, and threw it down onto the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The householder was taken aback, and thinking, "Since she threw it down from the roof, surely she has no possessions beyond this," he ordered his servants, "Go and see who threw down this cloth." They looked, and soon they saw the young woman crouching there. When they questioned her, she said, "I heard the qualities of the Blessed One being proclaimed, and terrified by the fear of poverty, I offered the garment I had obtained to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Tathāgata." They reported this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada was supremely amazed, and he clothed the young woman in garments and adorned her with ornaments of every kind.

Then, her life being short, she died and was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. As soon as she was born, garments appeared for her such as no other god or goddess possessed.

By the nature of things, a god or goddess, not long after being born, gives rise to three thoughts: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then she saw that she had died and passed from among humans, that she had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that she had offered a cloth to the Blessed One.

Then the goddess who had formerly offered the cloth, wearing earrings and rings that gleamed and swayed, her body adorned with necklaces and chains, wearing a crown adorned with all kinds of precious jewels, her body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaf, spṛkkā and other fragrances, that very night filled the fold of her garment with divine flowers: utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndāravas. Lighting up the whole of the Jeta Grove with a great light, she strewed the flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the goddess who had formerly offered the cloth, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she would come to realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, the goddess who had formerly offered the cloth shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she three times uttered words of joy:

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, has carried me over the mountain of bones, has shut the doors to the lower realms, has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and has established me among gods and humans. What he has done for me was not done by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my kin and the host of my relatives, nor by the departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And she said further:

"The path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils,
Utterly dreadful, has been cut off by your power.
The way to the heavens, richly endowed with merit, has been opened,
And I have also gained the path to nirvāṇa.

Today, relying on you, I have obtained
The eye that is utterly pure, rid of faults.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering,
And have attained the state of peace in which the noble ones delight.

O lord of supreme humans, worshipped by humans and gods,
You who have abandoned the sickness of birth, aging and death,
O Sage, so hard to behold in a thousand existences,
To have seen you today has borne fruit."

Then, delighted, her necklace swaying,
She bowed down and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
She turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then the goddess who had formerly offered the cloth, like a merchant who has made a profit, like a farmer whose crops have flourished, like a hero victorious in battle, like a sick person freed from every illness, went back to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had come to the Blessed One.

The monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were dwelling intent on diligence, and they saw that a great light had appeared near the Blessed One. When they had seen it, doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Rather, the woman who offered the cloth, having offered her cloth to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada while he was collecting offerings of faith, died and was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Last night she came to me, and when I had taught her the Dharma she saw the truths and went back to her own abode.

"Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: 'We shall honor the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and we shall not fail to honor them.' Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called The Parrot.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with great merit, receiving robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time King Bimbisāra was reigning in the city of Rājagṛha. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, blessed with good harvests and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and fights had been quelled, and there were no riots, no civil strife, no robbers, no famine and no diseases. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free from harm, with every thorn rooted out, he ruled his kingdom as one would care for an only son.

That king was full of faith, virtuous and of noble intent, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, greatly compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, and loving toward his subjects.

Then one day, longing to see the Blessed One, he sat with his cheek resting on his hand, his mind turned inward in brooding thought. His ministers said, "Your Majesty, why are you so downcast?" The king said, "For a long time I have not seen the Blessed One. For a long time I have not seen the Sugata. Now I wish to see the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One, who had entered upon his daytime retreat, heard King Bimbisāra's longing with his divine ear, pure and surpassing that of humans.

Now, there is nothing at all that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize or do not comprehend. And the buddhas, the blessed ones, who possess great compassion, who are devoted to benefiting the world, who have the single guard, who are sole heroes, without equal, who never speak in two ways, who abide in calm abiding and insight, who illuminate the three knowledges, who are well trained in the three trainings, who are skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet, the four bases of miraculous power, stand perfectly firm, who for a long time have been practiced in the four means of attraction, who are fearless through the four fearlessnesses, who roar the great and true lion's roar of the supreme bull, who have fully abandoned the five factors, who have completely transcended the five destinies, who possess the six factors, who have perfected the six perfections, who dwell in the six constant abidings, who are rich in the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who dwell in the nine successive meditative attainments, who have the power of the ten powers, whose fame pervades the ten directions, and who are far more exalted than the lord of the thousand-fold world, by the nature of things look upon the world with the eye of a buddha three times by day and three times by night. Their vision of wisdom turns to this: "Who is declining? Who is flourishing? Who is in need? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted by harm? Who is in need, in danger and afflicted by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation and in its fruits? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I make master of the wealth of the seven noble riches? In whom who has not yet generated roots of virtue shall I generate them? In whom who has already generated roots of virtue shall I ripen them? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

On this it is said:

"The ocean, the dwelling of sea monsters,
May sometimes let the hour of its tide go by;
But for the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time go by."

Then, in order to benefit King Bimbisāra, when the three months of the summer rains had passed and he had made his robes, the Blessed One, his robes finished, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and set out wandering through the country. Traveling by stages, he came to a forest. In that forest lived a parrot that knew human speech, and it saw the Blessed One from a long way off. It went very swiftly to the Blessed One and said, "Come, Blessed One! Welcome, Blessed One, welcome! Please do me a kindness. Please consider staying in this very forest."

Then, in order to benefit the parrot, the Blessed One spread a mat of grass at the foot of the tree where the parrot lived and sat down with his legs crossed. The great śrāvakas settled at the feet of other trees. Then the parrot, fearing that humans or nonhumans, yakṣas or rākṣasas, wild animals or beasts of prey might harm the Blessed One and the śrāvakas, flew back and forth around that forest the whole night long.

Then, when dawn broke, it circumambulated the Blessed One three times and asked his forgiveness: "Blessed One, since I have been born in the womb of an animal, I have no means at all to honor the Blessed One, so please forgive me. Even so, I would like to go ahead and announce to King Bimbisāra that the Blessed One is coming." The Blessed One said, "Do so."

Then it set out ahead of the Blessed One, and in due course reached the king. At that time King Bimbisāra was on the upper floor of his palace with only his women, amusing himself with music, delighting and enjoying himself. Then the parrot that knew human speech said to the king, "O King, know this: the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, is coming to your land, so it is fitting that Your Majesty prepare a meal."

Then the king came down very swiftly from the upper floor of the palace, and attended by a host of great ministers, he had seats prepared for the Blessed One and went out to meet the Blessed One with parasols, victory banners, flags, incense, perfumes and flowers of every kind. Then, with great reverence, he invited the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas inside and satisfied them with fine food.

Then the parrot thought, "All this abundance for the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's śrāvakas is my doing." Realizing this, it was joyful, glad and delighted, and with joy, gladness and happiness arising in it, it flew back and forth in front of the king, until a hawk carried it off and killed it. Because it died having brought forth a mind of joy toward the Blessed One, it was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

By the nature of things, a god or goddess, not long after being born, gives rise to three thoughts: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then he saw that he had died and passed from among the animals, that he had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because his mind had been gladdened toward the Blessed One.

Then the god who had formerly been a parrot thought, "It is not fitting for me to go and see the Blessed One only once a day has passed. I will go to see the Blessed One before the day is over."

Then the god who had formerly been a parrot, wearing spotless, swaying ring earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a crown adorned with various precious jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, on that very night filled the fold of his garment with divine flowers: utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and mandāravas. Illuminating the whole of the Jeta Grove with a great radiance, he scattered the flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the intentions, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the god who had formerly been a parrot, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the god who had formerly been a parrot, with the vajra of wisdom, destroyed the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truths, he uttered words of joy three times: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, has carried me across the mountain of bones, has closed the doors to the lower realms, has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and has established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and the host of my kin, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, so full of faults,
Utterly dreadful, you have cut off by your power.
You opened the way to the higher realms, rich in merit,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have obtained
The utterly pure eye that has cast off faults.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And gained the peaceful state in which the noble ones delight.
Lord, best of humans, honored by humans and gods,
Free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Sage so hard to see in a thousand existences,
Today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then, his necklace swaying, filled with joy,
He bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
He turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, the god who had formerly been a parrot went back to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One.

The monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were intent on exertion, and they saw that a great light had appeared near the Blessed One. Having seen it, doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was that? Last night, did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Did you see the parrot that invited me to that forest grove for a night's lodging?"

The monks replied, "Blessed One, we saw it."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, that very parrot died and was born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three."

The monks asked, "Venerable One, what deeds did the god who was formerly a parrot perform, by which he was born as a parrot? And what deeds did he perform, by which he was born among the gods and came to see the truths?"

The Blessed One said, "The god who was formerly a parrot himself performed and accumulated those deeds, whose accumulations are complete, whose conditions have ripened, which have come upon him like a flood, and which inevitably arrive. Since the god who was formerly a parrot performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the guide who tames beings, the unsurpassed one, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī. At one time a layman there was lax in the training, and through the ripening of that deed he was born as a parrot. Because he gladdened his mind toward me, he was born as a god. Because he kept the remaining points of training, he came to see the truths.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white; and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Messenger.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, had committed himself, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to spend the rains retreat at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where Prasenajit, king of Kosala, was, and on arriving he praised the king, saying, "May you be victorious! May you live long!" and made this request: "Your Majesty, please know that I have not seen the Blessed One for a long time, and I thirst with longing to see the Blessed One. I wish to see the Blessed One."

Then the king said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, "Householder, what have you heard about where the Blessed One now intends to spend the rains retreat?"

Anāthapiṇḍada said, "Your Majesty, I have heard that the Blessed One has committed himself to spend the rains retreat at Rājagṛha."

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the others, the people of the palace retinue, the townspeople and the ministers, summoned a man as a messenger and instructed him: "Come here, man. Go to where the Blessed One is, and on arriving, bow your head at the Blessed One's feet and, on our behalf, ask, 'Blessed One, are you free of ailment, free of discomfort? Do you move about with ease? Are you well, are you strong, are you at ease, without distress, and do you dwell in comfort?' And say this: 'Venerable One, the king of Kosala and the people of the palace retinue living in Śrāvastī long to behold the face of the Blessed One. Since we have not seen the Blessed One for a long time, we thirst with longing to see the Blessed One. As we long to see the Blessed One, out of compassion, may the Blessed One please come to Śrāvastī.' That is what they say."

Then that man heeded the instructions of Prasenajit, king of Kosala, the ministers, the people of the palace retinue and the townspeople, and set out for Rājagṛha. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Then, after searching all through the city of Rājagṛha, he went to where the Blessed One was, and on arriving, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, please know that Prasenajit, king of Kosala, and the people of the palace retinue living in Śrāvastī bow their heads at the Blessed One's feet and ask, 'Blessed One, are you free of ailment, free of discomfort? Do you move about with ease? Are you well, are you strong, are you at ease, without distress, and do you dwell in comfort?' And they also say this: 'Since we have not seen the Blessed One for a long time, we thirst with longing to see the Blessed One. As we long to see the Blessed One, out of compassion, may the Blessed One please come to Śrāvastī.'"

The Blessed One said, "Friend, if King Bimbisāra permits me to go, I will go."

Then that messenger made the request to King Bimbisāra, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, King Bimbisāra has given his consent for the Blessed One to go. Since the Blessed One now knows that the time for it has come, may he please set out." So he urged him.

Then the Blessed One consented to that man by remaining silent. Then, when the three months of the summer rains had passed, the Blessed One, having made his robes and finished the robes, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and set out for Śrāvastī with a large retinue of attendants.

The messenger, too, mounted a chariot and set out. Then, seeing the Buddha, the Blessed One, going on foot, he got down from the chariot, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: "Out of compassion, may the Blessed One please accept my chariot."

The Blessed One said:

"Abiding in the chariot of the bases of miraculous power
And of right effort,
Unharmed by the thorns of the afflictions,
I travel all over the earth."

The messenger said, "Although the Blessed One travels on the feet of miraculous power, still, to benefit me and out of compassion, please ride."

Then, in order to benefit the messenger, the Blessed One, by miraculous power, sat upon the chariot. Then the Blessed One, riding in the chariot, arrived at Śrāvastī, and the messenger announced it to the king. Then the king, the ministers, the people of the palace retinue and the townspeople went out to receive the Blessed One, and that night they stayed in that very Jeta Grove in order to listen to the Dharma.

That messenger was short-lived: after hearing the Dharma, he died that very night, and having died, he was born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Not long after being born, a god or goddess, by the nature of things, gives rise to three thoughts: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then he saw that he had died and passed from among humans, that he had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because his mind had been gladdened toward the Blessed One.

Then the god who had formerly been the messenger thought, "It is not fitting for me to go and see the Blessed One only once a day has passed. I will go to see the Blessed One before the day is over."

Then the god who had formerly been the messenger, wearing spotless, swaying ring earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a crown adorned with various precious jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, on that very night filled the fold of his garment with divine flowers: utpalas, kumudas, lotuses, white lotuses and mandāravas. Illuminating the whole of the Jeta Grove with a great radiance, he scattered the flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the intentions, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the god who had formerly been the messenger, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the god who had formerly been the messenger, with the vajra of wisdom, destroyed the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truths, he uttered words of joy three times: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, has carried me across the mountain of bones, has closed the doors to the lower realms, has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and has established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and the host of my kin, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, so full of faults,
Utterly dreadful, you have cut off by your power.
You opened the way to the higher realms, rich in merit,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have obtained
The utterly pure eye that has cast off faults.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And gained the peaceful state in which the noble ones delight.
Lord, best of humans, honored by humans and gods,
Free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Sage so hard to see in a thousand existences,
Today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then, his necklace swaying, filled with joy,
He bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
He turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, the god who had formerly been the messenger went back to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One.

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, who was on the upper floor of his palace, saw that great light, and when day broke he asked the Blessed One, "Blessed One, what was that? Last night, did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Great king, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Rather, that messenger of yours, his mind gladdened toward me, died and was born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Last night he came into my presence; I taught him the Dharma, he came to see the truths, and he went back to his own abode."

Then the king was amazed and said, "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dharma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Even a small thing done toward these becomes a great ripening!"

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, praised and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, rose from his seat and departed.

Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, there are these three that are declared supreme. What are the three? The Buddha, declared supreme; the Dharma, declared supreme; and the Saṅgha, declared supreme.

"What is the Buddha, declared supreme? Among whatever beings there are, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed or many-footed, whether having form or formless, whether having perception, without perception, or neither having perception nor without perception, among them the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha is taught to be supreme. Whoever delights in the Buddha delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be only the supreme, whether among gods as gods or among humans as humans. This is called the Buddha, declared supreme.

"What is the Dharma, declared supreme? Among whatever phenomena there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, among them the Dharma of freedom from attachment is taught to be supreme. Whoever delights in the Dharma delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be only the supreme, whether among gods as gods or among humans as humans. This is called the Dharma, declared supreme.

"What is the Saṅgha, declared supreme? Among whatever groups, gatherings, multitudes or assemblies there are, among them the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas is taught to be supreme. Whoever delights in the Saṅgha delights in the supreme, and it should be known that for those who delight in the supreme, the ripening too will be only the supreme, whether among gods as gods or among humans as humans. This is called the Saṅgha, declared supreme."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, section fourteen.

The Buffalo.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was wandering through the land of Kosala together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and came to a certain forest. In that forest there were a great herd of buffalo and five hundred buffalo herders.

Now, among them there was a buffalo that was strong, possessed of supreme strength, and whenever it caught the scent of other people, it would chase after them. The Blessed One, too, went in that direction. Then the buffalo herders saw the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas from far away, and they called out loudly, "Blessed One, there is a vicious buffalo here! Please do not come along this path!"

The Blessed One said, "Friends, I know that the time for this has come here, so do not be afraid."

Then that buffalo, seeing the Blessed One from far away, raised its tail straight up and charged toward where the Blessed One was. Then the Blessed One emanated in front of himself five maned lions with tossing manes, emanated five great men on his right and left flanks, and above emanated a great boulder of iron. Then the buffalo, seeing great terror in every direction, went to the Blessed One's feet, licked the Blessed One's feet with its tongue, and looked up at the Blessed One with a cowed face.

Then the Blessed One, in a language it could understand, taught it three phrases of Dharma: "Good friend, it is thus: all formations are impermanent; all phenomena are without self; nirvāṇa is peace." He also caused it to remember its former lives, and hearing this, it wept. Then the Blessed One spoke these verses to it:

"You have been born as an animal;
What can I do for you now?
You have already been born in a state without freedom;
What good is it to weep in vain?
Here, toward me, the compassionate Victor,
Give rise to a mind of faith.
It would be well to leave the animal birthplace,
And then you will go to the higher realms."

Then that vicious buffalo, scorning its own body, stopped eating; and since creatures born in the animal birthplace have a fierce digestive fire, it quickly died and was born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Not long after being born, a god or goddess, by the nature of things, gives rise to three thoughts: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? Through what karma was I born?" Then he saw that he had died and passed from among the animals, that he had been born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because his mind had been gladdened toward the Blessed One.

Then the god who had formerly been the buffalo thought, "It is not fitting for me to go and see the Blessed One only once a day has passed. I will go to see the Blessed One before the day is over."

Then the god who had formerly been the buffalo, wearing spotless, swaying ring earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a crown adorned with various precious jewels, his body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, on that very night filled the fold of his garment with divine flowers: utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and mandāravas. Illuminating all those forests with a great radiance, he scattered the flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the intentions, latent tendencies, constitution and nature of the god who had formerly been the buffalo, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the god who had formerly been the buffalo, with the vajra of wisdom, destroyed the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truths, he uttered words of joy three times: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, has carried me across the mountain of bones, has closed the doors to the lower realms, has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and has established me among gods and humans. Such a thing was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and the host of my kin, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, so full of faults,
Utterly dreadful, you have cut off by your power.
You opened the way to the higher realms, rich in merit,
And I have gained the path to nirvāṇa as well.
Today, relying on you, I have obtained
The utterly pure eye that has cast off faults.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering
And gained the peaceful state in which the noble ones delight.
Lord, best of humans, honored by humans and gods,
Free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
Sage so hard to see in a thousand existences,
Today I have seen you, and it has borne fruit."

Then, his necklace swaying, filled with joy,
He bowed and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
He turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, a farmer whose crops have flourished, a hero victorious in battle, or a sick man freed from every illness, the god who had formerly been the buffalo went back to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One.

Then those buffalo herders saw that great light. Having seen it, doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, who was it that came into the Blessed One's presence last night and made everything bright with divine radiance?"

The Blessed One said, "That buffalo of yours, his mind gladdened toward me, died and was born in the excellent divine realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Last night he came into my presence; I taught him the Dharma, he came to see the truths, and he went back to his own abode."

Then those buffalo herders were utterly astonished and amazed. They thought, "If even this one, born in the animal birthplace, met the Blessed One, a spiritual friend, was born among the gods and came to see the truths, why should we not attain something special too?"

Then they satisfied the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with fine food, and went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Through diligence, practice and effort they abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did the god who was formerly a buffalo perform, by which he was born as a buffalo? What deeds did he perform, by which he was born among the gods and came to see the truths? What deeds did these buffalo herders perform, by which they became buffalo herders? And by performing what deeds did they go forth and directly realize arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives these very ones performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations are complete, whose conditions have ripened, which have come upon them like a flood, and which inevitably arrive. Since these very ones performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the guide who tames beings, the unsurpassed one, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"At that time, when the monks were holding an assembly to settle questions of doctrine, a monk who was a master of the three baskets was present in that assembly with a following of five hundred. In it there were also monks who were still in training and monks beyond training, and they put questions to the master of the three baskets. He was unable to answer them, and growing angry, he let fly harsh words: 'What do these creatures, like buffalo of the forest, know?' And his disciples too said, 'What do these, who are like buffalo herders, know?'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The monk who was the master of the three baskets is this very buffalo, and those disciples are these buffalo herders. Through that deed he was born as a buffalo for five hundred lifetimes, and the disciples became five hundred buffalo herders. Because his mind was gladdened toward me, he was born as a god. Because they had obtained the state of a monk and kept moral discipline, they came to see the truths and directly realized arhatship.

"Therefore, monks, you should strive to abandon faults of speech, so that such faults as those of the buffalo and the buffalo herders do not arise, and so that you may attain such a wealth of good qualities as that god's. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Upoṣadha.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, there was a son of the gods called Upoṣadha, who would always go into the presence of the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma. Then, on a later occasion, the son of the gods Upoṣadha, together with a retinue of five hundred attendants, went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side in order to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, having understood the intentions, the latent tendencies, the constitution and the nature of the son of the gods Upoṣadha, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. When he had heard it, the son of the gods Upoṣadha, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of a real self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he uttered words of joy three times:

"Venerable Blessed One, you have dried up for me the ocean of blood and tears, carried me over the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established me among gods and humans. Such a thing as this was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by my household and the host of my kinsmen, nor by my departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And he said further:

"The path to the lower realms, so very fierce,
Laden with many evils, you have cut off by your power.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, you have opened,
And I have gained as well the path to nirvāṇa.
Today, relying on you, I have gained
The utterly pure eye, free of all faults.
I have crossed beyond the ocean of suffering
And gained the peaceful state that delights the noble ones.
Lord, supreme among humans, worshiped by humans and gods,
Free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
O Sage, hard to see in a thousand existences,
To have seen you today bears fruit."

Then, with his necklace swaying, filled with joy,
He bowed down and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
He turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like a merchant who has made a profit, like a farmer whose crop has flourished, like a hero victorious in battle, like a sick man freed from every illness, the son of the gods Upoṣadha returned to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One.

At that time the monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were devoted to diligent practice, and they saw that a great radiance had appeared around the Blessed One. When they saw it, a doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. The son of the gods Upoṣadha, together with a retinue of five hundred attendants, came to see me. I taught him the Dharma, he saw the truth, and he went back to his own abode."

Then a doubt arose in those monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, where did the son of the gods Upoṣadha come from? From what was his name given?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, do you wish to hear?"

They replied, "Venerable One, we wish to hear."

He said, "Then, monks, listen well and carefully and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"On a later occasion King Kṛkin went to see the Blessed One and to honor him. Then at one time two brahmins went to Ṛṣivadana on some business, and the two of them saw that king, endowed with great royal splendor and royal might. Then a longing for kingship arose in the two of them, and they asked a certain layman, 'O layman of the Buddha, what deed must one do so that whatever one thinks of and whatever one wishes will all be accomplished?'

"The layman said, 'Whoever keeps the eight-branched Upoṣadha in complete purity, whatever he thinks of and whatever he wishes will all be accomplished.'

"Then those two brahmins took the eight-branched Upoṣadha from the householder Chutö and kept it. One of them kept it in complete purity. When he died, he was born as the son of King Kṛkin; the son was given the name Sujāta, and after his father died he was placed on the throne. The other let his Upoṣadha lapse, and when he died he was born among the nāgas. Every single day, seven times over, burning sand rained down upon him, so that nothing but his bones was left.

"Then he thought, 'Of what is this the fruit? Of what is this the fruit and ripening, that I go on experiencing suffering such as this?' Then he thought, 'Because I was lax in the training of the eight-branched Upoṣadha that I had taken, I am experiencing suffering such as this, while the one who took it and kept it has gained a kingdom.' And again he thought, 'Even now I shall keep the eight-branched Upoṣadha. Then perhaps I may be freed from birth as a nāga.'

"Then, magically transforming himself into the guise of a brahmin, he came into the presence of the king. Having arrived, he praised the king, saying, 'May you be victorious! May you live long!' and said, 'Great king, I seek from you the eight-branched Upoṣadha. Your Majesty, please grant me the eight-branched Upoṣadha. If you do not grant it, Your Majesty's head will without doubt split into seven pieces.' Having said this, he vanished on the spot.

"Then the king was afraid and terrified; he was unhappy and dejected. He had a vessel holding a hundred thousand pieces of gold tied to the top of a banner, and had it proclaimed with bells throughout his whole land: 'Whoever teaches me the eight-branched Upoṣadha, to him I shall give these hundred thousand pieces of gold, and I shall honor him with great honors as well.' So he ordered.

"Then at one time an old woman, a carpenter's daughter, who lived there, pointed out a pillar to the king and said, 'In the past my father always made offerings to this pillar with incense, fumigants and flowers. Have it dug out and see.' Then the king ordered his attendants, 'Dig out this pillar!' When the king's servants had dug out the pillar, they found beneath it, written on golden plates, the eight-branched Upoṣadha, the five bases of training of a layman, and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening. Then the king wrote out the eight-branched Upoṣadha and gave it to that nāga. And twelve thousand sages dwelling at Ṛṣivadana directly realized the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.

"That nāga, too, kept the eight-branched Upoṣadha. He came out onto open ground and, abandoning his body, lay there while creatures fed upon him. Then he died and, together with a retinue of five hundred attendants, was born in the fine divine realm of the Thirty-Three. Monks, that is where Upoṣadha came from, and from that his name was given."

When the Blessed One had said this, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called The Geese.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas.
