Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time Prasenajit, king of Kosala, was reigning in Śrāvastī. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful and blessed with good harvests, filled with many folk and people; quarrels and fighting were stilled; it was free of unrest, internal strife, robbers, famine and disease, and rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Without causing harm, and with its thorns cleared away, he ruled the kingdom as one cares for an only son.

On a later occasion, when Prasenajit, king of Kosala, went to the Jeta Grove to see the Blessed One and to pay him homage, the king of Pañcāla had sent five hundred geese as a gift to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, and when the king went to the Jeta Grove he presented those five hundred geese. Then King Prasenajit granted those geese safety and released them in that very Jeta Grove.

Whenever the Blessed One, with his great retinue of śrāvakas, sat taking his meal, those geese would go into the presence of the Blessed One, and the Blessed One and those great śrāvakas would give them morsels of food. When they had eaten, they settled down content and delighted, their senses refreshed. Whenever the Blessed One rose from inner meditative absorption and taught the Dharma to the four assemblies, those geese would go into the presence of the Blessed One and listen to the Dharma.

Then, being short-lived, they died and were born in the fine divine realm of the Thirty-Three. Not long after a son or daughter of the gods is born, by the nature of things three thoughts arise: "From where did I die and pass on? Where have I been born? By what karma was I born here?" Then they saw that they had died and passed on from being geese, that they had been born in the fine divine realm of the Thirty-Three, and that this was because their minds had been gladdened by the Blessed One.

Then the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese thought, "It is not fitting for us to wait until a night has passed before going to see the Blessed One. We shall go to see the Blessed One before the night has passed."

Then the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese, wearing earrings and bracelets that glittered as they moved, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half necklaces, with crowns adorned with various precious jewels, their bodies anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā and the like, on that very night filled their laps with divine flowers, utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses and māndārava flowers. Illuminating the whole of the Jeta Grove with a great light, they strewed the flowers over the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the intentions, the latent tendencies, the constitution and the nature of the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese, taught them the Dharma in such a way that they would realize the Four Noble Truths. When they had heard it, the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of a real self, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, they uttered words of joy three times:

"Venerable Blessed One, you have dried up for us the ocean of blood and tears, carried us over the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and established us among gods and humans. Such a thing as this was not done for us by our fathers, nor by our mothers, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor by our households and the host of our kinsmen, nor by our departed ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brahmins."

And they said further:

"The path to the lower realms, so very fierce,
Laden with many evils, you have cut off by your power.
The way to the higher realms, rich in merit, you have opened,
And we have gained the path to nirvāṇa.
Today, relying on you, we have gained
The utterly pure eye, free of all faults.
We have crossed beyond the ocean of suffering
And gained the peaceful state that delights the noble ones.
Lord, supreme among humans, worshiped by gods and humans,
Free of the sickness of birth, old age and death,
O Sage, hard to see in a thousand existences,
To have seen you today bears fruit."

Then, with their necklaces swaying, filled with joy,
They bowed down and paid homage at his two feet,
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Foes,
They turned toward the world of the gods and went to the divine realm.

Then, like merchants who have made a profit, like farmers whose crops have flourished, like heroes victorious in battle, like sick men freed from every illness, the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese returned to their own abode with the very same splendor with which they had come into the presence of the Blessed One.

At that time the monks, not sleeping in the first and last watches of the night, were devoted to diligent practice, and they saw that a great radiance had appeared around the Blessed One. When they saw it, a doubt arose in them, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Blessed One, what was it? Last night did Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, or Śakra, lord of the gods, or the four world protectors come to see the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, nor Śakra, lord of the gods, nor the four world protectors who came to see me. Monks, did you see the five hundred geese that Prasenajit, king of Kosala, released here?"

"Venerable One, we saw them."

He said, "Their minds became gladdened toward me, and when they died they were born in the fine divine realm of the Thirty-Three. Last night they came into my presence; I taught them the Dharma, they saw the truth, and they went back to their own abode."

Then a doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese do, by which they were born as geese? What deeds did they do, by which they were born among the gods and saw the truth?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, earlier lives these very beings did and accumulated deeds whose causes had gathered and whose conditions had ripened, which bear down like a flood and inevitably come to pass. The deeds that the sons of the gods who had formerly been geese did and accumulated, who else will experience them? Monks, deeds that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense bases.

"The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"At that time these beings had gone forth, and because they were lax in the training, they were born as geese. Because they gladdened their minds toward me, they were born as gods. Because they kept the rest of the training, they came to see the truth.

"Therefore, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had said this, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Here ends the sixth section of summary verses from the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa.

The summary:

Suvarṇābha and Fragrant One,
Handsome, Strong, and Dugu,
Lotus Eyes and Drum Sound,
Son, Sun, and the Malla.

The story called Suvarṇābha.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a Śākya who was rich, with great wealth and abundant possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife became pregnant, and after eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son: a boy handsome, good to look at and beautiful, surpassing human complexion though not attaining the complexion of the gods, the color of gold from the Jambu River. His golden light illuminated the whole city of Kapilavastu.

Then his parents and other beings, seeing him, came to gaze at him, and were utterly amazed, wondering, "Where has such an extraordinary being come from?"

Then, when the birth celebration had been held, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "When he was born, the whole city of Kapilavastu was illuminated with golden light. Therefore let this boy be named Suvarṇābha."

Then the boy Suvarṇābha was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter and every other kind of excellent provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake. He was learned, clear-minded and upright, full of faith, virtuous and of good intentions, engaged in benefiting both himself and others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.

Some time later, intoxicated with pride in his good looks, he was amusing himself outside the city. A large number of Śākyas were going to the Nyagrodha Park. The boy Suvarṇābha saw them and asked, "Where are you going?"

They said, "We are going to the Nyagrodha Park to see the Buddha, the Blessed One."

When the boy Suvarṇābha heard the word "Buddha", a name he had never heard before, all the hair on his body stood on end. Utterly amazed, he thought, "Why, I too had better go and see the Buddha, the Blessed One." So he too went to the Nyagrodha Park. There the boy Suvarṇābha saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, with a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. The moment he saw him, his pride in his looks vanished. He bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One taught him the Dharma, and when he had heard that Dharma, he wished to go forth. Then, at one time, having asked leave of his parents, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and bowing with joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, if I may go forth and receive full ordination in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and attain the state of a monk, I too wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One stretched out his golden-colored hand, which was like the trunk of an elephant, and said this to the boy Suvarṇābha: "Come, young man, practice the holy life!" The instant he said this, his hair and beard were shaven, as though seven days had passed since they were shaved; his deportment was like that of one who had been fully ordained for a hundred years; and in his hands he held an alms bowl and a water vessel. Here it is said:

When the Tathāgata said to him, "Come,"
His head was shaven and his body clad in the patched robe.
Dressed in robes by the Buddha's intent,
At once he abode with his senses fully calmed.

Then he sat before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One gave him instruction in attention. Through effort, exertion and striving, he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable. Having fully ascertained that all kinds of conditioned things are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, he abandoned all afflictions and realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, regarding gold and a clod of earth as equal, with a mind like the sky and the palm of the hand alike, cool as sandalwood paste, having broken the eggshell with knowledge, having attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions and the analytical knowledges, indifferent to worldly gain, attachment and honors, he became worthy of the offerings, homage and respectful address of the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Then a doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Suvarṇābha do, by which he became so handsome, good to look at and beautiful, and, having gone forth, realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, earlier lives Suvarṇābha himself did and accumulated deeds whose causes had gathered and whose conditions had ripened, which bear down like a flood and inevitably come to pass. The deeds that Suvarṇābha himself did and accumulated, who else will experience them? Monks, deeds that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense bases.

"The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He was dwelling near the royal capital Bandhumatī. At one time the perfectly awakened Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the activities of a buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa in the element of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, like a fire whose fuel is spent.

"Then King Bandhumat performed the funeral honors for the remains of the Blessed One, and built a stupa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height, and he also instituted a festival for the stupa.

"Then at one time a certain householder went to the place where the stupa festival was being held, and he saw that a golden mirror had fallen from that stupa. He made it into an ear ornament for it, fastened it to the stupa, made offerings with incense, fumigants and flowers, bowed at its feet, and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain such qualities as these! May I please such a teacher as this, and may I never displease him!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the householder at that time, on that occasion, is this boy Suvarṇābha. Because he paid honor to the stupa of the perfectly awakened Buddha Vipaśyin, he came to have such exceptional good looks. Because he made that aspiration, he realized arhatship in this life.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had said this, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Sugandhi.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in the land of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a householder who was rich, with great wealth and abundant possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife became pregnant, and after eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son: a boy handsome, good to look at and beautiful, surpassing human complexion though not attaining the complexion of the gods. From his mouth came the scent of the utpala flower, and from his whole body came the scent of sandalwood.

Then, when the birth celebration had been held, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "Since the scent of the utpala comes from his mouth and the scent of sandalwood comes from his whole body, let this boy be named Sugandhi."

Then the boy Sugandhi was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter and every other kind of excellent provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Moreover, through the force and power of his former causes he was endowed with faith; he was virtuous and good-hearted, devoted to the welfare of himself and others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma. Whenever the boy Sugandhi, adorned with armlets, necklace and bracelets, went out into the street, the fragrance of sandalwood would pervade the whole city. Many people, catching the scent of divine incense, were filled with the greatest wonder and would say, "Oh, the power of merit!"

Some time later, the boy Sugandhi went to the Nyagrodha Park. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a mountain of jewels in motion. As soon as he saw him, joy toward the Blessed One arose in his mind. Having become joyful, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the boy Sugandhi, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the mountain of the view of a real self in the perishing aggregates, with its twenty towering peaks, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he asked his parents' leave and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very five-sectioned wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable. He ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, dispersal and destruction, and, abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and like the palm of his hand; he became cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he turned his back on the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of the worship, reverence and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become curious, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Sugandhi perform, such that the scent of the utpala comes from his mouth, and the scent of sandalwood comes from his whole body?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives Sugandhi himself performed and accumulated deeds whose collected causes have come together and whose conditions have ripened, which have become like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Since Sugandhi himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Deeds performed and accumulated, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago in times past, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Some time later, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the deeds of a buddha, passed completely into nirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted.

"Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for the Blessed One's relics, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height, and also instituted a festival for the stūpa. A certain householder, having developed faith in it, offered various kinds of incense and perfumed unguents, made offerings of fumigants and flowers, and made this aspiration: 'Through this root of virtue, this arising of the mind, and this giving away of what is to be given, may I too attain qualities such as these! May I please such a teacher as this, and may I not displease him!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the householder at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this boy Sugandhi. Because he paid honor to the stūpa of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, he has become fragrant in this way. Through the aspiration he made, he has directly realized arhatship in this life.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the fifteenth fascicle.

The story called Fair Form.

He became one worthy of the worship, reverence and respectful address of the whole world, even of non-human beings. Wherever he set his foot, those places too became pure. Thus he was renowned as one of great merit and greatness.

Some time later, he went to the Nyagrodha Park. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very five-sectioned wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable. He ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, dispersal and destruction, and, abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and like the palm of his hand; he became cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he turned his back on the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of the worship, reverence and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become curious, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Fair Form perform, such that his body has become like this and he has attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives Fair Form himself performed and accumulated deeds whose collected causes have come together and whose conditions have ripened, which have become like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Since Fair Form himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Deeds performed and accumulated, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago in times past, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Some time later, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the deeds of a buddha, passed completely into nirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted.

"Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for the Blessed One's relics, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. There King Bandhumat, together with his host of kinsmen and attended by his host of ministers, held a festival for the stūpa.

"Some time later, one day, a poor man went into the circumambulation path of the stūpa, and there he saw withered flowers and the stūpa covered with dust. Then, recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, he gave rise to faith. He took up a broom, swept the stūpa and cleared away the withered flowers. Then, seeing the stūpa free of dust and free of dirt, he was filled with joy, bowed at its feet, and made this aspiration: 'Through this root of virtue and this arising of the mind, may I too attain qualities such as these! May I please such a teacher as this, and may I not displease him!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the poor man at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Fair Form. Because he swept the stūpa, he has come to have a fair and beautiful form. Through the aspiration he made, he has directly realized arhatship in this very life.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Dugu.

As he played, made love and took his pleasure, his wife became pregnant, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son. She bore a boy who was handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, widely renowned for his greatness, and a delight to behold. When he was born, the whole city of Kapilavastu was filled with his renown.

These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter and every other kind of excellent provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Moreover, he was endowed with faith, virtuous and good-hearted, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, eager to give, delighting in generosity, rejoicing in giving abundantly, and abiding in great liberality. He gave many kinds of gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and the wretched and needy, and so drew them to him.

Then, some time later, the boy Dugu went to the Nyagrodha Park. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo of light a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a mountain of jewels in motion. Then the monks, having become curious, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Dugu perform, such that he has come to have great renown and to be dear and pleasing, and, having gone forth, has directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other former lives Dugu himself performed and accumulated deeds whose collected causes have come together and whose conditions have ripened, which have become like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Since Dugu himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago in times past, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Some time later, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the deeds of a buddha, passed completely into nirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted.

"Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for that Blessed One's relics, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height.

"Then some time later, in springtime, when the trees were in bloom and flowers of every kind had appeared, a householder said to the king, 'Together with Your Majesty, I wish to hang flowers on the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin.' The king said, 'Do so.' Then that householder, the king, the ministers and the attendants had it proclaimed with bells, prepared flowers of every kind, and hung the flowers on the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin. There many hundreds of thousands of living beings felt joy in their minds and generated roots of virtue."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the householder at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Dugu. Because he generated roots of virtue together with a great many people, this became the cause of his being dear and pleasing to the hearts of a great many people. By that very cause he became good to look upon and beautiful, and he has directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Lotus Eye.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas. Venerated and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a Śākya who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son: a boy handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, with eyes like blue lotuses, born bearing on his head a precious divine jewel of sapphire blue. He made the whole city of Kapilavastu take on the color of that sapphire jewel.

Then, when they had held the birth celebration, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall be given to this boy?" His relatives said, "Since this boy's eyes are like lotuses, let this boy be named Lotus Eye."

Then the boy Lotus Eye was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, cream of butter and every other kind of fine provision, and he grew up quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

He was endowed with faith, virtuous and of good intentions, devoted to benefiting himself and benefiting others, compassionate and magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, eager to give, delighting in generosity, rejoicing in lavish giving, and abiding in great liberality. Wherever he went, there he was worshiped and honored by gods and humans.

Then, some time later, the boy Lotus Eye went to the Nyagrodha Park, and there he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, with a radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns, like a moving Jewel Mountain, lovely in every way. The moment he saw him, his mind was filled with joy toward the Blessed One. Having given rise to joy, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. When he had heard it, the boy Lotus Eye shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he gave gifts and lavish gifts, satisfying monks, brahmins, the destitute and the poor and needy. Then he asked leave of his father and mother and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through striving, effort and exertion he came to know that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable. Having seen through every form of formation as subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment toward the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like the sky and like the palm of his hand; he had become cool like refined sandalwood; by knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from worldly gain, attachment and honors; and he became one to be worshiped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then one time, when he went for alms, a great many people looked at him and were amazed. So Lotus Eye went to the Blessed One and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, please make it so that my precious jewel is no more."

The Blessed One said, "Son, since this has arisen from karma, the precious jewel cannot be made to disappear. Nevertheless, it shall be made so that those who have faith see it, and those without faith do not see it." And the Blessed One did just that.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Lotus Eye perform, that he has become so greatly renowned and has attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Lotus Eye himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds whose causes were gathered and whose conditions had matured, which came on like a flood, and whose results must inevitably come. Since Lotus Eye himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruits.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Vipaśyin. He dwelt depending on the royal capital of Bandhumatī. Then at a certain time the perfectly complete buddha Vipaśyin, having performed all the deeds of a buddha, like a fire whose fuel is spent, passed into complete nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates.

"Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for the relics of that Blessed One, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage there and went on to the higher realms and to liberation.

"Then at a certain time, a caravan leader accomplished his aim in a voyage on the great ocean. On his return he brought back from it a great precious sapphire jewel. Seeing the stūpa of the Blessed One, he recalled the qualities of the Tathāgata and fastened that precious jewel to the finial of the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin. By its power he made all the directions and intermediate directions appear the color of sapphire. He also made offerings of lotus flowers and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain such qualities as these! May I please such a teacher as this, and may I not displease him!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the caravan leader at that time, on that occasion, was this very Lotus Eye. Through the ripening of that deed of fastening the precious jewel to the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin, a precious jewel appeared on his head. Because he made offerings of blue lotuses, his eyes became like blue lotuses. Because he made that aspiration, he directly realized arhatship in this very life.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Drum Sound perform, that he has become handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, and has also attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Drum Sound himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds whose causes were gathered and whose conditions had matured, which came on like a flood, and whose results must inevitably come. Since Drum Sound himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruits.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Vipaśyin. "Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for the relics of that Blessed One, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage there and went on to the higher realms and to liberation.

"Then at a certain time, a householder had people trained in music, with all kinds of musical instruments, and offered them to that stūpa. Every day they honored that stūpa with excellent strains of music.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the householder at that time, on that occasion, was this very Drum Sound. Because he offered all kinds of musical instruments to the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin, he came to have a voice like the sound of a drum, and by that very cause he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Son.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas. Venerated and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a Śākya who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth, and what came forth was a great lump of flesh and blood. When the parents, the others living in that house, the servants and the relatives saw it, they were displeased, saying, "What is this that has been born?"

Then, after a while, that householder went into the chamber of sorrow and sat there with his cheek resting on his hand, brooding, thinking, "What is this? To whom should I tell it? Who would know?"

Then the thought came to him: "This Buddha, the Blessed One, is all-knowing and all-seeing. He will know. I shall tell the Buddha, the Blessed One." So he went to where the Blessed One was, and when he had arrived he told the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "Householder, do not be afraid, do not be afraid! Place that lump of flesh and blood in well-carded cotton, and for seven days stroke it with your hand three times each day, and sprinkle it again and again with milk. After that it will burst open and a hundred sons will come forth, and all of them will have the strength of great wrestlers."

When the householder heard this, he was supremely amazed, and he thought, "That such sons should come to be mine is a gain well gained indeed!" He did just so, and when seven days had passed, that lump of flesh and blood burst open and a hundred sons came forth, every one of them handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, complete in all their limbs and features, and every one possessed of the strength of a great wrestler.

Then, as time went on, they were gradually raised and nourished until they were grown. All of them were proud, intoxicated with their good looks and youth, and as they roamed about here and there they went to the Nyagrodha Park. There they saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, with a radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns, like a moving Jewel Mountain, lovely in every way. The moment they saw him, their minds were filled with joy toward the Blessed One. Having given rise to joy, they bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood their dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions and natures, taught them the Dharma in such a way that they would realize the Four Noble Truths. When they had heard it, all of them shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, they asked leave of their father and mother and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through striving, effort and exertion all of them came to know that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable. Having seen through every form of formation as subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, they abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As arhats, free of attachment toward the three realms, they regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; their minds were like the sky and like the palm of the hand; they had become cool like refined sandalwood; by knowledge they had broken the shell of the egg; they had attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions and the analytical knowledges; they turned away from worldly gain, attachment and honors; and they became ones to be worshiped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did these hundred young men perform, that they have become brothers and possess the strength of great wrestlers?"

The Blessed One said, "These men, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds whose causes were gathered and whose conditions had matured, which came on like a flood, and whose results must inevitably come. Since they themselves performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruits.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Vipaśyin. He dwelt depending on the royal capital of Bandhumatī. Then at a certain time the perfectly complete buddha Vipaśyin, having performed all the deeds of a buddha, like a fire whose fuel is spent, passed into complete nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates.

"Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral honors for the relics of that Blessed One, built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage there and went on to the higher realms and to liberation.

"Then at a certain time a company of a hundred friends went out, and when they saw that stūpa they recalled the qualities of the Tathāgata. Together they anointed it with fragrant sesame oil and also paid homage with offerings of flowers, garlands and lamps. Then together they made this aspiration: 'Wherever we are born, may we be born there as brothers, coming forth together from one and the same womb! May we gain the might of great wrestlers' strength, and may we be endowed with good looks! In the future, too, may we please the perfectly complete buddhas, and may we not displease them!'

"Monks, what do you think? Those who were the company of friends at that time, on that occasion, are these great wrestlers. Because they honored that stūpa together, they have been born together in this way and have gained the might of great wrestlers' strength. Because they made that aspiration, they went forth in harmony as one and attained arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the sixteenth fascicle.

Sun.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas. Venerated and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and great mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in the land of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a Śākya who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son: a boy handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, born bearing a precious jewel on his head. From it, rays like the rays of the sun streamed out all around, and its light pervaded the whole city of Kapilavastu at night, making it bright as day.

When the parents, the servants living in that house, the relatives and the Śākyas dwelling in Kapilavastu saw this, they were amazed and swelled with joy.

Then, when they had held the birth celebration, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall be given to this boy?" His relatives said, "Since, as soon as this boy was born, he made the whole city of Kapilavastu bright as the sun, let this boy be named Sun."

Then the boy Sun was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, cream of butter and every other kind of fine provision, and he grew up quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

He was endowed with faith, virtuous and of good intentions, devoted to benefiting himself and benefiting others, compassionate and magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, loving toward all creatures, eager to give, delighting in generosity, rejoicing in lavish giving, and abiding in great liberality.

Then, some time later, the boy Sun went to the Nyagrodha Park, and there he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, with a radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns, like a moving Jewel Mountain, lovely in every way. The moment he saw him, his mind was filled with joy toward the Blessed One. Having given rise to joy, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. When he had heard it, the boy Sun shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he gave gifts and lavish gifts, satisfying śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute and the poor and needy. Then he asked leave of his father and mother and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through striving, effort and exertion he came to know that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable. Having seen through every form of formation as subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction, he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment toward the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like the sky and like the palm of his hand; he had become cool like refined sandalwood; by knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from worldly gain, attachment and honors; and he became one to be worshiped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then, whenever the venerable Sun went for alms, the brahmins and householders who lacked faith would scorn and revile him and mock him behind his back, saying, "Since he roams the highways, streets, crossroads and junctions like this, wearing a precious jewel on his head, the way of life of the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya is ruined! Their brahmin way of life is ruined!"

Then, deeply ashamed, he went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, please make my precious jewel disappear somehow."

The Blessed One said, "Son, since this was born of karma, it cannot be made to disappear. Even so, I shall make it so that those who have faith see it, and those without faith do not see it." And the Blessed One did just that.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what karma did Sun perform that he has become so greatly renowned and has attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "In other, former lives, Sun himself performed and accumulated deeds that have reached maturity, whose conditions have ripened, that have come upon him like a flood, and that are bound to bear fruit. Since Sun himself performed and accumulated these deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the guide who tames beings, the unsurpassed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Then, after some time, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the activities of a buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa, like a fire whose fuel is spent, into the realm of nirvāṇa in which no remainder of the aggregates is left.

"Then King Bandhumat performed the funeral rites for that Blessed One's remains and built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage to it there and went on to the higher realms and to liberation. Then, when the time came for worship at that stūpa, the faithful brahmins and householders worshiped it with incense, garlands of flowers, unguents of many kinds, parasols, victory banners, flags, and the sound of music.

"Then, after some time, a certain man played dice with the king, and as his winnings he gained a precious sunstone. Then, having developed faith, he fastened it to the pinnacle of the Blessed One Vipaśyin's stūpa, bowed at its foot, and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, by this generation of the mind, and by this complete giving up of something to be given, may I too attain such qualities as these! May I please such a Teacher as this, and never displease him! And may I come forth from my mother's womb wearing just such a precious jewel on the crown of my head!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the gambler at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Sun. Because he paid homage to the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin and fastened the precious jewel to it, a precious jewel appeared on his head; and by that very cause he became handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, and he realized arhatship.

"So, monks, the result of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the result of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the result of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Banner of the Mallas.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, respected, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas in the country of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time there lived in Kapilavastu a Śākya who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love, and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son, a boy who was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, surpassing the complexion of humans, though not reaching the complexion of the gods. At the moment the boy was born, the gods raised divine banners all around, and they beat divine musical instruments as well.

They also scattered divine blue lotuses, lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses, and the whole city of Kapilavastu was filled with his renown. In every house, too, banners were raised on his account. Then, when the birth feast for his birth had been held, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "Since, when this boy was born, renown spread throughout the whole world, let this boy be named Renown."

Then the boy Renown was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other fine provision besides, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake. He was a person of faith, virtuous and of good intent, devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.

Then, some time later, the boy Renown went to the Nyagrodha Park. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving Jewel Mountain, beautiful in every way. As soon as he saw him, joy toward the Blessed One arose in his mind. When joy had arisen, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding his intentions, latent tendencies, constitution, and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. When he had heard it, the boy Renown shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty high mountain peaks of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he gave gifts and abundant gifts, satisfied the śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute, and the poor and needy, and then, asking leave of his father and mother, he went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through diligence, effort, and exertion, he understood this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes to be unsteady and unstable; he ascertained that all kinds of formations are of a nature to decay, to fall, to scatter, and to perish; and having abandoned all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was the same toward empty space and the palm of his hand; he became cool, like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he broke the shell of the egg; he obtained the knowledges, the higher perceptions, and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from worldly gain, attachment, and honors; and he became one to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

He used robes that were offered on request, and seldom used those not offered on request. He used food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites that were offered on request, and seldom used those not offered on request.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what karma did Renown perform that, as soon as he was born, the gods raised banners and he became renowned throughout the world, and that, having gone forth, he attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives, Renown himself performed and accumulated deeds that have reached maturity, whose conditions have ripened, that have come upon him like a flood, and that are bound to bear fruit. Since Renown himself performed and accumulated these deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the guide who tames beings, the unsurpassed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Then, after some time, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the activities of a buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa, like a fire whose fuel is spent, into the realm of nirvāṇa in which no remainder of the aggregates is left.

"Then King Bandhumat performed the funeral rites for that Blessed One's remains and built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage to it there and went on to the higher realms and to liberation.

"Then, after some time, King Bandhumat held a festival at that stūpa, and at that stūpa festival the wrestlers raised banners. Then, after some time, one of the king's wrestlers threw another wrestler and won the wrestler's banner. He took it and, with a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of living beings playing music of every kind, went to where the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin stood. When he arrived, he called to mind the qualities of the Blessed One, fastened the banner to the central pole on top of the stūpa, and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain such qualities as these! May I please such a Teacher as this, and never displease him!'

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the wrestler at that time, on that occasion, was this very Renown. Because he paid homage and service to the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin, he experienced boundless happiness in saṃsāra, and by that very cause he has now also realized arhatship.

"So, monks, the result of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the result of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the result of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the section called Various Avadānas, the seventh summary verse, is complete.

The summary verse:

Suprabhā and Supriyā,
Śuklā, Somā, Kuvalayā,
Sundarī and Muktā,
Kacaṅgalā, Kṣemā,
And Virūpā are taught as a set.

Suprabhā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, respected, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a merchant who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love, and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, clothed in divine ornaments and wearing a precious jewel at her throat. A light came forth from it that illuminated all of Śrāvastī.

Then, when the birth feast for her birth had been held, they set about naming her, asking, "What name shall we give this girl?" Her relatives said, "Since, as soon as this girl was born, all of Śrāvastī was illuminated by the light of the precious jewel, let this girl be named Suprabhā, Fair Radiance."

Then the girl Suprabhā was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry her on their laps, two nurses to suckle her, two nurses to wash away her dirt, and two nurses to play with her. These eight nurses raised and nourished her with milk, curds, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other fine provision besides, and she grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake. That girl was a person of faith, virtuous and of good intent, devoted to her own welfare and the welfare of others. Whoever came to her to beg, she would unfasten the ornament from her throat and give it to them. And after she had given it, another ornament would appear.

Then, when the girl had gradually grown up, many sons of kings, sons of ministers, and sons of merchants came to ask for her hand. Harassed by them, her father sat with his cheek resting on his hand and thought, "If I give her to one, the others will become my enemies." And he sat there downcast.

Then, after some time, the girl saw her father downcast and said, "Father, why are you sitting there so downcast?" He then told her the matter in full. The girl said, "Father, do not be troubled. Seven days from now I myself will choose a husband."

Then the merchant informed King Prasenajit, and had it proclaimed throughout Śrāvastī with a bell: "Seven days from now the girl Suprabhā will choose a husband herself. Whatever you have to do, do it."

When the seven days had passed, the girl Suprabhā mounted a chariot, raised a banner made of a dyed monastic robe, had the form of the Buddha, the Blessed One, painted in a picture, and entered the street reciting praises. Then, to the sons of kings, the sons of ministers, and the sons of merchants there, who were gazing at her with longing, she explained clearly, with many kinds of words, "I do not wish to slight you in any way; it is only that I am not one who seeks sensual pleasures at all. I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, and I shall go forth in his presence." And with that, they turned back.

The girl Suprabhā went into the presence of the Blessed One, bowed at the Blessed One's feet, and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, understanding her intentions, latent tendencies, constitution, and nature, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she would realize the Four Noble Truths. When she had heard it, the girl Suprabhā shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty high mountain peaks of the view of the perishable collection, and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she also accomplished the higher perceptions.

Then the girl Suprabhā rose from her seat, draped her upper robe over one shoulder, placed her right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Blessed One with palms joined, and said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable One, if I too may go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a nun, then I too wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One, knowing that she would lead many who were to be trained into this teaching, said, "Girl, go, and look to your assembly as well."

Then the girl Suprabhā came out of the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta and went into the midst of a great crowd that had gathered. There each of them thought, "I shall carry her off by force," and they tried to seize her. Then, as they pressed upon her, the girl Suprabhā rose up into the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings, and displayed miracles of many kinds. Ordinary people are quickly won over to faith by miraculous power, and so they saw that miracle that brings gods and humans to faith. When they saw it, their hair stood on end, and, falling like trees cut off at the root, they bowed at her feet and entreated her, "Noble lady, come down, come down! Since you have realized such qualities as these, it is impossible that you would now indulge in sensual pleasures."

Then the girl Suprabhā descended from the sky, sat in the midst of the great crowd, and taught the Dharma in such a way that, on hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings saw the truths. Then the Blessed One entrusted her to Mahāprajāpatī, who gave her the going forth and full ordination.

Then, through diligence, effort, and exertion, she understood this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes to be unsteady and unstable; she ascertained that all kinds of formations are of a nature to decay, to fall, to scatter, and to perish; and having abandoned all afflictions, she realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, she regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; her mind was the same toward empty space and the palm of her hand; she became cool, like refined sandalwood; with knowledge she broke the shell of the egg; she obtained the knowledges, the higher perceptions, and the analytical knowledges; she turned away from worldly gain, attachment, and honors; and she became one to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what karma did Suprabhā perform that she is beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, that a precious jewel appeared at her throat, and that, having gone forth, she realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives, Suprabhā herself performed and accumulated deeds that have reached maturity, whose conditions have ripened, that have come upon her like a flood, and that are bound to bear fruit. Since Suprabhā herself performed and accumulated these deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the guide who tames beings, the unsurpassed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He lived in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Then, after some time, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, having carried out all the activities of a buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa, like a fire whose fuel is spent, into the realm of nirvāṇa in which no remainder of the aggregates is left.

"Then King Bandhumat performed the funeral rites for that Blessed One's remains and built a stūpa made of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height.

"Then, after some time, King Bandhumat's chief queen, having grown old, took the many kinds of ornaments off her body and offered them to that stūpa. Then she bowed at its foot and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, by this generation of the mind, and by this complete giving up of something to be given, may I too attain arhatship!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was King Bandhumat's chief queen at that time, on that occasion, is this Suprabhā. Because she fastened ornaments of many kinds to the stūpa of the Blessed One Vipaśyin, she became beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, complete in all her major and minor limbs; and through the aspiration she made, she has now realized arhatship.

"So, monks, the result of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the result of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the result of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Supriyā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, respected, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites, was staying with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the wife of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, complete in all her major and minor limbs, and utterly dear to the hearts of all the people living in Śrāvastī.

Then, when the birth feast for her birth had been held, they set about naming her, asking, "What name shall we give this girl?" Her relatives said, "Since this girl is dear to the hearts of all people, let this girl be named Supriyā, the Very Dear."

She remembered her former lives, and as soon as she was born she spoke this verse:

Whatever gift is given, be it much or little,
Grows from the ground of an excellent field.
Therefore the wise, with diligence, here in the world,
Give with faith to the Buddha, lord of gods and humans.

When her father and mother and the others living in that household heard her speak these words, they were frightened and alarmed and grew uneasy. With their hair standing on end, they said, "Alas! This girl is a piśācī!"
