She said, "Mother, I am neither a piśācī nor a rākṣasī. I am a girl, and I wish to give gifts."

Then her mother told the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, "The girl says this." The householder was delighted, pleased, and overjoyed, and he invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to a meal in his house, and on her behalf he had the dedication of the gift recited.

Then, when the girl had gradually reached seven years of age, she asked leave of her father and mother and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One, and she became beloved, cherished, dear to the heart, and pleasing to all the nuns.

Then, at one time, there came a great famine like an intermediate eon of famine, and many hundreds of thousands of living beings died there for lack of food and drink. Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, go and tell Supriyā on my behalf: 'For three months, provide the four assemblies with robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites.'"

Then the venerable Ānanda went to Supriyā and said, "The Blessed One has commanded: 'For three months, provide the four assemblies with robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites.'"

Supriyā joined her palms, received the Blessed One's command upon the crown of her head, and said, "As commanded."

Then Supriyā set out for Śrāvastī to visit the town where she would go for alms. Then, after a while, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard this news and came before Supriyā in great haste. He said, "Supriyā, where are you going?"

She said, "The Blessed One has commanded it. I have been appointed to the work of a provider for three months."

Anāthapiṇḍada said, "I will provide all of that for you. You need not do it."

Supriyā said, "Father, since you have seen the truths and directly perceive even the treasures hidden beneath the earth, what would be so wonderful in your providing this? But I am acting as a provider in order to benefit the poor."

In the same way, five hundred laymen, Queen Mallikā, the kṣatriya maiden Rainy Season, Ṛṣidatta the overseer of the queens' household, Purāṇa, Viśākhā the mother of Mṛgāra, and King Prasenajit each offered, saying, "You need not do it." Then she went into a forest, and there nonhuman beings in human guise also made her the same offer.

Even after these offers had been made, she herself served the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas for three months with robes, food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites.

During those same three months, through diligence, effort, and exertion, she understood this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes to be unsteady and unstable; she ascertained that all kinds of formations are of a nature to decay, to fall, to scatter, and to perish; and having abandoned all afflictions, she realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, she regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; her mind was the same toward empty space and the palm of her hand; she became cool, like refined sandalwood; with knowledge she broke the shell of the egg; she obtained the knowledges, the higher perceptions, and the analytical knowledges; she turned away from worldly gain, attachment, and honors; and she became one to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then, when the three months had passed, the Blessed One made his robes, and when the robes were finished, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and set out with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas from Śrāvastī for Rājagṛha. Supriyā met the Blessed One on the road and said, "I hope you are not weary."

Then, after a while, they reached a forest with water, and as it was midday and there were no provisions, she asked the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas to sit down.

Then she placed the alms bowl in her left hand and spoke these words: "If there is a maturation of merits, may my alms bowl become filled with food of various kinds, both soft and hard." Then the gods filled it with divine nectar. Then Supriyā, following the order of the rows, filled the alms bowls of the entire Saṅgha of monks with food, and there the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, foremost among my śrāvaka nuns who have made merit is this nun Supriyā."

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Supriyā perform, that she was born into a wealthy family, beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, honored by all people, and, having gone forth, directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives Supriyā herself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations were complete and whose conditions had matured, which have come on like a flood and will come without fail. Since Supriyā herself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element; they do not ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames those to be trained, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"Then early one morning the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and, attended by the assembly of monks and leading them, went into Vārāṇasī for alms. At that time a certain merchant had gone with his servants to a pleasure garden, taking with them a great deal of food, both soft and hard. Then a servant girl of his, carrying a basket of cooked rice, was following behind her master. That servant girl saw the Blessed One with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas on the road, and she was filled with joy, and this thought arose in her: 'What can my master do to me? Make me a slave twice over? I must not let slip this chance to offer a meal to the Blessed One.'

"Then, resigning herself to being killed, bound, and beaten, she opened the basket of cooked rice and satisfied the Blessed One with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with various kinds of food. Then she went to the merchant, and after a while the merchant asked, 'Girl, where is that basket of cooked rice?' She said, 'I offered food to the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa.' When the merchant heard this, he was utterly amazed. Then, glad, pleased, and overjoyed, he said, 'Girl, from this day on you are released from slavery; go! While I lay asleep, you kept watch for me.'

"Then she joined her palms and said to the householder, 'Will you permit me to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One?' Then the householder gave her an alms bowl and robes as well, and she took the alms bowl and robes her master had given her and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. For nine thousand years she did the work of an attendant in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and she offered cooked rice, porridge, soups and drinks, regular meals in turn, invitations as guests, garlands of lamps, and kaṭhina robes, and she offered gifts and great gifts. And she made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue of having offered gifts and great gifts to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, accomplished through hardship, by the resolve I have raised, and by giving away the things to be given, may I attain going forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? She who at that time, on that occasion, was the servant girl is this very Supriyā. Because she offered food to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, she was born into a wealthy family, beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, and honored by all people. Through the aspiration she made, she has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, deeds that are entirely black have a maturation that is entirely black as well. Deeds that are entirely white have a maturation that is entirely white as well. Mixed deeds have a maturation that is mixed as well. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and apply yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Śuklā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, among the Śākyas, there lived a Śākya called Rohiṇa, who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, enjoyed himself, and made love with her. But though he played, enjoyed himself, and made love, he had neither son nor daughter, and resting his cheek on his hand, he thought, "Although I possess much household wealth, I have neither son nor daughter. So after I pass away, since I have no son, all that I have will pass into the king's control." And he sat brooding.

Then śramaṇas, brahmins, soothsayers, friends, relatives, and other kinsfolk urged him, "Make supplication to the gods!" So, sonless and wanting a son, he made supplication to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra (Indra), Brahmā, and the rest, and to other special gods as well; that is, he also made supplication to the gods of parks, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads, the gods of three-way junctions, the gods who receive bali offerings, the gods born together with one, the gods who share one's nature, and the gods who constantly follow one.

There is a saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of supplication, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of supplication, each person would surely have a thousand sons, like a wheel-turning king. Rather, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together, aroused with desire; the mother is in season and has her menses; and a gandharva has arrived. From the coming together of these three conditions sons and daughters are born.

So he went on devoting himself to supplication, and a certain being died and passed from one class of beings and entered his wife's womb, and she conceived. Then the master of the house said, "My good lady, if you give birth to a boy, that is well. But if instead you give birth to a girl, I will drive you out of the house together with her."

Then after a while, when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth. She bore a girl who was beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, surpassing human complexion though not attaining that of the gods, clothed in a white garment, and unstained by the impurities of the womb.

Then after a while the Śākya Rohiṇa heard, "Your wife has given birth; she has borne a girl," and he went inside in a rage. Then his wife presented the girl clothed in a divine garment. When the Śākya Rohiṇa saw the girl, he was utterly amazed. He held the birth celebration and then held a naming, asking, "What name shall be given to this girl?" The relatives said, "Since she was born wearing a white garment, let this girl be named Śuklā."

Then the girl Śuklā was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry her on their laps, two nurses to suckle her, two nurses to wash away her dirt, and two nurses to play with her. These eight nurses raised and nourished her with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other excellent provision, and she grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake. As much as the girl Śuklā grew, so much did her garment also grow, and it never became soiled, nor did any dirt stain her body.

Then, when the girl Śuklā had gradually grown up, many princes and sons of merchants came to ask for her hand. Troubled by them, her father rested his cheek on his hand and thought, "If I give her to one, the others will become my enemies." And he sat brooding.

Then after a while the girl saw her father sitting brooding and said, "Father, why are you sitting there brooding?" Then he explained the matter to her in full. Then the girl said, "Father, do not be unhappy. I do not seek the pleasures of the senses. I will go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Father, please give me your permission."

Then after a while, having asked her parents, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, and the very garment in which she had been born became the complete set of five Dharma robes. Then, through diligence, application, and effort, she understood that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unstable and impermanent; she realized with certainty that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction; she abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, regarding gold and a clod of earth as equal, with a mind like space and like the palm of the hand, cool as sandalwood paste, having broken the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, indifferent to worldly gain, attachment, and honor, she became one to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Śuklā perform, that she was born into a wealthy family, beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, clothed in a white garment, and, having gone forth, directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives Śuklā herself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations were complete and whose conditions had matured, which have come on like a flood and will come without fail. Since Śuklā herself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element; they do not ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames those to be trained, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"Then at one time there was the wife of a merchant, a woman endowed with faith, virtuous and of good intention, who went to Ṛṣivadana on some business. There she saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. As soon as she saw him, she bowed at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught her the Dharma, and she gained faith. She offered a meal in her house to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and she offered kaṭhina robes to the Saṅgha of monks. Then in time, having asked her parents, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

"Monks, what do you think? She who at that time, on that occasion, was the merchant's wife is this nun Śuklā. Because she offered kaṭhina robes to the Saṅgha of monks, she was born wearing a white garment. Because she kept the state of pure conduct, she has directly realized arhatship in this life.

"Thus, monks, deeds that are entirely black have a maturation that is entirely black as well. Deeds that are entirely white have a maturation that is entirely white as well. Mixed deeds have a maturation that is mixed as well. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and apply yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the seventeenth section.

The story called Candra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a brahmin who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He had mastered the three Vedas, and he was able to explain word by word the glossaries of names together with the ritual lore, the analysis of letters, and, as the fifth, the legendary histories. He served as teacher to five hundred brahmin youths, instructing them in reciting the brahmanical mantras.

Then, wanting a son, he took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, enjoyed himself, and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself, and made love, his wife conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth. She bore a girl who was beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, complete in all her major and minor limbs.

Then they held the birth celebration and then held a naming, asking, "What name shall be given to this girl?" The relatives said, "Since most of the children in our family are named Candra, let this girl be named Candra."

Then the girl Candra was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry her on their laps, two nurses to suckle her, two nurses to wash away her dirt, and two nurses to play with her. These eight nurses raised and nourished her with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other excellent provision, and she grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake. Then, as the girl Candra gradually grew up, she became learned, clear-minded, and quick of intellect, skilled in her tasks, endowed with mindfulness, and able to retain what she had heard.

Then after a while, when her father was teaching the mantras to the brahmin youths, she learned them merely by hearing them. And having heard them, she was able to explain those treatises, connecting what came before with what came after. Then her fame spread throughout all Śrāvastī. Even non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) came every day to see her and debated with her.

Then, when the Blessed One had fully awakened into unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, he came to Śrāvastī, and most of the learned, and those reckoned learned, went there to see the Blessed One. Then, no longer seeing them, she said to the people of her household, "Why do those who know the treatises not come? What is the reason for this?" They said, "The Blessed One, the omniscient Śākyamuni, has come here, and they have all turned to him."

Then, hearing the word "buddha," which she had never heard before, she felt every hair on her body stand on end. Then the girl Candra, having heard the word "buddha," went to the Blessed One. There she saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. As soon as she saw him, she bowed at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the girl Candra's disposition, latent tendencies, constitution, and nature, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she would realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, the girl Candra, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishing collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she went forth under Mahāprajāpatī.

Then, through diligence, practice, and effort, she understood that this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unstable and impermanent; she realized with certainty that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction; she abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, regarding gold and a clod of earth as equal, with a mind like space and like the palm of the hand, cool as sandalwood paste, having broken the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, indifferent to worldly gain, attachment, and honor, she became one to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then, when the Blessed One told the monks, "Monks, you must recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half month," Mahāprajāpatī said at that time, "May the Blessed One please transmit the Prātimokṣa Sūtra! May the Sugata please transmit the Prātimokṣa Sūtra!" The Blessed One said, "The Tathāgatas, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not transmit the Dharma to nuns word by word. If there is someone among you who can retain it from a single telling, then I will transmit it."

Now at that time the nun Candra was seated, gathered in that very assembly. Then the nun Candra rose from her seat, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "I will retain it from a single telling. May the Blessed One please transmit the Prātimokṣa Sūtra! May the Sugata please transmit the Prātimokṣa Sūtra!" Then the Blessed One transmitted it in full, and from that single telling the nun Candra learned it.

There the Blessed One said to the monks, "Foremost among my śrāvaka nuns who are greatly learned and who retain what they have heard is this nun Candra."

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did the nun Candra perform and accumulate, that she was born into a wealthy family, beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, and became one who retains what she has heard?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives Candra herself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations were complete and whose conditions had matured, which have come on like a flood and will come without fail. Since Candra herself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element; they do not ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames those to be trained, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"Then at one time the daughter of a brahmin went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa. She received the scriptural transmission from her preceptor, studied it, and learned it by heart, and she became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense sources, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible. But she was not able to give rise to the ultimate wisdom. The preceptor under whom she had gone forth had been declared by the Blessed One Kāśyapa foremost among those who retain what they have heard."

"Then, at the time of her death, that nun made this aspiration: 'Just as my preceptor was declared foremost among those who retain what they have heard, so may I too, in the future, go forth in the teaching of that Blessed One of whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa prophesied to the brahmin youth Uttara, "Brahmin youth, when the lifespan of beings is a hundred years, you will become the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha called Śākyamuni," and may the Blessed One Śākyamuni declare me foremost among those who retain what they have heard.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? She who at that time, on that occasion, was the brahmin's daughter is this nun Candra. Because she made that aspiration, she has been declared foremost among those who retain what they have heard. Because she received the scriptural transmission there, studied it, and learned it by heart, she has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, deeds that are entirely black have a maturation that is entirely black as well. Deeds that are entirely white have a maturation that is entirely white as well. Mixed deeds have a maturation that is mixed as well. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and apply yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Kuvalayā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time in the city of Rājagṛha there took place the festival called the Meeting of the Nāga Kings Giri and Valgu, and many people gathered there from all of the six great cities. Then a master of the dance came from the south, and he had a daughter called Kuvalayā, beautiful, good to look upon, and lovely, complete in all her major and minor limbs, and proud with the intoxication of youth and health. Whenever she came among the spectators, all the spectators gazed at her with longing, and she captivated even those of little discernment.

When the festival took place there, the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa also came. Then the girl Kuvalayā said to the crowd, "Hey! In the city of Rājagṛha, is there anyone among humans who equals me in beauty, or surpasses me?" The crowd said, "There is the śramaṇa Gautama with his following." Kuvalayā said, "Is he a human, or is he a god?" The crowd said, "He is a human, but he is omniscient."

Then, having heard those words, Kuvalayā adorned herself with all her ornaments and went to the Blessed One. Having arrived, she stood before the Blessed One and danced, sang, and played music. She also displayed the signs of a woman, the marks of a woman, the gestures of a woman, and the playful wiles of a woman. Those monks there who were not free of desire were thrown into confusion by her, not knowing what to do.

Then, in order to train the monks in whom desire was strong and to remove Kuvalayā's intoxication with her beauty and youth, the Blessed One performed a miracle, a miracle of such a kind that Kuvalayā became old and decrepit, gray-headed, her teeth broken, bent like a roof beam. Then, the moment this was emanated, Kuvalayā saw herself as ugly, and her intoxication with beauty and youth vanished. And the monks in whom desire was strong became disenchanted.

Then Kuvalayā, freed of her intoxication, bowed her head at the Blessed One's feet and implored the Blessed One, "May the Blessed One please teach me the Dharma in such a way that I may be completely freed, with little difficulty, from this body full of pus."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the disposition, latent tendencies, constitution, and nature of Kuvalayā and of those monks who were not free of desire, taught the Dharma in such a way that they would realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, some, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishing collection and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Some directly realized the fruit of once-returning. Some directly realized the fruit of non-returning. And some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhatship.

Kuvalayā too gained faith and went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Through effort, application, and striving she understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable, and she cut through to the certainty that all forms of conditioning factors are subject to decay, collapse, scattering, and destruction. She abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat she became free of attachment to the three realms. Her mind held gold and a clod of earth as equal, and the sky and the palm of her hand as equal. She became cool like refined sandalwood. With knowledge she had broken the shell of the egg. She attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. She turned her face away from the gains, cravings, and honors of existence, and she became worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Those actors too, through that very weariness, abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable, it is wonderful that the Blessed One made the actress's daughter Kuvalayā, who was intoxicated with her looks and her youth, weary through old age, and established her all the way to the consummation of utmost security, nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, now that I am free of desire, free of aversion, free of delusion, completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and turmoil, now that I am all-knowing, possessed of omniscience, and have gained mastery over wisdom and over all that is to be known, what is so wonderful in my making the girl Kuvalayā, proud with the intoxication of her looks and youth, weary through old age, and establishing her all the way to the consummation of utmost security, nirvāṇa? In a past time, while I still had desire, still had aversion, still had delusion, and was not yet completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and turmoil, I made the girl Kuvalayā weary through old age and established her in the five bases of discipline. Listen well and carefully to that, and keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago, in a past time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king called Brahmadatta ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and blessed with good harvests, full of people and of many inhabitants. Disputes and quarrels were stilled; there was no turmoil, no internal strife, no banditry or theft, no famine, and no disease; and it was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. He protected the kingdom without harm, its thorns cleared away, as one cares for an only son.

"Then at one time the king played, enjoyed himself, and made love with his queen. Afterward, from their playing, enjoying, and making love, the queen became pregnant. When eight or nine months had passed, a son was born: she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, of fine complexion, golden in color, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a high nose, a well-formed nose, and thick eyebrows, complete in all his limbs and lesser limbs.

"Then, when the birth festival for his birth had been held, they set about naming him, asking what name should be given to this boy. The relatives said, 'This boy's father is the king of the land of Kāśi, and the boy himself is handsome, good to look at, and beautiful. Therefore this boy shall be named Kāśisundara.'

"Then the boy Kāśisundara was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two wet nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other excellent kind of provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

"When he had grown up, he was consecrated as crown prince. Then, while he was ruling as king, he understood that kingship is full of many faults and is the root of many harms, and he went forth among the sages. He dwelled in a hollow of the snow mountains, living on fruits, roots, and water, wearing deerskin and bark, and performing fire offerings.

"Some time later he went into a mountain hollow for fruits and roots. There, at one point, a kinnarī girl saw the young sage and became enamored of him. She danced, sang, and played music, and she displayed a woman's marks, a woman's signs, a woman's gestures, and a woman's amorous play.

"Then at one point the sage Kāśisundara taught the Dharma to that girl: 'Lady, you have grown old. Your voice, which at first was sweet and soft, has at the end become harsh.' When he had taught such a Dharma and she had heard it, the kinnarī girl was no longer intoxicated with her looks. Then faith arose in her, and she made this aspiration: 'When you fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, may I become your disciple.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? I was the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the young sage. That kinnarī girl is this very Kuvalayā."

Then the monks asked the Blessed One, "Venerable, what deeds did Kuvalayā do, by which she became handsome, good to look at, and beautiful? What deeds did she do, by which she directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Kuvalayā herself, in other former lives, did and accumulated deeds whose accumulation had come together and whose conditions had matured, which were bound to arise like a rushing flood, and which would inevitably come to fruition. Since Kuvalayā herself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, good and bad deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in a past time, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years, there appeared in the world the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, the Blessed One called Krakucchanda, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one. He dwelled relying on the royal palace of Sundara.

"Then at one time a master of actors came from the south. At that time, when the Blessed One had led King Sundara to see the truths, the king commanded the master of actors, 'Perform for me a drama about the Buddha.' They received the king's command on the crowns of their heads and said, 'Your Majesty, we shall do as you command.' Then they composed a drama of the Buddha, rehearsed it well, and performed it before the king together with his assembly of ministers. There the master of the actors himself entered in the guise of the Buddha, and the other actors entered in the guise of monks. The king was delighted, pleased, and overjoyed, and he gave a great heap of wealth to the troupe of actors headed by their master.

"Then they gained faith in the teaching of the Blessed One. Having given gifts and great gifts, they made a true aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, by the generating of this intention, and by this relinquishing of things to be given, may we too please the buddhas of the future, and may we not displease them.'

"Monks, what do you think? Those who were the actors are these, Kuvalayā and the others. Through the aspiration they made then, they have now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Sundarī.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and blessed with good harvests, full of people and of many inhabitants. Disputes and quarrels were stilled; there was no turmoil, no internal strife, no banditry or theft, no famine, and no disease; and it was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. He protected the kingdom without harm, its thorns cleared away, as one cares for an only son.

Then at one time the king played, enjoyed himself, and made love with his queen. Afterward, from their playing, enjoying, and making love, the queen became pregnant. When eight or nine months had passed, a child was born: she gave birth to a daughter who was handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, complete in all her limbs and lesser limbs.

Then, when the birth festival for her birth had been held, they set about naming her, asking what name should be given to this girl. The relatives said, "This girl is the daughter of the king of Kāśi, and her looks are fine. Therefore this girl shall be named Kāśisundarī."

Then the girl Kāśisundarī was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry her on their laps, two wet nurses to suckle her, two nurses to wash away her dirt, and two nurses to play with her. These eight nurses raised and nourished her with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other excellent kind of provision, and she grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, when the girl Kāśisundarī had grown up, six kings of the land sent messengers to King Brahmadatta with this message: "I have heard that a daughter was born to you. Do not give her to anyone else; give her to my son."

Then King Brahmadatta entered his chamber of sorrow, rested his cheek on his hand, and thought, "If I give her to one, the others will become my enemies." And he sat there brooding.

Then at one point the girl Kāśisundarī, adorned with every ornament, went to her father. Seeing her father overcome with sorrow, she asked him, "Father, why are you grieving?" Her father told her what had happened. Then the girl Kāśisundarī said to her father, "Father, please send messengers to the kings of the land saying, 'Seven days from now the girl Kāśisundarī will choose her own husband. Do whatever you must do.'"

When seven days had passed, those six kings of the land assembled. The girl Kāśisundarī, riding in a chariot and raising a banner of dyed monastic robes, holding in her hand an image of the Buddha, the Blessed One, went into the gathering of kings and said, "O kings of the land, listen! I do not care for your looks, your youth, your lineage, your wealth, or your power. I am not one who seeks sensual pleasures. I am a disciple of the Buddha, the Blessed One, whose image is painted on this cloth, and I shall go forth in his teaching."

Having said this, she went to Ṛṣivadana, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "Venerable, if I may go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya and receive full ordination and the state of a nun, I too wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One entrusted her to Mahāprajāpatī, who gave her the going forth and full ordination. Through effort, application, and striving she understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable, and she cut through to the certainty that all forms of conditioning factors are subject to decay, collapse, scattering, and destruction. She abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat she became free of attachment to the three realms. Her mind held gold and a clod of earth as equal, and the sky and the palm of her hand as alike. She became cool like refined sandalwood. With knowledge she had broken the shell of the egg. She attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. She turned her face away from the gains, cravings, and honors of existence, and she became worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Then those princes, remembering her looks, her youth, and her beauty, became drunk with the intoxication of desire, and even though she had gone forth, they kept pressing their suit. When they had made their appeal, she rose up into the sky like a king of geese spreading its wings and displayed various kinds of miracles. Ordinary people are quickly brought to faith by miraculous power. When those princes saw that utterly marvelous miracle, which brings gods and humans to faith, their hair stood on end. They bowed at her feet and begged her forgiveness: "Sister, since you have directly realized such qualities, it is impossible that you would indulge in sensual pleasures. Please forgive us."

Then the girl Kāśisundarī descended from the sky, sat down in the midst of a great crowd of people, and taught them such teachings. When they had heard it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained great distinction.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable, what deeds did Kāśisundarī do, by which she became handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, and by which, having gone forth, she directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Kāśisundarī herself, in other former lives, did and accumulated deeds whose accumulation had come together and whose conditions had matured, which were bound to arise like a rushing flood, and which would inevitably come to fruition. Since Kāśisundarī herself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, good and bad deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in a past time, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was thirty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, the Blessed One called Kanakamuni, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one.

"Then at one time there was a princess, full of faith, virtuous, and of good intention. She had a monastery built, filled it with every requisite, and offered it to the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas. And during the time of the perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa, she also went forth and cultivated loving-kindness for ten thousand years.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time was the princess is this Kāśisundarī. Because she offered the monastery, she became handsome, good to look at, and beautiful. Because she went forth during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and cultivated loving-kindness for ten thousand years, she has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black.

The ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Muktā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a merchant called Jaya, rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, enjoyed himself, and made love with her. Afterward, from their playing, enjoying, and making love, his wife became pregnant. When eight or nine months had passed, a child was born: she gave birth to a daughter who was handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, with a garland of pearls on her head.

Then, when the birth festival for her birth had been held, they set about naming her, asking what name should be given to this girl. The relatives said, "As soon as this girl was born, a garland of pearls appeared on her head. Therefore this girl shall be named Muktā."

Then the girl Muktā was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry her on their laps, two wet nurses to suckle her, two nurses to wash away her dirt, and two nurses to play with her. These eight nurses raised and nourished her with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other excellent kind of provision, and she grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, as the girl Muktā gradually grew up, whenever her garland of pearls was taken off, it appeared again. Seeing the destitute and the needy, the girl distributed her wealth among them.

Then, when she reached the age to be given in marriage, princes, ministers' sons, and many merchants' sons came to ask for her. Her father entered his chamber of sorrow, rested his cheek on his hand, and thought, "If I give her to one, the others will become my enemies." And he sat there brooding.

Then the girl said to her father, "Father, why are you troubled?" He told her everything that had happened. The girl said, "Father, I am not one who seeks sensual pleasures. I wish to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One."

Then at a later time the youngest son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, called Supriya, said to his father, "Please ask for that girl as my bride." So the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent a messenger to the merchant Jaya, saying, "Give the girl Muktā to my son. If you do so, we will become kin, and we will be friends for as long as we live."

Then the householder Jaya told his daughter of this matter. She said, "If he promises that, once he has matured and grown up, he will go forth together with me in the teaching of the Blessed One, then I will make him my husband." He did so, and some time later, on a certain occasion, both of them left home and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Then, through her own effort, application, and striving, she understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable, and she cut through to the certainty that all forms of conditioning factors are subject to decay, collapse, scattering, and destruction. She abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As an arhat she became free of attachment to the three realms. Her mind held gold and a clod of earth as equal, and the sky and the palm of her hand as alike. She became cool like refined sandalwood. With knowledge she had broken the shell of the egg. She attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. She turned her face away from the gains, cravings, and honors of existence, and she became worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable, what deeds did Muktā do, by which she was born wearing a garland of pearls on her head, and by which, having gone forth, she directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Muktā herself, in other former lives, did and accumulated deeds whose accumulation had come together and whose conditions had matured, which were bound to arise like a rushing flood, and which would inevitably come to fruition. Since Muktā herself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, good and bad deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in a past time, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, guide who tames beings, unsurpassed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one. He dwelled in the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"Then at one time a caravan leader set out on the great ocean, accomplished the purpose of his voyage without mishap, and returned. He brought back with him a supremely fine garland of pearls. His wife was handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, and she fastened it on her head.

"Now there lived in Vārāṇasī a householder who was full of faith, virtuous, and of good intention, devoted to his own benefit and the benefit of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma. This thought occurred to him: 'Let me collect offerings from the people, so that the quinquennial festival in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa is not interrupted.' So he petitioned King Kṛkin: 'I wish to collect offerings and hold the quinquennial festival of the Blessed One.' The king commanded, 'Do so.'

"Then the householder mounted an elephant and went through the highways, crossroads, and junctions of the city of Vārāṇasī, collecting offerings. At one point the caravan leader's wife took the garland of pearls off her head and gave it to the collection.

"Some time later the caravan leader came and, seeing that the garland of pearls had been taken from her head, asked, 'My good lady, where is the garland of pearls?' She said, 'My lord, I have given it to the collection of offerings for the teaching of the Blessed One. Please be glad of it; please have faith in it.'

"Then at one point the caravan leader bought it back for a price in jewels and gave it to his wife, but she would not take it back, saying, 'I have given it away completely.' Her husband said, 'My good lady, I have bought this with a great deal of gold and silver; why do you not want it?' Then the young woman took it, gathered many flowers, and also taking incense, garlands of flowers, and the like, went to Ṛṣivadana. There she anointed the perfumed chamber with incense and strewed it with flowers, and she placed the garland of pearls on the head of the Blessed One, and it stayed on the head of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

"Then faith arose in her, and she made this aspiration: 'May I too attain such qualities as these. May I please just such a teacher as this, and may I not displease him.'

"Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the caravan leader's wife is this Muktā. Because she paid honor to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, she became handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, and a garland of pearls appeared on her head. And for that very reason she has now also directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black, the ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white, and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Kacaṅgalā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas in the land of Kacaṅgalā, in the Kacaṅgalā forest.

At that time there lived in the land of Kacaṅgalā an old woman called Kacaṅgalā. Carrying a pitcher, she went to a well to draw water. Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, go and tell that old woman, 'Give water for the Blessed One to drink.'" When Ānanda had told her, she said, "Noble one, I will bring it myself."

Then, at one point, Kacaṅgalā filled the pitcher with water and went to the Blessed One. Kacaṅgalā saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, well adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent like a moving mountain of jewels. The moment she saw him, a mother's love for a son arose in her, and streams of milk flowed from both her breasts. Saying, "My son, my son!" she went to embrace the Blessed One.

Then the monks tried to stop her, and the Blessed One said, "Monks, do not stop this old woman. Why is that?

For five hundred lifetimes
She was my mother without a break.
With a mother's love for her son,
She embraces my body.
If she were prevented
From embracing my body,
She would at that very moment
Vomit warm blood from her mouth.
Seeing this love for a son,
And mindful of gratitude for her kindness,
With a heart full of tenderness and compassion,
I let her embrace my body."

Then, after a while, when her love for her son had calmed, she sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma. The Blessed One understood her disposition, her latent tendencies, her elements and her nature, and taught her the Dharma in such a way that she came to realize the Four Noble Truths. When she had heard it, Kacaṅgalā, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishing aggregates (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, she spoke these verses:

What a good son ought to do
For a mother who has borne hardships,
That which brings the mind to liberation,
You have done for me.
Exerting yourself for me,
You drew me up out of the lower realms
And set me in the higher realms and in liberation;
You have raised me to an exceedingly great distinction.

Then, after a while, she made her request to the Lord and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One. Through diligence, striving and effort she came to know that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five sections is in motion and unstable. She determined that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, she directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, she was free of attachment to the three realms. To her, gold and a clod of earth were the same; her mind was like space and like the palm of the hand; she had become cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge she had broken the eggshell of ignorance; she had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; she paid no heed to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and she became one to be worshipped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Thereafter, whenever the Blessed One gave the nuns a brief instruction and then withdrew into seclusion, Kacaṅgalā would explain it to the nuns. On that account the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, among my nun disciples who expound the discourses in detail, the foremost is the nun Kacaṅgalā."

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did Kacaṅgalā perform, that she went forth only when she was old? What action did she perform, that she became a slave woman? What action did she perform, that she did not come to carry the Blessed One in his last dwelling in a womb? And why was it that she went forth, directly realized arhatship, and was declared foremost among those who expound the discourses in detail?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Kacaṅgalā herself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together and whose conditions are fulfilled, which come on like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Who else would experience the actions that Kacaṅgalā herself performed and accumulated? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, when I was practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, she was my mother for five hundred lifetimes in succession. Whenever I wished to go forth, she obstructed me, and by the ripening of that action she went forth only when she was old. When I was practicing generosity, she put obstacles in the way of my giving, and because of that she became a pauper. Because she did not perform the kind of action that would have made her renowned for greatness, as Mahāmāyā was, she did not carry me in my last dwelling in a womb.

"Furthermore, she went forth in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and there she called the nuns, both those still in training and those beyond training, by the word 'slave woman,' and because of that she became a slave woman. There she trained, recited the texts, and became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense sources, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible; because of that, she has now directly realized arhatship and been declared foremost among those who expound the discourses in detail.

"Thus, monks, wholly black actions have a wholly black ripening; wholly white actions have a wholly white ripening; and mixed actions have a mixed ripening. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves to wholly white actions alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, Eighteenth Section. The story called Kṣemaṅkarā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was respected, revered, honored and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time King Prasenajit of Kosala and King Brahmadatta were at odds with each other. Then, at one point, King Prasenajit of Kosala went to the border of Brahmadatta's country and set up camp there. King Brahmadatta, for his part, armed his fourfold army, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps and the infantry, and set up camp on the bank of a river.

Then, at one point, King Prasenajit of Kosala brought his chief queen there, and he played, made merry and enjoyed himself with her. King Brahmadatta too played, made merry and enjoyed himself with his queen. Then, on one and the same day, a daughter was born to King Prasenajit of Kosala and a son was born to King Brahmadatta. Then, for a time, drums of rejoicing were beaten in the palaces of both kings, and gifts were given to the beggars.

Then, at one point, King Prasenajit asked his men, "What has happened in Brahmadatta's palace, that they are celebrating like this?" and they told him, "A son has been born to King Brahmadatta." King Brahmadatta asked in the same way, and was told, "A daughter has been born to King Prasenajit."

Then King Brahmadatta sent a messenger to King Prasenajit, saying, "I have heard that you are holding a festival because a daughter has been born to you. A son has been born to me as well, so give that daughter to my son. If we do this, we shall become kin, and there will be no enmity between us for as long as we live." King Prasenajit agreed, saying, "Let it be so." Then the two became friends with each other and lived at ease.

King Brahmadatta held a birth celebration for the boy who had been born to him and gave the boy the name Kṣemaṅkara. King Prasenajit of Kosala also held a birth celebration for the daughter who had been born to him and gave the girl the name Kṣemaṅkarā. Then both were nursed and raised, and in time they gradually grew up.

Then the boy sent the girl necklaces, bracelets, garlands, earrings and neck ornaments. When the girl had grown up, she found faith in the teaching of the Blessed One and came to see the faults in sensual pleasures. She asked her attendants, "Where have these gifts come from?" and the attendants explained it all to her in detail, with the reasons.

When she heard this, she said to her father, "Father, I have no interest in sensual pleasures. I wish to go forth into the teaching of the Blessed One, so please, Father, give me your permission."

The king said, "Daughter, because I came to be at ease when you were born, this is not something I can undo."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala sent a messenger to King Brahmadatta, saying, "This girl wants to go forth, so come and take her." Then, at one point, King Brahmadatta set a date, saying, "I will come seven days from now, so make whatever arrangements and preparations are needed."

Then the girl Kṣemaṅkarā heard the talk that she would be taken as a bride in seven days. Kṣemaṅkarā was frightened, terrified and unhappy, and shuddering, she went up onto the roof of the palace. Turning toward the Jeta Grove, she prayed to the Buddha, the Blessed One.

And she said:

Great sage, who abides in love and compassion and dwells in meditative concentration,
Tamer, possessed of a peaceful mind, knower of the ways of perfect peace and discipline,
I go to you, Protector, for refuge; so, Protector, I pray,
Free me, who have no protector, from the lower realms, as is fitting.

On that occasion, there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not perceive or do not understand. The buddhas, the blessed ones, possessed of great compassion, intent on benefiting the world, possessed of a single guardianship, sole heroes, without equal, who do not speak in two ways, abiding in calm abiding and insight, illuminators of the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet are firmly planted on the four bases of miraculous power, long familiar with the four means of attraction, fearless with the four fearlessnesses, who roar the great true lion's roar of the bull, who have entirely abandoned the five factors, who have wholly passed beyond the five destinies, endowed with the six factors, who have perfected the six perfections, who abide in the six constant abidings, rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, teachers of the eightfold path, skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, possessed of the strength of the ten powers, whose renown pervades the ten directions, and who are far more exalted even than those who hold sway over a thousand worlds, by their very nature look upon the world with the eye of a buddha three times by day and three times by night. Their wisdom-vision engages, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is beset by harm? Who is in want, in danger and beset by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and set in the higher realms, in liberation and in the fruit? Whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I establish in sovereign mastery of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I generate roots of virtue not yet generated? In whom shall I ripen the roots of virtue already generated? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, the dwelling of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the hour of its tide pass by,
But toward his children who are to be trained
The Buddha never lets the time pass by.

Then the Blessed One saw that the time had come to train Kṣemaṅkarā. He went there by miraculous power, and having arrived, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she came to realize the Four Noble Truths. When she had heard it, Kṣemaṅkarā attained the fruit of non-returning and also gained the superknowledges. Then Kṣemaṅkarā, having passed beyond the desire realm and gained the remedy, came to abide in fearlessness.

Then, at one point, when the seven days had passed and the time had come to take the bride, the prince arrived together with many hundreds of people and came before the sacrificial altar. The family priest gave out parched rice, butter and unbroken white mustard seeds. Then, just as the young man and the girl were about to join hands, Kṣemaṅkarā rose up into the sky like a king of geese spreading its wings, and many living beings saw her display miracles of various kinds.

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, King Brahmadatta, the prince Kṣemaṅkara, and the other beings who had come to see the spectacle were utterly amazed. They bowed at her feet and implored her, "Young woman, since you have directly realized such qualities as these, it is impossible for you to engage in sensual pleasures. Please forgive us."

Then Kṣemaṅkarā came down from the sky and sat in the midst of the great crowd, and she taught the Dharma in such a way that, on hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings saw the truths.

Then the girl Kṣemaṅkarā asked her father's leave and went to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One entrusted her to Mahāprajāpatī. She was given the going forth, and through diligence, striving and effort she came to know that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five sections is in motion and unstable. She determined that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, she directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, she was free of attachment to the three realms. To her, gold and a clod of earth were the same; her mind was like space and like the palm of the hand; she had become cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge she had broken the eggshell of ignorance; she had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; she paid no heed to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and she became one to be worshipped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

On that account the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, among my nun disciples of great wisdom and great eloquence, the foremost is this nun Kṣemaṅkarā."

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did Kṣemaṅkarā perform, that she has been declared foremost among those of great wisdom and great eloquence?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Kṣemaṅkarā herself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together and whose conditions are fulfilled, which come on like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Who else would experience the actions that Kṣemaṅkarā herself performed and accumulated? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"Then, at one point, the daughter of a merchant there went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa. She made gifts and donations to the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and for twelve thousand years she kept the state of celibate conduct, yet she attained no store of qualities at all. The preceptor under whom she had gone forth had been declared by the Blessed One Kāśyapa foremost among the wise. Then she made this aspiration: 'Just as my preceptor has been declared foremost among the wise, so too in the future, may I go forth into the teaching of the one whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa prophesied when he said to the brahmin youth Uttara, "Brahmin youth, when the lifespan of beings is a hundred years, you will become the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Complete Buddha called Śākyamuni," and may I become foremost among the wise.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the merchant's daughter at that time, on that occasion, is this nun Kṣemaṅkarā. Because she made gifts and donations, she was born into a wealthy royal family. Because she kept the state of celibate conduct for twelve thousand years, she has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, wholly black actions have a wholly black ripening; wholly white actions have a wholly white ripening; and mixed actions have a mixed ripening. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves to wholly white actions alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Virūpā.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was respected, revered, honored and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time King Prasenajit of Kosala was reigning in Śrāvastī. During his reign the land was wealthy, prosperous, at ease, blessed with good harvests and full of people and inhabitants; quarrels and fighting had been stilled; there was no strife, no civil unrest, no banditry, no famine and no disease; and it was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free of harm, its thorns cleared away, he ruled the kingdom as one cares for an only son.

Then, at one point, the king played, made merry and enjoyed himself with one of his queens. As he played, made merry and enjoyed himself with her, the queen conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth: she bore a daughter marked by eighteen kinds of ugliness. A birth celebration was held for her, and she was given the name Rastha.

Then, when in due course she was ready to be given in marriage, no matter to whom she was offered, no one would take her, because she was so very ugly.

Then, at one point, a very wealthy caravan leader named Gaṅga came from the south. King Prasenajit thought, "This caravan leader Gaṅga knows nothing of her defects, so I really must give her to him." Then, when night had fallen and it was dark, the king summoned Gaṅga by messenger, adorned the girl with every ornament, and gave her to him as his wife. Since Rastha had been given to Gaṅga, the name "Gaṅga's Rastha" came into being.

Then, the next day, when dawn broke, the caravan leader Gaṅga looked at the girl and saw that she was exceedingly ugly. When he saw her he was alarmed, but out of regard for the king he did not dare to cast her off, and he kept her shut away in his own house.

Then, at one point, the caravan leader Gaṅga set out for a festival and went to join his circle of friends. His friends had made a rule among themselves: "Whoever does not come to a certain pleasure garden together with his wife must pay a fine of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to the friends." Then Gaṅga came back to his house, went into the chamber of sorrow, and sat brooding, his cheek propped on his hand. Then he thought, "It would be far better for me to pay the fine. I cannot show her to them; the moment they saw her, there would be ugly gossip."

Then Gaṅga locked the door, took the five hundred kārṣāpaṇas for the fine, and went off to join his friends.

Then great sorrow arose in the girl, and she thought, "What good is it to live a life like this? As long as I stay alive, my husband will be unhappy and I will be unhappy too. Now the time has come for me to kill myself." Then she took a rope and went into an inner room to hang herself.

On that occasion, there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not perceive or do not understand. The buddhas, the blessed ones, possessed of great compassion, intent on benefiting the world, possessed of a single guardianship, sole heroes, without equal, who do not speak in two ways, abiding in calm abiding and insight, illuminators of the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, who have crossed the four floods, the soles of whose feet are firmly planted on the four bases of miraculous power, long familiar with the four means of attraction, fearless with the four fearlessnesses, who roar the great true lion's roar of the bull, who have entirely abandoned the five factors, who have wholly passed beyond the five destinies, endowed with the six factors, who have perfected the six perfections, who abide in the six constant abidings, rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, teachers of the eightfold path, skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, possessed of the strength of the ten powers, whose renown pervades the ten directions, and who are far more exalted even than those who hold sway over a thousand worlds, by their very nature look upon the world with the eye of a buddha three times by day and three times by night. Their wisdom-vision engages, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is beset by harm? Who is in want, in danger and beset by harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and set in the higher realms, in liberation and in the fruit? Whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desire, shall I pull out by the hand?
