Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I establish in sovereign mastery of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I generate roots of virtue not yet generated? In whom shall I ripen the roots of virtue already generated? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

The ocean, the dwelling of sea monsters,
May perhaps let the hour of its tide pass by,
But toward his children who are to be trained
The Buddha never lets the time pass by.

Then the Blessed One, while staying in the Jeta Grove, sent forth golden-colored rays of light. With them he lit up that house as if a thousand suns had risen, and he also went there by miraculous power. He untied the noose from her neck and let the girl breathe again.

There are six marvelous and wondrous things that arise in the world: a tathāgata; the Dharma and Vinaya taught by a tathāgata; being born as a human; being born where the noble ones dwell; having complete faculties; and aspiring to virtuous qualities. These marvelous and wondrous things arise in the world.

Then the Blessed One taught the girl the Dharma suited to her. When she had heard it, the girl, with the vajra of wisdom, shattered the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishing aggregates and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Then, having found faith, she served the Blessed One a meal and also offered him robes. Then the girl's ugliness disappeared; she became beautiful, and like a daughter of the gods she sat there lighting up the inner room with radiance. The Blessed One then went back.

Then the friends thought, "Surely this man's wife must be extraordinarily beautiful, and out of a jealous nature he would rather pay the fine than show her. Let us get him drunk on various kinds of liquor, take his keys, go to his house and look at his wife." Then they made him dead drunk on various strong liquors, took his keys, went to his house, opened the doors and saw the girl. When they saw her they were amazed, and thought, "No wonder Gaṅga would not show her to us!"

Then they went back, roused Gaṅga from where he lay asleep under the influence of the liquor, and said, "Gaṅga, to have so beautiful a wife, you have truly found a fine prize!"

At this Gaṅga became even more unhappy, thinking, "I have paid the fine, and on top of that I have become the butt of ugly talk." Then, still unhappy, he came back to his house, opened the door and looked at his wife. Seeing her as exceedingly beautiful, like a forest goddess sitting in a grove of blossoming flowers, he asked, "Good lady, what is this? What did you do to come to have such an exceptional form?" Then she told her husband everything that had happened, and when he heard it, he too found faith in the Blessed One.

Then, at one point, the girl in due course asked her husband's leave and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One. Through diligence, striving and effort she came to know that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five sections is in motion and unstable. She determined that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, she directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, she was free of attachment to the three realms. To her, gold and a clod of earth were the same; her mind was like space and like the palm of the hand; she had become cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge she had broken the eggshell of ignorance; she had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; she paid no heed to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and she became one to be worshipped, honored and respectfully addressed by the gods, together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, feeling doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Rastha do that she was born into a wealthy family? What deeds did she do that she became ugly, yet went forth and directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Rastha herself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds that have reached their fullness, whose conditions have come together, which bear down like a flood, and which will inevitably come about. Since Rastha herself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived the wife of a merchant who was fierce, coarse and harsh-tempered.

"When buddhas do not appear in the world, pratyekabuddhas appear in the world: compassionate toward the wretched and destitute, living in remote dwellings, the sole recipients of the world's offerings. Then, at one time, an ugly pratyekabuddha came to her house, and she reviled him at length, saying, 'What does an ugly one like this want in my house?' and she drove him out of the house.

"Then, to benefit her, that pratyekabuddha rose up into the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings, and displayed miracles of many kinds. Then the merchant's wife was filled with remorse. She begged his forgiveness, offered him food, and made this aspiration: 'May I not experience the karmic ripening of having reviled a pratyekabuddha. May I attain qualities such as these. May I please a teacher even more exalted than this one, and may I not displease him.'

"Monks, what do you think? She who at that time, on that occasion, was the merchant's wife is this very Rastha. Through the karmic ripening of having offered food to the pratyekabuddha, she was born into a wealthy royal family. Because she spoke ugly words and drove him from the house, she became ugly. Moreover, she went forth under the Blessed One Kāśyapa. There she trained and recited the teachings, and became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense sources, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible, and she guarded the state of the holy life. Because of that she has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black deeds is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white deeds is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Here ends the eighth summary verse of the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa.

The summary:
Samudra and Sumanas,
Hiraṇyapāṇi, Tripiṭa,
Yaśomitra, the Apparitionally Born,
Sundara and Kapphiṇa,
Bhadrika and Rāṣṭrapāla:
These are taught in this section.

The story called Samudra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, palace attendants, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a caravan leader who took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he sported, delighted and made love with her. As he sported, delighted and made love, at one point this thought arose in him: "As long as I am in the prime of youth, I should increase my wealth. Later, when I am old, I will enjoy it in comfort."

Then the caravan leader bought an oceangoing ship along with a company of five hundred merchants as his attendants, and together with his wife he set out onto the great ocean. Then, after a time, his wife became pregnant, and on that very ocean the child was born: she gave birth to a boy who was beautiful, handsome and lovely. Having held a birth celebration for him, they gave him the name Samudra, Ocean.

Then, after a time, the caravan leader accomplished the purpose of the voyage and returned from the great ocean without mishap. Later, when the boy Samudra had grown up, his father appointed him caravan leader and sent him off to the great ocean with five hundred merchants as his attendants. Travelling on by stages, he saw villages, towns, cities, provinces, royal capitals and markets, and came to the shore of the ocean. There he hired a ship for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and he also took on the five kinds of hired men who live by wages: those who launch the ship, those who bail out the water, the oarsmen, the bird-handlers, and the helmsmen. Then, having proclaimed the departure three times by ringing a bell, he set out upon the great ocean.

When they had gone out onto the great ocean, the black wind of the rākṣasas drove the ship this way and that. Samudra the caravan leader favored the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas), and, terrified of an untimely death, he set about praying to the six teachers; yet the wind drove the ship around all the more. Then, after a time, the other merchants too set about praying to thousands of gods, and they said:

"Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāyu, Agni and Mahendra,
The various sages and gods, and the many nāgas dwelling on the earth:
In you we have faith, yet here the harm of death has come upon us.
Swiftly dispel these sufferings, we pray, and protect us travellers!"

But though they cried out in lament like this, there was no one at all to give them refuge.

Then, after a time, a layman who was aboard that ship said, "O friends, neither the six teachers nor the other gods can do anything for you. Go for refuge from the depths of your hearts to the god who is truly present, the Buddha, the Blessed One, and he will be your refuge."

Then the five hundred merchants headed by Samudra the caravan leader cried out with one voice and went for refuge to the buddhas, the blessed ones.

Now, there is nothing at all that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not perceive or do not understand. The buddhas, the blessed ones, possess great compassion and are devoted to benefiting the world. They are the sole protectors, the sole heroes, without equal, never speaking with a double tongue. They abide in calm abiding and insight, illuminate the three knowledges, are well trained in the three trainings, and are skilled in the three bases of discipline. They have crossed the four floods; the soles of their feet stand firmly on the four bases of miraculous power; they have long been versed in the four means of attracting others; through the four fearlessnesses they are without fear; and they roar the great and genuine lion's roar of the bull among men. They have entirely abandoned the five factors and have completely passed beyond the five destinies. They possess the six qualities, have perfected the six perfections, and dwell in the six constant abidings. They are rich in the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, teach the eightfold path, and are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments. They possess the strength of the ten powers, their fame spreads throughout the ten directions, and they are far more exalted even than those who hold sway over a thousand.

As is the very nature of things, three times by day and three times by night they survey the world with the buddha eye, and their vision of wisdom proceeds with the thought: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into danger? Who is afflicted by harm? Who is in want, in danger and afflicted by harm? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is sliding into the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation and in the fruit? Whom, sunk in the mire of sense desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I set in sovereign command of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I produce the roots of virtue not yet produced? In whom shall I ripen the roots of virtue already produced? Whom, already ripened, shall I set free?"

On this it is said:

The ocean, home of the sea monsters,
May perhaps let the time of its tide pass by;
But for the children who are to be trained,
The Buddha never lets the time pass by.

Then the Blessed One, while staying in the Jeta Grove, sent forth rays of light the color of gold, more brilliant than a thousand suns, and these lit up those merchants on every side. He also sent forth rays of loving-kindness, cultivated fully over a thousand eons; these refreshed them, and turned back the black wind of the rākṣasas.

Then, after a time, Samudra the caravan leader accomplished the purpose of the voyage and returned from the great ocean without mishap. Made weary of the world by that very brush with death, he gave gifts and lavish gifts, brought relief to his kinsfolk, and satisfied ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and the needy. Then, with his whole retinue of five hundred merchants, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through striving, exertion and effort he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that every kind of formation is by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, his mind was like empty space and like the palm of the hand, he became cool like sandalwood paste, with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg, and he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges. He turned away from the gains, the cravings and the honors of existence, and he became one to be worshipped, revered and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable Blessed One, it is wondrous that the Blessed One gave back to these five hundred merchants headed by Samudra the lives they held so dear, saved them from distress, and established them in nirvāṇa, the utmost and final goal."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, now that I am free from attachment, free from aversion and free from delusion, completely freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and agitation, all-knowing, knowing all aspects, and have gained mastery over all wisdom and all that is to be known, what great wonder is there in this, that I gave these five hundred merchants headed by Samudra the lives they held so dear, saved them from distress, and established them in nirvāṇa, the utmost and final goal? Even in the past, when I still had attachment, still had aversion, still had delusion, and was not yet completely freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and agitation, I protected these very merchants. Listen to that well and closely, keep it in mind, and I shall explain.

"Monks, long ago in times past, on the shore of an ocean, there lived a sage endowed with the five superknowledges, who practiced fierce austerities, ate roots and fruits for food, wore deerskins and bark for clothing, and performed the fire offering. He was compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, loving toward all creatures, and one who protected those who had fallen into distress.

"Then, at one time, five hundred merchants of Vārāṇasī wished to go out onto the great ocean. Travelling on by stages, they reached the shore of the ocean. When they saw that sage, faith arose in them; they bowed at his feet and made this request: 'Lord, if any distress should befall us when we have gone out onto the ocean, we pray that you, Lord, will protect us.' He consented, saying, 'I shall do so.'

"Then those merchants gathered jewels and set out back toward Jambudvīpa. Then, at one point, they were driven all around by the black wind of the rākṣasas, and that sage protected them. Then, having accomplished the purpose of the voyage, they returned without mishap, went to the sage and said: 'O great sage, what is it you are seeking to accomplish, dwelling here in hard striving and with this compassionate nature?'

"He said: 'May I become a buddha who, for a blind world without a guide and without a leader, ferries across beings who have not crossed over, frees those not yet free, comforts those not yet comforted, and brings to complete nirvāṇa those who have not yet attained complete nirvāṇa.'

"They said: 'When you have become a buddha, please think of us as well.'

"The sage said: 'I shall do so.'"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the sage at that time, on that occasion, was I. Those merchants were these men headed by Samudra; at that time too I protected them. Moreover, they went forth in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and since they brought their faculties to maturity there, they have now realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black actions is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white actions is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Sumanas.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and venerated by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the renowned Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in Śrāvastī there lived a householder who was rich, of great wealth and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, a rival to Vaiśravaṇa in wealth. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, delighted and made love with her. As he played, delighted and made love, every son that was born to them died.

At that time the elder Aniruddha used to go about that household for alms. Then the thought arose in the householder: "This elder Aniruddha is renowned as great through the ripening of his merit. I shall make a request of him, saying, 'If a son is born to me, I will offer him to you as your disciple.'"

Then the householder invited the elder Aniruddha into his house, served him a meal, and made this request: "Elder, if a son is born to me and does not die, I will offer him to the elder as a disciple."

The elder Aniruddha said: "Do not forget the promise you have made."

Then, some time later, he again played, delighted and made love. As he played, delighted and made love, his wife conceived, and a sweet fragrance came forth from her body. Then, after a time, when eight or nine months had passed, the child was born: she gave birth to a boy who was beautiful, handsome and lovely, wearing a small garland of the heavenly sumanas flowers.

Then, having held a birth celebration for him, they gave him the name Sumanas. Then they invited the elder Aniruddha into the house for a meal and offered the boy to him. The elder Aniruddha then gave him dyed robes and also pronounced a blessing, saying, "May you live long!" Later, when seven years had passed since his birth, his parents gave him over to the elder Aniruddha. The elder Aniruddha gave him the going forth and gave him instruction in meditative attention. Through striving, exertion and effort he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that every kind of formation is by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, his mind was like empty space and like the palm of the hand, he became cool like sandalwood paste, with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg, and he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges. He turned away from the gains, the cravings and the honors of existence, and he became one to be worshipped, revered and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

He was one of keen faculties: when he was sewing a robe made of rags from the rubbish heap, at each single stitch of the needle he would enter into and arise from the eight liberations.

Then, some time later, the elder Aniruddha instructed him: "Son, go and fetch water from the river Khangden."

So the novice Sumanas took a water jar and went to the bank of the river Khangden. Having bathed there and filled the jar with water, he went through the sky. At times he sent the jar on ahead and the novice Sumanas came along behind it; at times the novice Sumanas went ahead and the jar came along behind him.

At that time the Blessed One had arisen from his meditative seclusion and was teaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. There the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you see this novice coming along with his jar filled with water, mindful, his faculties perfectly composed?

"Having thoroughly abandoned desire and aversion,
And being free of ignorance,
He bears his final body:
How very beautiful is that little one!"

When the Blessed One had thus praised and extolled the novice Sumanas before the Saṅgha of monks, the monks became doubtful and asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable One, what actions did this Sumanas perform, that he was born beautiful, handsome and lovely, as if wearing a garland of heavenly sumanas flowers, and that he is of keen faculties and has realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, the actions that Sumanas himself performed and accumulated in other, former lives have gathered their conditions, their causes have matured, and they now come upon him like a flood, inescapably. Since Sumanas himself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, the actions one has performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

"The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago in times past, in the ninety-first eon, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Vipaśyin. He was staying near the royal capital of Bandhumat.

"At that time there lived a caravan leader in whom, from his youth, the wish to go forth had arisen, but he had been unable to go forth. When he grew old, regret arose in him and he thought, 'I did not do well in failing to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.' Then he hung sumanas flowers on the stupa of the Blessed One's hair and nails. He also served a meal to the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas, bowed at his feet, and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, by this arousing of the mind, and by this giving away of things to be given, may I please the future tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, blessed ones, and may I not displease them. In whosever teaching I go forth, may I there realize the noble qualities while still in my youth.'

"Moreover, he went forth in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and there for ten thousand years he kept the conduct of pure life; because of that, he has now realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black actions is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white actions is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Hiraṇyapāṇi.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and venerated by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the people of the palace, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the renowned Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in Śrāvastī there lived a householder who was rich, of great wealth and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, a rival to Vaiśravaṇa in wealth. He had no son and no daughter. He sat with his cheek resting on his hand, brooding, and thought: "Although my house is full of riches, I have no son and no daughter, so after I am gone, since I have no son, everything I own will pass to the king."

Then ascetics, brahmins, soothsayers, friends, relatives and other kinsfolk urged him, "Pray to the gods!" In the world, indeed, there is the saying that sons and daughters are born through prayer. But it is not so: if sons and daughters were born through prayer, then each person would have a thousand sons, like a wheel-turning king. Rather, sons and daughters are born when three conditions come together. What are the three? The father and mother, roused by desire, come together; the mother is in season and fertile; and a gandharva is present. It is when these three conditions come together that sons and daughters are born.

So he was devoting himself to prayer, and a certain being died and passed from another class of beings and entered his wife's womb.

Some women of a wise nature have five special qualities. What are the five? They know when a man is impassioned and when he is not; they know the right time and the fertile season; they know when they have conceived; they know by whom they have conceived; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl: if it is a boy, it lies on the right side of the womb, and if it is a girl, it lies on the left side of the womb.

Then she, overjoyed, told her husband: "My lord, I have conceived a child. Since it lies on the right side of my womb, it will surely be a boy. Please rejoice!"

He too was overjoyed. Raising the upper part of his body and stretching out his right hand, he uttered words of joy: "I shall see the face of the son I have long wished for! May my son be worthy and not unworthy! May he do my duties! May he support us in return for our raising him! May he enjoy his inheritance! May my family line long endure! And after we have passed away and died, may he give gifts, whether many or few, and make merit on our behalf, and dedicate the offering, saying, 'Wherever these two have been born and gone, may this follow them there!'"

Then, knowing that she had conceived, in order to care for the child he kept her at ease in the upper story of the mansion. In cold weather she was given things to keep her warm, in hot weather things to keep her cool, and the foods the physician prescribed: foods not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent and not too astringent, foods free of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency and astringency. She was adorned with necklaces and garlands, and like a daughter of the gods roaming in the Nandana Grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat, never coming down to the ground below, and she was kept from hearing any unpleasant sound at all.

Then, when eight or nine months had passed, the child was born: she gave birth to a boy who was beautiful, handsome and lovely, complete in all his limbs and parts. On his two hands there appeared two gold coins stamped with marks, which had arisen from the ripening of his karma; and whenever these were taken, others would appear.

Then, having held a birth celebration for him, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said: "As soon as he was born, two gold coins arising from the ripening of his karma appeared on his two hands. Therefore let this boy's name be Hiraṇyapāṇi, Gold in Hand."

Then the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two wet nurses, two nurses to wash away dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other kind of fine provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

He was full of faith, virtuous and of good intentions, devoted to the benefit of himself and others, and compassionate. Whenever he went out into the street and saw ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and the needy, he would stretch out his two hands, and from them would come heaps of gold and silver coins stamped with marks, as many as were needed. Then his fame spread throughout all Śrāvastī.

Then, some time later, the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi went to the Jeta Grove. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as he saw him, joy toward the Blessed One arose in his mind. With joy arisen, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then, after the Blessed One had taught him the Dharma, he said to the venerable Ānanda: "Master, I wish to serve a meal to the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas."

The elder Ānanda said: "Son, kārṣāpaṇas are needed."

Then the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi stood before the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, stretched out his two hands, and piled up a great heap of gold and silver. When the elder of the Saṅgha, the other monks and the elder Ānanda saw this, they were utterly amazed.

Then the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi served a meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, understanding his intention, latent tendencies, disposition and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the four noble truths. On hearing it, the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain of the view of the perishing aggregates with its twenty lofty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truths, he divided his wealth among his relatives, satisfied ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and the needy, asked leave of his parents, and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through striving, exertion and effort he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that every kind of formation is by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, his mind was like empty space and like the palm of the hand, he became cool like sandalwood paste, with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg, and he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges. He turned away from the gains, the cravings and the honors of existence, and he became one to be worshipped, revered and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable One, what actions did Hiraṇyapāṇi perform, that two gold coins stamped with marks came forth from his two hands, and that he went forth and realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, the actions that Hiraṇyapāṇi himself performed and accumulated in other, former lives have gathered their conditions, their causes have matured, and they now come upon him like a flood, inescapably. Since Hiraṇyapāṇi himself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, the actions one has performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

"The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons;
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"Then the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, having carried out all the deeds of a buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, like a fire whose fuel is spent. King Kṛkin performed the funeral honors for his relics and built a stupa of the four kinds of precious substances, one league in circumference and one krośa in height.

"When the festival of that stupa was being held, a gambler fastened two gold coins to the central pole of the stupa. Then he bowed at its foot and made this aspiration: 'Wherever I am born, may I always have gold in my hands!'"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the gambler at that time, on that occasion, was this Hiraṇyapāṇi. Because he fastened two gold coins to the stupa, he has come to have this distinction; and through the aspiration he made, he has now realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black actions is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white actions is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the nineteenth section.

The story called Tripiṭa.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, esteemed, respected and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the people of the royal court, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas, the renowned Blessed One, the Buddha, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time Prasenajit, king of Kosala, was ruling as king in Śrāvastī. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, happy and blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Quarrels and fighting had been quelled, and there was no strife, no internal unrest, no banditry, no famine and no disease. It was rich in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle and buffalo. Free of harm, with all thorns removed, he protected his kingdom as one cares for an only son.

Then, after some time, he played, made love and enjoyed himself with his queen. As he played, made love and enjoyed himself, the queen conceived a child, and when eight or nine months had passed a child was born: a boy, clothed in a dyed robe, wearing the dress of a renunciant, and remembering his former lives. As soon as he was born he asked, "Are the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda and the others, staying right here in Śrāvastī?"

His mother was amazed and, swelling with joy, said, "Son, the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas are staying right here in Śrāvastī."

Then, after some time, she told the matter to King Prasenajit: "A son of yours has been born, clothed in a dyed robe, wearing the dress of a renunciant, and remembering his former lives, and he asks where the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas are staying."

Then, in order to benefit the child, King Prasenajit invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to a meal. The Blessed One, attended by the assembly of monks and placed at the head of the Saṅgha of monks, went to where King Prasenajit's meal was laid out, and on arriving sat down on the seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, took the child in his lap, brought him before the Blessed One, and said, "Blessed One, as soon as this son of mine was born he remembered the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas."

The Blessed One then said to the child, "Tripiṭa, may you be free from illness."

And the child said, "Homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha."

King Prasenajit was utterly amazed.

Then, when seven years had passed since his birth, still wearing those very dyed robes, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is unsteady and unstable, and he ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, and had a mind like empty space and the palm of the hand. He became cool, like sandalwood paste. With knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg. He attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges. He turned away from the gains of existence, from craving and from honors. He became one worshipped by the gods together with Indra and Upendra, one to be praised and spoken of with reverence.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Blessed One, the Buddha, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did Tripiṭa perform, that he was born clothed in a dyed robe, wearing the dress of a renunciant, and remembering his former lives, and that after going forth he realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Tripiṭa himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated those actions which, once the accumulations are gathered and the conditions come together, come forth like a flood and will without fail bear their fruit. Since Tripiṭa himself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer element of earth, nor do they ripen in the element of water, the element of fire or the element of wind. Actions performed and accumulated, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the accumulation is complete and the time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the perfectly complete Buddha called Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

Then, at one time, the son of King Kṛkin went to Ṛṣivadana. There he saw the Blessed One, the Buddha, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels; and as soon as he saw him, faith arose in him. Faith having arisen, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One, understanding his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught him the kind of Dharma that brings disenchantment with saṃsāra, and on hearing it he came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa.

Then he made a request to the king: "Father, I wish to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Please grant me permission."

The king said, "Before long you must be consecrated as regent, so I can do nothing about this."

The son said, "I have no wish for a kingdom, which is full of faults and has become an enemy of the Dharma. If you will not permit me to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, I will not eat." Then, since his father did not give permission, he went without food for one day, two days, three days, up to six days.

Then his companions made a request to the king: "Please consider, Your Majesty: it would be good if the prince went forth, but it would not be good if he were to die here."

So the king gave his permission, but bound him to a promise, commanding him, "Until you have learned the Tripiṭaka, the Three Baskets, do not come to meet me."

Then, after some time, having received his father's permission, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, before long he had learned the Three Baskets and became a teacher of the Dharma, eloquent in knowledge and in liberation. He then thought, "Surely I have not broken the promise I made before." Thinking this, he went to his father, and when they met, his father asked, "Son, have you learned even a little?"

He said, "I have learned the Three Baskets."

Then he taught his father such Dharma that, on hearing it, the king was delighted. Joy arose in him, and he said, "My only son, what do you need?"

He said, "I wish to invite the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas and to offer them the six requisites."

The king said, "The royal palace is vast; do whatever you please."

Then Tripiṭa satisfied the Blessed One and his retinue of twenty thousand monks with excellent food, and to each monk he offered a set of the six requisites. Then, bowing at his feet, he made this aspiration: "Having now obtained going forth with difficulty, by this root of virtue of honoring the Tathāgata together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, by this generating of the mind, and by this complete relinquishing of things to be given, wherever I am born, may I be clothed in a dyed robe, possessed of this dress of a renunciant, and remember my former lives."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the son of King Kṛkin is this very Tripiṭa. For that very reason he was born into a wealthy family, handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, and remembering his former lives.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black actions is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white actions is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Yaśomitra.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, esteemed, respected and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the people of the royal court, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas, the renowned Blessed One, the Buddha, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a caravan leader who was rich, with much wealth and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love and enjoyed himself with her.

At that time a terrible famine struck, and even by begging one could not obtain food. The soothsayers too had foretold that no rain would fall. Then, after some time, the caravan leader's wife conceived a child, and when eight or nine months had passed a child was born: a boy, handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, complete in all his major and minor limbs. And on the very day the boy was born, the drought came to an end. Then his fame spread throughout all of Śrāvastī.

Then, having held the birth celebration for him, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "Since his fame has spread everywhere, let this boy be named Yaśomitra."

Then the boy Yaśomitra was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him in their laps, two wet nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other excellent kind of provision, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, when the boy Yaśomitra had grown up, he went to the Jeta Grove on some business. There he saw the Blessed One, the Buddha, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and made beautiful by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels; and as soon as he saw him, faith arose in him. Faith having arisen, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One then taught him the kind of Dharma that brings disenchantment with saṃsāra, and on hearing it he came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa. Having asked his father and mother, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is unsteady and unstable, and he ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal, and had a mind like empty space and the palm of the hand. He became cool, like sandalwood paste. With knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg. He attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges. He turned away from the gains of existence, from craving and from honors. He became one worshipped by the gods together with Indra and Upendra, one to be praised and spoken of with reverence.

From his two eyeteeth flowed water possessing the eight qualities, and so he was never troubled by thirst. When, in the hot season, the thirsty monks gathered in the Saṅgha for the midday drink, he did not come. Then the monks who were his friends asked him, "Why are you never troubled by thirst?"

He said, "From my two eyeteeth flows water possessing the eight qualities, and so I am never troubled by thirst."

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Blessed One, the Buddha, the one who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did this Yaśomitra perform, that he is handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, that water possessing the eight qualities flows from his two eyeteeth, and that after going forth he realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Yaśomitra himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated those actions which, once the accumulations are gathered and the conditions come together, come forth like a flood and will without fail bear their fruit. Since Yaśomitra himself performed and accumulated those actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer element of earth, nor do they ripen in the element of water, the element of fire or the element of wind. Actions performed and accumulated, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the accumulation is complete and the time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the perfectly complete Buddha called Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"Then, at one time, the son of a merchant went forth under an old monk. But he was lazy and did not want to serve others. So his fellow practitioners of the holy life had that same elder appoint him as an attendant. Then, thinking, 'I am the attendant,' he grew full of himself, and he took to accepting service from monks far senior to him. Because of this his roots of virtue were exhausted.

"Later, at one time, he was struck by illness, and the elder, following the physician's instructions, had him drink medicinal ghee. During the night he grew thirsty and, at a loss what to do, thought, 'I will drink some water.' He went to his own water vessel and saw that there was no water. In the same way he went to his preceptor, his teacher, and the Saṅgha's quarters, and saw that they too had no water. Then, after a while, he went to the bank of the river Varaṇā, and it too was without water.

"Displeased, in order to make his fellow practitioners of the holy life disenchanted, and to show that what is given in faith is a heavy thing, he climbed a tree that stood on the far side of the river Varaṇā, tied a cloth there, reflected on his own deeds, and remained there, resting on his deeds.

"Then, after a while, when the next day dawned, he told the story to his fellow practitioners of the holy life. When his fellow practitioners of the holy life heard what had happened they were displeased and told one another of it. Then his preceptor gave him water, but he could not see that either.

"Displeased, the preceptor informed the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and the Blessed One Kāśyapa declared, 'Strike the gaṇḍī gong!' The keeper of the monastery struck the gaṇḍī, and the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, assembled. The story spread throughout the city of Vārāṇasī, and many hundreds of thousands of beings gathered. Then his preceptor had him sit before the head of the row, filled a pitcher with water, gave it to him and said, 'Son, distribute this water to the Saṅgha.'

"Then, seeing the result directly before his eyes, that very disenchantment led him to generate faith in the Blessed One and the śrāvakas, and with intense resolve he distributed that water to the Saṅgha. Then, in order to benefit him, the Blessed One stretched out his arm, like the trunk of an elephant, and with the hand that gives relief from all fears received that water. And though the great śrāvakas also took of it, it was not exhausted; even when it had been distributed to the entire Saṅgha, it was not exhausted.

"Then, seeing that wondrous miracle, which inspires faith in gods and humans, many hundreds of thousands of living beings came to see the truth. And in his own mind stream too, the roots of virtue were restored.

"When he had recovered from his illness, he made sure that the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, never lacked for water, and for twelve thousand years he distributed water to the Saṅgha. Later, when the time of his death arrived, he made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, this generating of the mind, and this complete relinquishing of things to be given, may I please, and never displease, the one of whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa prophesied to the brahmin youth Uttara, "Brahmin youth, when beings live for a hundred years, you will become the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha called Śākyamuni." And from between my eyeteeth too may water possessing the eight qualities flow.'

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was that monk is this very Yaśomitra. Because for twelve thousand years he distributed water to the Saṅgha and made that aspiration, in this life water flows from between his eyeteeth; and for that very reason he has realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of wholly black actions is wholly black; the ripening of wholly white actions is wholly white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called The Apparitionally Born.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was honored, esteemed, respected and worshipped by kings, by great ministers, by the wealthy, by the people of the royal court, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas. Worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnarīs and mahoragas, the renowned Blessed One, the Buddha, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and supplies for the sick, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, had undertaken to spend the rains retreat in the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three, not far from the Pārijāta, king of trees, upon a stone slab like a white woolen blanket; and there he was teaching the Dharma to the mother who bore him and to the other gods of the Thirty-Three.

At that time the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had undertaken to spend the rains retreat at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the fourfold assembly went to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, and on arriving they bowed their heads at the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana's feet and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana instructed them with a talk on the Dharma, inspired them, roused them and delighted them. Having instructed, inspired, roused and delighted them with many kinds of talk on the Dharma, he fell silent.

Then the fourfold assembly rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, have you heard anything of where the Blessed One has now undertaken to spend the rains retreat?"

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said, "Friends, I have heard that the Blessed One has undertaken to spend the rains retreat in the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three, not far from the Pārijāta, king of trees, upon a stone slab like a white woolen blanket, and that he is staying there teaching the Dharma to the mother who bore him and to the other gods of the Thirty-Three."

Then the fourfold assembly praised and rejoiced in what the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, bowed at his feet, rose from their seats and departed.

Then, when the three months of the rains had passed, the fourfold assembly went to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, and on arriving they bowed their heads at the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana's feet and sat down to one side. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana instructed the fourfold assembly with a talk on the Dharma, inspired them, roused them and delighted them. Having instructed, inspired, roused and delighted them with many kinds of talk on the Dharma, he fell silent.

Then the fourfold assembly rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, please be aware: it has been a long time since we saw the face of the Blessed One, and we thirst for the sight of the Blessed One. We wish to see the Blessed One. If it would be no trouble for the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, may the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana go to where the Blessed One is, and on arriving, pay homage at his feet and ask, 'Are you free of trouble? Are you free of ailment? Do you move about with ease? Are you keeping well? Are you strong? Are you at ease? Are you free of discomfort? Do you abide in comfort?' And please also tell him this: 'Venerable One, the fourfold assembly of Jambudvīpa wish to see the Blessed One. They say this: "Venerable One, the people of Jambudvīpa do not have such miraculous power and might as would let them go to the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three in order to see the Blessed One, approach him and serve him. But the gods of the Thirty-Three do have such miraculous power and might as lets them go to Jambudvīpa in order to see the Blessed One, approach him and serve him. Therefore, out of compassion, may the Blessed One please come down from the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa."'"

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the fourfold assembly by remaining silent. Then the fourfold assembly, understanding that the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had consented by remaining silent, bowed their heads at the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana's feet, rose from their seats and departed.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the fourfold assembly had not long departed, entered into such a meditative absorption that, as his mind settled in equipoise, in the time it takes a strong man to stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanished from Śrāvastī and arrived in the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three, not far from the Pārijāta, king of trees, where the stone slab like a white woolen blanket lay.

At that time the Blessed One was seated in the midst of an assembly of many hundreds of gods, teaching the Dharma. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw the Blessed One seated in the midst of an assembly of many hundreds of gods, teaching the Dharma, and when he saw this he smiled and thought, "Just as in Jambudvīpa the Blessed One is surrounded by the fourfold assembly, so here too he is seated with a great assembly."

Then the Blessed One, knowing in his own mind the mind of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Maudgalyāyana, these beings have no independence of their own. When I think, 'Go,' then they go; when I think, 'Come,' then they come. Knowing my intention with their minds, they come and go."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was and, on arriving, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana looked over the whole assembly of gods and said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, oh, what a varied assembly of gods has gathered and is seated here! Within this assembly of gods there are gods who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Buddha, were born here after leaving their bodies. There are also those who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and of the moral discipline dear to the noble ones, were born here after leaving their bodies."

Then the Blessed One, agreeing with what the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it is so; it is just so. Oh, what a varied assembly of gods has gathered and is seated here! Within this assembly of gods there are gods who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Buddha, were born here after leaving their bodies. There are also gods who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and of the moral discipline dear to the noble ones, were born here after leaving their bodies."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, agreeing with what the Blessed One had said and with what the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it is so; it is just so. Oh, what a varied assembly of gods has gathered and is seated here! Within this assembly of gods there are gods who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Buddha, were born here after leaving their bodies. There are also those who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and of the moral discipline dear to the noble ones, were born here after leaving their bodies."

Then another son of the gods, agreeing with what the Blessed One had said and with what the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śakra, lord of the gods, had said, spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it is so; it is just so. Oh, what a varied assembly of gods has gathered and is seated here! Within this assembly of gods there are gods who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Buddha, were born here after leaving their bodies. There are also those who, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and of the moral discipline dear to the noble ones, were born here after leaving their bodies."

Then some of the gods rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, we, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Buddha, were born here after leaving our bodies." And other gods said this: "Venerable One, we, endowed with faith grounded in understanding of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and of the moral discipline dear to the noble ones, were born here after leaving our bodies."

Then and there many hundreds of gods, many thousands of gods, and many hundreds of thousands of gods, having each declared in the presence of the Blessed One the fruit of stream-entry that they had attained, vanished on the spot.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the gods had departed, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, the fourfold assembly in Jambudvīpa bow at the feet of the Blessed One, and they ask: Are you free from harm? Are you free from trouble? Do you move about with ease? Are you well? Are you strong? Are you at ease? Are you free from discomfort? Do you dwell in comfort?"

The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana, may you and the fourfold assembly dwelling in Jambudvīpa be well."

Maudgalyāyana said, "Venerable One, the fourfold assembly in Jambudvīpa long to see the face of the Blessed One, and they also say this: 'Venerable One, the people of Jambudvīpa do not have such miraculous power and might as to go to the divine realm of the Thirty-Three in order to see the Blessed One, to approach him, and to honor and serve him. But the gods of the Thirty-Three do have such miraculous power and might that the gods of the Thirty-Three can come to Jambudvīpa in order to see the Blessed One, to approach him, and to honor and serve him. Therefore, out of compassion, we pray that the Blessed One come down from the divine realm of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa.'"

The Blessed One said, "In that case, Maudgalyāyana, go to Jambudvīpa and announce to the fourfold assembly: 'Listen! Seven days from now the Blessed One will come down from the divine realm of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa, to the foot of the udumbara tree in the Apadjara Forest, near the city of Sāṃkāśya.'"

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and entered into such a meditative absorption that, as soon as he settled his mind, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanished from the divine realm of the Thirty-Three and arrived in Jambudvīpa.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana came to Jambudvīpa and announced to the fourfold assembly, "Listen! Seven days from now the Blessed One will come down from the divine realm of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa, to the foot of the udumbara tree in the Apadjara Forest, near the city of Sāṃkāśya."

Then, when seven days had passed, the Blessed One came down from the divine realm of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa, to the foot of the udumbara tree in the Apadjara Forest, near the city of Sāṃkāśya. When the Blessed One came to the city of Sāṃkāśya, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered in order to see the Blessed One.

Then there appeared there a monk who was apparitionally born. He invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, to a meal. Then, when the time of the midday meal arrived, the moment he formed the thought, there appeared divine seats covered with great canopies of silk, and divine food, both soft and hard. Then that apparitionally born monk satisfied the Blessed One with divine food, and he also showed fine hospitality to the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, his latent tendencies, his constitution, and his nature, taught him the Dharma accordingly. Having heard it, the apparitionally born monk realized that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he thoroughly ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. Having become an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like empty space and the palm of the hand; he became cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from the gains, attachments, and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of offerings, veneration, and respectful address from the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having grown doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who resolves all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did the Apparitionally Born perform, so that he was born apparitionally, and so that whatever he thinks of and whatever he wishes for is all accomplished the very moment he forms the thought?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the Apparitionally Born himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds that have come to maturity, whose conditions have been fulfilled, that arise like a flood, and that will inevitably come. Since the Apparitionally Born himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the ninety-first eon, when beings lived for eighty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Vipaśyin. He dwelt near the city of Bandhumatī.

"Some time later, five monks undertook to spend the rains retreat in a secluded forest dwelling far from any village. Of these, one monk served as attendant to the other four monks, and through their diligence, practice, and effort those four abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. The remaining monk bowed at their feet and made an aspiration: 'Just as these have directly realized arhatship by relying on me, so by this root of virtue, by this resolve, and by this giving away of things to be given, may I go forth and never be troubled over the finest requisites.'

"Monks, what do you think? The monk who served as attendant at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Apparitionally Born."

The monks asked, "Venerable One, what deeds did the Apparitionally Born perform, so that he was born apparitionally?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

"At that time there lived a merchant there. When his wife was giving birth to a child, she was racked by painful feelings, and she cried out in distress and wept. When he heard her cries, he became deeply unhappy. He went into the chamber of sorrow and sat brooding, his cheek resting on his hand, and this thought occurred to him: 'Oh, what if I were to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, and make the aspiration that I may never experience dwelling in a womb!' Through that very disenchantment he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and he made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue and this resolve, wherever I am born, may I be born apparitionally there. May I never experience dwelling in a womb.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the merchant at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Apparitionally Born. Because he made that aspiration, he was born apparitionally. And because he brought his faculties to maturity there, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black as well; the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white as well; and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed as well. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Sundara.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time in Kapilavastu there lived a Śākya who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like Vaiśravaṇa's, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, made love, and enjoyed himself with her. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son, a boy who was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, surpassing the complexion of humans though not attaining the complexion of the gods. When he was born, many most wondrous things occurred, and these adorned the entire city of Kapilavastu.

Then, having celebrated his birth with a birth feast, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall be given to this boy?" His relatives said, "Since the city of Kapilavastu was made beautiful when he was born, this boy shall be named Sundara."

Then the boy Sundara was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to clean him, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and all other kinds of fine provisions, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, when he had grown up, he went to the Nyagrodha Park in order to see the Blessed One. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. The moment he saw him, his mind filled with joy toward the Blessed One. Filled with joy, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, his latent tendencies, his constitution, and his nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, the boy Sundara shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he asked his father and mother for permission and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through diligence, practice, and effort he realized that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he thoroughly ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. Having become an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like empty space and the palm of the hand; he became cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from the gains, attachments, and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of offerings, veneration, and respectful address from the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having grown doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who resolves all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Sundara perform, so that he is handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, surpassing the complexion of humans though not attaining the complexion of the gods, and so that when he was born many most wondrous things occurred, which made the whole city of Kapilavastu beautiful?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Sundara himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated deeds that have come to maturity, whose conditions have been fulfilled, that arise like a flood, and that will inevitably come. Since Sundara himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for forty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Krakucchanda. He dwelt near the royal capital, the city of Śobhāvatī. Later King Śobha built a stupa for his hair and nail clippings.

"Then, some time afterward, when a festival took place, a group of friends went to that stupa. When they saw the stupa, faith arose in them and they hung flowers on it. One of those friends said, 'I have nothing, so I will not do anything,' and he left the group of friends. But then regret arose in him, and he gathered flowers of many kinds and offered them to that same stupa."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The friend who at that time, on that occasion, felt regret and offered flowers at the stupa of the hair and nails of the perfectly complete Buddha Krakucchanda was none other than this Sundara.

"Monks, Sundara also performed and accumulated other deeds. Monks, long ago, in times past, there lived a merchant in the city of Vārāṇasī who saw a pratyekabuddha who was ill. Faith arose in him, and he bowed at his feet and offered him almsfood, and he also offered him clothing. Monks, what do you think? The one who was the merchant at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Sundara.

"Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he was a poor woodgatherer. He went to gather wood in a mountain valley, and there he saw a stupa, and grass had grown up in the courtyard around that stupa. Faith arose in him, and he pulled out the grass, took up a broom, and swept the stupa and the courtyard of the stupa. Then he bowed at its foot and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue and this resolve, may I become handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful. In the future, may I please the perfectly complete buddhas, and may I never displease them.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the poor woodgatherer at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this very Sundara.
