Because he swept the stupa and the courtyard of the stupa, wherever he has been born he has been handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful. And for that very reason he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black as well; the ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white as well; and the ripening of mixed deeds is mixed as well. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves solely to entirely white deeds. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the twentieth section.

The story called Kapphiṇa.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time in the south a king called Thoughtful was ruling. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Quarrels and fighting had ceased; there was no unrest, no internal strife, no banditry, no famine, and no disease; and it abounded in sāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. He ruled his kingdom without harm, with its thorns removed, as one would care for an only son.

Then, some time later, he played, made love, and enjoyed himself with his queen. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, the queen conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son, a boy who was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, complete in all his major and minor limbs. Then, having celebrated his birth with a birth feast, they named him Kapphiṇa.

Then the boy Kapphiṇa was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to clean him, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and all other kinds of fine provisions, and he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

On the very day that the king's son Kapphiṇa was born, sons were also born to eighteen thousand ministers, and every one of them had the strength of a great champion. Each of them, too, was given a name suited to his own circumstances.

Then, some time later, King Thoughtful died, and after him his son Kapphiṇa was installed as king. All of those eighteen thousand sons of ministers were appointed as the king's ministers.

Later, King Mahākapphiṇa went hunting, attended by the eighteen thousand ministers. Looking at his whole great army before him and behind him, he asked the ministers, "Tell me, who else is there now who has a great army such as mine?"

The ministers, speaking to please him, said, "Your Majesty, there is no one who has one."

Then some merchants who had traveled from the Middle Country to the south presented gifts to King Mahākapphiṇa. The king said, "Merchants, who is the king of that country?"

The merchants replied, "Your Majesty, in some lands an assembly of many rules; in some lands a king rules."

Then, some time later, King Mahākapphiṇa sent messengers to the six great cities, beginning with Śrāvastī, saying, "Even if you happen to be standing, do not sit down, but come quickly! If you do not do so, you will be severely punished."

When they heard these words, the kings who lived in the six great cities were frightened, terrified, and dismayed, and they shuddered. They assembled, gathered together, reached an agreement, and came to Śrāvastī. Then they went to the Blessed One and told the Blessed One the matter in full. The Blessed One reassured them and said, "Bring that messenger to me." So they instructed the messenger, "There is a king above our kings; go before him for now."

Then the Blessed One, knowing that the messenger was coming, transformed the Jeta Grove, the park of the prince, into the four kinds of jewels, so that it resembled Sudarśana, the city of the gods. He stationed the Four Great Kings as its gatekeepers. He also arrayed elephants like Airāvaṇa, horses like Balāhaka, chariots like Nandighoṣa, and men like fearsome yakṣas. The Blessed One emanated himself in the guise of a universal monarch. He also emanated a lion throne about seven palm trees high, and the Blessed One sat upon it.

When the messenger saw such splendors, he was utterly amazed. Then the Blessed One wrote a letter and said to the messenger, "Tell King Kapphiṇa that I say: 'The moment you see this letter, even if you happen to be standing, do not sit down, but come quickly! If you do not come, I will come with a great host of troops.'"

The messenger went and delivered the letter and the message to King Mahākapphiṇa, and did all that he had been told. Then King Mahākapphiṇa, attended by the eighteen thousand ministers, traveled stage by stage until he reached Śrāvastī. The kings of the land went out to meet King Mahākapphiṇa, invited him into the city with great honor, and when he had rested from his journey they informed the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that he was coming, emanated everything as before. When King Mahākapphiṇa went to the Jeta Grove, the moment he saw it, the pride he took in his appearance and the pride he took in his power vanished. But his arrogance about his strength still remained.

Then the Blessed One formed a worldly thought, thinking, "It would be good if Śakra, lord of the gods, came bringing Indra's bow." The very moment the Blessed One formed that thought, Śakra, lord of the gods, in the guise of a charioteer, presented Indra's bow.

Then the Blessed One gave it to King Mahākapphiṇa, but King Mahākapphiṇa could not even lift it, let alone draw it. Then the Blessed One emanated seven great iron drums, and he himself drew that bow into the shape of a half moon and shot an arrow, which pierced all seven great iron drums straight through. From them came forth a sound:

Set out on renunciation!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching!
As an elephant crushes a hut of reeds,
Crush the army of the Lord of Death!
Whoever, in this very Dharma and Vinaya,
Conducts himself with heedfulness
Will fully abandon the cycle of births
And bring suffering to an end.

That sound rang out as far as the realm of the Akaniṣṭha gods. Then King Mahākapphiṇa's arrogance about his strength vanished as well, and the thought occurred to him, "Oh! What is this?"

Then the Blessed One, understanding the workings of King Mahākapphiṇa's mind, made the guise of a universal monarch disappear and spoke this sūtra:

"Monks, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, possesses the ten powers, is fearless with the four fearlessnesses, claims the lofty place of the leader of the herd, turns the Brahmā wheel, and in the assembly roars the true lion's roar, namely: When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are formations; conditioned by formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name and form; conditioned by name and form are the six sense sources; conditioned by the six sense sources is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; conditioned by birth arise old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and distress. Thus this whole great mass of suffering comes to be.

"That is to say: When this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; from the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; from the cessation of consciousness, name and form cease; from the cessation of name and form, the six sense sources cease; from the cessation of the six sense sources, contact ceases; from the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; from the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; from the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; from the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases; from the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; from the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and distress cease. Thus this whole great mass of suffering ceases.

"Monks, my Dharma is well spoken, clearly laid open, cuts off the flow, and is rightly and well taught, down to gods and humans. In a Dharma thus well spoken, clearly laid open, cutting off the flow, and rightly and well taught, down to gods and humans, it is only fitting that a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith should strive in the Teacher's teaching. It is fitting that he apply himself. It is fitting that he be heedful. It is an easy thing for the flesh and blood of the body to dry up entirely, until only skin, sinews, and bones are left. But one who has undertaken diligence in the Dharma, who is capable, diligent, enthusiastic, and valiant, should never give up diligence midway, until he has attained whatever is to be attained through unrelenting effort. Why is that? The lazy person dwells in suffering, mingled with evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, that bring renewed existence, that are feverish, that have suffering as their ripening, and that lead to future birth, old age, and death; and his great aim falls utterly into ruin. One who has undertaken diligence dwells in happiness, unmingled with evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, that bring renewed existence, that are feverish, that have suffering as their ripening, and that lead to future birth, old age, and death; and his great aim is brought to complete fulfillment.

"Monks, the Teacher himself is present here before you and teaches the Dharma, which brings peace, leads to complete nirvāṇa, and leads to perfect awakening. This scripture spoken by the Sugata is worthy to be drunk as the very essence. Therefore, monks, those who rightly see their own aim, the aim of others, and the aim of both should each train well in this, thinking, 'How can our going forth become meaningful, fruitful, productive of happiness, and ripen in happiness? And how can the honor shown by those whose clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick we enjoy become of very great fruit, very great benefit, very great splendor, and very great extent?' Monks, you should train in this way."

When this discourse on the Dharma had been spoken, King Mahākapphiṇa, together with his retinue of eighteen thousand ministers, shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through exertion, striving, and effort he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, with a mind for which gold and a clod of earth were equal and to which space and the palm of the hand were alike, become cool like refined sandalwood, having broken the shell of the egg with knowledge, having obtained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, turning away from gain, from attachment, and from honors in existence, he became one worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did the venerable Kapphiṇa perform, that he was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, that together with his retinue of eighteen thousand ministers he came to possess the strength of a great champion, and that, having gone forth, he also directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Kapphiṇa himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together, whose conditions have ripened, which are present like a rushing flood, and which inevitably come to pass. Since Kapphiṇa himself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen on the external earth element, nor do they ripen on the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely on the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the accumulation is complete and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, ninety-one eons ago, when people lived for eighty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He dwelt in dependence on the royal capital Bandhumatī. Then, at one time, a ship captain returned from the great ocean bringing many precious jewels, and he invited the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas, for meals for three months. He also built a monastery and offered it to the Saṅgha of the four directions. Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the ship captain was none other than this Kapphiṇa.

"Monks, Kapphiṇa also performed and accumulated other actions. Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king called Brahmadatta ruled. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and quarrels were stilled; there were no disturbances, no uprisings, no robbers, no famines, and no diseases; and it was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Endowed with the Dharma, a Dharma king, he ruled in accordance with the Dharma. Later, attended by eighteen thousand ministers, he went to a pleasure grove whose trees were in full bloom, a woodland resounding with the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds. In that pleasure grove he saw a pratyekabuddha who was ill, and for three months he served him with wholesome food. After the pratyekabuddha had passed into complete nirvāṇa, he built a stūpa for his relics and, together with his assembly of ministers, anointed it with sesame oil. Because of this, he and his retinue came to possess the strength of a great champion. Moreover, during the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa he went forth, and because he ripened his faculties there, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black. The ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white. The ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandoning entirely black actions and mixed actions, you should devote yourselves solely to entirely white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Bhadrika. The Buddha, the Blessed One, honored, esteemed, revered, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, ship captains, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; the Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then, twelve years after the Blessed One had attained perfect, complete awakening, when those twelve years had passed and he came to the city of Kapilavastu, many thousands of Śākyas, Droṇodana, Amṛtodana, and others, saw the truths; only King Śuddhodana did not. Then King Śuddhodana, seeing those excellent qualities of his son, was supremely amazed, and this thought arose in him: "If my son had not gone forth, he would have become a wheel-turning king, victorious to the four frontiers, endowed with the Dharma, a Dharma king. Now that he has gone forth as a shaven renunciant, he is most unbecomingly attended. I had better have one person from each Śākya household go forth."

Then King Śuddhodana had a bell sounded in the city to assemble all the Śākyas. When all the Śākyas had gathered, King Śuddhodana said, "O Śākyas, listen! Even if Prince Sarvārthasiddha had not gone forth, you alone would have had to serve him. Now that he has gone forth, let one person from each Śākya household go forth in order to serve him."

Then five hundred sons of the Śākyas, Bhadrika, Aniruddha, Revata, Devadatta, and others, set out to go forth. Then Upāli, their barber and attendant, seeing them going forth, wept. The Śākyas asked him, "Upāli, why are you crying?" Crying out "Alas, alas! Woe, woe!" and lamenting, he said, "If you go forth, who will there be now to support me with food and clothing?" The Śākyas said, "Then, Upāli, spread out a cloth." When he had spread out the cloth, the Śākyas heaped up in a great pile the necklaces, half-necklaces, jewels, pearls, beryls, armlets, and finger rings that they wore on their bodies, and gave them to him.

Then the barber Upāli, seeing them going forth and looking at the many kinds of ornaments, gave rise to proper attention: "These Śākyas are endowed with lineage, good looks, youth, and wealth. Yet they have cast off their wives and these ornaments like spittle and gone forth. Then why should I, who own nothing at all, send these ornaments home? I had better leave them and go forth after these men myself."

Then the barber Upāli went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, if even such as we may go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and may go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a monk, then I too wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." Then the Blessed One said, "Come, monk," and so he went forth.

Then the five hundred Śākyas, Bhadrika and the others, now in the garb of monks, were made to bow to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. But they recognized Upāli's feet, and because they were endowed with lineage, good looks, and wealth, they could not bring themselves to bow to Upāli. Thereupon the Blessed One said to the venerable Bhadrika, "Bhadrika, since in this teaching of mine there is no regard for lineage, good looks, youth, power, or the purity of the four castes, bow to him!" Then the five hundred Śākyas, Bhadrika and the others, letting the nature of the Dharma prevail, bowed at his feet like a tree cut down at the root. The very moment they bowed at his feet, this great earth quaked in six ways.

Then the venerable Bhadrika, through exertion, striving, and effort, understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, with a mind for which gold and a clod of earth were equal and to which space and the palm of the hand were alike, become cool like refined sandalwood, having broken the shell of the egg with knowledge, having obtained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, turning away from gain, from attachment, and from honors in existence, he became one worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

He was a great being, compassionate toward the miserable and the destitute. Later, one morning, having put on his lower garment and his Dharma robe and taken his alms bowl, he set out into Śrāvastī for alms. Then, at one point, he went for alms to the house of a lowborn family. At that time King Prasenajit of Kosala, mounted on his chief elephant called Ekapuṇḍarīka, had set out with his driver Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa to see the Blessed One. King Prasenajit of Kosala saw Bhadrika, his faculties calm, his mind calm, possessed of a supremely disciplined and utterly peaceful mind, wearing robes of rags from a rubbish heap and carrying poor food, coming out of that lowborn family's house. Seeing him, he asked his driver Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa, "Is that not the monk Bhadrika?" The driver said, "It is as Your Majesty says; it is he." Then King Prasenajit of Kosala fainted, swooned, and fell to the ground. When he had been sprinkled with water, he revived, and once he had recovered his senses, his driver Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa helped him up.

Then King Prasenajit went before the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, I have seen something marvelous. Bhadrika, the king of the Śākyas, wearing robes of rags from a rubbish heap and carrying poor food, having received alms with a most peaceful deportment that inspires faith in gods and humans, was coming back out of the house of a lowborn family. At that, I thought this:

'The teaching of the Blessed One is truly what brings perfect discipline. When one relies on it, one comes to such contentment, and it is most wondrous that even those raised in comfort become so disciplined in their ways.'"

The Blessed One said, "Great king, there is something else about Bhadrika that is even more wondrous; listen! Great king, whether this Bhadrika dwells in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, he utters these words of joy three times: 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! When I had not yet gone forth, I lived within the royal palace, very well guarded by great ministers, townspeople, and country people, and protected by walls, moats, gates, and bolts; yet my heart feared others and was without joy, I was suspicious of everyone, and I could not even sleep. Now that I have no regard even for body and life, I can dwell at ease wherever I am.'"

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did the venerable Bhadrika perform and accumulate in other, former lives, that he was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, that he was born into a wealthy royal family, and that, having gone forth, he also directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Bhadrika himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together, whose conditions have ripened, which are present like a rushing flood, and which inevitably come to pass. Since Bhadrika himself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen on the external earth element, nor do they ripen on the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely on the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the accumulation is complete and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, a beggar lived in the city of Vārāṇasī. Overcome by a hungry body and weakness, he was wandering here and there when he saw a girl carrying cakes. Wanting the cakes, the beggar went after the girl, snatched one cake by force, and ran off this way and that. The girl followed close behind him. Then the beggar, without hesitating, plunged into the river Varaṇā.

"At times when buddhas do not appear, pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, compassionate toward the miserable and the destitute, living in remote dwellings, the sole field of offering for the world. At one point a pratyekabuddha came before that beggar. When the beggar saw the pratyekabuddha's peaceful deportment, great joy arose in him, and with that great joy, offering it up along with his own misery, he presented the cake to the pratyekabuddha. Then, in order to make his joy vast, the pratyekabuddha rose up into the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings and displayed various kinds of miracles. When the beggar saw that utterly marvelous miracle, which inspires faith in gods and humans, he bowed at his feet like a tree cut down at the root and made this aspiration: 'Through this root of virtue of offering to one worthy of offerings who has accomplished his vows, through this generation of the mind, and through this giving away of a gift, wherever I am born, may I be born there into a high family and attain qualities such as these! May I please teachers even more exalted than this one, and may I never displease them!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the beggar was none other than this Bhadrika. Through the ripening of that action of offering a cake to the pratyekabuddha, he was born into the wealthy family of the Śākyas. Moreover, during the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa he went forth, and because he kept the conduct of the holy life there for ten thousand years, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black. The ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white. The ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandoning entirely black actions and mixed actions, you should devote yourselves solely to entirely white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Rāṣṭrapāla. The Buddha, the Blessed One, honored, esteemed, revered, and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, ship captains, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; the Buddha, the Blessed One, worshipped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas in the land called Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, in the Sthūlakoṣṭhaka forest.

At that time, in the land of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, a king called Kauravya was ruling. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and quarrels were stilled; there were no disturbances, no uprisings, no robbers, no famines, and no diseases; and it was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Endowed with the Dharma, a Dharma king, he ruled in accordance with the Dharma.

Now the son of his younger brother, called Rāṣṭrapāla, was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, complete in all his major and minor limbs. The Blessed One saw that the time had come to discipline him. In the morning he put on his lower garment and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and, going before the Saṅgha of monks and attended by the assembly of monks, went into Sthūlakoṣṭhaka for alms. Rāṣṭrapāla saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. The moment he saw him, his mind became joyful toward the Blessed One. Joy having arisen in him, he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and asked to go forth.

Then the Blessed One said to him, "Son, have your father and mother given you permission?" Rāṣṭrapāla replied, "Venerable One, they have not given permission." The Blessed One said, "Son, tathāgatas and the śrāvakas of tathāgatas do not let anyone go forth or receive full ordination without the permission of his father and mother."

Then Rāṣṭrapāla went to his father and mother. Having arrived, he spoke in praise of the Buddha: "I have seen the Blessed One, the perfectly complete Buddha Śākyamuni, who, having given up the flourishing kingdom of a wheel-turning king and sixty thousand queens, shaved his head and put on the patched Dharma robe, and is now dwelling right here in Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, going about for alms. It is fitting that you permit me to go forth after the Blessed One who has gone forth." But his father and mother did not give permission. Then he fasted for one day, two days, three days, up to six days.

Then Rāṣṭrapāla's father and mother went to where their son Rāṣṭrapāla was. Having arrived, they said this to their son Rāṣṭrapāla: "Son Rāṣṭrapāla, understand this! You have lived in comfort and you want a pleasant life. You have never known hardship, and the holy life is hard to practice. Dwelling in solitude is hard. Living alone is hard to delight in. Taking up residence in the wilderness, in forest thickets, and in remote dwellings is hard even to think of. Son Rāṣṭrapāla, stay right here and enjoy the pleasures of the senses. Give gifts too, and make merit too." But though they spoke thus, the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla said nothing at all.

Then the parents of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla urged his relatives, saying, "O relatives, entreat our son Rāṣṭrapāla!" Then the relatives of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla went to where the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla was. Having arrived, they said this to the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla: "Son Rāṣṭrapāla, understand this! You have lived in comfort and you want a pleasant life. You have never known hardship, and the holy life is hard to practice. Dwelling in solitude is hard. Living alone is hard to delight in. Taking up residence in the wilderness, in forest thickets, and in remote dwellings is hard even to think of. Son Rāṣṭrapāla, stay right here and enjoy the pleasures of the senses. Give gifts too, and make merit too." But though they spoke thus, the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla said nothing at all.

Then the parents of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla urged Rāṣṭrapāla's friends, saying, "O young men, entreat our son Rāṣṭrapāla!" Then the friends of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla went to where Rāṣṭrapāla was. Having arrived, they said this to the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla: "Dear Rāṣṭrapāla, understand this! You have lived in comfort and you want a pleasant life. You have never known hardship, and the holy life is hard to practice. Dwelling in solitude is hard. Living alone is hard to delight in. Taking up residence in the wilderness, in forest thickets, and in remote dwellings is hard even to think of. Dear Rāṣṭrapāla, stay right here and enjoy the pleasures of the senses. Give gifts too, and make merit too." But though they spoke thus, the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla said nothing at all.

Then the friends of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla went to where Rāṣṭrapāla's father and mother were. Having arrived, they said this to the parents of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla: "Father and mother, please understand this! What good would it be if dear Rāṣṭrapāla were to die? Allow him to go forth with genuine faith from home into homelessness. If he comes to delight in the going forth, then, as he will be alive, you will see him. If he does not delight in it, there is no place for a son to go other than his father and mother." The parents said, "Young men, if, after our son Rāṣṭrapāla has gone forth, he will come to meet us, then we give our permission on that condition."

Then the friends of the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla went to where the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla was. Having arrived, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla: "Dear Rāṣṭrapāla, your father and mother have given you permission to go forth, but they say they will grant it only if, after you have gone forth, you will come to meet them." Rāṣṭrapāla said, "Yes, I will meet them."

Then the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla gradually regained the might and strength of his body and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder's son Rāṣṭrapāla said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, my father and mother have given me permission. If I may go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a monk, then I too wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." When he had made this request, the son of good family Rāṣṭrapāla went forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, received full ordination, and attained the state of a monk.

Having gone forth in this way, through exertion, striving, and effort he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, with a mind for which gold and a clod of earth were equal and to which space and the palm of the hand were alike, become cool like refined sandalwood, having broken the shell of the egg with knowledge, having obtained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges, turning away from gain, from attachment, and from honors in existence, he became one worthy of the worship, veneration, and respectful address of the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Thereupon the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, foremost among my śrāvaka monks who dwell in the wilderness is this one: the monk Rāṣṭrapāla."

Then the monks, having become doubtful, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla perform, that he was born into a wealthy family, that he was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, and that, having gone forth, he also directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, Rāṣṭrapāla himself, in other, former lives, performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have come together, whose conditions have ripened, which are present like a rushing flood, and which inevitably come to pass. Since Rāṣṭrapāla himself performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen on the external earth element, nor do they ripen on the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen solely on the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the accumulation is complete and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, an enemy army came against the king of Videha and his palace retinue. At a loss for what to do, he fled into the forest thickets. There, at midday, tormented by the heat of the sun's rays, he and his troops wandered this way and that and could not find the road.

"At times when buddhas do not appear in the world, pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, compassionate toward the miserable and the destitute, living in remote dwellings, the sole field of offering for the world. At that time a pratyekabuddha who was living by that wilderness road, moved by compassion, showed the king of Videha the road and also showed him a pool of water, and so he saved the precious lives of the king and his retinue. Then the king, faith having arisen in him, led him to his own city and served him for three months with every kind of requisite. After the pratyekabuddha had passed into nirvāṇa, the king built a stūpa for his relics and made this aspiration: 'Through this root of virtue, through this generation of the mind, and through this giving away of a gift, may I too attain such qualities as these! May I please teachers even more exalted than this one, and may I never displease them!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king was none other than this Rāṣṭrapāla.

"Monks, Rāṣṭrapāla also performed and accumulated other actions. In this very Fortunate Eon, when people lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He dwelt in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park. At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, King Kṛkin was ruling. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, with good harvests, and filled with many people and inhabitants. Disputes and quarrels were stilled; there were no disturbances, no uprisings, no robbers, no famines, and no diseases; and it was rich in śāli rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. Endowed with the Dharma, a Dharma king, he ruled in accordance with the Dharma.

"Then his youngest son went to Ṛṣivadana, and there he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. The moment he saw him, his mind became joyful toward the Blessed One. Joy having arisen in him, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma. Then the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught him the Dharma. Faith arose in him, and he served the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his retinue, went for refuge, and took up the bases of training. After the Blessed One had passed into complete nirvāṇa, he also fastened a small parasol to his stūpa.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the prince at that time, on that occasion, is none other than this Rāṣṭrapāla. Rāṣṭrapāla also performed and accumulated other deeds. Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a brahmin whose work was digging roots. Once, when he had gone to dig roots and was wandering about in the forest, he saw there a pratyekabuddha who was ill. Faith arose in him, and he attended to him; and when the pratyekabuddha had recovered from his illness, he offered him food as well and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain qualities such as these! May I please a teacher who is even more exalted than this one, and may I not displease him!'"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the root-digging brahmin at that time, on that occasion, is none other than this Rāṣṭrapāla. Through the karmic maturation of that deed he never once experienced suffering in saṃsāra, and now too he has been born into a wealthy royal family, handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful. By that very cause he has directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, wholly black deeds have a wholly black ripening; wholly white deeds have a wholly white ripening; and mixed deeds have a mixed ripening. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Here ends the ninth group of the summary verses of the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa.

The summary verse:

Subhūti and the Elder,
Hastaka, and the one Nourished with Care,
Saṃsāra and Guptika,
Virūpa and Gaṅgika,
Dīrghanakha and Truly Lovely:
these are taught in this group.

The story called Subhūti.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now, after the Blessed One had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, he appointed śrāvakas to benefit the people to be trained in the various regions. At that time, those who were meditators stayed on the terraces of Mount Meru, devoting themselves to meditative concentration.

Then one day Suparṇa, king of the birds, seized a young nāga from the depths of the great ocean, carried it up onto the terraces of Mount Meru, and began to devour it. As that young nāga was dying, it made its mind joyful toward the great śrāvakas, and then it died. Having died, it entered the womb of the chief wife of a brahmin named Bhūti in Śrāvastī. After eight or nine months had passed, a son was born to her: she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful.

When the birth festival had been celebrated, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" The relatives said, "Since this boy's father is Bhūti, let this boy be named Subhūti."

The boy Subhūti was raised and nurtured, and when he had grown up, through the power and force of causes from the past he became impatient, wrathful, and given above all to malice. So his parents sent him away from the household, and he went forth among the sages. There too he devoted himself to meditative concentration, and he lived in dependence on a forest.

In that forest there also dwelt a deity who had seen the truth. Feeling compassion for him, the deity thought, "Because this son of good family is given above all to wrath and malice, he will not attain any distinction. I shall bring him to see the Blessed One." So that deity spoke in praise of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha in Subhūti's presence. A wish to see the Blessed One arose in Subhūti, and by the deity's magical power he was led into the Blessed One's presence.

Then he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a light surpassing a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, wholly excellent. The very moment he saw him, the spite he had harbored toward sentient beings vanished. Joy then arose in him, and he bowed at the Blessed One's feet and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would come to realize the Four Noble Truths. When he had heard it, Subhūti, son of good family, shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty towering peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Through diligence, effort and exertion, and by cultivating loving-kindness, he tamed his mind. He understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he cut through to the certainty that all kinds of formations are of a nature to decay, to fall, to scatter and to be destroyed. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, he was free of attachment to the three realms. Gold and a clod of earth were equal to him; his mind was like space and like the palm of his hand; he had become cool, like rubbed sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges; he paid no heed to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became an object of worship, veneration and respectful address for the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the venerable Subhūti considered from where he had died and passed on, where he had been born, and through what deed he had been born, and he saw that for five hundred lifetimes he had died as a nāga and been born again only as a nāga. Then this thought arose in him: "Because I brought about the conditions for aversion in this way, I was born only as a nāga for five hundred lifetimes, and for that very reason I underwent great suffering. Now I must act so that others do not come to feel aversion toward me, lest, possessed of it, after parting from the body they fall into the lower realms, the bad destinies, the ruinous states, and are born among the beings of the hells." So he took up and abided in the path of dwelling free of affliction.

Whenever he wished to stay for alms within the Saṅgha, or in a village, a district or a region, he would first of all survey the area where he would go about, thinking, "When they see me, surely no one, down even to an ant, will become hostile in mind on some account?" If so, he gave up that way of going about and changed to another, and so the minds of those beings became joyful. Although he was an arhat, he endured hardships such as these.

Then this thought arose in the venerable Subhūti: "Come now, I shall benefit many beings." By his magical power he emanated five hundred garuḍas. Seeing them, the nāgas were frightened and terrified, and in their misery they were all at a loss as to what to do. Then Subhūti protected them completely by the power of his magic. When their minds had become joyful, he gave them instruction in loving-kindness. Then again he emanated himself in the form of a great nāga and harried five hundred garuḍas; they too were frightened, and he gave them instruction in loving-kindness. In this way he tamed five hundred of the nāga race and five hundred of the garuḍa race.

On account of this, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, foremost among my śrāvaka monks who dwell free of affliction is this one: Subhūti, son of good family."

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable One, what deeds did the venerable Subhūti perform, that he has been declared foremost of those who dwell free of affliction?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, in other former lives Subhūti himself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations are gathered and whose conditions have matured, that are present like a flood and will inevitably come. Since Subhūti himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

"The deeds of embodied beings
are not lost even in a hundred eons;
when conditions gather and the time arrives,
they ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of beings to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"There this one went forth. He gave gifts and great gifts, kept the discipline of pure conduct for ten thousand years, and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue, this generation of mind, and this giving away of things to be given, in the future, in the teaching of the one of whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa prophesied to the brahmin youth Uttara, "Brahmin youth, when the lifespan of beings is a hundred years, you will become the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha called Śākyamuni," may I go forth, and may I become foremost of those who dwell free of affliction.'

"If you ask through what deeds he was born as a nāga: not having abandoned the afflictions, with his faculties confused, and not having brought the paths of action to completion, he gave rise to a hostile mind toward monks in training and beyond training and uttered the words 'venomous snake,' and therefore he was born as a nāga. Because he gave gifts and great gifts and kept the discipline of pure conduct, he has now directly realized arhatship and has been declared foremost of those who dwell free of affliction.

"Thus, monks, wholly black deeds have a wholly black ripening.

"Wholly white deeds have a wholly white ripening, and mixed deeds have a mixed ripening. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to wholly white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the twenty-first section.

The story called the Elder.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, esteemed, revered and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, townspeople, guild masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, a recipient of robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka feeding place.

At that time there lived in Rājagṛha a guild master who was rich, with much wealth and great resources, with vast and extensive holdings, possessed of wealth like Vaiśravaṇa's, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her, his wife conceived a child; and before the child was born, he went on for a time playing, enjoying himself and making love with that same wife. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her, while that first child remained in the womb, in the course of time ten sons were born from the mother's belly one after another, yet that first child stayed on in the womb.

Then in time the householder's wife fell ill. Though she was treated with medicines of roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits, the illness did not subside. When she was struck by a mortal illness and was close to death, she said to her husband, "My lord, please know this: my first son is in here. When I have died, cut open my right side with a blade and take out the boy who has been there from the first." Having said this, she spoke these words:

"All that is gathered ends at last in loss;
all that is high ends at last in a fall;
all who meet end at last in parting;
all who live end at last in death."

And she died. When she had died, they adorned a bier with blue, yellow, red and white cloths, carried her to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove, and summoned Jīvaka, the king of physicians.

Throughout the city of Rājagṛha the word went round: "A certain woman had a child remaining in her womb for so many years. Ten other sons were born to her, yet the first child who stayed in the womb was never born. Today Jīvaka, king of physicians, is to cut open the belly of the dead woman with a blade and take out the first boy who has remained in the womb." When the word had gone round, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, and the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa, gathered at the charnel ground of the Cool Grove to watch.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, go and tell the monks this: 'The Blessed One wishes to go and walk in the charnel ground. Those of you who wish to see a marvel, come along.'"

Then, after a while, the Blessed One, attended by the great śrāvakas, the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Aniruddha, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Revata and others, went to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove. And the crowd, seeing the Blessed One, made way for him.

Then the physician Jīvaka cut open the woman's right side. The boy came out by himself: his hair was white, his limbs were covered with wrinkles, every part of his body had grown old, his faculties were decrepit, he was emaciated and of little strength. The moment he came out, he looked at the crowd and spoke these words: "Listen! Do not speak harsh words to your superiors, or to those like superiors, or to your father and mother, or to your preceptors and teachers, lest you undergo an experience such as mine, who stayed sixty years in my mother's belly between the stomach and the intestines!" Having said this, he remained without saying anything more.

Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, since even a being in his final existence undergoes an experience such as this, be done with all birth in existence! Be done with all the requisites of birth in existence!"

Then the Blessed One said to the boy, "Boy, are you old?"

"Blessed One, I am old."

"Boy, are you old?"

"Sugata, I am old."

From that circumstance he was given the name the Elder.

Then, on that occasion, the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma that, on hearing it, many hundreds of beings became disenchanted and attained great distinction.

That Elder remained in the household life for ten years, and when he had reached the age of seventy he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. He undertook to spend the rains retreat on Vulture Peak Mountain together with twenty-five monks. There the elder of the Saṅgha laid down a rule: "No one who still remains an ordinary being shall take part in the pravāraṇā." Then in time, when three months had passed, twenty-four of the monks attained arhatship, while the Elder alone remained at the level of an ordinary being.

Then, during the pravāraṇā, the elder of the Saṅgha barred him again and again, eight times over, drove him out of the assembly and sent him away. So he took a blade, went into an inner room, and weeping and lamenting in many ways, he said:

"Though all the forests have burst into flame
and the mountains have already turned yellow,
still my sinful mind
has not been set free.

"Though the sound of the mountain streams has fallen still
and the rivers too are dwindling,
still my sinful mind
has not been set free.

"Though these birds born from eggs
have grown faint in their calls and cries,
still my sinful mind
has not been set free.

"Though the leaves of these forests are yellow
and the trees have shed their foliage,
still my sinful mind
has not been set free.

"Though the elders who give instruction
have already gone off in every direction,
still my sinful mind
has not been set free.

"While I remain an ordinary being,
how can I go before the Teacher?
What need is there to live without purpose?
I shall kill myself with the blade."

At that moment, there is nothing that the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not know, do not see, do not realize or do not understand. The buddhas, the blessed ones, possessed of great compassion, intent on benefiting the world, endowed with a single protection, solely heroic, without equal, never speaking in two ways, abiding in calm abiding and insight, illuminating the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, having crossed the four floods, the soles of their feet planted firmly on the four bases of miraculous power, long familiar with the four means of gathering, fearless through the four fearlessnesses, roaring the great true lion's roar of the bull among men, having entirely abandoned the five factors, having wholly transcended the five destinies, endowed with the six factors, having completely perfected the six perfections, abiding in the six constant abidings, rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, teachers of the eightfold path, skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, possessed of the strength of the ten powers, their fame spreading through all the ten directions, surpassing even the lord of the thousand, by their very nature look upon the world with the buddha eye three times by day and three times by night, and their seeing wisdom engages, thinking: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who is in want? Who has fallen into hardship? Who is beset by harm? Who is beset by want, hardship and harm? Who is inclining toward the lower realms? Who is sliding toward the lower realms? Who has fallen into the lower realms? Whom shall I draw out of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruits? Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I pull out by the hand? Whom, lacking the seven noble riches, shall I establish in sovereign mastery of the seven noble riches? In whom shall I generate roots of virtue not yet generated? In whom shall I ripen roots of virtue already generated? Whom, already ripened, shall I liberate?"

Here it is said:

"The ocean, home of the sea monsters,
might let the hour of its tide pass by;
but for the children to be trained,
the Buddha never lets the hour pass."

Then, at that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, took thought, went to him by his magical power, and taught him the Dharma suited to him. When he had heard it, the venerable Elder understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he cut through to the certainty that all kinds of formations are of a nature to decay, to fall, to scatter and to be destroyed. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. As an arhat, he was free of attachment to the three realms. Gold and a clod of earth were equal to him; his mind was like space and like the palm of his hand; he had become cool, like rubbed sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges; he paid no heed to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became an object of worship, veneration and respectful address for the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Having attained arhatship, the Elder thought, "Let me see whether there are any whom I too can train." He saw some five hundred merchants out on the ocean, caught and whirled about by the black wind of the rākṣasas, and he thought, "I shall protect these people who have met with suffering from that suffering. Perhaps I shall then be able to train them." So the Elder went there by his magical power and protected them from that danger. Faith arose in them, and they all went forth. He gave them instruction in mental attention, and through diligence, effort and exertion they all abandoned every affliction and directly realized arhatship.

But no one knew of their qualities, and the Group of Six began to mock them, muttering, "That old fool sits with five hundred men gathered around him and keeps them at his side; these too will be just like him and will never be tamed."

Then the venerable Ānanda, who was kind to his companions in the pure life and intent on benefiting others, wishing to speak with the venerable elder, went to where the venerable elder, the Elder, was. When he arrived, he exchanged with the venerable elder, the Elder, face to face, many kinds of pleasant and delightful conversation, and then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the elder, the Elder: "If you would give me leave to ask and to have my questions answered, I would ask the venerable elder, the Elder, about certain points."

"Venerable Ānanda, ask, and when I have heard, I will explain it to you."

"Venerable elder, Elder, what dharmas should a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, keep in mind without interruption?"

"Venerable Ānanda, a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, should keep two dharmas in mind without interruption: calm abiding and insight."

"Elder, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience? When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience?"

"Venerable Ānanda, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on insight. When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on calm abiding. And so, venerable Ānanda, the mind of a learned noble śrāvaka who has fully cultivated calm abiding and insight is liberated by way of the elements."

"Elder, what are the elements?"

"Venerable Ānanda, they are the element of abandonment, the element of freedom from attachment, and the element of cessation."

"Elder, what is it that, once abandoned, is called the element of abandonment? What is it that, once one is free of attachment to it, is called the element of freedom from attachment? What is it that, once it has ceased, is called the element of cessation?"

"Venerable Ānanda, the abandonment of all formations is called the element of abandonment. Freedom from attachment to all formations is called the element of freedom from attachment. The cessation of all formations is called the element of cessation."

Then the venerable Ānanda praised and rejoiced in what the elder, the Elder, had explained, and went to where the five hundred monks were. When he arrived, he said this to the five hundred monks: "Venerable ones, what dharmas should a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, keep in mind without interruption?"

"Venerable Ānanda, a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, should keep two dharmas in mind without interruption: calm abiding and insight."

"Venerable ones, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience? When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience?"

"Venerable Ānanda, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on insight. When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on calm abiding. Venerable Ānanda, the mind of a learned noble śrāvaka who has fully cultivated calm abiding and insight is liberated by way of the elements."

"Venerable ones, what are the elements?"

"Venerable Ānanda, they are the element of abandonment, the element of freedom from attachment, and the element of cessation."

"Venerable ones, what is it that, once abandoned, is called the element of abandonment? What is it that, once one is free of attachment to it, is called the element of freedom from attachment? What is it that, once it has ceased, is called the element of cessation?"

"Venerable Ānanda, the abandonment of all formations is called the element of abandonment. Freedom from attachment to all formations is called the element of freedom from attachment. The cessation of all formations is called the element of cessation."

Then the venerable Ānanda praised and rejoiced in what the five hundred monks had explained, and went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, what dharmas should a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, keep in mind without interruption?"

"Ānanda, a monk who dwells in the wilderness, who dwells at the foot of a tree, who dwells in an empty house, should keep two dharmas in mind without interruption: calm abiding and insight."

"Venerable One, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience? When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, what benefit does one come to experience?"

"Ānanda, when calm abiding has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on insight. When insight has been practiced, cultivated and made much of, one is liberated in dependence on calm abiding. Ānanda, the mind of a learned noble śrāvaka who has fully cultivated calm abiding and insight is liberated by way of the elements."

"Venerable One, what are the elements?"

"Ānanda, they are the element of abandonment, the element of freedom from attachment, and the element of cessation."

"Venerable One, what is it that, once abandoned, is called the element of abandonment? What is it that, once one is free of attachment to it, is called the element of freedom from attachment? What is it that, once it has ceased, is called the element of cessation?"

"Ānanda, the abandonment of all formations is called the element of abandonment. Freedom from attachment to all formations is called the element of freedom from attachment. The cessation of all formations is called the element of cessation."

"Venerable One, it is marvelous how the Teacher and the śrāvakas, in the supreme words, agree and accord in exactly this way: meaning with meaning, word with word, and letter with letter."

"Why so? Venerable One, I went to where the senior monk, the Elder, was, and when I put this very meaning to the senior monk, the Elder, in these words and these letters, he answered me with this very meaning, in these words and these letters, exactly as the Blessed One has now declared it. I rejoiced in and praised what the senior monk, the Elder, had explained, and went to where the five hundred monks were. When I put this very meaning to the five hundred monks in these words and these letters, they too answered me with this very meaning, in these words and these letters, exactly as the Blessed One has now declared it. Venerable One, it is marvelous how the Teacher and the śrāvakas, in the supreme words, agree and accord in exactly this way: meaning with meaning, word with word, and letter with letter."

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, do you know who the elder monk is?"

He replied, "Venerable One, the elder monk is an arhat. His defilements are exhausted; he has done what had to be done and completed his task; he has laid down the burden and attained his own goal; he has completely exhausted the fetters that bind to existence; and through perfect knowledge his mind is utterly liberated. And those five hundred monks, every one of them, are likewise arhats. Their defilements are exhausted; they have done what had to be done and completed their task; they have laid down the burden and attained their own goal; they have completely exhausted the fetters that bind to existence; and through perfect knowledge their minds are utterly liberated."

When the Blessed One and the venerable Ānanda had spoken of and proclaimed the elder monk and the five hundred monks in this way, doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Blessed One, the Buddha, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did the Elder perform, that he remained in his mother's womb for sixty years? Venerable One, what actions did he perform, that he became dull-witted, and yet went forth and realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives the Elder himself performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have gathered and whose conditions have ripened, which are now present like a flood, and which will inevitably come to pass. Since it was the Elder himself who performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide who tames beings, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"There, the son of a merchant went forth under a certain elder. That elder was an arhat who had abandoned attachment. Then, some time later, a festival took place in that land, and the young monk roused the elder, saying, 'Get up! Let us go to the village for alms.'

"The elder said, 'Son, you go on ahead for now, and busy yourself with something virtuous.'

"A second and a third time the young monk roused the elder, saying, 'Get up! Let us go to the village for alms,' and a second and a third time the elder said, 'Son, you go on ahead, and busy yourself with something virtuous.'

"Then that greedy young monk spoke harsh words: 'Then don't come out of the house for sixty years! I am going.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the young monk at that time, on that occasion, is this elder monk. Through the ripening of that action, speaking harsh words with a mind of hatred toward an arhat, he remained in his mother's womb for sixty years.

"Moreover, because he was formerly stingy with the Dharma, he became deficient in wisdom, and his faculties ripened only with great difficulty. Because he trained there, recited the teachings, and became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense sources, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible, he has now gone forth in my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and realized arhatship.

"Therefore, monks, you should strive to abandon faults of speech, so that faults such as the Elder's, from when he was an ordinary being, do not arise. And you should attain a collection of qualities like the one he gained by attaining arhatship. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Hastaka.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a merchant who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played with her, made love, and enjoyed himself. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son, a boy who was handsome, good to look at, and beautiful, of fine complexion, golden in color, complete in all his limbs and smaller parts, and who by nature remembered his former lives.

Then he took hold of his own hands, kissed them, stroked them, and hugged them, and uttered these words: "Ah, at last, after a very long time, I have found my two hands! Ah, at last, after a very long time, I have found my two hands!"

Then, when the birth celebration had been held, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?" His relatives said, "As soon as he was born, he took hold of his hands, kissed them, stroked them, and hugged them. Therefore let this boy be given the name Hastaka."

Then the boy Hastaka was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on their laps, two wet nurses to nurse him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, cream of butter, and every other kind of excellent provision, and he grew swiftly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, at a time when a danger arose in that land, the crowds of people became frightened, and, at a loss what to do, they hid their possessions from one another. The boy Hastaka, however, hid his two hands, and said to the crowds of people, "Oh, do not harbor hostile thoughts toward those worthy of offerings! Do not speak harsh words! Oh, at last, after a very long time, I have found my two hands!"

Then, some time later, the boy Hastaka went to the Jeta Grove. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as he saw him, his mind took joy in the Blessed One. Joy having arisen, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding his inclinations, latent tendencies, constitution, and nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the four noble truths. Having heard it, Hastaka destroyed with the vajra of wisdom the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, he asked his father and mother for leave and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through effort, application, and striving, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable, and he resolved that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to dispersal, and to destruction. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship.

Becoming an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and like the palm of the hand; he became cool like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions, and the analytical knowledges; he no longer looked to the gains, attachments, and honors of existence; and he became one worshiped by the gods together with Indra and Upendra, an object of their offerings and respectful speech.

Even after he had attained arhatship, he taught the Dharma to the monks in the same way, saying, "Oh, do not harbor hostile thoughts toward those worthy of offerings! Do not speak harsh words! Ah, at last, after a very long time, I have found my two hands!"

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did Hastaka perform and accumulate, that even though he has attained arhatship he still says, 'Ah, at last, after a very long time, I have found my two hands!'?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, this is the fruit of action seen directly. Do you wish to hear what he is thinking of when he speaks this way?"

"Venerable One, we wish to hear it."

"Monks, in other, former lives Hastaka himself performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have gathered and whose conditions have ripened, which are now present like a flood, and which will inevitably come to pass. Since it was Hastaka himself who performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide who tames beings, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One called Kāśyapa. He was staying near the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"At one time there were two monks there who were friends. Of the two, one was an arhat and also very learned; the other was an ordinary being and of little learning. The learned arhat was known to all, possessed of great merit, a receiver of robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, and he received many invitations. Wherever he was invited, he took his friend the monk along as his attendant śramaṇa.

"Then one day, when the arhat had been invited and was about to set out, he looked for his attendant śramaṇa but could not find him. Since he was nowhere to be seen, the arhat took another monk with him. Then some frivolous young monks there said, 'Venerables, look! Today he did not take his attendant śramaṇa, but took someone else.'

"At that, the monk grew angry, and, with a mind of hatred toward the arhat, he spoke harsh words: 'If from now on I ever wash his alms bowl, may these two hands of mine cease to exist!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the monk's friend at that time, on that occasion, is this Hastaka. Because he spoke harsh words with a mind of hatred toward an arhat, he was without hands for five hundred lifetimes. Later, heartfelt remorse arose in him, and he confessed his wrong as a wrong, acknowledging it, laying it bare, and clearing it away; because of this he has regained his hands. Because he trained there, recited the teachings, and became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense sources, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is impossible, he has now realized arhatship.
