"Thus, monks, actions that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; actions that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed actions have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Nourished with Care.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, respected, revered, and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, people of the palace retinue, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a brahmin who was rich, with much wealth and great means, with vast and extensive possessions, possessed of wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played with her, made love, and enjoyed himself. As he played, made love, and enjoyed himself, his wife conceived, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a son, a boy of poor complexion, unpleasant to look at, and ill-favored. As soon as he was born, his mother's two breasts ran dry of milk.

Some time later the brahmin summoned another nurse for him, but through the ripening of the boy's actions her milk too dried up. Then, when no milk came even after every means of producing milk had been tried, he was nourished with great care, and so he was given the name Nourished with Care, Nourished with Care. He was known as one of little merit, and he was indeed of little merit: when he grew up, he could not find even a bellyful of food.

Then he saw monks, their lower robes neatly worn and their upper robes neatly draped, carrying alms bowls as black as bees, going into Śrāvastī for alms, and he saw them coming back out with their hands full and their bowls full. Seeing this, he wished to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, and he asked his father and mother for leave and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Even after going forth, he could not find even a bellyful of food, and he grew weary of it. Through that very weariness, and through effort, application, and striving, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is unsteady and unstable, and he resolved that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to dispersal, and to destruction. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. Becoming an arhat, free of attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and like the palm of the hand; he became cool like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the higher perceptions, and the analytical knowledges; he no longer looked to the gains, attachments, and honors of existence; and he became one worshiped by the gods together with Indra and Upendra, an object of their offerings and respectful speech.

Some time later, he took up the task of sweeping the Blessed One's Perfumed Chamber. When he had swept it, he put on his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. There he obtained plenty of good alms, and with them his faculties and great elements were satisfied. His faculties satisfied, he passed the night until dawn in the meditative concentrations, the liberations, and the absorptions.

Then the thought came to him: "Ah, this is a good method. I shall make a request of the Saṅgha of monks." So he made this request of the whole Saṅgha of monks: "Venerables, I am of little merit. Only when I have swept the Perfumed Chamber and then go for alms am I fed. Therefore, may the Saṅgha have compassion for me, and may no one else sweep the Perfumed Chamber."

The Saṅgha then made a rule that no one should sweep the Blessed One's Perfumed Chamber, and so, at his ease, he would sweep the Perfumed Chamber and afterward go into Śrāvastī for alms.

At that time the venerable Śāriputra, too, having undertaken to spend the rains retreat in the Jeta Grove together with a retinue of five hundred, arrived in Śrāvastī, and out of reverence for the Teacher he swept the Perfumed Chamber. When the venerable Nourished with Care noticed this, he said, "Elder, by sweeping the Perfumed Chamber you have struck me in the belly."

The elder said, "What is wrong?"

Nourished with Care said, "Elder, whenever I have not swept the Perfumed Chamber, I do not find any alms."

Then the elder Śāriputra said, "If that is so, do not be disheartened. Wherever I am invited, I will give you food there."

Then an invitation came for the elder Śāriputra together with his retinue of five hundred, and Nourished with Care set out with them as well. But when they came near the householder's door, through the ripening of Nourished with Care's actions a great quarrel broke out in that household. The venerable Nourished with Care thought, "This quarrel has broken out because I am of little merit." So he turned back, went to the monastery, and stayed there fasting.

The next day the venerable Śāriputra said, "Why did you not come?"

He replied, "Does the elder not know how a quarrel broke out there because I am of little merit?"

So that day the elder Śāriputra put him in front, and they went into the house. But even though he sat among the Saṅgha, and food was served to those on his right and his left, the man serving forgot him, and so, right there in the midst of the Saṅgha, he went without food for a second time.

Some time later the elder Ānanda heard of this. Having heard it, he said to Nourished with Care, "In that case, stay right here in the Jeta Grove, and I will bring your food to you."

The elder Ānanda possessed such memory that he had learned eighty thousand collections of Dharma from the Blessed One and twenty thousand from other monks. Yet through the obscuration of Nourished with Care's actions, even the elder Ānanda forgot, and there too he went without food for a third time.

Then, when four days had passed, the elder Ānanda made a special effort and gave him alms. But as Ānanda was coming back out, dogs snatched it away, and there too he went without food for a fourth time.

Then, when five days had passed, the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard of it. He took alms for Nourished with Care and set out by his miraculous power, but through the ripening of Nourished with Care's actions, the king of birds, a garuḍa, struck the food with the tip of his wing and threw it into the ocean, and there too he went without food for a fifth time.

Then, when six days had passed, the elder Śāriputra heard of it and thought, "Ah, surely it must be I myself who fetches the alms for Nourished with Care." So the elder Śāriputra took alms for him, vanished from that very household, and came to the door of Nourished with Care's dwelling. But through the ripening of Nourished with Care's actions, that door became enclosed by rock. Thinking, "I shall open the door by miraculous power," the elder Śāriputra set the alms bowl down on the ground, but through the ripening of Nourished with Care's actions it sank eighty thousand yojanas down, onto the golden ground below. The elder Śāriputra drew it up from there as well by miraculous power, and, thinking, "I shall put the food in his mouth," he put the food into his mouth; but through the ripening of his actions his mouth vanished, and the food fell outside.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, knowing that Nourished with Care had no share in it, grew weary, and there too the venerable one went without food for a sixth time.

Then, on the day when seven days had passed, the venerable Nourished with Care, in order to stir weariness in beings, to show that actions are not lost, and to make known the power of actions, filled his alms bowl with ashes, sat down before the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, mixed the ashes with water and drank them, and passed completely into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. When the monks saw this, they grew weary, and they performed the funeral rites for his remains.

Then doubts arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what actions did Nourished with Care perform, that even though he attained arhatship he went without food for six days, and on the seventh day passed completely into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives Nourished with Care himself performed and accumulated actions whose accumulations have gathered and whose conditions have ripened, which are now present like a flood, and which will inevitably come to pass. Since it was Nourished with Care himself who performed and accumulated these actions, who else would experience them? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The actions of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their very fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived the wife of a householder who was full of faith, virtuous, and good-hearted. Without interruption she gave gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and needy, and beggars. Later her husband died, and after a time her son became master of the household. He was miserly and stingy, clinging to his possessions, one who would not give even a bali offering to the crows, and whenever he saw śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and needy, or beggars, he felt hostility.

"His mother, as had been her custom before, went on giving gifts and abundant gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute, the wretched and needy, and beggars. Then her son, overcome by miserliness, said, 'Mother, do not give gifts without my consent.'

"She said, 'My only son, in this house that is the custom of the household.'

"Then he set aside a separate portion of food for her, but even so she gave half of that food away and ate only half herself.

"Then he, his mind overcome by miserliness and clouded by anger, forbade her again and again, but whatever means he used to forbid her, he could not stop her. So he said to his mother, 'Mother, there is something to be done; please go into the inner room of the house.' Then she, being by nature honest, went into the inner room. He shut the door and cut off her food for a day, and she said, 'Son, I am hungry.'

"At that he spoke harsh words: 'Eat ashes!'

"Then, after a time, she met with misery, discomfort, and harm, and though she cried out piteously, he kept her fasting for six days and did not let her out, and she died. Yet he, clouded by miserliness, felt no remorse at being parted from his mother."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the householder's son at that time, on that occasion, is this Nourished with Care. Through the ripening of that action of harming his mother, he was born for one eon in the great hell of beings, Avīci. For that very reason, even though he has now realized arhatship, he went without food, and passed completely into nirvāṇa after eating ashes.

"Monks, Nourished with Care also performed and accumulated other actions. Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a brahmin devoted to the gods, who was honored, respected, revered, worshiped, and esteemed by all the brahmins, householders, and people living in Vārāṇasī.

"By the nature of things, when buddhas do not appear in the world, pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, compassionate toward the wretched and needy, living in remote dwellings, the sole worthy recipients of offerings in the world. At one time a pratyekabuddha went into Vārāṇasī for alms, and the brahmin saw him coming back out with his hands full and his bowl full. Miserliness arose in him, and he said, 'Let me see your alms bowl; bring it here.' Since the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not operate unless they direct their minds to it, the venerable one showed it to him. Then the brahmin threw it to the ground and kicked it. The pratyekabuddha then went without food, yet no remorse arose in the brahmin.

"Monks, what do you think? The one who was the brahmin at that time, on that occasion, is this Nourished with Care. Moreover, he went forth during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and because he kept the life of pure conduct there, he has now realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, actions that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; actions that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed actions have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story of Saṃsāra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, people of the court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a householder who was rich, of great wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, who had the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth. She bore a boy who was handsome, good to look upon and beautiful, complete in all his limbs and features. The moment he was born, he looked at the people of the household and spoke these words: "Alas, saṃsāra is suffering! Saṃsāra is the utmost suffering!" Having said this, he remained without saying anything more.

Then they held the birth feast for him, and as they were giving him a name, asking, "What name shall we give this boy?", his relatives said, "As soon as he was born, he cried out, 'Saṃsāra, saṃsāra!' Therefore let this boy be named Saṃsāra."

The boy Saṃsāra was then entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to hold him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of butter, and every other kind of fine provision, so that he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

As he gradually grew up, since he naturally remembered his former lives, he taught the Dharma to groups of people, saying, "O people, do not speak harsh words to your superiors, to those who are like superiors, to your father and mother, to preceptors and to teachers! Saṃsāra is suffering! Saṃsāra is the utmost suffering!"

Then some time later, while wandering about here and there, he came to the Jeta Grove. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, and wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as he saw him, his mind became joyful toward the Blessed One. With joy arisen, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One then taught him a Dharma discourse that brings weariness with saṃsāra. Having heard it, the boy Saṃsāra came to see the faults of saṃsāra and the benefits of nirvāṇa. He asked his father and mother for leave and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he was decisively certain that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship.

As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and the palm of his hand; he had become cool like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the eggshell of ignorance; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he was indifferent to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of the worship, veneration and respectful address of the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Even after he had become an arhat, he taught the Dharma to the monks, saying, "Venerable ones, do not speak harsh words to your superiors, to those who are like superiors, to your father and mother, to preceptors and to teachers! Saṃsāra is suffering! Saṃsāra is the utmost suffering!"

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Saṃsāra do, that for five hundred lifetimes he came forth from his mother's womb as a corpse, dead, and that he went forth and directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the deeds that Saṃsāra himself did and accumulated in other, earlier lives have gathered their causes and fulfilled their conditions; they are present like a swelling flood, and they will come without fail. Since Saṃsāra himself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time has come,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when beings lived for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, called Kāśyapa. He dwelt in the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana, in the Deer Park.

"At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, the son of a merchant went forth under an elder. That elder was an arhat who had abandoned attachment. Then, some time later, a festival took place in that land. The young monk urged the elder, saying, 'Get up, let us go to the village for alms.' The elder said, 'Son, it is still early. Go for now and do something virtuous.' Two and three times the young monk urged the elder, saying, 'Get up, let us go to the village for alms,' and two and three times the elder said, 'Son, it is still early. Go and do something virtuous.' Then that young monk, greedy for food, spoke with harsh speech: 'For five hundred lifetimes may you never come out of the house alive! I am off.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the young monk at that time, on that occasion, is this very one. Because he spoke harsh words with a mind of hatred toward an arhat, by the ripening of that deed he came forth from his mother's womb as a dead corpse for five hundred lifetimes. Now he has been born as a human being, and remembering that, he says, 'Saṃsāra is suffering! Saṃsāra is the utmost suffering!' Because remorse arose in him and he confessed his offense to the elder, and because he kept the life of pure conduct, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, actions that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; actions that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed actions have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

From the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa, the twenty-second and final section.

The story of Guptika.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, people of the court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At the time when the Blessed One, invited by Lac Ear, brought to faith the many people to be tamed in the land of Baskets, the whole multitude of people living in the land of Baskets was inclined toward the Buddha, flowed toward the Dharma and flowed toward the Saṅgha.

At that time there lived in the land of Baskets a householder who was rich, of great wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, who had the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth. She bore a boy, and as soon as he was born his whole body was found to be densely covered with boils. When those boils burst, his flesh turned into a festering mass; pus and blood oozed from his body, and an exceedingly foul stench came from it.

Then his father, by the force of his power as a lord, himself treated him with wealth, mantras, medicines and servants. Yet because the force of the power of karma prevailed, the disease did not subside, and his whole body remained like that. Since he was ashamed and kept himself hidden with clothing, he was given the name Guptika, "the Hidden One."

Then some time later, when the boy Guptika had grown up, his friends of the same age, who went back and forth between the city of Śrāvastī and the land of Baskets, said to his father, "Sir, if you take him to Śrāvastī, there are physicians, medicines and the like there, so he could surely be cured of that disease."

When his father heard these words, he gave him many jewels and servants and sent him to Śrāvastī. In due course he went with his friends of the same age to Śrāvastī. But although there were many physicians, riches, medicines and servants there, they could not cure that disease of his, which had arisen from his karma.

Then some time later he went to the Jeta Grove. There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, and wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as he saw him, his mind became joyful toward the Blessed One. With joy arisen, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, understanding his disposition, his latent tendencies, his temperament and his nature, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard it, he understood that the five aggregates of appropriation are a disease, a boil, a thorn, an evil, impermanent and suffering. Knowing that all conditioning factors are impermanent, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Striving, exerting himself and making effort, he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he was decisively certain that all forms of conditioning factors are by nature subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship.

As an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was like space and the palm of his hand; he had become cool like refined sandalwood; with knowledge he had broken the eggshell of ignorance; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges; he was indifferent to the gains, attachments and honors of existence; and he became one worthy of the worship, veneration and respectful address of the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

His friends of the same age also became weary of the world, and through that very weariness they went forth. They went to where the venerable Guptika was, and having arrived, they spoke thus to the venerable Guptika: "Venerable Guptika, what in the world is subject to destruction, and what in the world is not subject to destruction?"

"Venerable ones, form is subject to destruction; nirvāṇa, its cessation, is not subject to destruction. Venerable ones, feeling, perception, conditioning factors and consciousness are subject to destruction; nirvāṇa, their cessation, is not subject to destruction.

"Venerable ones, what do you think? Is form permanent, or is it impermanent?"

"Venerable Guptika, it is impermanent."

"Venerable ones, is what is impermanent suffering, or is it not suffering?"

"Venerable Guptika, it is suffering."

"Venerable ones, would a learned noble śrāvaka grasp at what is impermanent, suffering and subject to change as a self, thinking, 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Guptika, he would not."

"Venerable ones, what do you think? Are feeling, perception, conditioning factors and consciousness permanent, or are they impermanent?"

"Venerable Guptika, they are impermanent."

"Venerable ones, is what is impermanent suffering, or is it not suffering?"

"Venerable Guptika, it is suffering."

"Venerable ones, would a learned noble śrāvaka grasp at what is impermanent, suffering and subject to change as a self, thinking, 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Guptika, he would not."

"Therefore, venerable ones, whatever form there is, whether past, future or present, external or internal, coarse or subtle, inferior or excellent, far or near, all of it should be seen thus as it really is with perfect wisdom: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.' Whatever feeling, perception and conditioning factors there are, and whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future or present, internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or excellent, far or near, all of it should be seen thus as it really is with perfect wisdom: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Venerable ones, the learned śrāvaka who sees in this way becomes weary of form, and becomes weary of feeling, perception, conditioning factors and consciousness. Being weary, he becomes free from attachment. Being free from attachment, he becomes liberated. When liberated, the knowledge and vision of liberation arises in him alone: 'My birth is exhausted, the life of pure conduct has been lived, what had to be done has been done, I will know no existence other than this one.'"

When this Dharma discourse was spoken, the eye of Dharma regarding phenomena, free of dust and stainless, was purified in those friends of the same age.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Guptika do, that his body became so ugly, so diseased and so foul-smelling? And what deeds did he do, that his intelligence became sharp and clear, and that he went forth and directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the deeds that Guptika himself did and accumulated in other, earlier lives have gathered their causes and fulfilled their conditions; they are present like a swelling flood, and they will come without fail. Since Guptika himself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time has come,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a merchant who was on bad terms with another merchant. That other merchant offered much wealth to the king and petitioned him: 'Your Majesty, this merchant has committed an offense. Please punish and chastise him.' The king consented and had him punished. The other merchant then summoned him to his own house and had him beaten with whips. When blood came from his body, he had a great quantity of powdered virulent poison sprinkled on it, so that the man's body became a festering mass of rotting flesh.

"When that merchant's friends heard what had been done to him, they joined together and cured him of that disease with special provisions. Then, through that very weariness, he left home and went forth, and without a teacher he cultivated the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and directly realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.

"Then this thought arose in him: 'That merchant has generated great demerit in his own mind stream. Before he is lost, I should certainly go to him and stir weariness in him.' He went before him, rose up into the sky above, and displayed miracles of various kinds. Ordinary people are quickly brought to faith by miraculous powers. Like a tree cut off at the root, the merchant fell and bowed at his feet, and joining his palms he entreated that blessed one: 'Great one worthy of offerings, please come down! I have wronged you, and I shall rise out of it by relying on you alone.' He begged the pratyekabuddha's forgiveness, served him food, offered him robes, and made this aspiration: 'May I not experience the ripening of the deed by which I wronged you in anger! Through this honor that I have shown, may I attain qualities such as these! May I please a teacher even more exalted than this one, and may I never displease him!'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the merchant at that time, on that occasion, is this Guptika. Through the force of that deed he died under the whip for five hundred lifetimes, and for that very reason he has now obtained such a body. Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa he went forth together with his friends of the same age, and because they kept the life of pure conduct there, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, actions that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; actions that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed actions have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story of Virūpa.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshiped by kings, great ministers, wealthy men, people of the court, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and known by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and other requisites, was staying together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there lived in the land called Bharga a householder who was rich, of great wealth and great means, with vast and extensive holdings, who had the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. As he played, enjoyed himself and made love, his wife became pregnant, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth. She bore a boy who had eighteen kinds of ugliness. His parents, out of love for their son, raised him. But when he had gradually grown up, his parents drove him out of the house because of his ugliness. Wherever he went, there too many people drove him away because he was so unpleasant to see. Even creatures born in the animal realm treated him with contempt; what need is there to speak of humans? Driven out of the city, he stayed in a deserted pleasure grove. Sometimes, when he found fruits and roots, he ate them; at other times, when he found no fruits or roots, he lived on grass, flowers and leaves.

Then the Blessed One, seeing that the time had come to tame Virūpa, said to four great śrāvakas, "Monks, come, let us tame Virūpa." The Blessed One, attended by the great śrāvakas, then went to the deserted pleasure grove. When Virūpa saw the Blessed One, he was ashamed and fled this way and that. Then the Blessed One blessed him so that he could not flee anywhere at all. Then the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas entered the absorption of cessation. Rising from cessation, the Blessed One transformed himself into an ugly man, and having done so, he took a bowl filled with food and went over to Virūpa.

When Virūpa saw him, he was delighted and said, "Great friend, where have you come from? Come here! The two of us shall stay together." Then the Blessed One gave him food, and when his senses were satisfied, the Blessed One changed back into his own appearance.

When Virūpa saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, he said, "Now that you have become handsome, by the power of what deed has this happened?"

The Blessed One said, "I have a spell called Gladdening the Mind; this is its power."

Then Virūpa gave rise to a gladdened mind toward the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas who had entered the absorption of cessation. Because of that, his ugliness vanished and he became handsome. He went forth and directly realized arhatship.

Then doubt arose in the monks, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Virūpa do, that he became so ill-colored, so unbearable to touch, and possessed of eighteen kinds of ugliness, and that he went forth and directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, the deeds that Virūpa himself did and accumulated in other, earlier lives have gathered their causes and fulfilled their conditions; they are present like a swelling flood, and they will come without fail. Since Virūpa himself did and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Rather, virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been done and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred eons.
When the conditions gather and the time has come,
They ripen into their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, called Tiṣya. Later he dwelt at a certain royal palace.

"Then the Perfectly Complete Buddha Tiṣya considered, and saw that at that time there were two bodhisattvas who were close to awakening: the bodhisattva Śākyamuni and Maitreya. Of these, he saw that Maitreya's own mind stream had ripened but those he was to tame had not ripened, while Śākyamuni's own mind stream had not ripened but those he was to tame had ripened.

"Then, in order to ripen the mind stream of the bodhisattva Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Complete Buddha Tiṣya went up onto the Snow Mountain, entered a cave of jewels, sat down with his legs crossed, and entered the absorption of the fire element.

"At that time the bodhisattva Śākyamuni had gone up onto the Snow Mountain, king of mountains, in search of fruits and roots. As he wandered about here and there, he saw the Perfectly Complete Buddha Tiṣya, his body well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, adorned with a halo a fathom wide, possessing a radiance surpassing a thousand suns, and wholly excellent, like a moving mountain of jewels. As soon as he saw him, he attained such one-pointedness of mind that for seven days and nights he stood on one foot and praised him with a single verse:

O bull among men, no other great ascetic like you is found in the god realms or on earth;
Nowhere at all in this world is there one, nor in the palace of Vaiśravaṇa;
Nor in the supreme abodes, the palaces of the gods, nor in the directions or the intermediate directions;
Though one roam the whole wide earth with its mountains and forests, where could one be found?

"Thus he praised him. Then the Perfectly Complete Buddha Tiṣya, seeing that the mind stream of the bodhisattva Śākyamuni had ripened, gave him his approval, saying:

Excellent, excellent, holy being!
Excellent brahmin, today,
By this power and perfected diligence
In praising well the Tathāgata,
Nine eons have been cut short.

"Thus he spoke. Then that Blessed One, attended by gods renowned as mighty, remained inside that cave. There was a god of lesser renown who lived in that cave, and he could not get into the cave. So he made his eyes hideous and menaced the Blessed One. Although he menaced him for a long time, he was unable to harm the Blessed One, and so he gained faith, thinking, 'This sage is a good one, one accomplished in his discipline.' Then he manifested his full body, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, begged his forgiveness, and also served him food."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the god living in that cave at that time, on that occasion, is this Virūpa. Through the ripening of that deed he experienced endless suffering in saṃsāra, and now too, for that very reason, he has become ugly. Because he later gave rise to a gladdened mind, his ugliness vanished, he became handsome, went forth and directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, actions that are wholly black have a ripening that is wholly black; actions that are wholly white have a ripening that is wholly white; and mixed actions have a ripening that is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly black actions and mixed actions, and devote yourselves solely to wholly white actions. Monks, you should train in this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Gaṅgika.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed and worshipped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, the townspeople, guild leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshipped and acknowledged by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with great merit and receiving robes, food, bedding, seats, medicine for the sick and medical supplies, was dwelling together with the community of śrāvakas in the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.

At that time there lived in Vārāṇasī a householder who was rich, with much wealth and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, enjoyed himself and made love with her. But though he played, enjoyed himself and made love, no son was born and no daughter, so he rested his cheek on his hand and thought, "Although my house is endowed with much wealth, I have neither son nor daughter. Because there is no son, after I pass away everything I own will fall to the king." Thinking this, he sat absorbed in brooding.

Then śramaṇas, brahmins, soothsayers, friends, relatives and other kin urged him, "Pray to the gods!" So, wanting a son by that woman, he prayed to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā and the others, and to other distinguished gods as well. That is, he prayed also to the gods of the parks, the gods of the forests, the gods of the crossroads, the gods of the three-way junctions, the gods who receive bali offerings, the gods born together with a person, the gods of like nature, and the gods who constantly follow behind. There is a saying in the world that sons and daughters are born because of prayer, but that is not so. If sons and daughters were born because of prayer, it would follow that each person would have a thousand sons, like a great wheel-turning king. In fact, sons and daughters are born from the coming together of three conditions. What are the three? The father and mother come together, aroused with desire; the mother is in season and fertile; and a gandharva is present. From the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.

Then, while he was devoted to praying, a certain being died and passed from a certain class of beings and entered the womb of his wife. Some women who are wise by nature have five special qualities. What are the five? They know when a man is aroused and when he is not aroused; they know the time and the fertile period; they know when a child has been conceived; they know from whom the child has been conceived; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl. If it is a boy, it rests on the right side of the womb; if it is a girl, it rests on the left side of the womb.

Then, overjoyed, she told her husband, "My lord, a child has been conceived in me. Since it rests on the right side of my womb, it will certainly be a boy. Please rejoice!" He too was overjoyed. Raising the upper part of his body and stretching out his right arm, he uttered words of joy: "I shall see the face of the son I have long wished for! May my son be well formed, and not ill formed! May he carry out my duties! May he support us in return for being supported! May he enjoy his inheritance! May my family line long endure! And after we have passed away and died, may he give gifts and make merit for our sake, whether much or little, and dedicate the reward, saying, 'Wherever these two are born and go, may this go to them!'"

Then, knowing that she had conceived, he kept her at ease on the upper floor of the mansion in order to care for the child. In the cold season she had the requisites for cold, and in the hot season the requisites for heat. She was given the foods prescribed by the physicians, foods not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent and not too astringent; she was nourished with foods free of the bitter, the sour, the salty, the sweet, the pungent and the astringent. Her body was adorned with necklaces and garlands, and like a divine maiden wandering in the Nandana grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat without ever descending to the ground below. And he saw to it that she heard no unpleasant sound whatsoever.

Then, when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth. A boy was born, handsome, good to look at and beautiful, complete in all his major and minor limbs. When he was born, they held a birth celebration and named him Gaṅgika. Then the boy Gaṅgika was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, the cream of butter and all other excellent kinds of provisions, so that he grew quickly, like a lotus in a lake.

He was also endowed with roots of virtue conducive to penetration. Finding no joy in living at home, he bowed at the feet of his father and mother and made this request: "Father and mother, please permit me to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One." But because he was their only son, his parents would not allow it.

Then this thought occurred to Gaṅgika: "Gaining birth as a human being is hard to find. The appearance of a Tathāgata is also hard to find. And besides, having complete faculties is hard to find as well. Well then, what means is there for me to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One?"

Then he thought: "Well then, I shall make an aspiration and bring about my own death, so that I may gain a human birth and go forth very quickly."

Having thought this, he drank poison, but he did not die. He leapt into fire, but he did not die. He leapt from a cliff, but he did not die. He leapt into the river Varaṇā, and there too he did not die. Then the thought occurred to him: "What other means is there for me to die?"

Then he thought: "Well then, King Ajātaśatru is fierce, violent, harsh and rash. I shall go to his palace and break into it at night." So he went to the city of Rājagṛha, and when night had come and darkness had fallen, he was breaking into the house. The guards seized him alive and brought him before King Ajātaśatru, saying, "Your Majesty, this man is a thief, a violator of the palace, an offender. At night he broke into the palace." Then the king sentenced him to death for committing a crime.

Then the executioners, wearing blue garments, with garlands of karavīra flowers about their necks and weapons in their hands, led him away. Proclaiming loudly on the highways, the streets, the crossroads, the junctions of three roads and the places of public announcement, they took him out through the southern gate of the city and led him to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove. As he was being led, he said to the executioners, "Hey! Before the king's order is reversed, lead me on quickly!"

Then the executioners reported this to the king. The king had him brought back and asked, "Man, why do you wish to give up your precious life?" Then he told the king the whole story in detail.

Then King Ajātaśatru, his hair standing on end like a kadamba flower, his eyes filled with tears and his face weeping, uttered words of joy: "Ah! Since he strives like this to give up his precious life in order to go forth, his mind stream is fully ripened. He has thoroughly understood the faults of saṃsāra. He has truly gained perfect faith."

Then the king sighed and said, "My son, I hold power over your life. Now go, and go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One." With these words the king released him.

He went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Through diligence, application and effort he understood that this very five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that all kinds of formations are subject to decay, falling, scattering and destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship. Having become an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal. His mind was like space and like the palm of the hand. He had become cool, like sandalwood paste. With knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg. He had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges and the discriminating knowledges. He paid no heed to worldly gain, attachment or honors. He became worthy of veneration, of reverence and of respectful address by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, foremost among my śrāvaka monks who went forth through faith is this one: Gaṅgika, the son of the merchant of Vārāṇasī."

Then the monks felt doubt, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Gaṅgika perform, through whose ripening fire could not harm his body, neither poison, nor weapons, nor water could bring about his death, and he also attained arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, in other, former lives Gaṅgika himself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations have been gathered, whose conditions have matured, which come on like a flood, and which will inevitably arrive. Since Gaṅgika himself performed and accumulated these deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element. They do not ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred aeons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a low-caste thief who stole goods from the charnel grounds. Once he robbed some travelers and obtained their goods, and afterward he was pursued by a band of ruffians. At that time, in one part of the charnel ground, a pratyekabuddha was absorbed in the attainment of cessation. In front of him the low-caste charnel-ground thief threw down the goods and hid right there.

"Then the ruffians saw the pratyekabuddha. They struck him with stones, they cut at him with weapons and they burned him with fire. Yet because he was absorbed in the attainment of cessation, they could not move even the hem of his robe. Then, when the ruffians had grown weary and gone back, the pratyekabuddha slowly arose from his meditative absorption.

"Then the low-caste charnel-ground thief offered food to that pratyekabuddha and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain qualities such as these! Just as he cannot be harmed by others, so may I too, wherever I am born, be unharmed by others. May I please a teacher even more exalted than he is, and may I not displease him.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the low-caste charnel-ground thief is none other than this Gaṅgika. Moreover, he went forth in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and because he there kept to the holy life, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black. The ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white. The ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to entirely white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Dīrghanakha.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was respected, revered, honored and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka feeding place.

At that time there lived in the village of Nālada a brahmin named Tiṣya, who had taken as his wife Śārī, the daughter of the brahmin Māṭhara. When Śāriputra entered Śārī's womb, that woman, whenever she debated on the treatises with her brother Dīrghanakha, would bring her brother to defeat. Then this thought occurred to Dīrghanakha: "It seems that a being renowned for great merit has taken conception in her womb, and this is its power. Well then, I had better leave beforehand and settle in some other region." So Dīrghanakha went to the south and studied many treatises.

Then, in due course, Śāriputra was born. When he was sixteen years old he had mastered the grammar of Indra, and with the treatises he defeated every opponent in debate. Then, in due course, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Some time later the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha heard: "Your nephew defeated all those tīrthikas and has now professed himself a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama." When he heard this, a strong sense of defeat arose in him, and the thought arose that to all the treatises there is no end.

Then, in due course, he arrived at Rājagṛha. At that time the Blessed One had risen from seclusion and was teaching the fourfold assembly the Dharma, rich in every flavor, like the unboiled honey of bees. Śāriputra too was standing before the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.

Then the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha saw the Blessed One seated, surrounded by his assembly like the shape of a crescent moon, teaching the Dharma, and Śāriputra standing there holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. Seeing this, he said to the Blessed One, "Gautama, I accept nothing at all."

The Blessed One said, "Agnivaiśyāyana, this view that you hold, 'I accept nothing at all': do you not accept that either?"

"Gautama, this view that I hold, 'I accept nothing at all': that too I do not accept."

"In that case, Agnivaiśyāyana, if you know thus and see thus, this view will be abandoned, given up and discarded, and no other view will link on, be taken up or arise."

"Gautama, since I know thus and see thus, this view is abandoned, given up and discarded, and no other view will link on or arise."

"In that case, Agnivaiśyāyana, you will be in accord with many people and alike with them. Since many people also see thus and speak thus, you too are just like them. Agnivaiśyāyana, those śramaṇas or brahmins, whoever they may be, who definitively abandon that view and do not take up another view are said to be fewer than the few in this world.

"Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three standpoints of views. What are the three? Agnivaiśyāyana, here some see thus and speak thus: 'I accept nothing at all.' Again, here some see thus and speak thus: 'I accept everything.' Again, here some see thus and speak thus: 'I accept one thing and do not accept another.'

"Agnivaiśyāyana, of these, the view of those who see thus, 'I accept everything,' leads to attachment and not to freedom from attachment. It leads to aversion and not to freedom from aversion. It leads to delusion and not to freedom from delusion. It leads to bondage and not to release. It leads to affliction and not to purification.

It leads to increase and not to decrease; it leads to delight, to grasping and to intense clinging.

"Agnivaiśyāyana, of these, the view of those who see thus, 'I accept nothing at all,' leads to freedom from attachment and not to attachment. It leads to freedom from aversion and not to aversion. It leads to freedom from delusion and not to delusion. It leads to release and not to bondage. It leads to purification and not to affliction. It leads to decrease and not to increase; it leads to no delight, no grasping and no intense clinging.

"Agnivaiśyāyana, of these, as for the view of those who see thus, 'I accept one thing and do not accept another': first, what they accept leads to attachment and not to freedom from attachment. It leads to aversion and not to freedom from aversion. It leads to delusion and not to freedom from delusion. It leads to bondage and not to release. It leads to affliction and not to purification. It leads to increase and not to decrease; it leads to delight, to grasping and to intense clinging. What they do not accept leads to freedom from attachment and not to attachment. It leads to freedom from aversion and not to aversion. It leads to freedom from delusion and not to delusion. It leads to release and not to bondage. It leads to purification and not to affliction. It leads to decrease and not to increase; it leads to no delight, no grasping and no intense clinging.

"Here the learned noble śrāvaka trains in reflecting thus: 'If I were to see thus and speak thus, "I accept everything," then I would quarrel with both of these: with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept nothing at all," and with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept one thing and do not accept another." If I quarrel, there will be dispute. If there is dispute, there will be harm.' Seeing rightly that this involves quarreling, involves dispute and involves harm, he abandons that view and does not take up another view. In this way that view is abandoned, given up and cleared away, and no other view links on, is taken up or arises.

"Here the learned noble śrāvaka trains in reflecting thus: 'If I were to see thus and speak thus, "I accept nothing at all," then I would quarrel with both of these: with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept everything," and with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept one thing and do not accept another." If I quarrel, there will be dispute. If there is dispute, there will be harm.' Seeing rightly that this involves quarreling, involves dispute and involves harm, he abandons that view and does not take up another view. In this way that view is abandoned, given up and cleared away, and no other view links on, is taken up or arises.

"Here the learned noble śrāvaka trains in reflecting thus: 'If I were to see thus and speak thus, "I accept one thing and do not accept another," then I would quarrel with both of these: with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept everything," and with the one who sees thus and speaks thus, "I accept nothing at all." If I quarrel, there will be dispute. If there is dispute, there will be harm.' Seeing rightly that this involves quarreling, involves dispute and involves harm, he abandons that view and does not take up another view. In this way that view is abandoned, given up and cleared away, and no other view links on, is taken up or arises.

"Agnivaiśyāyana, this body is material and gross, arisen from the four great elements as its cause. The noble śrāvaka should dwell contemplating it as ceaselessly arising and perishing. He should dwell contemplating freedom from attachment, contemplating cessation and contemplating relinquishment. When the noble śrāvaka dwells contemplating its ceaseless arising and perishing, then whatever desire for the body, affection for the body, cherishing of the body, dwelling upon the body, attachment to the body and intense clinging to the body he has, his mind does not remain overpowered by it.

"Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant, painful, and neither painful nor pleasant. When the learned noble śrāvaka experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time the other two, the painful feeling and the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, cease for him. At that time the noble śrāvaka experiences only the pleasant feeling, and that pleasant feeling too is impermanent and subject to cessation. When the noble śrāvaka experiences a painful feeling, at that time the other two, the pleasant feeling and the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, cease for him. At that time the noble śrāvaka experiences only the painful feeling, and that painful feeling too is impermanent and subject to cessation.

When the noble śrāvaka experiences a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, at that time the other two, the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling, cease for him. At that time the noble śrāvaka experiences only the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, and that feeling which is neither painful nor pleasant is also impermanent and subject to cessation.

"He thinks: 'What is the basis of these feelings? What gives rise to them? What is their origin? What brings them into being? The basis of these feelings is contact. What gives rise to them is contact. Their origin is contact. What brings them into being is contact. When this or that contact arises, this or that feeling arises; when this or that contact ceases, this or that feeling ceases, is stilled, becomes cool and comes to an end.' Having thought this, whenever he experiences any feeling, whether pleasant, painful, or neither painful nor pleasant, he understands, correctly and as it really is, the arising of those feelings, their passing away, their decline, their danger and the escape from them. Since he understands, correctly and as it really is, the arising of those feelings, their passing away, their decline, their danger and the escape from them, he dwells contemplating every feeling that arises as impermanent, contemplating it as perishing, contemplating its cessation and contemplating its relinquishment.

"When he experiences a feeling that lasts as long as the body, he understands, correctly and as it really is, 'I am experiencing a feeling that lasts as long as the body.' When he experiences a feeling that lasts as long as life, he understands, correctly and as it really is, 'I am experiencing a feeling that lasts as long as life. When life reaches its end and I am parted from the body, all my feelings without exception will cease right here; they will come to an end without remainder, be completely exhausted and be finished.'

"He thinks: 'At the time of parting from the body, even if I experience a pleasant feeling, that itself is the end of suffering. At the time of parting from the body, even if I experience a painful feeling, or a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, that itself is the end of suffering.'

"When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he experiences it unbound, and not bound. When he experiences a painful feeling, or a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he experiences it unbound, and not bound. Unbound from what? I declare that he is unbound from attachment, aversion and delusion; unbound from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness and distress; unbound from suffering."

At that time the venerable Śāriputra had been fully ordained for half a month, and he was standing at the Blessed One's side, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. Then the venerable Śāriputra thought: "The Blessed One speaks only of the abandoning of these various dharmas. He speaks only of freedom from attachment to them, only of their cessation, only of their relinquishment. Well then, I too had better dwell contemplating the abandoning of these various dharmas. I had better dwell contemplating freedom from attachment, contemplating cessation and contemplating relinquishment."

Then the venerable Śāriputra, dwelling in contemplation of these various dharmas as impermanent, contemplating them as perishing, contemplating freedom from attachment, contemplating cessation and contemplating relinquishment, freed his mind from the defilements without grasping.

And in the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha there arose, with regard to dharmas, the Dharma eye, free of dust and free of stain. Then the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha, having seen the Dharma, heard the Dharma, understood the Dharma and plumbed the depths of the Dharma, crossed beyond hesitation and crossed beyond doubt. No longer depending on others and no longer led by others, he gained fearlessness in the teachings of the Teacher's doctrine. He rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, if I may go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination and attain the state of a monk, I wish to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha went forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, received full ordination and attained the state of a monk. Having gone forth in this way, that venerable one dwelt alone and secluded, heedful, ardent and resolute. Dwelling alone and secluded, heedful, ardent and resolute, he realized in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and with perfect faith go forth from home into homelessness. Having accomplished it and experienced it, he knew fully: "My births are exhausted. I have lived the holy life. I have done what was to be done. I know no further existence beyond this one." That venerable one became an arhat, his mind perfectly liberated.

Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, foremost among my śrāvaka monks who have attained the discriminating knowledges is this one: the monk Sthūlakoṣṭhaka."

Then the monks felt doubt, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts, "Venerable One, what deeds did Sthūlakoṣṭhaka perform, so that he became a great expounder of the treatises, and after going forth directly realized arhatship?"

The Blessed One said, "In other, former lives Sthūlakoṣṭhaka himself performed and accumulated deeds whose accumulations have been gathered, whose conditions have matured, which come on like a flood, and which will inevitably arrive. Since Sthūlakoṣṭhaka himself performed and accumulated these deeds, who else would experience them? Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element. They do not ripen in the water element, the fire element or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds performed and accumulated ripen solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred aeons.
When the conditions gather and the time arrives,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, five hundred ruffians led by a chieftain set out as thieves. After traveling for some time, they came to a khadira forest, and their leader said, 'You lotus-eyed ones, look and see whether there are any other people here. Then we will make an offering to the yakṣa and go on.'

"The ruffians searched all around, and seeing a pratyekabuddha sitting in that khadira forest, they seized him and led him before their chieftain. Then the chieftain of the ruffians commanded, 'Kill him!'

"Then, in order to benefit them, the pratyekabuddha rose into the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings, and displayed many kinds of miracles. Then the chieftain of the ruffians fell at his feet like a tree cut at the root, confessed his wrongdoing, offered him food, and made this aspiration: 'May I too attain qualities such as these! May I please a teacher even more exalted than he is, and may I not displease him.'"

The Blessed One said, "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the chieftain of the ruffians is this great Sthūlakoṣṭhaka. Moreover, he went forth in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and there for ten thousand years he kept to the holy life. Because of that, he has now directly realized arhatship.

"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black. The ripening of entirely white deeds is entirely white. The ripening of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon entirely black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourselves to entirely white deeds alone. Monks, this is how you should train."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The story called Truly Lovely.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was respected, revered, honored and worshiped by kings, great ministers, the wealthy, palace attendants, merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas. Worshiped and renowned among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras and mahoragas, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possessed of great merit, who received robes, alms food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and other requisites, was dwelling together with his Saṅgha of śrāvakas near the city of Kuśinagarī, at the Upavartana of the Mallas, in the grove of the twin sāla trees.

Then, when the time had come for the Blessed One to pass into parinirvāṇa, he said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, tonight at midnight the Tathāgata will pass into parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. Prepare the Tathāgata's couch between the twin sāla trees, with its head toward the north."

"Venerable One, I will do so," he replied. The venerable Ānanda, just as the Blessed One had told him, prepared the couch between the twin sāla trees with its head toward the north. Then he went to where the Blessed One was, and when he arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, I have prepared the Tathāgata's couch between the twin sāla trees, with its head toward the north."

Then the Blessed One went to where the couch was, and when he arrived he lay down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other. Having placed one foot upon the other, endowed with the perception of light, with mindfulness and with vigilance, he held in his mind only the perception of nirvāṇa. And there, at midnight, the Blessed One passed into parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates.

The very instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, the great earth shook violently, meteors fell, the horizons blazed, and from the sky divine drums resounded. The instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, passed into parinirvāṇa, the twin sāla trees, finest of the trees of the forest, bowed down and scattered flowers over the Tathāgata as he lay in the lion's posture.

The very instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, a certain monk spoke this verse:

These two finest trees of the sāla grove,
Graced with beauty,
Scatter flowers all around
Upon the Teacher who has passed beyond sorrow.

The very instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, Śakra, lord of the gods, spoke this verse:

Alas, all formations are impermanent;
Their nature is to arise and to perish.
Having arisen, they cease;
Their stilling is bliss.

The very instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, spoke this verse:

In this world all sentient beings
Must surely cast off their bodies.
Even such a Teacher as this,
Who had no equal in this world,
The Tathāgata who attained the powers,
The One with Eyes, has passed into parinirvāṇa.

The very instant the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, the venerable Aniruddha spoke these verses:

The Protector, whose mind was steadfast,
When the breath that moves out and in had ceased,
Resting in the unmoving and the peaceful,
The One with Eyes passed into parinirvāṇa.

When the Teacher, endowed with the supreme in every aspect,
Passed away,
Then a great terror arose,
Then the hair stood on end.

With a mind that did not falter
He accepted the feelings.
Like a lamp that has gone out,
His mind was fully liberated.

When seven days had passed since the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, the venerable Ānanda, circumambulating the funeral pyre that had been raised for the Blessed One, spoke these verses:

The Guide's precious body, of great miraculous power,
He who has gone to the world of Brahmā,
Was burned by flames that sprang from his own body.
It had been wrapped in five hundred pairs of cloths.

With a full thousand garments and Dharma robes
The body of the Buddha had been wholly wrapped.
Yet there, of the cloths, the inner and the outer,
These two were not burned at all.

When a hundred years had passed since the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka was reigning in the city called Pāṭaliputra. During his reign the land was prosperous, flourishing, and happy, with good harvests, full of many folk and people; quarrels and fighting were stilled, and there was no strife, no internal unrest, no robbers, no famine, and no disease; it was rich in sāli rice, sugar cane, cattle, and buffalo. He was righteous, a Dharma king who ruled in accordance with the Dharma.

Then, some time later, he sported, made merry, and took his pleasure together with his queen. As he sported, made merry, and took his pleasure, the queen later conceived, and when eight or nine months had passed a son was born. She gave birth to a boy who was handsome, good to look upon, and beautiful, whose eyes were like the eyes of the kuṇāla bird.

Then, after the birth feast had been held for him, they set about naming him, asking, "What name shall this boy be given?" The relatives said, "From the very moment he was born his eyes have been like the eyes of the kuṇāla bird, and so this boy shall be named Kuṇāla."

Then the boy Kuṇāla was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him on the lap, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to wash away his dirt, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses reared and nourished him with milk, curds, butter, ghee, and the cream of butter, and with every other kind of fine provision, and he grew up swiftly, like a lotus in a lake.

Then, adorned with every ornament, he was taken onto the king's lap. The king gazed at him again and again and took his fill of delight in his perfect looks, and he said, "In all the world there is no one equal in looks to my son."

Now at that time, in the land of Earth-Holder, there was a village called Great Flower Load. There a son was born to a certain householder, one who surpassed the complexion of humans though he had not attained the complexion of the gods. When he was born, there appeared a jeweled pool filled with fragrant divine water, and a great pleasure garden, perfect in flowers and fruits, which was able to move; wherever the boy went, there the pool and the pleasure garden would appear. The boy was given the name Sundara.

Then, some time later, when the boy had grown up, some merchants from the village of Great Flower Load went on some business to the land of Pāṭaliputra. Taking gifts with them, they went before King Aśoka. They bowed at the king's feet, offered their gifts, and sat down before him. Then King Aśoka showed them his son Kuṇāla and asked, "O merchants, in all your wanderings, have you ever before seen, anywhere at all, anyone of such distinguished looks as this?"

Then the merchants joined their palms, bowed low, and bowed at his feet, and having begged not to be held at fault, they said to the king, "Your Majesty, in our land there is a boy called Sundara, who surpasses the complexion of humans though he has not attained the complexion of the gods. When he was born, there appeared a jeweled pool filled with fragrant divine water, and a great pleasure garden, perfect in flowers and fruits, which is able to move; wherever the boy goes, there the pool and the pleasure garden appear."

When King Aśoka heard this, he was utterly amazed and wished to see him, and he sent a messenger with this message: "King Aśoka wishes to come to see the boy Sundara, so do whatever needs to be done or prepared." At this most of the people were frightened, thinking, "If the king comes here with a great army, will that not bring great harm?"

So they made ready a fine mount for the boy and sent him to King Aśoka with a gift of a hundred thousand pearl necklaces. Traveling on by stages, he came to the city of Pāṭaliputra and, bearing the hundred thousand pearl necklaces, went before King Aśoka. Then King Aśoka saw the beauty of the boy Sundara's looks and the radiance of his complexion, and the divine pool and the pleasure garden, and the instant he saw them he was utterly amazed.

Then King Aśoka, wishing to show this wonder to the elder Upagupta, took the boy Sundara with him and went to the Kukkuṭārāma. At that Kukkuṭārāma there dwelt eighteen thousand arhats, headed by Upagupta, and twice that number of trainees and virtuous ordinary beings. The boy bowed at the elder's feet and sat down before him to listen to the Dharma, and the elder Upagupta taught him the Dharma.

That boy's mental continuum was fully ripened, and on hearing the Dharma he wished to go forth. He asked leave of King Aśoka and went forth in the presence of the elder Upagupta. Through application, practice, and effort, he understood that this very wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes is moving and unstable, and he ascertained that all kinds of formations are by nature subject to decay, to falling, to scattering, and to destruction. Abandoning all afflictions, he directly realized arhatship.

Having become an arhat, free from attachment to the three realms, he regarded gold and a clod of earth as equal; his mind was the same toward space and the palm of his hand; he had become cool like sandalwood paste; with knowledge he had broken the shell of the egg; he had attained the knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges; he turned away from worldly gain, craving, and honors; and he became one worthy to be worshiped, honored, and respectfully addressed by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then a doubt arose in King Aśoka, and he asked the elder Upagupta, "Venerable one, what deeds did Sundara perform, that he came to have such looks as these? What deeds did he perform, that there appeared a jeweled pool filled with fragrant divine water, and a great pleasure garden, perfect in flowers and fruits, that is able to move?"

The elder Upagupta said, "Great king, in other, former lives, Sundara himself performed and accumulated those deeds, whose collections have come together and whose conditions have matured, which arise like a flood and will inevitably come to pass. Since Sundara himself performed and accumulated those deeds, who else would experience them? Great king, deeds that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the outer earth element, nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds that have been performed and accumulated ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

The deeds of embodied beings
Are not lost even in a hundred aeons.
When they have gathered and their time has come,
They ripen as their fruit.

"Great king, long ago, at the time when the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, with a retinue of five hundred, was wandering through the land of Magadha, wishing to compile the Dharma.
