At one point, a certain poor merchant saw that most of the community of monks were overwhelmed by grief at being parted from the Teacher, were weary from their journeying, and had their bodies covered with dust. Compassion arose in him, and he invited the five hundred monks headed by Mahākāśyapa to a bath performed with due ceremony. He offered warm water scented with various perfumes, washed the bodies of the monks, and washed their robes as well. He also satisfied them with fine food, and then he took refuge and received the bases of training, and he made this aspiration: 'May I go forth in this very teaching of the Blessed One Śākyamuni and directly realize arhatship.'

"What do you think, great king? The one who at that time, on that occasion, was the poor merchant is this monk Sundara. Because he gave the monks a bath performed with due ceremony, he now has such distinguished looks as these, and there appeared a jeweled pool filled with fragrant divine water, and a great pleasure garden, perfect in flowers and fruits, that is able to move. Because he took refuge and received the bases of training, he has directly realized arhatship in this very life.

"Thus, great king, wholly black deeds have a wholly black ripening, wholly white deeds have a wholly white ripening, and mixed deeds have a mixed ripening. Therefore, great king, abandon wholly black deeds and mixed deeds, and devote yourself only to wholly white deeds. Great king, this is how you should train."

Then King Aśoka praised what the elder Upagupta had taught, rejoiced in it, rose from his seat, and departed.

Here ends the tenth summary verse of the Hundred Avadānas, and the Hundred Avadānas Beginning with Pūrṇa is complete.

This was translated and finalized by the Indian preceptor Jinamitra and the chief editor-translator, Bandé Devacandra.

Translator's notes

The summary verse names the stories of this first chapter. Some of its names are hard to split with certainty. གང་པོ་བཟང may be "Pūrṇabhadra" or "the good Pūrṇa". ཟླ་བ་ཆེ་བ་པད་མ is read here as "Great Candra and Padma", but it could also mean "Candra and Mahāpadma". The lazy one and the caravan leaders are given in their meanings. The Sanskrit title is romanized as the Tibetan spells it. ཆོས་ཤིག in the Buddha's words to the monks is read in its usual sense in this genre, "get ready". The cold hells are given in English, in the order this text lists them. The phrase རྣམས་གྱིན་ད་འཛུམ་མི་སྟོན does not read well as written. It is translated as "do not show a smile without reason", which the parallel stanza earlier in the same set of verses supports. The future buddha's name, written གང་པོ་བཟང, is probably Pūrṇabhadra. It is kept here as "the good Pūrṇa" so that it matches the summary verse. In the third of Ānanda's verses the Tibetan reads "rnams gyin da 'dzum mi ston," which makes little sense; given the parallel line in the preceding verse and the Sanskrit formula (nākāraṇaṃ ... smitam), it is taken as a scribal slip for a phrase meaning "without reason." The order of the cold hells follows this text (Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Hahava). The buddha name rin chen ldan is rendered Ratnavat as the standard Sanskrit equivalent ("Possessor of Jewels"). The "king who turns the wheel by force" renders stobs kyi 'khor los sgyur ba (balacakravartin). The boy's name dga' byed ("one who causes delight") is explained by the text itself; its Sanskrit original cannot be identified with confidence (perhaps Nandaka or Nandana), so it is translated as "Delighter." The opening words "le lo can zhes bya ba ni" give the title of this story, "The Lazy One." "Nandana Grove" renders dga' ba'i tshal, the pleasure grove of the gods. The phrase "grum po bzhin du lnga re 'dug pa" is obscure; it is taken in its evident sense of sitting idle "like a cripple." "Pūraṇa" renders rdzogs byed, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, foremost of the six tīrthika teachers. "Lord of the thousandfold world" renders brgya phrag bcu pa la dbang byed pa (Skt. daśaśatavaśavartin), an epithet of Brahmā. As in the earlier smile passage, "rnams gyin da 'dzum mi ston" in Ānanda's third verse is taken as a scribal slip for a phrase meaning "without reason," following the parallel line and the Sanskrit formula. The future buddha's name, stobs dang brtson 'grus dang mthu rtsal dang shin tu ldan pa, is translated into English because its Sanskrit form cannot be fixed with confidence (perhaps something like Balavīryaparākrama). "Restraining his own mind" renders "bdag gi sems la brgyad bkag nas," where brgyad ("eight") makes no sense; the evident sense is that he checked his own mind, perhaps reading rgyab bkag. "A quarter of a coin" renders zho'i bzhi cha gcig, a quarter of a small silver unit, stressing the trifling price. In Ānanda's second verse, the Tibetan reads gsum mchog ("supreme three"), which makes no sense; it is taken as a slip for gsung mchog ("supreme speech"), which fits the line. In the fourth verse the syllables gyin da are unclear; they are rendered "for no reason," in line with the parallel phrase in the preceding verse. The buddha name Spos mchog is rendered Gandhottama. The weaver's name Zla ba is rendered Candra ("Moon"). The future buddha's name, Tshar tshar bla ma, could not be identified with a Sanskrit form with confidence; it is translated by meaning as "Supreme Fringe," echoing the strips of fringe (tshar tshar) the weaver offered. The name of the guild master's son, Che ba, could not be identified with a Sanskrit form with confidence, so it is translated by meaning as "Great." The syllables gyin da in the fourth verse of Ānanda's request are unclear and are rendered "for no reason," in line with the parallel phrase in the preceding verse. The herb named shi ri ka is given as "śirika," following the Tibetan spelling; it cannot be securely identified. The text here names the future buddha Śākyamuni; this is translated as it stands. The "sūtra like a youth" (gzhon nu lta bu'i mdo) is taken as the Daharasūtra, the discourse by which Prasenajit was won over to the Buddha. In the last verse, the syllables གྱིན་ད in "the protectors, the perfect buddhas ... display a smile" do not make sense as written; following the context and the stock form of this verse, the line is taken to mean "not without reason," and is translated so. The rare term སྟོབས་ཀྱི་འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བའི་རྒྱལ་པོ is rendered as balacakravartin, a wheel-turning king who rules by force, as distinct from the universal monarch proper. པད་མའི་བླ་མ is taken as the standard rendering of the buddha name Padmottara. In "those two learned that the Blessed One had come to their country," the two are the two kings of Pañcāla; it is the Blessed One's miraculous power that emanates the fourfold army. In the last verse, the syllables གྱིན་ད do not make sense as written; following the context and the stock form of this verse, the line is taken to mean "not without reason." Pūraṇa (རྫོགས་བྱེད) is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, one of the six non-Buddhist teachers. The Tibetan says "the fire died out," although only flowers, incense and water are named; the fire is evidently that of the burning incense. In the last verse, the syllables གྱིན་ད do not make sense as written; following the context and the stock form of this verse, the line is taken to mean "not without reason." The future buddha's name མི་གཡོ་བ is given as Acala. The text reads ཇི་ལྷར, evidently a copyist's slip for ཇི་ལྟར ("how"), which is translated. "Lotus Filament" renders པད་མའི་ཟེ་བ, the name of a battle formation; the exact Sanskrit term is not certain. The second account of Ajātaśatru's rout has རྒྱབ་ཀྱིས་བལྟས་པ ("looked back") where the earlier ones have རྒྱབ་ཀྱིས་ཕྱོགས་པ ("turned his back"); it is rendered in the same sense. The river ཆུ་ཀླུང་ཁང་ལྡན is taken as the Ajiravatī, the river at Śrāvastī, whose name ("having courtyards") this Tibetan appears to render; the identification is probable but not certain. In Ānanda's third verse the syllables གྱིན་ད are obscure; they are read, in line with the parallel verse and the Buddha's reply, as "without a reason." The Buddha's name མི་འཇིགས་སྦྱིན ("Giver of Fearlessness") is given as Abhayada. In the summary verse, བསྟོད་མཆོག་སྦྱིན is divided into two titles, "Praise" and "the Boon-Giver," to yield the ten stories of the decade; this division is uncertain. The colophon line ends with the misspelling རྫོགས་སྷོ for རྫོགས་སོ. The buddha's name ཤིང་རྟ་སྐལ་ལྡན ("Fortunate Chariot") is given as Bhagīratha, the name that སྐལ་ལྡན་ཤིང་རྟ usually renders; the identification is probable rather than certain. The phrase གང་ན་ལས་ཐམས་ཅད་པ is read as "together with Viśvakarman," taking གང་ན as a slip; ལས་ཐམས་ཅད་པ is the standard rendering of Viśvakarman, the divine craftsman. གུ་ལང is rendered as Śiva, whose epithet (Paśupati, "lord of cattle") it represents. "Five factors" (yan lag lnga) abandoned and "six qualities" (yan lag drug) possessed follow the stock Avadānaśataka epithet (pañcāṅgaviprahīṇa, ṣaḍaṅgasamanvāgata). The phrase rendered "whose accumulations had matured" (tshogs rnyed) renders the stock labdhasambhāra, more literally "having obtained the accumulations." The country called འདམ་བུ་ཚལ (and འདམ་བུའི་ཚལ) is rendered literally as "Reed Grove"; I could not identify its Sanskrit name with confidence. "Kalandaka Feeding Ground" renders བྱ་ཀ་ལན་ད་ཀ་གནས་པ (Skt. Kalandakanivāpa). The brahmins' invocation of Śakra, རུས་པ་མེད་མའི་སྐྱེས་བུ, is rendered literally ("husband of the Boneless Lady"). It evidently translates a Vedic epithet of Indra (perhaps one referring to Ahalyā, as in Ahalyājāra), but I cannot identify the underlying Sanskrit with confidence; སྐྱེས་བུ could also be simply "man." The buddha's name དབང་པོ་འདུལ is given as Indradamana, the form found in the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka. The rendering "latticework" for ཀེག་ཙེ is tentative; the architectural terms in the description of the monastery are not all certain. The text names the festival as the Five-Year Festival, but in the clause on its continuing in future times it reads "festival of the fifth day" (ཞག་ལྔ་པ); this may be a slip for ལོ་ལྔ་པ, but it is translated as written. The word ཐོར in "the monks heard those very words" is unclear; it is taken as "here and there" (scattered), though it could also be read as "at dawn". The name of the past buddha, རིན་པོ་ཆེའི་རི་བོ, is translated by its meaning, Jewel Mountain, since its Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. The phrase rendered "twenty-one modulations" (ཁོང་དུ་འཁྱིག་པ) refers to the melodic modes or modulations (probably mūrchanā) of Indian music theory. The clause about the six great cities is terse; it is taken to mean that Supriya had outplayed the musicians there and declared those cities of no account. "Putting him off" renders བསྒྱངས, taken in its sense of delaying or deferring. "Elements of mind" (སེམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས) may refer to the elements of consciousness. The name of the future pratyekabuddhas, སྐད་སྙན, is translated by its meaning, Sweet Voice, since its Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. In Ānanda's verse, གྱིན་ད is taken as "for no purpose", in line with the parallel "without cause or condition". The name of the past buddha, རྟོགས་མཛད, is translated by its meaning, Realizer, since its Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. The man's plea, "since I am worthy of the sublime gift" (bdag ni dam pa stsal ba'i 'os lags kyis), is terse and its exact sense is uncertain; it may mean that he is a fit recipient of the Buddha's excellent gift of protection. "Broken the shell of the egg" is the stock image of breaking through the eggshell of ignorance. The monks' remark that "everything is accomplished by the Blessed One's mere intention" is translated as it stands, though the Buddha's reply addresses the karmic background of the man's story. The name dbang po'i rgyal mtshan is rendered Indradhvaja. "Show the openness of his house" renders khyim yangs par bstan pa literally; the intended sense, probably the king's generous hospitality, is not entirely certain. The brahmin's words "I am worthy of receiving the sublime" (dam pa stsol ba'i 'os) are terse; they echo the same formula in the preceding story. Thags zangs ris is identified as the asura king Vemacitrin, and nor sbyin as Dhanada, an epithet of Kubera. The name of the past buddha, bde mdzad, is rendered Śaṅkara, its usual Sanskrit equivalent. "The finest sandalwood" renders tsan dan sa mchog, whose exact variety is uncertain. The goddess named bde sogs could not be identified with confidence; her name is translated by its meaning as "Gatherer of Bliss." The elephants sa srung gi bu and rab brtan are identified as Airāvaṇa and Supratiṣṭhita, and dga' byed kyi tshal as the Nandana Grove of the Thirty-Three. The name of the future buddha, lha'i zas sbyin, could not be identified with confidence in Sanskrit and is translated by its meaning, "Giver of Divine Food." In the summary verse, several story titles are rendered by their meaning (the Ten-Headed, Soft Complexion, Cool Light, the Boatman, Rising Fragrance, Sweet Voice), since I cannot be fully certain of the Sanskrit forms; they likely correspond to the Avadānaśataka titles Daśaśiras, Sūkṣmatvac, Śītaprabha, Nāvika, Gandhamādana, and Valgusvara. The Ten-Headed and the others are the titles of the following stories in this section. The text reads ཡེ་ནི at the start of the explanation of the three conditions; I have taken it as ཡང་ནི, "rather," which the sense requires. The phrase rendered "a sprinkling of perfumed water" uses the word that elsewhere means empowerment; here, as an offering to a stūpa, it plainly means a ritual sprinkling or ablution. The final exhortation in the Tibetan addresses the monks with a singular "you"; it is rendered as in the parallel passages. The name of the future pratyekabuddha, literally "Supreme Lotus," is rendered Padmottara, its evident Sanskrit form. The future pratyekabuddha's name, literally "Supreme Wheel," is rendered Cakrottara, its evident Sanskrit form, on the pattern of Padmottara in the previous story. The phrase rendered "give birth ... crying out in distress" reads literally "was giving birth to a son and uttering bad sounds." "Three weeks, twenty-one days" renders the Tibetan's doubled expression of the period of the birth celebration. "Set his mind firmly on an aspiration" renders སེམས་ལ་རྟས་པར་བྱས, which in this genre stands for the Sanskrit idiom of making a resolve (praṇidhāna); the content of the aspiration follows later in the story. In Ānanda's second verse, བླ་ཡིས is read as བློ་ཡིས, "by your own understanding," which the sense requires. In the fourth verse, the unclear གྱིན་ད is rendered "without reason," as the context of the stock verse demands. "Bam po seven" marks the beginning of the seventh section (fascicle) of the collection. The "brahmin's son who was swollen with pride" is given descriptively, as the Tibetan gives it; it likely refers to the proud brahmin youth (Skt. perhaps Mānastabdha) whom the Buddha converted, but the identification is not certain. The "twenty peaks" are the twenty forms of the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), four for each of the five aggregates. The name of the future pratyekabuddha, འཁོར་བ་རྒལ, is translated by its meaning ("Crosser of Saṃsāra"), since the Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. In the verse "do not display a smile without reason," the written གྱིན་ད makes no sense in context; it has been read as a scribal slip for an expression meaning "without cause" (matching the parallel line earlier in the same set of verses). The story title སྤོས་ཀྱི་ངད་ལྡང is translated by its meaning ("Wafting Fragrance"), as its Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. As in the previous episode, the written གྱིན་ད in the verse line "Do not display a smile without reason" makes no sense as it stands and has been read as an expression meaning "without cause." The phrase ཆུ་ཞེང་གབ་པ describing the nyagrodha tree is rendered as "as tall as it was broad"; the exact sense of གབ་པ here is uncertain. As in the earlier episodes, the written གྱིན་ད in the verse line "Do not display a smile without reason" has been read as an expression meaning "without cause." In Ānanda's verse, གྱིན་ད (in "do not display a smile without purpose") makes no sense as written; it is taken as a slip for a phrase meaning "idly, without purpose," which the parallel verse requires. In the summary verse, ཁམ་རེ ("Morsel") and ཞི་ལྡན ("Peaceful") are translated by meaning, since their Sanskrit titles cannot be fixed with confidence; the other titles follow the standard Sanskrit forms. The "members of the association" (མཛའ་སྡེ་བོ) are the companions of a lay society or club whose offering was told in the preceding story. གས་བ (twice) makes no sense as written and is read as གསོ་བ, "to heal" / "remedy"; འཆི་མ is read as མཆི་མ, "tears." The river ཆུ་ཀླུང་ཟློག་བྱེད is translated by meaning ("Turner-Back") since its Sanskrit name cannot be identified with confidence. In the description of nirvāṇa, གཞའ་གསང is obscure; the phrase is rendered by its evident sense, "the ultimate end." The queen's name, བློ་ངན་མ, is rendered by its meaning, "Evil-Minded," as its Sanskrit original could not be identified with confidence. "Cleared away the thorns of the realm" renders the idiom for having subdued enemies and troublemakers. The clause about the king, literally "having become without entanglement in sensual passion," is taken to describe his prior character, contrasting with the anger that now overcomes him. The phrase ཕེའུ་བཏབ, rendered "tried to calm him," is obscure. Dharmapāla's plea to his father (ཡབ་ཅིག་ཕའོ་འཚལ་ལ་ནི་བུ་སྡུག་ལ) appears corrupt as transmitted; it is rendered by its evident sense, reading a greeting such as ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ. ལ་གོར་དུ in the monk's reaction is uncertain and is rendered "eager." The palace name ཞི་བའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན could not be identified with a Sanskrit original and is translated by its meaning, "Great Sound of Peace." The description of the vulture (བྱ་རྒོད་སྟང་ཟིལ་བཅག་པའི་འཕྲོ་ལྟ་བུ) is obscure and is rendered by its apparent sense, "of fearsome, overbearing aspect." The verse's third line reads "freed from fears" (འཇིགས་པ་དག་ལས); the familiar form of this saying has "freed from what is dear" there, but the line is translated as it stands. Guhyaka, "the hidden one," is an epithet of yakṣas used in addressing the yakṣa. Kauśika is a name of Śakra. "The sacred fire" renders མེ, "fire," here meaning the household sacrificial fire as an object of veneration. Maitrakanyaka's name means "Maitra's girl," which the advice at the end of this passage explains. The passage opens with ཡེ་ནི, which in context must carry the sense "rather, in fact" (perhaps a slip for ཡང་ནི); the meaning follows the stock Avadāna formula of the three conditions for conception. ཆོས་འཐུན་པ་པ is taken as the stock sahadharmika deities, "those who share his nature." In this passage ཚ་བ is the ordinary word for heat and pungent taste, གཟུགས་བཟང is the adjective "handsome," and པད་མ is "lotus," not the names listed for earlier pieces. The four places are identified from the Sanskrit Maitrakanyaka story: ལོངས་སྤྱོད་བྱེད = Ramaṇaka, རྟག་ཏུ་མྱོས = Sadāmatta, དགའ་བྱེད = Nandana, ཚངས་པའི་བླ་མ = Brahmottara. Among the five hired crew, མཉན་པ is here a common noun for a ship's hand ("boatman") rather than a name, and བྱིའུ་ཟུལ་མཁན is understood as the keeper of the birds released to find land; that identification is tentative. The training formula after "you should not harm them" is compressed in the Tibetan; it is read as a resolution the monks are to adopt, that the faults of Maitrakanyaka's time as an ordinary being not arise and that qualities like those he gained as a god be attained. The gems རྡོའི་སྙིང་པོ and སྤུག are rendered conventionally as emerald and sapphire; their exact identification is uncertain. ཕོ་བྲང་འཁོར་གྱི་མི is rendered literally as "people of the royal court" (the Sanskrit stock list has "townspeople"). "Five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra" renders ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, corresponding to the stock Sanskrit pañcagaṇḍaka, referring to the five destinies. In Ānanda's own statement the text reads བྱེད ("doer"), which makes no sense there; it is translated as ཕྱེད ("half"), the reading found in the Blessed One's reply. The rain of Mahendra (དབང་ཆེན) is the rain sent by the great Indra, lord of the gods. The prince's name, ལེགས་པར་གསུངས་པ་ཚོལ་བ, "Seeker of Well-Spoken Words," corresponds to Subhāṣitagaveṣin, the hero of the parallel story in the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka. The eight nurses and their duties follow the stock avadāna description. In the king's verse, རབ་བཟང and པད་མ are ordinary words here ("most excellent," "lotuses"), not the names listed earlier. The opening "Anāthapiṇḍada" is the title of this story. སྒོ་སྐྱེས་བཙུགས་པ is taken as a door-post or threshold pillar (perhaps Skt. indrakīla) set in the ground, an image of immovability. རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག is read as Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, and the pair བླ་དྲང་སྲོང་སྦྱིན and གནའ་མི as Ṛṣidatta and Purāṇa, Prasenajit's chamberlains known from the Sanskrit sources. "Twin sāla trees" renders ཤིང་ས་ལ་ཟུང; ཉེན་ཀོར is taken as Upavartana, the Mallas' sāla grove near Kuśinagara, as in the Sanskrit parinirvāṇa narratives. The passage ends as the Blessed One begins to speak; his words follow in the next piece. The six teachers are identified with the standard Sanskrit forms of their names. In the verse, རྐང་པ་རེག་པ is read as རིག་པ་རྐང་པ, "knowledge and conduct" (vidyā-caraṇa), since "feet touching" makes no sense in context. The "first to fourth ascetic" are the four stages of attainment, from stream-enterer to arhat. In the monks' closing words, འཁོར་བའི་འགུག ("hook" or "grip" of saṃsāra) and གཞའ་གསང ("security", apparently rendering Skt. yogakṣema) are unusual spellings and are translated by their evident sense. དཔོན་པོ, "official, chief," is read as དབོན་པོ, "nephew," which fits Aśoka's following words about his relatives and the Buddha Kāśyapa; this reading is not certain. ཤིང་མྱ་ངན་འཚང is taken as the aśoka tree (usually ཤིང་མྱ་ངན་མེད). The monk's name མྱ་ངན་མེད is rendered Aśoka. In the herd leader's thought, དམ་བསྲུངས "hold fast, keep together" is rendered by its evident sense. The phrase rendered "I simply lived at my ease" (bsod nyams su 'dug 'dug) is unusual; it seems to mean Aśoka grew complacent, relying on his kinship with the Buddha. The brahmin youth Bla ma is rendered by the Sanskrit name Uttara, the name under which Kāśyapa's prophecy to the future Śākyamuni is told. In the summary verse for the next group of ten (stories of hungry ghosts), the items "the lower stream" (chu smad) and "the cesspit" (phyis khung) are tentative literal renderings; I could not identify the corresponding story titles with confidence. The Tibetan tshal za, the man the guild leader instructs, is rendered "workman"; it seems to denote a servant or laborer, perhaps one working in the sugarcane plantation. The pratyekabuddha's reflection, "there is no help for it," renders a terse phrase (byas kyis med do) whose exact force is somewhat uncertain. The phrase rendered "He was unwell" (na dbu can) is unusual; it may mean he suffered from an illness of the head, but the general sense of being ill is clear from the physician's prescription that follows. The ghosts are first introduced with the feminine form ཡི་དགས་མོ ("female hungry ghost"), although they themselves say they were five hundred guild leaders and are referred to elsewhere simply as hungry ghosts; the translation uses the neutral "hungry ghosts." The "dedication of the offering" renders ཡོན་གྱི་རབས (Skt. dakṣiṇādeśanā), the recitation that dedicates the merit of a gift. "The gong" renders གཎྜཱི (gaṇḍī), the wooden sounding board struck to assemble the monks. Uttara renders ཆུ་སྨད, which names both the boy and the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) under which he was born, Uttarāṣāḍhā; the name is given from the mansion, and the story corresponds to the Uttara tale of the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka. The opening sentence begins mid-thought from the previous piece, completing the three questions the newly born gods ask themselves. In Uttara's reply to his mother, the text reads ནད་ལྟར ("like an illness"), which makes no sense in context; the translation follows the evident reading ད་ལྟར ("now"). In the account of the stolen cloth, the text reads དེ་གཤེགས་ནས ("he having departed"), which does not fit the action; the translation follows the evident reading དེ་བཤགས་ནས ("having cut it up"), since the monk then patches it onto a seat. "Deep weariness with saṃsāra" renders སྐྱོ་བ (Skt. saṃvega). "Nuns still in training and nuns beyond training" renders the technical pair slob pa and mi slob pa (Skt. śaikṣa and aśaikṣa), noble disciples still on the path and arhats. "Regular offerings" renders ནར་མ, the standing donations made to the community. "Struck the gong without pause" renders གཎྜཱི་མཇུག་མེད་པ་བརྡུངས, literally "struck the gong without an end," apparently the continuous signal sounded at a monk's death; the exact sense is uncertain. The closing scene places the visit in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, although this story is set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī; the translation follows the text as it stands, which repeats a stock passage. འདམ་བུ་སྦྱིན་གྱི་བུ (literally "son of the reed-giver") is rendered Maudgalyāyana: in this collection the disciple who tours the realm of hungry ghosts is Maudgalyāyana, and this appears to be an older Tibetan rendering of his name, distinct from the more common མོའུ་འགལ་གྱི་བུ. "Sons" (བུ) is the title of the new story (Sanskrit Putrāḥ). ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པ, ཆོས་འཐུན་པ, རྟག་ཏུ་ཕྱི་བཞིན་འབྲང་བ are the stock classes of personal deities (sahaja, sahadharmika, nityānubaddha) in this formula. In the phrase about the honey, མ་བསྐོལ་བ is read as "unboiled", i.e. pure. ཕྱིས་ཁུང, literally "cesspit," is the title and the boy's name; it is rendered as Jāmbāla ("filth, mire"), the name of the corresponding story in the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka, with the literal sense given once. The second wife (ཆུང་མ་ཕྱི་མ) is the one who conceived; the first wife (ཆུང་མ་སྔ་མ), the barren one, is the one who gave the drug and became the hungry ghost woman. སྤྲེའུ་རྫིང་གི་འགྲམ་གྱི་ཁང་པ་བརྩེགས་པ is the Kūṭāgāra Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada (Monkey Pond). གོར་མ་ཆག་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ is rendered "a man of unbroken accomplishment," Pūraṇa taking the boy's love of filth for the indifference of an accomplished ascetic. In "who far surpass even the lord who holds sway over a thousand" (བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་བཅུ་པ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་པ, literally "one who has power over ten hundreds"), the referent is uncertain; it likely corresponds to Sanskrit daśaśatavaśavartin, perhaps the ruler of a thousandfold world system. འཁོར་བ་འཇིག ("Destroyer of Saṃsāra") is the standard Tibetan rendering of Krakucchanda, the buddha of this Fortunate Eon whose era is that of a forty-thousand-year lifespan. མཛེས་ལྡན is here the name of a royal capital, kept as Sundara. In the arhat's final thought, ཉོན་མོངས་པ is taken to mean the afflicted monk himself; the arhat keeps silent so as not to provoke him into further harmful speech. In the summary verse, the story titles are rendered from the Tibetan; དཔལ་ལྡན་མ ("Glorious One," a woman) is given as Śrīmatī, a likely but unconfirmed Sanskrit form; ནེ་ཙོ is "parrot" and མ་ཧེ "buffalo." The heading "Here ends the fifth decade" renders "the fifth summary verse is complete," each summary verse marking a group of ten stories. "Gave up eating" renders ཁ་འཚོས, read in context as the snake's fasting before its death (compare the Sanskrit avadāna motif of renouncing food); the exact sense of the Tibetan expression is not certain. "Departed ancestors" renders སྔོན་གྱི་མཚུན, corresponding to Sanskrit pūrvapreta. Here རུས་པའི་ལ་བསྒྲལ་བ means being carried across the mountain of bones (accumulated over countless rebirths), not the ritual sense of བསྒྲལ་བ. "Conqueror of Foes" renders the epithet དགྲ་ཐུབ. ངེས་ཤས་ཆེར་ཆགས་པ is rendered "intense attachment"; context (the buried treasure) suggests attachment to wealth, and ངེས may be a slip for ནོར "wealth", but the text is translated as it stands. The boy's name ཟླ་བ ("Moon") is given as Candra; the Sanskrit could also be Soma, so the identification is not certain. "Recite the dedication of the offering" renders ཡོན་གྱི་རབས་གདོན་པ, the recitation dedicating the merit of a gift (dakṣiṇādeśanā) to the named person. The Buddha's reply to the monks appears to continue through the account of the father in the charnel ground; it is rendered as his continuing speech, though the Tibetan may also be read as resumed narration. "Remains of the dead" renders ཤི་བའི་རུས་བུ, literally "the bones of the dead one," here the son's body. The festival name སཱ་ལ་གཅོག་པ, "Plucking of the Sāla," corresponds to the Indian spring festival of gathering sāla blossoms (compare Sanskrit śālabhañjikā). In the father's story, སྲོག་ཕངས་པ་བྱིན is read as the king granting the father his life at the son's petition. "Many-storied palace" renders ཁང་པ་བརྩེགས་པ (kūṭāgāra), here an upper-storied building in Ajātaśatru's palace at Rājagṛha, not the Kūṭāgāra Hall at Vaiśālī named elsewhere in the text. The "festival on the fifteenth day" renders ཚེས་བཅྭ་ལྔ་ལ་སྐབས་འབྱེད་པ, the full-moon festival occasion. ཤང་ཤང་ཏེའུ is taken as the jīvaṃjīvaka bird. "The view of the perishable collection" renders འཇིག་ཚོགས་ལ་ལྟ་བ (satkāyadṛṣṭi), whose twenty peaks are the twenty forms of the view of self in relation to the five aggregates. "Departed ancestors" renders སྔོན་གྱི་མཚུན, the deceased forebears (pūrvapretas). "The story called The Garment" renders the section heading གོས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི, which opens a new tale. "An eighth of a māṣaka" renders ཞོའི་བརྒྱད་ཆ, an eighth of a zho, a small unit of weight and money; the point is the smallest possible gift. "The goddess who had formerly offered the cloth" renders the descriptive epithet སྔོན་རས་འབུལ་འབུལ་བའི་ལྷའི་བུ་མོ, kept as a description rather than a personal name. "The lord of the thousand-fold world" renders བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་བཅུ་པ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་པ, literally "one who rules over the tenfold hundred," i.e. the lord of a thousand-world system, a Brahmā. The stock list of numbered qualities (single guard, five factors abandoned, six factors possessed, six constant abidings) is given as this text states it. "The view of the perishable collection" renders satkāyadṛṣṭi, the view of a real self in the aggregates; its "twenty peaks" are the twentyfold forms of that view. Spṛkkā is a fragrant plant used in unguents. "Toward me" in the Buddha's explanation follows the Tibetan, referring to the parrot's devotion to the present Buddha. "The Messenger" is the title of this new story. In the verse, the Tibetan reads ཡང་དག་སྩོལ ("right bestowing"), which makes little sense here; it is translated as ཡང་དག་རྩོལ, "right effort", the evident reading. The bases of miraculous power (ṛddhipāda) and right effort are factors of awakening; the Buddha plays on the messenger's offer of a chariot, and the messenger in turn plays on "the feet of miraculous power." "Five great men" follows the Tibetan མི་ཆེན་པོ. Parallel accounts of this kind of taming place masses of fire (མེ) at the Buddha's sides, so མི may be a slip for མེ ("five great fires"); the text is translated as written. "Stopped eating" renders ཁ་འཚོས, taken in context as fasting, which the following clause about the animal's fierce digestive fire explains. "A master of the three baskets" renders སྡེ་སྣོད་གསུམ་པ (tripiṭaka), a monk learned in all three collections of scripture. In the new story, བསྙེན་གནས (Skt. upoṣadha, the fast-day observance) is the name of the god who appears in it; it is given in its Sanskrit form. The householder named ཆུ་སྟོད (literally "Upper Waters") could not be identified with a Sanskrit name with confidence; his name is given in Tibetan phonetics as Chutö. The king's son ལེགས་སྐྱེས is rendered Sujāta, the usual Sanskrit equivalent. The name of the god Upoṣadha is evidently being linked to the eight-branched upoṣadha observance that the story goes on to tell. "Your Majesty" renders the royal honorific ལྷ. The phrase ཐང་ལ་ཕྱུང་སྟེ་ལུས་བོར་ནས་དེ་ཁ་འཚོས་ཏེ་འདུག is somewhat obscure. It is taken to mean that the nāga came out onto open ground and gave up his body to be fed upon, a motif familiar from other upoṣadha-keeping nāgas. In the verse, the Tibetan reads "joyful (དགའ་བ) to see in a thousand existences". The parallel verse in the preceding story has དཀའ་བ, "hard to see", which the sense requires, so this is taken as a copyist's slip and translated as "hard to see". The summary verse lists the titles of the ten stories of this section. སྡུ་གུ could not be identified with confidence and is given in phonetics as Dugu. The other titles are translated by meaning, except Suvarṇābha ("Golden Light"), the hero of the first story. The householder's act with the fallen golden mirror is terse in the Tibetan (དེའི་རྣ་བའི་གོང་རྒྱན་དུ་བཅོས་ནས); it is taken to mean that he fashioned it into an ornament and fixed it back on the stupa. "Five-sectioned wheel of saṃsāra" renders ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, matching the stock Sanskrit avadāna phrase pañcagaṇḍaka saṃsāracakra (the wheel divided into the five destinies). Nyagrodha Park is the Nyagrodhārāma near Kapilavastu. The boy's name, བྱད་བཟང, is rendered by its meaning, "Fair Form," since the Sanskrit original cannot be confirmed with certainty; the corresponding Sanskrit Avadānaśataka story may name him Vapuṣmān ("having a beautiful body"), which fits the explanation given for the name. The boy's name, སྟོབས་ལྡན, is rendered by its meaning, "Mighty," since its Sanskrit form (perhaps Balin or Balavān) cannot be confirmed. In the list of requisites the text reads གདོན ("graha"), evidently a slip for གདན ("seats"), as in the parallel stock passages; "seats" is translated. The name སྡུ་གུ, kept as "Dugu" for consistency with earlier usage, is explained in the text from སྡུག "dear, beloved"; its Sanskrit original is uncertain (possibly Priya). The hero's name, པད་མའི་མིག, is rendered by its meaning, "Lotus Eye," since the text explains it from his lotus-like eyes; the underlying Sanskrit (perhaps Padmākṣa) cannot be confirmed with confidence. The "twenty lofty peaks" are the twenty forms of the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi). "Five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra" renders ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, the stock Avadāna image of the five destinies. The closing sentence continues into the next piece. The new hero's name, རྔ་སྒྲ, is rendered by its meaning, "Drum Sound," as the text explains it from his drum-like voice; the Sanskrit original cannot be confirmed with confidence. A krośa (རྒྱང་གྲགས) is a measure of distance, a fraction of a league. The new story's title, བུ, simply means "son" and is rendered as "The Son"; it may stand for a Sanskrit title such as Putra, but this is not certain. ཚན་པོ་ཆེ is taken as "great wrestler" (Skt. mahānagna), the stock term for a champion of physical strength in the Avadāna literature. The hero's name, ཉི་མ, is rendered by its meaning, "Sun," as the text explains it; the Sanskrit original (perhaps Sūrya) cannot be confirmed with confidence. "Sunstone" renders མེ་ཤེལ (Skt. sūryakānta, a "fire crystal"). The short line "The Banner of the Mallas" is the title of the new story that begins here, rendered following the name already established for གྱད. སྙན་གྲགས is rendered by its meaning, "Renown," as the Tibetan itself explains the name; its Sanskrit original (possibly Yaśas) cannot be confirmed with confidence. "The view of the perishable collection" is satkāyadṛṣṭi; "five spokes" renders ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, the five destinies of saṃsāra. The names in the summary verse are identified from the parallel decade of the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka: འོད་བཟང་མ Suprabhā, རབ་སྡུག་མ Supriyā, དཀར་མོ Śuklā, ཟླ་བ Somā (a woman here, distinct from the earlier Candra), ཨུད་པ་ལ Kuvalayā, མཛེས་ལྡན་མ Sundarī, མུ་ཏིག Muktā, ཀ་ཙང་ག་ལ Kacaṅgalā, མི་སྡུག Virūpā. བ་དེ་བྱེད་མ is read as བདེ་བྱེད་མ, Kṣemā, the line being an evident miswriting. The crowd's address སྲུ་མར་སྤྱོན་མར་སྤྱོན is obscure as written; it is rendered as a respectful plea for her to come down (མར་སྤྱོན), which fits her descent that follows. སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ is Mahāprajāpatī. Names in the list of would-be donors are identified as follows: ཕྲེང་རྒྱུད་མ Mallikā, དྲང་སྲོང་སྦྱིན Ṛṣidatta, གནའ་མི Purāṇa, རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག Viśākhā the mother of Mṛgāra. The kṣatriya maiden དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ could not be identified with confidence and is given by its meaning, "Rainy Season." The merchant's words "While I lay asleep, you kept watch for me" render the Tibetan literally; the sense is that she made merit on his behalf while he was heedless. "Regular meals in turn" renders a term for food offered to the Saṅgha on a regular rotation. The Tibetan name of Śuklā's father, སྣར་མ, is the usual rendering of the asterism Rohiṇī; the masculine form Rohiṇa is given as the likely Sanskrit, but it is not certain. In "a mind like space and like the palm of the hand," the formula means an arhat's mind is even and unobstructed. The girl's name ཟླ་བ, "moon," is kept as Candra for consistency with its earlier use in this text; as a woman's name the Sanskrit would properly be Candrā. The list of brahmanical learning follows the standard formula (nighaṇṭu, kaiṭabha, akṣaraprabheda, and itihāsa as the fifth). "The view of the perishing collection" is the view of a real self in the transitory aggregates (satkāyadṛṣṭi), whose twenty forms are pictured as mountain peaks. "Ultimate wisdom" refers to the knowledge that brings final liberation, arhatship. The brahmin youth བླ་མ is given as Uttara, the usual Sanskrit name of the future Śākyamuni in the time of Kāśyapa. The festival is named after the nāga kings རི་བོ and ཡིད་འོང, given here as Giri and Valgu, following the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka's Girivalgusamāgama festival; the identification is likely but not certain. The phrase rendered "the consummation of utmost security" (གཞའ་གསང་གི་མཐར་ཐུག་པ) appears to correspond to the stock Sanskrit atyantaniṣṭha yogakṣema preceding nirvāṇa; the Tibetan wording is unusual and the rendering follows that parallel. "The five bases of discipline" (བརྟུལ་ཞུགས་ཀྱི་གནས་ལྔ) likely corresponds to the five training precepts. The sage's teaching to the kinnarī is given in the past tense in the Tibetan and is translated as it stands. The king is called མཛེས་པ, while the palace is མཛེས་ལྡན (Sundara); both are taken as Sundara, the king evidently bearing the name of his capital. ཟློས་གར་མཁར is read as ཟློས་གར་མཁན, "actors", an evident slip. The section heading "The story called Sundarī" marks the start of the next avadāna. "Kings of the land" renders ཉི་འོག་གི་རྒྱལ་པོ, literally "kings beneath the sun," i.e. the rulers of the surrounding regions. The princes address the nun with སྲུ, literally "aunt," a respectful term of address, rendered "Sister." The merchant's name རྒྱལ་བ (later རྒྱལ) is rendered Jaya, the usual Sanskrit for this Tibetan; the original may instead be Jina. The phrase rendered "whenever her garland of pearls was taken off, it appeared again" (ཕོག་ན་ཕྱིར་ཞིང་བྱུང) is terse; the sense of ཕོག is inferred from context. Anāthapiṇḍada's son is given the Sanskrit masculine form Supriya, consistent with the earlier name Supriyā listed for the same Tibetan. "Collect offerings" renders དད་པ་སྡུད་པ, literally "collect faith," meaning to gather donations given in faith. "The quinquennial festival" renders ལོ་ལྔ་པའི་དུས་སྟོན (Skt. pañcavārṣika). The "perfumed chamber" is the Buddha's dwelling (gandhakuṭī). "Withdrew into seclusion" renders nang du yang dag 'jog las gshegs pa; the particle las ("from") would literally suggest "came out of seclusion," but the sense, matching the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka (pratisaṃlayanāya praviśati), is that the Buddha gave a brief instruction and then withdrew, after which Kacaṅgalā explained it in detail. "Mahāmāyā" renders sgyu 'phrul chen mo, the Buddha's mother in his final life. The heroine's name, bde byed ma, and the prince's, bde byed, are given as Kṣemaṅkarā and Kṣemaṅkara on the standard equivalence bde byed = Kṣemaṃkara; the corresponding Sanskrit Avadānaśataka story calls her Kṣemā, so the exact Sanskrit form behind this Tibetan is not certain. The king's reply, "this is not something I can undo" (ngas bcos su med), is understood as his saying that the betrothal he made, which brought him peace at her birth, cannot be revoked. "Those who hold sway over a thousand worlds" renders brgya phrag bcu pa la dbang byed pa ("those who have power over ten hundreds"), the stock epithet in which the buddhas are said to surpass such world-rulers. The girl's name ར་སྠ is a Sanskrit name written in Tibetan letters; it is given here as spelled, "Rastha"; its intended Sanskrit form is uncertain. The caravan leader's name གང་ག is rendered Gaṅga. "No wonder Gaṅga would not show her to us" renders the friends' remark ending in yus so, taken as acknowledging that his keeping her hidden was understandable. Rastha's name is kept as given earlier in this text. The names in the summary verse are identified from the parallel ninth decade of the Sanskrit Avadānaśataka; རྫུས་ཏེ་སྐྱེས་པ is translated literally as "the Apparitionally Born," since its exact Sanskrit title is uncertain. ཡུལ་འཁོར་སྲུང here is the monk Rāṣṭrapāla of the avadāna, not the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose Tibetan name is spelled the same way. The boy born at sea is called Samudra, "ocean," as in the Sanskrit collection. The five kinds of hired crew are given in Tibetan terms whose exact nautical functions are not all certain; "bird-handlers" renders བྱེའུ་ཟུལ་མཁན literally, presumably the men who kept shore-sighting birds, but the identification is tentative. The epithet གཞའ་གསང་གི་མཐར་ཐུག་པ qualifying nirvāṇa is obscure; it is rendered by its evident sense, corresponding to the stock Sanskrit phrase for nirvāṇa as the absolute culmination (atyantaniṣṭha). "Those who hold sway over a thousand" renders the stock epithet daśaśatavaśavartin, usually understood of Indra and similar lords. The merchants address the sage as bhagavat, rendered "Lord", as is usual when the title is given to a ṛṣi rather than to the Buddha. The divine flowers named in the last sentence are sumanas (jasmine) blossoms, which give the boy his name. The river ཆུ་ཀླུང་ཁང་ལྡན could not be identified with a known Sanskrit name and is given in phonetics as Khangden; its words mean roughly "possessing houses". In the verse, ཆུ་ཆུན is taken as an affectionate term for the young novice ("that little one"); the reading is not certain. "Gathered their conditions ... come upon him like a flood, inescapably" renders the stock Avadāna formula for the ripening of karma. "The Nandana Grove" renders དགའ་བའི་ཚལ, the pleasure grove of the gods of the Thirty-Three. The child's name, literally "Three Baskets" (Sanskrit Tripiṭaka, "the Three Collections"), is kept as Tripiṭa to match the earlier pieces. In "the dress of a renunciant," the first occurrence reads dag sbyong, evidently a slip for dge sbyong ("śramaṇa, renunciant"), which the later occurrences have. "Like a flood" renders dba' rgal, read as the stock simile of actions surging forth like a torrent. The line rendered "Surely I have not broken the promise I made before" is obscure in the Tibetan (gnyer dgum gor ma chag) and is translated by its evident sense. In "it would be good if the prince went forth, but it would not be good if he were to die here," the phrase de'u re is read in that sense. "Eloquent in knowledge and in liberation" renders rig pa dang grol bar smra ba, a stock epithet of a skilled Dharma speaker. Among the classes of beings, gdon sbyin is an evident slip for gnod sbyin, yakṣa. The river chu klung zlog byed, literally "the Averter," is taken as the Varaṇā, the river bounding Vārāṇasī whose name derives from a root meaning "to ward off." The phrase rendered "remained there, resting on his deeds" (las la rten cing 'dug) is terse; it may imply that he sat in contemplation of his karma rather than any act of self-harm, and the story continues with him alive. The king of trees yongs 'du sa brtol is the Pārijāta (also called Pārijātaka or Kovidāra), the celestial coral tree of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three; the stone slab "like a white woolen blanket" is the Pāṇḍukambala stone on which the Buddha spent this rains retreat teaching his mother. "Faith grounded in understanding" renders shes nas dad pa, the Tibetan for avetyaprasāda, the unwavering confidence of the noble disciple in the Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, together with the moral discipline dear to the noble ones (āryakānta śīla); these four are the factors of stream-entry. The city སྣང་ལྡན is taken as Sāṃkāśya, the traditional site of the Buddha's descent from the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, which fits this episode. The forest name ཨ་པད་ཛ་ར is a transliteration that I could not identify with confidence; it is given as spelled, "Apadjara." The monk's first aspiration, ཡོ་བྱད་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་དག་གིས་བྲེལ་བར་མ་གྱུར་ཅིག, is rendered "may I never be troubled over the finest requisites," that is, never be burdened with procuring them; this matches the frame story, in which whatever he wishes for appears the moment he thinks of it. Krakucchanda's capital མཛེས་ལྡན and its king མཛེས་པ are given here as Śobhāvatī and Śobha. Calling them "Sundara" would confuse them with the boy Sundara, whose name has the same Tibetan form མཛེས་པ. The identification is probable but not certain, and it differs from the "Sundara" used for མཛེས་ལྡན earlier in the text. The name of Kapphiṇa's father, རྟོག་ལྡན, could not be identified with a Sanskrit form with confidence, so it is translated by its meaning, "Thoughtful." The elephant, horse, and chariot are compared to the celebrated mounts Airāvaṇa (ས་སྲུང་གི་བུ), Balāhaka (སྤྲིན་གྱི་ཤུགས་ཅན), and Nandighoṣa (དགའ་བྱེད་སྒྲ); these identifications are probable. "The five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra" (ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ) refers to the five realms of rebirth in the older fivefold scheme. "Having broken the shell of the egg with knowledge" is the stock image of breaking out of the eggshell of ignorance. The strength of a "great champion" renders ཚན་པོ་ཆེ (Skt. mahānagna). The final paragraph opens the next tale, titled "Bhadrika," with the stock setting formula. The driver's name ཁ་ལོ་པ་རྒྱུ་བའི་བུ་རིང་པོ is taken as Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa ("Dīrgha, son of Cārāyaṇa"), Prasenajit's well-known attendant; the elephant's name པད་མ་དཀར་པོ་གཅིག་པུ is rendered Ekapuṇḍarīka ("Lone White Lotus"). ཕྱག་འཚོལ in the Buddha's command is read as ཕྱག་འཚལ ("bow"). "Letting the nature of the Dharma prevail" renders ཆོས་ཉིད་བཙན་པར་བྱས་ནས, i.e., subordinating their caste pride to the Dharma. The phrase རང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་བསྔོས་ཏེ, rendered "offering it up along with his own misery," is obscure; it may mean that he gave despite his own hardship. ཁུར་བ is taken as a kind of cake. The place name ཡུལ་གསུས་པོ་ཆེ is identified as Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, the Kuru town associated with Rāṣṭrapāla in the Avadānaśataka. The king's name སྒྲ་མི་སྙན ("Unpleasant Sound") is the standard Tibetan rendering of Kuru/Kaurava; it is given as Kauravya, the name of the Kuru king in the Rāṣṭrapāla story. The Tibetan calls Rāṣṭrapāla both the son of the king's younger brother and a "householder's son"; both are translated as they stand. In the summary verse, ལག་པ་ཅན is taken as Hastaka and རྒན་པོ as the story of the Elder (Sthavira), following the tenth decade of the Avadānaśataka; འདེ་གུས་གསོས ("Nourished with Care") and ཡང་དག་སྡུག ("Truly Lovely") could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally. In this decade མི་སྡུག་པ and གང་གཱ་པ are story titles (Virūpa, Gaṅgika), rendered accordingly. སྲིད་སྲུང་ལས་ཕྱུང is taken as "sent him away from the household." "Dwelling free of affliction" renders ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པ, the Tibetan for Subhūti's traditional distinction as foremost in araṇāvihāra (dwelling without conflict). The "five spokes" of the wheel of saṃsāra render ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, the five destinies. སྐབས་འབྱེད་པ / སྐབས་དབྱེ་བ is taken as the pravāraṇā, the ceremony closing the rains retreat (usually དགག་དབྱེ in Tibetan), as the following passage on exclusion from the assembly suggests. In the story title and the Buddha's question, རྒན་པོ (Skt. sthavira) means both "old man" and "elder", which is the point of the naming. "The lord of the thousand" renders བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་བཅུ་པ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་པ ("one who holds sway over ten hundred"), a stock comparison in this epithet series whose referent is not certain. In the Elder's first full answer the Tibetan begins one sentence with དེ་ནས ("then"), where the parallel answers have none; it is read as continuing the Elder's reply ("And so"). The text reads "mother's lta" in the Buddha's concluding statement; this is evidently a slip for ltо, "womb," as in the monks' question, and is translated accordingly. The name rendered "the Elder" (rgan po) is kept as established earlier in the text; it is distinct from the title "senior monk" or "elder" (gnas brtan, sthavira) that precedes it. The phrase rendered "stroked them" (mthang la 'jor bar byed) is obscure; the sense of caressing the newly found hands is clear from context, but the exact gesture is uncertain. The opening line, "The story called Hastaka," is the title of the new avadāna. "Attendant śramaṇa" renders the Tibetan for one who follows behind a monk on his rounds (Skt. paścācchramaṇa). "Mixed actions" renders a term meaning actions both black and white. "Perfumed Chamber" renders the term for the Buddha's own dwelling (Skt. gandhakuṭī). The idiom rendered "struck me in the belly" means that Śāriputra's sweeping has deprived him of his food. The last clause, literally "the mouth became nonexistent and it was cast outside," is taken to mean that his mouth closed up and the food dropped away. "Eat ashes!" renders a curse whose verb as written ('gom, "tread") is odd; the sense is fixed by the later statement that he "passed into nirvāṇa after eating ashes." "Threw it to the ground" renders an unclear verb (pho nas), read as "dropping" or "knocking down." "A brahmin devoted to the gods" (lha la rten pa) could possibly be a personal name, but no Sanskrit form can be identified with confidence. The monks' question says Saṃsāra "came forth from his mother's womb as a corpse, dead" for five hundred lifetimes, which the narrative of this passage does not otherwise describe; it is translated as it stands, and the explanation presumably follows in the account of his past deeds. "Five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra" renders ཕོལ་མིག་ལྔ་པ, the standard Avadāna image of the wheel with five sections (pañcagaṇḍaka), one for each destiny. The young monk's curse literally says he should not come out "of the house" alive; the story's fulfillment shows it was understood as the womb. Two names could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally: རྒྱ་སྐེགས་ཀྱི་རྣ་བ་ཅན, "Lac Ear" (possibly Skt. Jatukarṇa), the one who invited the Buddha, and the land སློ་མ་ཅན, "the land of Baskets." The line naming the twenty-second and final section is a section marker that the Tibetan places here, before the last stories. In the opening sentence the phrase མེད་ན་མ་ལ is obscure; it is taken in the sense "before he is lost," which fits the pratyekabuddha's compassionate intention. སྐྱེད་མོས་ཚལ་དུང་ཡག is rendered "a deserted pleasure grove"; དུང་ཡག could also be the grove's proper name. The past buddha རྒྱལ is given as Tiṣya, the name under which this well-known episode appears in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya; other sources call him Puṣya, and the Tibetan can render either. The verse of praise is in long lines of several metrical segments each and is rendered as four long lines. The particle མ་ལ, used several times to open Gaṅgika's reflections, is an exclamation ("well then"), not "mother". The address བུ་གཅིག in the king's words is rendered "my son"; it may allude to Gaṅgika being an only son. The passage on the executioners is translated as the Tibetan stands; in parallel avadāna accounts the blue garments and karavīra garland mark the condemned man. In the Dīrghanakha story, ཆད་པ in the debates between Śārī and her brother is the technical term for defeat in debate (nigraha), not the doctrinal "annihilation," and ཆད་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས likewise is a sense of defeat. The village སྤང་སྤོས་ཅན ("having spikenard") is rendered Nālada, the spikenard (nalada) village known as Śāriputra's birthplace. མེའི་ཆ་ལུགས་ཅན་གྱི་བུ is Dīrghanakha's clan name, Agnivaiśyāyana. In the list of those who honored the Buddha, བླ་མར་བྱས is the verb "revered," not the name Uttara. In the third reflection the Tibetan reads གཅིག་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་འདོད་དོ ("one accepts everything") where the parallel clauses have བདག་ནི; this is evidently a copyist's slip, and it is translated as "I accept everything." Here བྱམས་པ in ལུས་ལ་བྱམས་པ is "affection for the body," not the name Maitreya. Two readings are taken as copyists' slips. In the first list of what the śrāvaka understands about feelings, ངེས་པར་འགྱུར་བ is read as ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ ("escape"), as in the repeated list that follows. In Śāriputra's reflection, "speaks only of the experience (མྱོང་བ) of these dharmas" is read as "the abandoning (སྤོང་བ)," which the next sentence requires. The arhat whom the Buddha names at the end, after Dīrghanakha's ordination, is called Sthūlakoṣṭhaka (in other sources Mahākauṣṭhila). The Tibetan གྱད་ཀྱི་ཉེ་འཁོར is taken as the Upavartana of the Mallas, the traditional site of the parinirvāṇa near Kuśinagarī. The robbers' "offering to the yakṣa" appears, from the sequel, to be a human sacrifice for which they seek a victim, though the text does not say so explicitly. The place name Earth-Holder (sa 'dzin) and the village name Great Flower Load (me tog khur chen) are translated literally, as their Sanskrit forms could not be identified with confidence. The boy's name mdzes ldan, "the Beautiful One," is rendered Sundara, its most likely Sanskrit form. In Ānanda's verse, "bza' shing" is read as the cloths or garments wrapping the body, in line with the known tradition that the innermost and outermost wrappings of the Buddha's body did not burn. The phrase "a hundred thousand pearl necklaces" may instead mean a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand, as is common in avadāna literature. The elder ཉེ་བར་སྲུང is identified as Upagupta, the elder associated with King Aśoka at the Kukkuṭārāma; the usual Tibetan rendering is ཉེ་བར་སྦས, but this form is plainly the same figure. "The wheel of saṃsāra with its five spokes" refers to the five destinies of rebirth.
